title: ProtoVis-Nav: Prototypical Visual Imagination for Visual-Spatial Aligned UAV Navigation
authors: Guangyuan Sui,Yunzhong Hou,Chi Harold Liu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision language navigation (VLN) is very challenging for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) since small errors in 3D motion prediction can lead to navigation errors and collisions. Unable to fathom execution outcomes in 3D environments, existing methods often struggle to predict accurate navigation waypoints from language instructions. To solve this, we introduce the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework, shortened as ProtoVis-Nav, which forces the model to imagine an outcome-associated local visual representation for the intended next UAV movement. Specifically, we predict feature prototypes and use their linear combination to estimate the visual feature of the target region. In this manner, the VLN model first imagines the local visual representation of the next intended location, and then uses predicted prototypes as context for generating the final action, promoting alignment between visual context and waypoint outputs. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the ProtoVis-Nav framework and show substantial improvements over existing baselines. Data and code are available at link.
introduction:
Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) is a challenging problem in embodied AI, enabling agents to navigate complex environments while following natural language instructions Gu et al. (2022); Park and Kim (2023). Although early VLN research predominantly centered on indoor navigation for ground-based robots Krantz et al. (2020); Ku et al. (2020); Zhou et al. (2024); Huang et al. (2023), a growing body of recent work focuses on Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) Cai et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2023); Wu et al. (2025); Zhang et al. (2025d); Xiao et al. (2025),
where navigation involves a more challenging 3D action space and requires precise motion control and reliable 3D trajectory planning Wang et al. (2024a).
Despite the rapid progress of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) Bai et al. (2025); Wang et al. (2025a); Hong et al. (2025); Team et al. (2026), applying them to UAV navigation remains difficult as they struggle to navigate 3D environments accurately and safely Wang et al. (2025b); Xiao et al. (2025).

A major reason for these navigation errors is the inability to associate motion predictions with their potential outcomes Nie et al. (2025).
In fact, most methods directly predict continuous waypoints from visual observations and language instructions Arafat et al. (2023).
Since their training objective penalizes only the waypoint error, the model can hardly anticipate the execution outcomes of its own actions Koh et al. (2021), increasing the risk of generating trajectories that are potentially unsafe in the 3D environment.

To address this problem, an emerging trend in visual language navigation is to equip the agent with future-aware visual predictive capabilities, often framed as navigation world models Bar et al. (2025).
Specifically, they usually predict the future observation via a specific video generation model Koh et al. (2021); Bar et al. (2025) or as outputs of the same VLN model Yao et al. (2025); Huang et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026). UAV navigation requires accurate fine-grained motion control grounded in local visual evidence Ding et al. (2026). In fact, precise flight actions are often determined by small and localized visual regions (e.g., a narrow gap to fly through). This raises a key question: rather than generating the global future scene, can we enforce future-aware grounding by strictly focusing on these localized visual regions most critical to the upcoming movement?

In this work, we propose the Prototypical Visual Imagination framework for UAV navigation, dubbed as ProtoVis-Nav. The method is motivated by a simple idea: rather than modeling an entire future scene or a long-horizon latent rollout, the agent should focus on the exact regions most relevant to its precise movement by imagining an outcome-associated local visual representation.
To this end, we project the next intended UAV location onto the current image plane, crop the surrounding local region, and use its visual feature as the supervision target. Compared with using the entire future frame or the future-frame center, this projected region provides a supervision target that more directly grounds 3D motion prediction in the current image space, while avoiding the intractable imagination of future observations.
Plus, we introduce a prototype-based feature prediction method. Instead of using multi-layer perceptrons to directly estimate the target feature, this approach predicts a set of Prototypical Visual Imagination (PVI) tokens, which are then combined through a softmax-normalized mixing matrix, so that their linear combination matches the target-region feature. The predicted PVI tokens are less susceptible to overfitting and are then used as context for waypoint prediction, encouraging tighter alignment between visual context and continuous action outputs.

We experimentally verify the effectiveness of the proposed method on OpenUAV Wang et al. (2024a) and HUGE-Bench Guo et al. (2026). Results show that ProtoVis-Nav substantially improves navigation performance over strong baselines and leads to more reliable continuous UAV navigation.

title: HEIR: Harness Egocentric Intent for Human-Robot Interactions
authors: Yichi Zhang,Bo Wang,Zhenghan Zhu,Yutong Han,Jiayin Zou,Gao Kejun,Chang Liu,Shaoxuan Xie,Chi Zhang,Shi Haoyang,Zongxuan Lai,Sen Cui,Guocai Yao,Miao Liu
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
The research community has witnessed revolutionary progress driven by data-centric approaches, enabling the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs) [7, 10, 12, 44, 16] and vision-language models (VLMs) [43, 2, 29]. Tremendous efforts have been invested in reproducing this success in embodied AI, leading to rapid advances in vision-language-action models (VLAs) [6, 22, 54, 5, 4] and world-action models (WAMs) [65, 30, 66]. More recently, inspired by LLM agents that harness external tools, agentic robot systems [1, 17] have been developed to orchestrate multiple execution modules for long-horizon tasks.

Much of this progress remains fundamentally task-centric, where robots execute given instructions while humans remain peripheral to the formulation. This paradigm is insufficient for robots intended to serve, assist, and collaborate with people in real-world scenarios, where humans are not merely obstacles to avoid, but active participants whose behaviors, intentions, and requests continuously shape the task. We therefore argue that embodied AI should increasingly embrace a user-centric perspective, placing situated human context at the core of robot decision-making and execution.

Studying this new paradigm in the data-driven era requires datasets that capture not only robot sensory and action signals, but also how humans perceive, communicate, and interact with robots throughout task execution. Existing Human–Robot Interaction (HRI) datasets [46, 64], however, are largely collected in controlled tabletop settings and focus on short-horizon interactions, providing limited coverage of situated human behaviors. Meanwhile, egocentric vision has been increasingly explored for robot learning [60, 13], yet limited effort has studied how intentional cues from the human perspective can complement robot observations during HRI.

To bridge this gap, we introduce HEIR, Harnessing Egocentric Intent for Human–Robot Interactions, a dataset for studying user-centric human–robot interaction during long-horizon tasks in naturalistic household environments. As illustrated in Fig. 1, HEIR pairs human egocentric video, measured gaze, and speech with robot observations and teleoperated navigation–manipulation trajectories. These recordings capture the human and robot context surrounding each request, including referents visible only from the human perspective, while each continuous session preserves both multi-stage execution and state changes across requests. Our dataset further provides annotations of task intent, target objects, destinations, nominal plans, and realized navigation–manipulation stages, thereby linking situated human context to task semantics and robot behavior.

HEIR supports a hierarchical set of tasks spanning VLM-based user intent inference, subtask planning, and navigation and manipulation execution. In this paper, we evaluate how additional user-centric cues benefit intent modeling and long-horizon planning for HRI, benchmark prevailing navigation and manipulation methods through offline evaluation, and further report task success rates in real-robot experiments. We also provide episode-level experimental results and video demonstrations on long-horizon tasks to demonstrate how HEIR establishes an empirical foundation for studying user-centric robot interaction.

title: Collaborative Task Allocation for Heterogeneous Multi-Robot Systems Through Iterative Clustering
authors: David R. Martin,Brooks A. Butler,Scott Nivison,Magnus Egerstedt,Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque,Pramod Khargonekar
comment: Published in IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L) and presented at 2026 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA)
abstract: Multi-robot systems face the challenge of efficiently allocating teams of heterogeneous robots to tasks. The task allocation problem is complicated by collaborative interactions between robots where teams of robots develop emergent capabilities that enable them to complete tasks that would be inefficient or impossible for individual robots. To address these challenges, we present an iterative clustering algorithm for collaborative task allocation in heterogeneous multi-robot systems. This approach partitions the computationally intractable global optimization problem into smaller, tractable subproblems by iteratively forming clusters of robots and tasks, then optimizing assignments within each cluster. By ensuring robots remain clustered with their currently assigned tasks, we guarantee monotonic improvement in overall utility with each iteration. We analyze the convergence of the algorithm and characterize how cluster size constraints determine which suboptimal assignments could trap the algorithm. In simulation, iterative clustering consistently outperforms simulated annealing, and a group-based auction in both computation time and solution quality, and outperforms a hedonic game approach in solution quality.
introduction:
Multi-robot systems have demonstrated significant potential in numerous domains, including disaster relief [1], sensor fusion [2], construction [3], warehousing [4, 5], and beyond [6, 7]. Of particular interest are robot teams where collaboration enables new capabilities, allowing them to complete tasks that would be impossible or highly inefficient for individual robots. Recent examples highlight this synergistic potential: in [2], multiple drones equipped with cameras collaboratively estimate 3D object depth with higher accuracy than lidar, in [8], aquatic robots transport terrestrial robots across water bodies to reach otherwise inaccessible goals, in [3] and [5], robot teams collaborate to carry oversized payloads.

A challenge in collaborative multi-robot systems is the multi-robot task allocation (MRTA) problem, which is the process of determining optimal robot-to-task assignments that maximize system performance [7]. Researchers have addressed MRTA using diverse approaches, including the Hungarian algorithm [9], mixed integer programming [10], auctions [5, 11], game-theoretic approaches [12, 13], metaheuristics (such as simulated annealing [14] and evolutionary algorithms [15, 16]), clustering techniques [17, 18], and machine learning methods [3, 19]. Distributed algorithms such as group-based auctions [11] and game theoretic approaches [13] have shown a remarkable ability to scale efficiently to large systems.

Despite recent advances, existing algorithms struggle to account for collaborative synergy in multi-robot teams. Most existing approaches assume predetermined team sizes and capability requirements for each task [3, 10, 15]. However, in many systems, the optimal team size may be unclear. When resources are abundant and tasks are few, it may be advantageous to assign more resources to each task. Conversely, when resources are constrained, it may be necessary to reduce team sizes or omit less important tasks completely. Collaborative dynamics complicate resource allocation. Existing works that allow variable team sizes generally rely on assigning individual robots to tasks where they provide the greatest marginal contribution [12, 20]. However, these approaches struggle in situations where robots’ contributions are not easily separable from those of their teammates. For instance, a task requiring three robots might yield no utility until all three are assigned. In general, these methods fail in scenarios requiring simultaneous multi-robot reassignments, where a single reassignment provides no benefit.

To account for collaborative team effects, we model the MRTA problem as a coalition structure generation problem [21], partitioning robots into coalitions assigned to each task with the goal of optimizing total utility. While coalition structure generation is NP-hard [22], we propose a novel iterative clustering algorithm that scales effectively. The proposed method directly addresses the key limitations of existing methods by: (1) providing a computationally efficient solution to the coalition structure generation problem, (2) modeling team utility as a nonlinear function that can be greater than the sum of the individual robot contributions, and (3) determining appropriate team compositions for each task while accounting for this collaborative synergy.

The proposed method iteratively forms clusters of robots and tasks, then optimizes assignments within each cluster. We develop two variants of this approach: one that forms clusters randomly and another that uses heuristics to guide cluster formation. We prove that assignment utility increases monotonically with each iteration and analyze how cluster size constraints affect the algorithm’s ability to escape suboptimal solutions. In simulation, the iterative clustering approach achieves 99.9% of optimal utility for small problems, outperforms exisiting methods for large problems, and exhibits fast convergence that scales effectively to problems with up to 1000 robots and 500 tasks.

title: UAV-Flow++: A Unified Suite for Benchmarking and Learning Language-Guided UAV Flight
authors: Donglin Yang,Xiangyu Wang,Yantong Zhong,Wenhao Zheng,Zihan Ding,Yue Liao,Hongsheng Li,Ke Xu,Si Liu
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) are widely deployed across diverse applications, serving as aerial perception platforms for object detection, tracking, counting, and human behavior understanding [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], as well as enabling precision agriculture, infrastructure inspection, emergency response, and entertainment applications [6, 7, 8, 9].
In parallel, advances in motion planning and control have enabled increasingly autonomous flight and multi-UAV coordination in cluttered three-dimensional environments [10, 11, 12, 13]. These capabilities provide a technical foundation for UAVs to operate as embodied agents that interpret human intent and execute tasks in the physical world.
While modern UAVs are increasingly capable of autonomous flight, enabling them to follow high-level natural language instructions remains a fundamental challenge in achieving more intelligent human–UAV interaction. For example, executing a command such as “Fly 3 meters in front of me and take a photo" requires UAVs to transform abstract human intentions into executable physical actions.
This process demands that the system seamlessly interpret user intent, reason about the environment, and synthesize dynamically feasible, collision-free flight trajectories.

In pursuit of language-guided aerial autonomy, recent efforts have extended vision-language navigation (VLN) paradigms from ground robots to UAV platforms [14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20]. Leveraging large-scale simulated environments [21, 22, 23, 24, 9], these approaches enable UAVs to follow language instructions for long-horizon target search and goal-directed navigation tasks.
However, prevailing research mainly prioritizes high-level semantic reasoning and macro-level route synthesis
[14, 15, 25, 26, 27, 28]
, operating on the premise that short-range execution can be offloaded to standard low-level planners and control modules [10, 11, 12]. While this assumption has proven successful in many robotic systems, extending it to UAV platforms introduces additional challenges. UAVs must plan and execute dynamically feasible motions while avoiding obstacles in unconstrained 3D environments under real-world kinematic constraints [10, 11, 13]. As a result, enabling language-guided low-level flight maneuver remains a critical yet largely underexplored problem in the development of intelligent UAV systems.

We introduce the Flying-on-a-Word (Flow) task to formalize language-conditioned short-range maneuver execution. Given a concise instruction, egocentric observations, and UAV state estimates, the agent must interpret the intended motion and execute the corresponding flight behavior through closed-loop interaction. Flow covers primitive motion commands and object-interactive commands, assessing motion intent understanding and spatial context grounding.
To support systematic evaluation and policy learning on language-conditioned short-range UAV flight, we present UAV-Flow, the first large-scale benchmark that integrates real-world expert demonstrations with an interactive simulation suite. Specifically, UAV-Flow comprises 30,692 expert-piloted real-world trajectories spanning eight major motion categories and diverse visual contexts. Complementing these demonstrations, UAV-Flow-Sim provides 10,109 simulated trajectories in an interactive environment, enabling controlled policy training and closed-loop evaluation.
We further develop an automated evaluation method for UAV-Flow-Sim to assess task success by jointly considering maneuver execution quality and final state instruction compliance.

Next, we introduce a staged policy learning framework that jointly exploits expert demonstrations and simulation-based interaction to make effective use of task-specific data. In the first stage, imitation learning is used to ground the policy in the distribution of expert flight behaviors, enabling the model to acquire instruction-compliant maneuvers from offline demonstrations. However, during closed-loop execution, control deviations can lead the policy to states outside the demonstration distribution.
We further improve the policy through environment interaction in UAV-Flow-Sim, using task-level completion feedback to guide policy optimization.
Guided by this task-level feedback, we seek to learn more effectively from the action sequences of trajectories with higher completion scores. Therefore, we build upon GRPO [29] and introduce a tail-aware advantage derived from the group reward distribution, producing tail-aware GRPO (TGRPO). This advantage construction assigns greater weight to reward intervals reached by fewer trajectories within each group, strengthening learning from high-reward execution while making fuller use of outcomes that are sparsely represented in group.
For physical deployment, we use a ground-drone collaborative architecture in which the ground station performs VLA inference and the UAV executes the commands. The execution layer selects look-ahead waypoints according to the measured end-to-end delay, accounting for UAV motion during communication and inference to support continuous closed-loop flight.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

(1) We define the Flying-on-a-Word (Flow) task, which formulates language-conditioned UAV navigation as fine-grained, short-range trajectory execution from egocentric observations, assessing the policy’s ability to understand motion intent and execute object-grounded spatial behaviors.

(2) We build UAV-Flow, a real-world expert demonstration dataset, and UAV-Flow-Sim, an interactive simulation suite, together forming the large-scale real-world benchmark for language-conditioned UAV short-range navigation. We also provide an automated task-level closed-loop evaluation protocol in the simulation benchmark.

(3) We propose a staged policy learning framework that combines imitation learning and reinforcement learning through imitation pretraining on mixed real-world and simulated demonstrations, followed by closed-loop post-training with Tail-Aware GRPO (TGRPO).

(4) We have conducted extensive experiments. The pretrained FlowVLA policy achieves a success rate of 75.58%, which TGRPO post-training further raises to 93.16%, achieving the highest overall success rate among evaluated methods. Comprehensive ablation studies validate the effectiveness of the policy learning framework.

This paper is built upon UAVFlow [30], our conference version, and extends it in several important aspects. First, we further develop an upgraded closed-loop simulation evaluation suite, UAV-Flow-Sim, equipped with newly introduced automated task-level evaluation metrics for more fine-grained and reproducible assessment. Second, we develop FlowVLA with mixed-demonstration pretraining followed by online RL post-training, incorporating a tail-aware advantage into GRPO to strengthen learning from the action sequences of high-reward trajectories and improve success rates on challenging Flow tasks. Third, we provide a much more comprehensive experimental study, including comparisons with prior methods, ablation studies, and qualitative analyses. Compared with the conference version, the extended method achieves clear performance improvements and provides a more complete benchmark, training, and evaluation framework for language-conditioned UAV maneuvers.

title: XBot-Omni: An Omni-Modal Model for Embodied Understanding and Interaction
authors: Kerui Gu,Xing Fu,Shuoyang Sun,Cheng Peng,Jingru Duan,Huayu Gu,Zhenyu Chen,Jiaxin Huang,Cheng Wen,Rui Zhen,Kairui Chen,Zhihui Peng,Shaoli Huang
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
In embodied interaction, the meaning of nonverbal behavior, such as body gestures and facial expressions, depends on
the surrounding dialogue, visual scene, and its timing relative to speech.
For example, a pointing gesture must indicate the intended object
as the corresponding phrase is spoken.
Recent Omni models, including Qwen3.5-Omni-Plus (Team, 2026)
and Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, 2026), integrate text, vision,
and audio for multimodal understanding and response generation,
but do not directly generate body motion. Extending them to embodied
interaction requires deciding which actions to perform and coordinating
them with speech.

Co-speech methods generate holistic motion (Liu et al., 2024)
or strengthen gesture semantics through retrieval (Zhang et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025).
A common conversational pipeline passes synthesized speech to an
audio-to-gesture (A2G) module, as in RoboGesture (Wang et al., 2026).
However, speech-only conditioning can lose intent or scene information
not explicitly expressed in the reply, while still requiring waveform
release and audio feature extraction even during incremental processing
of an ongoing response.

Native representation sharing offers tighter integration:
MIBURI (Mughal et al., 2026) supports streaming gestures,
Motion-Omni (Ma et al., 2026a) jointly generates speech and
full-body motion offline, and DyaPlex (Nagano et al., 2026) couples
full-duplex speech with streaming motion and partner-motion perception.
Building on this direction, an embodied Omni model should also use
multimodal response context to guide explicit gesture semantics while
coordinating motion with unfolding speech.

We introduce XBot-Omni, extending the Omni paradigm to an expandable set of robotic modalities, including body motion and facial expression, with “X” denoting this extensibility. Its Thinker–Talker–Actor architecture combines Omni understanding, native speech conditioning, and explicit gesture-semantic control for streaming motion generation (Table 1). The Thinker interprets text, images, audio, and video to infer response intent and scene context, while the Talker generates streaming speech. Rather than treating motion as a downstream synthesis task, the Actor directly conditions on native Thinker representations for semantic and scene-referential guidance, and native Talker states for speech-coordinated movement, alongside a complementary branch for facial expression.

The Actor addresses three challenges through its Motion Generator, Semantic Action Controller, and Speech–Action Aligner. First, the Motion Generator incrementally consumes native Talker states, bypassing waveform release and audio re-encoding for
low-latency motion generation. Second, as semantically specific gestures are underrepresented in common co-speech datasets (Mughal et al., 2026),
the Semantic Action Controller derives explicit action requirements from Thinker representations, grounding gestures in communicative intent and visual context. For example, “the apple is right there” should elicit pointing toward the intended object rather than generic rhythmic motion. Finally, the Speech–Action Aligner associates Thinker-derived semantic events with speech progression estimated from Talker states, coordinating gesture preparation and expression with the corresponding spoken phrases.

To support context-aware embodied interaction, we curate interaction videos and collect robot-view recordings for Thinker training, capturing perceptual context, dialogue, and response decisions. For Actor training, we collect synchronized speech–motion recordings to learn expressive movements and their temporal
coordination with speech. The training pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning,

title: Inner Product Regularization for Imitation Learning
authors: Benjamin A. Christie,Tianyu Qiu,Amy H. Choi,David Fridovich-Keil,Dylan P. Losey
abstract:
Robots that learn from demonstrations should extrapolate their policy despite state perturbations such as sensor noise, scene variation, and compounding errors.
One approach to this robustness is regularization, i.e., adding an inductive bias during training that shapes the learned policy. Prior regularizers consider each state on its own and limit how sensitive the policy is to any perturbation at that state. By contrast, we explore how the policy’s output shifts when given the same perturbation at different states. Our insight is that, locally, the robot should respond to state perturbations in a consistent manner: e.g., if changing an irrelevant object position does not impact the policy at one state, that same change should not shift the policy output at a nearby state. Applying this insight, we develop inner product regularization (InneR). We theoretically show that the inner product on action space induces an inner product on state space through the policy Jacobian, and that the null space of this induced inner product governs which state perturbations have a first-order effect on the policy outputs; for stochastic policies, this inner product is the Fisher information of the action distribution with respect to state. Regularizing each inner product by itself only shrinks the policy’s sensitivity, but by clustering states whose inner products are aligned, averaging the inner products within each cluster, and then minimizing the smallest eigenvalues of that average, InneR shapes the learned policy so that nearby states share a common null space. Overall, InneR enforces consistent responses to state perturbations without limiting policy expressiveness, and can be appended to existing imitation learning pipelines for deterministic or stochastic policies. Our experiments compare InneR to behavior cloning and norm regularization methods across deterministic and stochastic policies. In simulated experiments, InneR makes learned policies more robust to irrelevant state dimensions and shifts between training and test distributions, whereas the norm penalties often perform worse than behavior cloning. On a real robot arm performing three manipulation tasks, InneR raises the average success rate of a diffusion policy from 18%18\% to 57%57\% without additional data.
introduction:
The goal of imitation learning is to extrapolate a generalized policy from a limited set of expert examples.
Consider Figure 1: during training, the robot is shown how to close the coffee machine, and at test time it must generalize that policy across new scenarios, which expose it to states that are not in its training dataset (Spencer et al., 2021).
For example, sensor noise shifts the measured pose of objects, the scene itself varies between trials, and small errors in the robot’s actions can compound over time.
Regularization techniques are often employed to enhance robustness in the face of these perturbations.
Instead of relying on additional data or expert oversight, regularization enforces an inductive bias on the learned policy during training.

Existing regularizers try to limit how sensitive the policy is to changes in state.
For instance, one standard approach is to minimize the norm of the model’s parameter vector Krogh and Hertz (1991); Liu et al. (2021).
Other recent techniques penalize the norm of the policy Jacobian with respect to state Hoffman et al. (2019); Scarvelis and Solomon (2024), or, for stochastic policies, the Fisher information of the action distribution with respect to input Shen et al. (2019); Gloeckler et al. (2023).
These penalties share a common structure: each state is treated on its own, and the policy is made less sensitive to every perturbation at that state.
But not every perturbation should be ignored, e.g., a policy that is robust to moving clutter in the background should still respond when its target object shifts to the right.
Uniformly shrinking the policy’s sensitivity dampens both responses, fundamentally limiting the robot’s ability to control each of its action dimensions.

We propose an alternate perspective on regularization in behavior cloning.
Instead of asking how much the policy changes at a given state, we focus on how the policy responds to the same perturbation at different states.
Our intuition is that — at least within a local neighborhood — the robot should respond to perturbations in a consistent manner.
For example, if a shift in lighting does not affect the robot’s policy at one state, the same shift should not affect the robot’s policy at a nearby state.
Conversely, if a perturbation does substantially impact the task (e.g., the target object moves), then the robot’s policy should change at both states.
This intuition implies structure, and therefore regularization, for the learned policy:

We propose inner product regularization (InneR) as a tool for enforcing this local null space consistency.
InneR works alongside standard imitation learning algorithms by clustering the states in each training batch according to their inner product alignment, averaging the inner product matrices within each cluster, and then penalizing the shared null space.
When we average the inner product matrix across a set of states, the smallest eigenvalues of that average measure how far the states are from sharing a common null space.
Regularizing the policy to minimize these eigenvalues therefore encourages consistency, and this consistency does not come at the cost of expressiveness.
Since the regularizer is zero for any family of full-rank Jacobians with a common row space, InneR can align the directions that the policy ignores without reducing the policy’s sensitivity to the directions that matter.

In summary, we make the following contributions:

Connecting local perturbations to the inner product on state space.
We show that the inner product on action space induces an inner product matrix on state space through the policy Jacobian, and that the null space of this matrix characterizes which local perturbations have no first-order effect on the policy.
For stochastic policies, we show that this matrix is the Fisher information with respect to state.

Aligning the null space using active subspace learning.
We show the smallest eigenvalues of the expected inner product are zero exactly when the individual inner products share a null space.
This yields an eigenvalue regularizer that enforces consistent responses to perturbations without reducing the rank of the policy.
This method contrasts with commonly-employed Frobenius and nuclear norm penalties on the Jacobian.

Localizing the regularization by inner product alignment.
We implement our theory with the InneR algorithm for deterministic or stochastic policies.
To encourage local consistency, InneR first measures the geometric alignment between inner product matrices.
InneR then clusters states which are already aligned, and regularizes each cluster separately so that the relevant state directions can change over the course of a task.

Comparing to alternative regularizers.
We compare InneR to unregularized and regularized imitation learning frameworks across multiple model types in controlled simulations and in the real world.

title: FORGE: Force-Aware Multi-Granularity Control for Efficient Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
authors: Liangjun Xing,Ke Fan,Kailin Li,Bin Wang,Xiaojie Niu,Qingwei Ben,Jiafei Cao,Wei Yao,Yebin Liu,Jingbo Wang,Weinan Zhang
abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated locomotion, balance regulation, and manipulation under frequent contacts, making teleoperated demonstration collection difficult: a practical controller must simultaneously provide precision, stability, and contact awareness. We propose FORGE, a force-aware multi-granularity control system with a coarse-to-fine command space spanning velocity navigation, planar foot placement, wrist-pose tracking, and optional force-conditioning inputs. Policy training requires no full-body human motion trajectories or joint-angle references; deployment consumes only sparse bilateral wrist poses relative to the pelvis, coarse motion commands, and optional desired wrist-load inputs. For sustained contact, FORGE combines a momentum observer with a learned correction trained using simulator contact-force supervision. At deployment, it estimates low-frequency, wrist-equivalent interaction forces from proprioception and reconstructed low-level arm PD torques, without wrist force/torque sensors. A quasi-static virtual-target loop uses this estimate and an optional desired applied-force input to adapt the wrist target. A frozen locomotion prior and asymmetric residual actions stabilize manipulation-induced whole-body corrections. Experiments evaluate unified-control stability, task-space tracking, quasi-static wrist-equivalent force estimation, squeezing forces during sustained contact with a rigid box, and downstream diffusion-policy execution of a squat-and-lift task across payload conditions. Website: bb0928.github.io/forge.
introduction:
Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinating manipulation with stepping, leaning, or posture adjustment under complex dynamics and frequent contacts [1, 2, 3]. Unlike fixed-base dual-arm robots, which benefit from stable support and mature teleoperation systems [4], humanoids must map operator intent to whole-body behavior under underactuation and changing contacts. Balance errors can compromise stability, joint errors can accumulate into end-effector drift, and rigid position control can disrupt sustained interaction. A practical controller must therefore jointly provide Stability, Precision, and Contact Awareness, including interaction-force estimation for regulating sustained contact.

Existing approaches satisfy these requirements only in part. Full-body tracking and large-scale motor-control models [5, 6, 7] provide broad motion repertoires, but dense motion-reference objectives do not directly expose task-space commands for precise foot placement, wrist targeting, and sustained contact. Decoupled locomotion/upper-body stacks [8, 9] preserve locomotion stability but can limit task-dependent whole-body coordination. Force-aware approaches [10, 11, 12] demonstrate learned force estimation and force-conditioned position control, yet sensorless estimation is difficult: external contact, friction, actuator behavior, and whole-body coupling are entangled in proprioception.

A unified controller must therefore support coarse-to-fine teleoperation: approaching a task region, adjusting stance, tracking wrist trajectories, and adapting to contact. Commands must remain composable as task demands change.

These limitations motivate FORGE, which forges a FORce-aware multi-Granularity policy for Efficient humanoid loco-manipulation. Its unified coarse-to-fine interface supports base velocity commands, planar foot-placement targets, Cartesian wrist-pose targets, and optional force-conditioning inputs, individually or jointly. Granularity-conditioned masking [13] activates the observations and rewards relevant to each command group. Training needs no full-body human trajectories or human joint-angle references; teleoperation supplies only bilateral wrist poses relative to the pelvis and coarse commands from wearable trackers, handheld VR devices, or vision-based pose estimation.

For sustained contact, a Physics-Informed Hybrid Force Estimator learns a simulator-supervised correction to a model-based momentum observer. At deployment, it uses arm joint states and reconstructed low-level PD torques without wrist force/torque sensors. The estimator captures the low-frequency component of the equivalent interaction force at each wrist. We combine this estimate with an optional command for the robot-applied force to adjust wrist position targets during sustained, quasi-static contact.

To stabilize mixed-objective training, we freeze a pretrained lower-body locomotion expert and learn an asymmetric residual policy that controls the upper body and applies corrective lower-body actions. This reduces exploration difficulty while preserving the locomotion prior and allowing task-dependent whole-body coordination.

Simulation and hardware experiments show that masking and asymmetric residual training improve unified-control stability and task-space tracking over their ablations, while the hybrid estimator reduces force-estimation error under the evaluated quasi-static contacts compared with analytical-only and learned-only estimators. To assess FORGE as a whole-body executor for visuomotor learning, we train a diffusion policy [14] on collected demonstrations; it commands FORGE to execute squat-and-lift across payloads.

Our contributions are a unified multi-granularity controller trained without full-body human motion references, physics-informed sensorless wrist-force estimation with contact-load adaptation, and asymmetric residual learning for stable whole-body loco-manipulation.

title: SALA: Semantically Aligned Latent Actions Enable Dual-Axis Scaling of Embodied Foundation Models
authors: Jiachun Jin,Zetong Zhou,Haonan Wang,Xiao Yang,Jun Zhu,Zhijie Deng
abstract:
Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts.
To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions.
Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control.
The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.
introduction:
Embodied foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models, connect visual observations and language instructions to robot actions, offering a path toward general-purpose robot control (Black et al., 2024; Brohan et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024).
Their generalization depends on diverse interaction experience across tasks, objects, and environments, yet collecting such data through robot teleoperation remains costly.
Egocentric human videos provide a complementary source of experience, capturing everyday manipulation without requiring robot hardware or teleoperation (Grauman et al., 2022; Hoque et al., 2026; Punamiya et al., 2026).
Using this experience for policy learning, however, requires bridging the human-to-robot embodiment gap: the same operation can involve different motions and control mechanisms across humans and robots, and is often performed in scenes that differ from the robot’s workspace.

Latent action models (LAMs) are a popular way to incorporate human videos into robot policy training without explicit action labels (Ye et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024b; Bu et al., 2025).
By encoding visual transitions in a shared latent space, they provide a common prediction target for human and robot experience.
Compared with world-action models (WAMs), which predict future video frames together with actions (Wu et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2026b; Li et al., 2026b), LAMs avoid explicit pixel prediction during policy learning, which can make training more efficient.
However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which constrains each latent to explain the transition within its own clip but does not relate human and robot executions of the same behavior.
Their latents therefore tend to cluster by visual appearance, such as the scene, rather than by the underlying action, so semantically similar human and robot actions need not lie close together.
Aligning human actions with their robot counterparts thus requires supervision that connects their meanings across embodiments.

Our insight is that language can provide this supervision.
Even when human and robot clips are unpaired, natural-language descriptions of their atomic actions, such as “grasp the cup”, relate a human clip to multiple robot clips with different degrees of semantic similarity, as illustrated on the left of figure 1.
We propose SALA, which trains a latent action tokenizer by translating these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents.
Robot latents, grounded in control by action reconstruction, serve as anchors, and the alignment moves only human latents toward them.
As the middle of figure 1 shows, the resulting latent actions are organized by action semantics rather than by scene, giving human videos a prediction target that is meaningful for robot control.

Once trained, the tokenizer labels videos from their frames alone, so its latent actions provide a unified supervision signal for training the policy on both human and robot videos, without action labels or atomic-action descriptions.
This makes human video a scalable source of supervision along two axes.
In pre-training, the policy can absorb large-scale general human videos spanning diverse everyday tasks.
In post-training, because human and robot latent actions are aligned, task-specific human videos, i.e., human demonstrations of the target task, supervise the same action expert that controls the robot.
Since such demonstrations require no robot, they offer a practical way to improve a policy on a new task, one that robot-only policies cannot exploit.

We evaluate SALA in simulation and on a real robot.
On RoboTwin 2.0 (Chen et al., 2025b), where videos of another robot arm stand in for human videos, SALA achieves a higher average success rate than existing LAMs and WAMs trained on the same videos, with the largest gain in domain-randomized scenes.
Analyses of the tokenizer show that language alignment organizes latent actions by atomic action semantics rather than by scene.
On a real robot controlled in a 63-DoF action space, including two 22-DoF dexterous hands, human video helps along both axes.
Pre-training on more general human video, up to 2,678 hours, consistently reduces the robot’s action prediction error on downstream tasks without additional robot data.
With teleoperated demonstrations fixed, post-training on more task-specific human video raises the average real-robot success rate from 53.75% to 72.5%.
The right of figure 1 shows both trends.

Our contributions are as follows:

We use language as relational supervision: atomic-action descriptions align human and robot latent actions from unpaired videos, with the alignment anchored on robot latents grounded in control.

We turn human videos into latent-action supervision for the same action expert that controls the robot, which enables scaling along two axes: general human video in pre-training and task-specific human video in post-training.

Experiments in simulation and on a 63-DoF real robot with dexterous hands show that SALA outperforms prior LAMs and WAMs trained on the same cross-embodiment videos in average success rate, and that human video scales along both axes: more general human video in pre-training keeps reducing the robot’s action prediction error, and more task-specific human video in post-training raises real-world success rates.

1. We use language as relational supervision: atomic-action descriptions align human and robot latent actions from unpaired videos, with the alignment anchored on robot latents grounded in control.

2. We turn human videos into latent-action supervision for the same action expert that controls the robot, which enables scaling along two axes: general human video in pre-training and task-specific human video in post-training.

3. Experiments in simulation and on a 63-DoF real robot with dexterous hands show that SALA outperforms prior LAMs and WAMs trained on the same cross-embodiment videos in average success rate, and that human video scales along both axes: more general human video in pre-training keeps reducing the robot’s action prediction error, and more task-specific human video in post-training raises real-world success rates.

title: Maximizing LLM Utility While Managing LLM Fallibility
authors: Ekta U. Samani,Christopher G. Atkeson
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can supply autonomous systems with plans, predictions, and judgments, but these contributions are sometimes wrong. This review asks how a system can maximize an LLM’s utility while managing its fallibility. Our answer is to adapt the system’s reliance on the LLM as evidence about the LLM’s performance accumulates. Systems built from imperfect components, such as noisy sensors and faulty software, have long worked in this way, and the classical methods they use can be applied to LLM-based systems as well. A system can change its reliance on an LLM in several ways, depending on the LLM’s role and on the other components in the system. Each change needs an estimate of the LLM’s reliability, and the LLM’s role and the kind of contribution it makes determine what to estimate. Classical methods from decision theory, estimation, and online learning then turn these estimates into reliance decisions. These decisions can reduce how often LLM errors affect the system. However, some errors matter even when they are rare. An independently verified mechanism can prevent such errors from being executed. Without one, adapting reliance using reliability estimates can still keep their risk within a bound. Studies on adapting reliance on LLMs are emerging but limited, and the reviewed comparisons suggest that adapting reliance can improve system performance.
introduction:
Large language models (LLMs) can supply plans [1, 2, 3], designs, and judgments [4], which we call LLM contributions, to robotic systems, and the gains from using them can be large. For example, COCO-TAMP [5] uses LLM knowledge about where household objects are usually stored and which objects tend to be found together to guide a robot’s search. Combining this knowledge with Bayesian state estimation reduced average planning and execution time by 62.7% in simulation compared with a baseline without this knowledge. However, a separate variant that asked the LLM to update location beliefs directly failed in three of five simulated trials with randomized object placements, while variants using Bayesian updates completed the tasks. These results illustrate both the value of LLM knowledge and the importance of how a system uses it. This review therefore asks how a system can maximize the utility of imperfect LLMs while managing their fallibility.

Systems built from imperfect components, such as noisy sensors and faulty software, faced the same question long before the advent of LLMs. Such systems tolerate these imperfections by limiting their reliance on any one component. In fault-tolerant software, for example, a system can rely on the majority vote of multiple versions of a program, so that a faulty version is overruled [6]. Methods from estimation, control, and online learning also help adapt reliance on imperfect components as evidence about each component’s performance accumulates. For example, an adaptive Kalman filter [7] weights each sensor by the uncertainty it estimates from that sensor’s measurements. A contextual bandit [8] learns which source works best in each context and a discounted bandit [9] gives old outcomes less weight so that it can track a non-stationary source. LLM contributions can also be uncertain, context-dependent, and non-stationary [10, 11]. An LLM-based system can therefore use the same methods to adapt its reliance on an LLM. For example, the system can weight the LLM’s contributions by their past performance, verify them before acting on them, or stop using the LLM altogether. Our hypothesis is that adapting reliance according to evidence about the LLM’s reliability can improve system performance.

Prior work already explores improving system performance by using the outcomes of LLM contributions to improve future LLM contributions. As shown in Fig. 1(b) and Fig. 1(c), feedback can be added to subsequent prompts [13, 14], or aggregated across many instances into fine-tuning data that updates the model’s parameters [15]. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) aggregates human feedback in the same way to improve the LLM [16].

However, work on adapting reliance on LLM contributions that may be erroneous is emerging and limited [17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22]. Existing surveys address robotic applications of foundation models [23], LLM uncertainty [24], planning [25, 26], routing [27], and safeguards [28, 29]. This review complements these surveys by showing how to apply classical methods to reliance decisions across LLM roles (Fig. 1(d)). Section 2 shows the ways in which we can change reliance on an LLM, depending on the role it plays in the system and on the other components in the system. Making such changes requires estimating the LLM’s reliability from evidence (Section 3) and then turning those estimates into reliance decisions with classical methods (Section 4). Some LLM errors matter even when they are rare. Section 5 shows what a system needs to prevent them from being executed and, when it cannot, how to keep their risk within a bound.

title: CT-SGAL-LIO: Causal Continuous Time Refinement of Discrete LiDAR Inertial Odometry
authors: Nam Tran,Thu Tran,Toan Nguyen,William J Beksi,Tuan Dang
comment: ICRA 2027 submissions
abstract: State-of-the-art LiDAR-inertial odometry methods, including those on richer state manifolds, achieve strong global accuracy, yet their pose stream alternates between propagation and correction and can oscillate over short horizons even when globally accurate. Most existing methods follow these approaches: they either modify the filter to enable faster updates or estimate a continuous-time trajectory from raw LiDAR and inertial data. The latter involves extra optimization, delaying state updates and becoming less robust during rapid rotations or accelerations. We propose CT-SGAL-LIO, a continuous-time refinement module that smooths the posterior pose stream of a discrete SGal⁡(3)\mathrm{SGal}(3) estimator without modifying the estimator itself. The key novelty is to perform continuous-time trajectory refinement directly on the projected SGal⁡(3)\mathrm{SGal}(3) posterior: we fit a cubic trajectory over a bounded window of recent poses and evaluate it at a small fixed lag. This places the query time within the observed interval, so the refined pose is obtained by interpolation rather than extrapolation, while preserving causal operation. CT-SGAL-LIO improves relative trajectory accuracy on 17 sequences from three public benchmarks. Across 17 sequences from GRAND-TOUR, MCD, and GEODE, CT-SGAL-LIO improves short-term motion accuracy while largely preserving global accuracy. RTE improves by up to 70% on GRAND-TOUR and on all seven GEODE sequences, with 9.9–51.1% reductions. A 19.5-min R-Campus run also reduces posterior jumps by 85.4% with only a 4.7 mm change in the end-to-start gap. We plan to release our source code and results to support community validation and reproducibility.
introduction:
LiDAR–inertial odometry (LIO) underlies mapping, planning, and control on mobile robots, and downstream consumers routinely query the pose stream at rates decoupled from the LiDAR scan rate.
State-of-the-art tightly coupled iterated filters, most recently formulated on the Galilean manifold SGal⁡(3)\mathrm{SGal}(3) [1], achieve strong global trajectory precision.
However, the state stream that such filters publish alternates between IMU-propagated states and LiDAR-corrected states, which can exhibit different local error characteristics.
As a result, a globally accurate trajectory can still contain short-horizon oscillations, visible even on our own baseline: on the GRAND-TOUR [2] HAUS_1 sequence, the discrete estimator we build on already achieves a low global error, yet its relative motion error over short intervals still fluctuates, and CT-SGAL-LIO reduces this short-term error by 67% without altering the global trajectory (Fig. 1).

Existing remedies for this local inconsistency modify the discrete estimator itself. One direction raises the state-update rate by restructuring the filter to process individual points rather than whole scans. A second direction replaces the discrete state altogether with a continuous-time trajectory representation fitted jointly to raw LiDAR and, where available, inertial residuals. This approach works well, but it has two drawbacks, discussed in Section II. Smooth parametric trajectories can struggle with aggressive motion, and fitting them with future measurements introduces delay. Neither direction considers a simpler alternative: keep the discrete LIO estimator and its map untouched, and refine only the pose stream after it is produced.

We answer this question with CT-SGAL-LIO, an online continuous-time refinement layer that treats the discrete posterior as an observation rather than as a state to be re-derived.
CT-SGAL-LIO maintains a persistent, bounded-memory buffer of recent posterior poses and fits a robust cubic trajectory over this window in a local SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) Lie-algebra chart.
The refined trajectory is evaluated at a fixed lag, placing the query time inside the observed window rather than at its boundary. This lets us obtain the pose by interpolation rather than extrapolation, without sacrificing causality. Because CT-SGAL-LIO consumes only the timestamped SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) projection of the estimator’s posterior state and feeds nothing back into the filter or its map, it is decoupled from the underlying estimator and can in principle attach to any discrete LiDAR-inertial system that exposes a pose stream. In this paper, we instantiate it on top of LIMOncello [1], the estimator whose SGal⁡(3)\mathrm{SGal}(3) posterior it refines.

Our contributions are as follows.

We propose a model-agnostic, causal, fixed-lag continuous-time refinement layer that operates purely on the posterior pose stream of a discrete LIO estimator, without coupling to raw sensor residuals or to the map.

We formulate this refinement as robust cubic trajectory fitting in a local SE⁡(3)\mathrm{SE}(3) Lie-algebra chart, combining iteratively reweighted least squares with a curvature prior tailored to short, bounded temporal windows.

We show that attaching CT-SGAL-LIO to LIMOncello’s
SGal⁡(3)\mathrm{SGal}(3) posterior consistently improves short-term motion
accuracy while generally preserving global trajectory accuracy across
17 sequences from three public benchmarks (GRAND-TOUR, MCD [3],
and GEODE [4]). Specifically, CT-SGAL-LIO 
reduces RTE by up to 70% on GRAND-TOUR and by 9.9–51.1% on all
seven GEODE sequences, while ranking first or second in RTE on all
six evaluated MCD sequences.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section II reviews discrete-time LIO, manifold state representations, continuous-time trajectory estimation, and fixed-lag smoothing.
Section III overviews the system architecture.
Section IV details the fixed-lag continuous-time refinement formulation.
Section V presents our experimental evaluation.
Section VI concludes the paper.

title: Informative Path Planning with Gaussian Processes: Error Bounds, Algorithms, and Benchmarks
authors: Kalvik Jakkala,Jennifer Wakulicz,Donald G. Dansereau,Srinivas Akella,Lantao Liu,Jason M. O'Kane
comment: preprint
abstract: Accurate environmental monitoring relies on Informative Path Planning (IPP) to deploy autonomous systems that maximize information gain. While Gaussian Processes (GPs) provide a robust mathematical foundation for modeling the environment, contemporary IPP approaches remain hindered by heuristic operational constraints and the lack of simultaneous theoretical guarantees for worst-case estimation error and approximation quality. Rather than introducing yet another heuristic, this paper presents a rigorous theoretical analysis of existing error bounds and algorithms to further develop the mathematical foundation for IPP.
introduction:
In an era defined by rapid climate change, ecological degradation, and shifting global ecosystems, accurate environmental monitoring has become critical for scientific understanding and informed decision-making. Characterizing complex, large-scale natural phenomena—such as ocean salinity, atmospheric pollutants, soil moisture, or glacial bathymetry—requires high-resolution data that is often dangerous, time-consuming, or prohibitively expensive to collect manually. To address this, an overarching framework of Robotic Information Gathering (RIG) has emerged, focusing on deploying autonomous systems to maximize information gain regarding these environmental data fields [9, 26]. At its core, RIG shares fundamental similarities with active learning; both domains seek to select the most informative data points to query in order to maximize model accuracy with minimal data collection effort.

Traditionally, environmental monitoring tasks have relied on geometric planners, such as boustrophedon (lawnmower) sweeps [10] or Voronoi-based coverage methods [6]. While these strategies successfully guarantee spatial visitation, they are inherently inefficient. By entirely ignoring the probabilistic data correlations within the environment, geometric sweeps frequently oversample highly predictable and redundant regions, wasting valuable time and energy.

Overcoming the limitations of geometric coverage requires addressing two interconnected problems: Sensor Placement (SP) and Informative Path Planning (IPP). While SP focuses on identifying optimal locations for static sensors, IPP routes mobile robots through informative regions while respecting operational constraints, such as motion constraints and limited onboard compute. To model data correlations, the vast majority of these approaches rely on Gaussian Processes (GPs) [42] because of their high sample efficiency and principled uncertainty quantification.

Within this GP framework, IPP encompasses two primary operational paradigms:

Offline IPP: The GP hyperparameters describing the environment are assumed to be known a priori. This serves as a critical theoretical foundation to study the core problem structure.

Online IPP: The GP hyperparameters are unknown beforehand and must be learned dynamically by the robot during the mission.

Despite the mathematical foundation provided by GPs, a critical gap remains regarding the strength of theoretical guarantees offered by IPP algorithms. A persistent trade-off exists between discrete and continuous planning methods. While optimizing submodular objectives like mutual information enables discrete greedy planners to achieve strict approximation factor guarantees, these approaches suffer from severe computational bottlenecks due to expensive matrix operations.

Conversely, planners operating in continuous spaces—such as Rapidly-exploring Random Trees (RRTs) [20] or Ergodic Control [35]—can offer asymptotic convergence, but they inherently lack finite-time approximation guarantees. Indeed most IPP approaches on continuous domains provide anytime algorithms that provide better solutions the longer they run.

Furthermore, a fundamental limitation persists across both paradigms: the reliance on heuristic operational constraints. Most contemporary approaches require explicitly setting a predefined cardinality limit on sensing locations or an ad hoc travel distance budget. Ideally, a planner would instead allow users to specify a maximum allowable uncertainty or error, autonomously determining the necessary sensing budget and travel distance required to satisfy that bound.

Crucially, because existing continuous methods—including ergodic exploration and sampling-based planners—typically plan over predetermined operational budgets (such as fixed time horizons or path lengths) and optimize spatial proxy distributions, they lack finite-time approximation guarantees on the resulting GP predictive variance and worst-case field estimation error.

To bridge the gap between heuristic planning and verifiable mapping quality, this work establishes a rigorous theoretical foundation for Informative Path Planning. Our core contributions are as follows:

Squared Error Bounds and Objective Formulation:
By leveraging existing probabilistic and deterministic error bounds, we contextualize the role of GP predictive variance in bounding true field reconstruction error—showing that it both lower-bounds expected mean squared error and, scaled by the RKHS norm, upper-bounds deterministic pointwise squared error. This formally establishes predictive variance as the mathematically ideal objective for offline GP-based IPP and provides a grounded blueprint for online formulations.

Theoretically Grounded Discrete Offline IPP:
We analyze a recent optimization algorithm, GreedyCover [22], for predictive variance and establish that its near-optimal approximation guarantee matches the fundamental hardness-of-approximation limit for the problem. Consequently, this establishes a theoretically grounded, complexity-optimal foundation for discrete offline GP-based IPP under bounded uncertainty constraints.

Comprehensive Benchmarking and Analysis: We evaluate prominent information-theoretic metrics and optimization methods, empirically demonstrating that GreedyCover delivers strong error reduction with substantial computational efficiency. These results establish the method as a robust solution for offline GP-based IPP under bounded uncertainty constraints while highlighting critical implications for tackling continuous-space and online formulations.

2. Online IPP: The GP hyperparameters are unknown beforehand and must be learned dynamically by the robot during the mission.

By leveraging existing probabilistic and deterministic error bounds, we contextualize the role of GP predictive variance in bounding true field reconstruction error—showing that it both lower-bounds expected mean squared error and, scaled by the RKHS norm, upper-bounds deterministic pointwise squared error. This formally establishes predictive variance as the mathematically ideal objective for offline GP-based IPP and provides a grounded blueprint for online formulations.

2. Theoretically Grounded Discrete Offline IPP:
We analyze a recent optimization algorithm, GreedyCover [22], for predictive variance and establish that its near-optimal approximation guarantee matches the fundamental hardness-of-approximation limit for the problem. Consequently, this establishes a theoretically grounded, complexity-optimal foundation for discrete offline GP-based IPP under bounded uncertainty constraints.

3. Comprehensive Benchmarking and Analysis: We evaluate prominent information-theoretic metrics and optimization methods, empirically demonstrating that GreedyCover delivers strong error reduction with substantial computational efficiency. These results establish the method as a robust solution for offline GP-based IPP under bounded uncertainty constraints while highlighting critical implications for tackling continuous-space and online formulations.

title: ACE-CaP-0: Real-World Code-as-Policies in the Era of Experience
authors: ACE-CaP Team,Changxu Wei,Yunpeng Qing,Guozheng Ma,Bowen Liu,Zexin He,Yilun Kong,Haoming Gu,Jingyuan Liu,Tianyu Zhu,Jianfei Wang,Junqiang Kou,Huinan Mo,Hao Lv,Pengbin Li,Yuesong Wang,Bo Li,Huan Zhou,Shunyu Liu,Chunxiao Liu,Bixuan Jin,Shaopeng Yin,Fei Wang,Zhi Hou,Jiaxing Huang,Changqing Zou,Dacheng Tao,Xiaogang Wang
abstract:
Recent advances in frontier models have pushed the boundaries of agentic robot control, enabling agents to perform complex robotic tasks through reasoning and interaction.
However, repeated calls to these models during execution can substantially increase task completion time.
Code as Policies (CaP) offers a route for coding agents to acquire physical skills through experience and retain them in executable programs, allowing the reasoning invested in development to be reused across runs.
Developing reliable code policies while limiting the cost of physical experimentation remains a central challenge.
We investigate human guidance as a source of priors for feasible actions and simulation as an auxiliary environment for exploring and testing candidate policies.
Our findings favor robot demonstrations available on request and simulation used selectively during real-world policy refinement.
These findings inform ACE-CaP-0, an agentic recipe that couples policy revision with experience acquisition through Demonstrations on Request and Simulation on Demand.
Across eight real-world manipulation tasks spanning alignment, multi-object handling, and bimanual coordination, the resulting frozen programs achieve 92.1% success (221/240 trials).
Mean execution times across tasks range from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes.
The programs execute with runtime perception and control, without a human or coding agent in the loop.
These results highlight CaP’s potential to turn experience into reliable, reusable physical skills.
introduction:
Foundation models are changing how robots acquire and execute skills.
Learned action models, including vision-language-action (VLA) and world action models (WAMs), combine pretrained knowledge with large-scale data and interaction experience to support generalist robot control [1, 2, 3].
Advances in frontier models (e.g., GPT-6 Astra [4] and Claude Fable 5.2 [5]) are expanding the role of agents in both robot control and policy development.
In agentic robot control, agents interpret observations, choose actions, and revise their decisions in response to physical feedback [6].
When execution relies on repeated model calls, however, inference latency can account for a substantial part of task completion time [7, 8].
Agents can also apply these capabilities during policy development, organizing experiments, diagnosing failures, and revising the policies a robot executes [9, 10].

Code as Policies (CaP) represents robot behavior as executable programs, allowing decisions made during development to be retained and reused across runs [11, 12].
Through demonstrations and experimentation, a coding agent can discover manipulation strategies and encode their action structure, geometric relationships, and motion parameters in code [13].
The resulting program can execute with runtime perception and control, without requiring the coding agent to select each action.
Its explicit task logic can be inspected and revised, supporting the accumulation of executable skills in embodied Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI) [14, 10].

Developing reliable code policies requires physical knowledge that a task instruction often leaves unspecified.
The agent must resolve choices about grasping, alignment, and coordination, yet a failed attempt may not reveal how to revise the program [13, 10].
Repeated physical trials also consume robot time and can require human scene resets [9, 15].
Policy development therefore couples two decisions: how to revise the program, and what experience to acquire next.
We ask: how should agents acquire experience to develop reliable code policies when physical experimentation is costly?

Human guidance can supply feasible strategies and motion references, while simulation provides an auxiliary environment for exploring and testing candidate implementations [13, 15].
We examine their use through six development conditions on charger insertion, with one development run per condition (Section 2).

What form of human guidance helps an agent develop a physically realizable policy, and when should it be provided?
Our results favor robot demonstrations paired with textual guidance and available on request during development.
Robot demonstrations supply motion references in the target embodiment, while on-request access lets the agent seek guidance for its current manipulation problem.

When and how should simulated experience support real-world program development?
Our results favor using simulation on demand to investigate current development questions within a real-world feedback loop.
Simulated experiments examine candidate revisions, while physical execution checks whether the sensing and action assumptions they rely on hold on the robot.

Building on these findings, we introduce ACE-CaP-0, a recipe that couples policy revision with experience acquisition through Demonstrations on Request and Simulation on Demand (Section 3).
During development, the coding agent chooses whether to request a robot demonstration, examine a candidate revision in simulation, or test the program on the robot.
The resulting program is frozen for evaluation and executes with runtime perception and control, without a human or coding agent in the loop.

We evaluate ACE-CaP-0 on eight real-world manipulation tasks requiring alignment, object reorientation, multi-object handling, and bimanual coordination (Section 4).
Development allows at most ten human-assisted scene resets per task, excluding resets for demonstration collection.
Each frozen program is then evaluated in 30 trials without further updates.
As summarized in Figure 1, the programs achieve 92.1% overall success (221/240 trials).
Mean physical execution times range from 0.97 to 2.27 minutes across tasks.
These results support CaP as a practical route from targeted experience to reliable, reusable physical skills.

1. What form of human guidance helps an agent develop a physically realizable policy, and when should it be provided?
Our results favor robot demonstrations paired with textual guidance and available on request during development.
Robot demonstrations supply motion references in the target embodiment, while on-request access lets the agent seek guidance for its current manipulation problem.

2. When and how should simulated experience support real-world program development?
Our results favor using simulation on demand to investigate current development questions within a real-world feedback loop.
Simulated experiments examine candidate revisions, while physical execution checks whether the sensing and action assumptions they rely on hold on the robot.
