title: AgriSense: Vision-Language Decision Support and Robotic Intervention in a Virtual Greenhouse Copy title
authors: Lyes Saad Saoud,Oualid Doukhi,Reza Ghorbani,Moussa Ayyash
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Autonomous greenhouse management is moving beyond static sensing and conventional control toward embodied systems that can perceive, navigate, regulate, and intervene at plant level. However, coupling multimodal predictions to robotic and environmental-control interfaces requires explicit output definitions and task-specific evaluation. This paper presents AgriSense, a framework integrating an Isaac Sim virtual greenhouse, a quadruped mobile manipulator, RGB and LiDAR–inertial sensing, environmental-reference execution, and a supervised vision–language decision-to-action (VLDA) module. Frozen DINOv2 and BERT encoders and a structured environmental encoder feed a concatenation-based network that jointly proposes twelve environmental references, a target zone, and a binary intervention flag. Checkpoint replay reproduces 41/43 target-zone decisions on the original split. Five-seed retraining on a source-grouped test set gives 43/44 correct decisions in each seed for the full, image-removed, and language-removed configurations; thus an incremental multimodal zone-accuracy benefit is not established. The full model’s temperature, humidity, and soil-moisture mean absolute errors are 0.249 ∘C, 2.030 and 0.997 percentage points, respectively. The sensor-only condition also matches full zone accuracy, while language-only reaches 68.64%. Separate real-image benchmarks reveal a substantial distribution-shift limitation. Five offline Point-LIO routes give rigidly aligned trajectory errors of 5.22–17.32 mm; 32 accepted virtual-arm targets meet geometric criteria, with eight boundary rejections. Six long-horizon climate cases and distinct fault protocols further characterize integration limits. Navigation and integrated treatment use simulator-state inputs; physical greenhouse accuracy and agronomic treatment efficacy are not established. The contribution is a reproducible multimodal decision-support interface and its component-level characterization in a virtual greenhouse, rather than a field-validated autonomous treatment system.
introduction:
Protected agriculture seeks to improve crop productivity while reducing water, energy, labor, and chemical inputs. Modern smart greenhouses already employ fixed sensors and automated controllers to regulate temperature, humidity, soil moisture, lighting, ventilation, and irrigation. Recent reviews in greenhouse AI, sensory-data integration, and greenhouse temperature prediction/control further emphasize plant-centric intelligence, multimodal sensing, and reliable embedded execution as active research directions (Al-Qudah et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025). However, most existing systems remain limited to greenhouse- or zone-level monitoring and regulation. Zone-level monitoring does not by itself provide a spatially localized inspection and intervention workflow. Such a workflow must associate observations with management zones and separate environmental references from plant-level treatment proposals.

Mobile robots have therefore been investigated for greenhouse mapping, row following, crop inspection, fruit detection, and pesticide spraying
(Sánchez-Molina et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2022; Abanay et al., 2022; Cañadas-Aránega et al., 2024b; Cheng et al., 2024; El Amraoui et al., 2024; Tan et al., 2025).
These studies demonstrate the potential of agricultural robotics, but many existing systems remain restricted to wheeled platforms, predefined task logic, isolated perception modules, or navigation-only demonstrations. Perception, spatial grounding, environmental regulation, and physical intervention are often evaluated independently rather than as components of a unified autonomy pipeline.

Agricultural digital twins are also increasingly used for greenhouse monitoring, prediction, visualization, and decision support
(Ariesen-Verschuur et al., 2022; Gund et al., 2025; Lang et al., 2025).
However, many of these platforms represent the greenhouse as a passive monitored process rather than an embodied robotic environment. In contrast, an embodied virtual greenhouse must represent robot motion, RGB and LiDAR observations, inertial sensing, local map construction, greenhouse-zone association, actuator feedback, and plant-level spray-intervention workflow. Isaac Sim is particularly suitable for this purpose because it supports physically based robotics simulation, multimodal sensor generation, robot–environment interaction, and compatibility with robot-learning workflows
(NVIDIA, 2026b; NVIDIA, 2026a; NVIDIA, 2026c).

Recent embodied multimodal models have shown that visual, textual, and continuous state inputs can support robot decision-making. PaLM-E demonstrated embodied multimodal reasoning from language, vision, and state-estimation inputs
(Driess et al., 2023), while RT-2 and OpenVLA connected vision–language representations with robotic actions
(Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025).
Nevertheless, directly mapping an unconstrained semantic-model output to greenhouse actuators would be unsafe. Navigation goals must be consistent with the local map, environmental setpoints must satisfy agronomic and actuator bounds, and plant-level interventions must satisfy confidence, freshness, reachability, and safety requirements. This motivates a hierarchical architecture in which multimodal reasoning generates structured decision proposals, while deterministic navigation, PI/PID reference-tracking controllers, and predefined manipulator primitives remain responsible for physical execution.

The research question is how to specify an image–text–environment proposal interface for greenhouse tasks and determine which inputs contribute to its predictions. AgriSense addresses this question through a three-output supervised model and grouped modality comparisons, with separate virtual experiments characterizing localization, environmental response, targeting and command admission. The model’s role is decision support; the supporting interfaces are studied within a common spatial setting.

Smart greenhouse systems commonly combine distributed sensors with rule-based, PI/PID, model-predictive, or learning-based controllers to regulate temperature, humidity, soil moisture, lighting, ventilation, and irrigation (Al-Qudah et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2025; Ding et al., 2018). These systems are effective for maintaining greenhouse- or zone-level microclimate conditions, but their sensing and actuation are generally spatially coarse. Measurements are typically obtained from fixed sensor nodes, while control actions are applied to an entire greenhouse compartment or management zone.

This architecture is suitable for broad environmental regulation but is less effective for localized conditions such as leaf disease, pest infestation, fruit-level anomalies, uneven water stress, or isolated crop damage. Addressing these conditions requires more than accurate sensing: the system must acquire close inspection views, associate each observation with a physical location, determine the appropriate response, and execute a localized action. In AgriSense, zone-level environmental regulation is therefore complemented by mobile robotic inspection and plant-level spray-intervention workflow.

Mobile agricultural robots have been investigated for greenhouse mapping, crop inspection, row following, fruit detection, harvesting, and pesticide spraying (Sánchez-Molina et al., 2024; Cañadas-Aránega et al., 2024b; Fujinaga, 2025; Tan et al., 2025). Representative systems combine 3D LiDAR perception with 2D LiDAR SLAM for greenhouse navigation (Jiang et al., 2022), use LiDAR-based row traversal to support strawberry-greenhouse spraying (Abanay et al., 2022), and apply multi-sensor fusion to greenhouse positioning and navigation (Cheng et al., 2024). Datasets such as GREENBOT further highlight the importance of multimodal sensing and localization for greenhouse robots (Cañadas-Aránega et al., 2024a).

These studies establish important foundations for greenhouse navigation. Nevertheless, localization and motion planning are often evaluated independently from environmental regulation, multimodal semantic reasoning, and localized intervention. Moreover, many greenhouse platforms are wheeled robots designed for relatively uniform aisles. Legged robots provide an alternative for environments containing narrow passages, uneven terrain, irrigation infrastructure, soil patches, and obstacles, although they introduce additional locomotion, stability, and manipulation constraints.

A local pose and map provide the spatial reference for associating observations and proposals with management zones.

Embodied multimodal models provide a mechanism through which robots can interpret visual observations, language instructions, and continuous state information. Prior work has demonstrated embodied reasoning from language, visual, and state-estimation inputs (Driess et al., 2023), connected vision–language representations with robotic actions (Zitkovich et al., 2023), and introduced an open vision–language–action architecture for robotic manipulation (Kim et al., 2025).

Directly applying an unconstrained vision–language output to greenhouse actuators, however, presents substantial safety and reliability risks. A predicted navigation goal may be inconsistent with the current local map, an environmental setpoint may fall outside agronomic or actuator limits, and a requested spray action may be unnecessary, stale, or physically unreachable. Consequently, AgriSense does not use the multimodal model as an end-to-end low-level controller.

The VLDA formulation generates environmental-reference, target-zone and binary intervention proposals. Deterministic navigation, PI/PID environmental controllers, and predefined manipulation primitives remain responsible for physical execution. The distinction between semantic proposal generation and validated control execution is central to the proposed architecture.

Agricultural digital twins are increasingly used for crop monitoring, environmental prediction, resource planning, visualization, and decision support
(Ariesen-Verschuur et al., 2022; Gund et al., 2025; Lang et al., 2025). Many existing agricultural twins emphasize process-level representations of crop growth or greenhouse climate. Although valuable for planning and monitoring, they do not necessarily model an embodied robot moving through the greenhouse, generating viewpoint-dependent RGB and LiDAR observations, updating a local map, and executing physical intervention primitives.

High-fidelity robotics simulators provide complementary capabilities. Isaac Sim supports physically based rendering, robot and sensor simulation, synthetic data generation, robot–environment interaction, and integration with robot-learning workflows
(NVIDIA, 2026b; NVIDIA, 2026a). These capabilities make it suitable for constructing an embodied virtual greenhouse in which sensing, localization, navigation, environmental monitoring, and manipulation can be evaluated within a shared spatial environment.

In AgriSense, the virtual greenhouse is not used only as a visualization interface. It provides a virtual environment for sensing, management-zone association, multimodal inputs, and separate localization/navigation tests, together with plant-level inspection and targeted intervention workflows.

The individual components used in AgriSense—LiDAR–IMU localization, PI/PID environmental regulation, multimodal representation learning, quadruped locomotion, and virtual-greenhouse simulation—are not independently new. The contribution is the explicit learned-proposal interface and component-level evaluation of its supporting workflow.

Table 1 compares named studies by task and output contract.

Agricultural studies provide more task-specific context. AgriVLN addresses instruction-following navigation in agricultural scenes (Zhao et al., 2025); visual-language-guided horticultural planning connects RGB observations and semantic maps to robot primitives (Cuaran et al., 2026); AgroGPT adapts conversational vision–language models to agricultural concepts (Awais et al., 2025); and AGRI-BT combines language-generated behaviour trees with CLIP-based perception in simulated greenhouse tasks (Salman et al., 2026). These approaches motivate an explicit distinction between a supervised predictor, a generative planner, and a low-level action policy. The present VLDA belongs to the first category: BERT encodes supplied text, and three supervised heads produce fixed-format proposals. Table 1 compares the tasks and output definitions of these systems.

The central contribution is the implemented multimodal proposal interface, specified through its input schema, three nonlinear prediction heads, training objective, and decoding rules. The evaluation combines checkpoint reproduction, five-seed modality ablations, explicit source-group splits, and separate image-transfer diagnostics. Navigation, offline localization, environmental regulation, manipulation, and fault tests assess the supporting system interfaces. This focus does not require claiming that ordinary feature concatenation is a new fusion mechanism. Instead, the experiments identify both useful component-level behaviour and limits on the role of the visual and language branches.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the system interfaces, virtual greenhouse, VLDA implementation, datasets, and evaluation protocols. Section 3 reports and discusses the prediction, localization, regulation, intervention, and fault-handling results. Section 4 concludes the paper. Detailed protocols, retained historical plots, and extended results are provided in a separate Supplementary Material file.

title: EgoX: Egocentric Cross-Embodiment Manipulation with Embodiment Dreaming
authors: Yaru Niu,Binghong Chen,Changwei Yao,Shangtao Li,Zhenlong Fang,Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran,Shuai Zhou,Yuemin Mao,Kalie Ching,Po-Ju Chao,Yudong Luo,Peiqi Yu,Heng Zhang,Hao Zhang,Bingqing Chen,Chen Qiu,H. Eric Tseng,Ye Yuan,Umar Iqbal,Changliu Liu,Jonathan Francis,Ding Zhao
abstract: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment’s dynamics. Across 13 task–embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+’s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments.
introduction:
Large-scale pretraining has driven rapid progress in natural language processing (Devlin et al., 2019; Brown et al., 2020) and computer vision (Radford et al., 2021; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), demonstrating the potential of learning reusable knowledge from diverse data. A corresponding ambition in robotics is to develop generalist models that accumulate manipulation knowledge across tasks and environments and can be adapted to different robot embodiments. We envision a future populated by robots with complementary physical capabilities: tabletop arms, wheeled mobile manipulators, humanoids, and quadrupeds offer different combinations of mobility, reach, and workspace access, while grippers, dexterous hands, and specialized tools support different forms of object interaction (Pfeifer et al., 2007; Baines et al., 2024; Kirschner et al., 2025). Their different ways of perceiving and interacting with the world also provide complementary experience for learning. However, collecting data and training models separately for every embodiment, task, and scene is costly and limits the reuse of this experience. How can we draw on experience across these embodiments to develop shared manipulation knowledge while allowing each robot to adapt it to its own body and environment?

Several complementary data sources offer a path toward this goal. Cross-embodiment robot learning draws on demonstrations collected across different bodies, sensors, and action spaces (O’Neill et al., 2024; Octo Model Team et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025; Doshi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2024; Gemini Robotics Team et al., 2025a). Egocentric human data captures diverse physical interactions in real-world settings beyond existing robot deployment environments (Kareer et al., 2025; Niu et al., 2025; Qiu et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2026). Simulation enables scalable data collection and has supported policy pretraining, sim-to-real transfer, and co-training with real-world demonstrations (Deshpande et al., 2026; NVIDIA et al., 2025; Maddukuri et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026b). Together, these sources can broaden the objects, scenes, and interaction strategies available for learning beyond the demonstrations collected for any individual robot. Realizing this potential, however, requires training recipes that can make effective use of heterogeneous experience. Demonstrations from different embodiments encode interactions through distinct morphologies, viewpoints, proprioception, action semantics, and motion dynamics, making it challenging to turn their combined experience into useful manipulation capabilities across robots.

Recent work has examined scaling laws and data composition for robot manipulation (Lin et al., 2025; Lin et al., 2026a; TRI LBM Team et al., 2025). Alongside these questions, we focus on how experience from heterogeneous embodiments should be collected, represented, and used for shared learning. Our central concern is the design of representations and learning interfaces that allow diverse demonstrations to contribute to a common manipulation model while preserving the differences that matter for each embodiment’s sensing and control. We treat humans, real robots, and simulated agents as embodiments on equal footing, each contributing its own observations and actions. Through joint pretraining and adaptation to target embodiments, we investigate how this shared experience can improve downstream manipulation across different robot bodies and end-effectors. Fig. 2 illustrates this perspective through corresponding stages of Kitchen-Bread performed by human, real-robot, and simulated embodiments.

We introduce EgoX (Fig. 1), an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework built around a single methodological premise: transfer should occur through semantically corresponding modalities, while sensing and control interfaces remain embodiment-specific. The framework has three components. First, EgoX organizes human, real-robot, and simulated demonstrations in a unified observation-action representation, grouping heterogeneous signals into anatomically or functionally relevant modalities and expressing poses in a unified egocentric frame system.
Second, MXT+, a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer, adopts a fine-grained modular design: within each embodiment, each observation modality has its own tokenizer and each action modality its own expert, while a shared Transformer trunk integrates information across modalities and embodiments.
Third, MXT+ uses embodiment dreaming, an auxiliary objective that predicts future embodiment latents from the current shared representation. This training-only branch encourages the trunk to encode how each embodiment’s visual and proprioceptive state evolves, without requiring pixel reconstruction or deployment-time computation.

We evaluate EgoX on five manipulation tasks, from long-horizon loco-manipulation to precise insertion and tool use (Kitchen-Bread, Kitchen-Cleanup, Sort, Insert, and Scoop), across six robot embodiments: G1-Dex5, xArm7-Dex4, G1-Sim-Dex3, LocoMan-Dex2, R1Lite-Gripper, Z1-Tool. Human demonstrations provide an additional pretraining source. Our experiments compare MXT+ variants with baseline policies across all tasks and ablate the pretraining mixture, embodiment dreaming objective, and MXT+’s modular design. Cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+’s average task progress from 0.63 to 0.80, yielding the highest average score among the evaluated methods and the best performance on 12 of 13 task–embodiment pairs. The gains from pretraining are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution (OOD) conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Broader pretraining mixtures transfer better, and embodiment dreaming raises task progress from 0.63 to 0.78 across seven settings while making the trunk’s latent geometry more similar across embodiments.
In summary, our contributions are:

A unified, modality-structured representation for egocentric cross-embodiment manipulation. EgoX organizes human, real-robot, and simulated demonstrations into a common observation–action structure based on anatomically or functionally corresponding modalities, while retaining embodiment-specific sensing and control interfaces.

A unified, modality-structured representation for egocentric cross-embodiment manipulation. EgoX organizes human, real-robot, and simulated demonstrations into a common observation–action structure based on anatomically or functionally corresponding modalities, while retaining embodiment-specific sensing and control interfaces.

MXT+, a modular cross-embodiment Transformer with embodiment dreaming. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns dedicated tokenizers and action experts to individual observation and action modalities, connected through a shared Transformer trunk. Embodiment dreaming encourages the trunk to model each embodiment’s transition dynamics through future-latent prediction used only during training.

A systematic study of cross-embodiment transfer. Experiments across five tasks and six diverse robot embodiments demonstrate the benefits of cross-embodiment pretraining, particularly under OOD conditions. Ablations show benefits from broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming also producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments.

title: Safe and Efficient Navigation Considering Texting Pedestrians via Attention-Aware Cost-map Tuning
authors: Shunya Tadano,Yusuke Tamura,Ankit A. Ravankar,Yasuhisa Hirata
comment: . Accepted at the 35th IEEE International Conference on Robot and Human Interactive Communication (RO-MAN 2026)
abstract:
Smartphone-distracted pedestrians deviate from social norms unpredictably and cannot be relied upon to yield to approaching
robots — a safety challenge that existing navigation methods are poorly equipped to handle, since they treat all pedestrians
uniformly regardless of attention state. We propose an attention-aware navigation framework that classifies each
pedestrian as attentive or distracted in real-time using 3D skeletal features and a Random Forest classifier, then dynamically
widens cost-map safety margins around distracted individuals to drive proactive avoidance. A within-subjects user study with 12
participants across 252 trials demonstrates significant improvements in perceived smoothness (p=0.003p=0.003) and predictability (p=0.034p=0.034) over both a LiDAR-only baseline and a
trajectory-prediction-only method, without any increase in travel time. Notably, trajectory prediction alone does not improve
subjective navigation quality unless coupled with attention-state-aware cost adjustment — confirming that appropriately responding to who is in front of the robot
can matter more than trajectory smoothness alone.
introduction:
Autonomous robots operating in shared human spaces must do more than avoid collisions — they must navigate in ways that are
safe, predictable, and socially acceptable to the people around them [1]. This requires robots to continuously interpret pedestrian behavior and adapt their motion accordingly [2].
Service robots deployed in hospitals, offices, and care facilities face this challenge routinely, where the cost of getting it wrong
is not merely inefficiency but physical risk. Despite significant advances in social navigation, however, a persistent gap remains:
existing methods treat all pedestrians as attentive, cooperative agents — an assumption that breaks down the moment someone picks
up their phone.
This gap is most consequential for service robots in healthcare and care facilities, which routinely share narrow corridors with distracted patients, visitors, and staff [3].

Smartphone-distracted pedestrians present a qualitatively different navigation challenge. Observational studies report that
12% to 45% of pedestrians in public spaces are actively distracted while walking, with texting shown to moderately
increase the rate of collisions and near-misses [4]. Distraction induces “inattentional blindness” [5],
alters gait parameters including walking speed and stride length [6], and significantly slows
responses to environmental changes [7]. Crucially, a distracted pedestrian is unlikely to notice an
approaching robot or adjust their path — placing the full burden of conflict resolution on the robot itself. No existing navigation
approach accounts for this asymmetry.

This paper proposes an attention-aware navigation framework that directly addresses this gap. The system classifies each pedestrian as attentive or distracted in real-time from 3D skeletal information and uses this classification to dynamically adjust cost-map safety margins during motion planning. As shown in Fig. 1, wider avoidance regions are assigned
around distracted pedestrians, allowing the robot to plan proactively rather than react to an unfolding conflict. A within-subjects experiment with 12 participants across 252 trials demonstrates that this approach significantly improves perceived smoothness and predictability of robot navigation while maintaining travel efficiency.

The contributions of this research are as follows:

Skeletal-based Distraction Classification: A pose-based module that classifies pedestrians as attentive or
distracted in real-time from 3D skeletal keypoints using a lightweight Random Forest classifier, designed for deployment
on mobile robot hardware.

Skeletal-based Distraction Classification: A pose-based module that classifies pedestrians as attentive or
distracted in real-time from 3D skeletal keypoints using a lightweight Random Forest classifier, designed for deployment
on mobile robot hardware.

Attention-Aware Cost Tuning for Legible Avoidance: A dynamic cost-map layer that modulates safety margins based on classified attention state, making avoidance behavior more legible and anticipatable around non-cooperative pedestrians.

Empirical Validation: A user study
demonstrating that attention-state classification — not trajectory prediction alone — is the critical factor connecting objective motion smoothness to perceived navigation
quality.

   理由：模型的输入主要是3D骨架特征，并不包含视觉和语言的组合，输出为机器人动作，但缺乏语言输入的元素，因此不符合VLA的定义。

   理由：虽然论文涉及机器人导航和避让，但并未明确提到使用类人机器人（humanoid）或涉及整体协调的操控任务，主要集中在行人行为的分类和成本地图调整上。

5. 最终标签总结

6. 如果有歧义，请说明最容易混淆的点

title: NSDL: Neuro-Symbolic Division of Labor for Multi-Robot Task Planning
authors: Xincheng Tan,Ke Wang,Yining Di,Minfeng Zhu
comment: . Submitted to ICRA 2027
abstract:
Planning for a heterogeneous robot team from a scene image and an
instruction involves two kinds of decisions. Some must be judged from
the scene: which goals are already met, how the task splits, and which
robot does what. Others follow from these and can be computed:
prerequisite actions, handoffs between robots, and timing. We argue
that each kind should go to the component suited to it: a small
vision-language model learns the first, and a deterministic solver
computes the second. In NSDL (Neuro-Symbolic Division of Labor), the
trained model writes its judgments as a plan sketch, which lists the
goals that still need action and the intended steps in order, each with
a robot. The solver expands the sketch into an executable joint plan.
The model calls two tools, a detector for evidence and the solver, and
is trained with the solver in the loop. We evaluate on the public
VIKI-L2 benchmark and on LOCUS-Bench, a new benchmark that grades the
two kinds of difficulty separately. NSDL outperforms end-to-end
planners and formalize-then-plan baselines on both benchmarks and with
three backbones from 3B to 8B; the 7B model reaches 97.0% out-of-distribution accuracy on VIKI-L2. Ordering and scheduling errors
nearly disappear once the solver writes the structure; the remaining
failures are misjudged states, and most goals the model misses are
ones it never lists. Code, model weights, and LOCUS-Bench are publicly
available at https://github.com/Xincheng-Tan/NSDL.
introduction:
Multi-robot systems combine robots with complementary capabilities for
tasks that no single robot completes alone. Planning for such a team
from a scene image and an instruction has become a task for
vision-language models (VLMs). The planner receives the instruction,
one image, and the capabilities of each robot, and returns a joint plan
that says which robot does what and in what order
[1, 2]. Large language models (LLMs) brought broad
reasoning to this setting [3, 4, 5], and VLMs connect it
to raw visual observation [6, 7, 2]. Trained
planners for this task build on small VLMs [2], whose capacity
is limited. Which decisions should such a model learn, and which should
a solver compute? The question applies to language-model planning in
general [8, 9].

The decisions in this task fall into two kinds. State judgment
covers whether each goal is already satisfied in the scene, how the
task decomposes into subtasks, and which robot takes which. No fixed
procedure computes these from the input; they require image evidence
and semantic understanding. Structural planning covers the
prerequisites and the scheduling that follow once intent and assignment
are fixed, such as opening a cabinet before stowing an item and
respecting end-effector capacity. Given a fixed action model, a
deterministic solver computes them correctly. Fig. 1
shows one failure of each kind on one scene, made by two planners: the
untrained Qwen2.5-VL-7B and VIKI-R 7B, an end-to-end planner trained on
the public VIKI-Bench. Both mark a plate that is already on the table as
still to be moved, and both stack picks onto a robot without a free
end-effector.

We argue that each kind should go to the component suited to it: the
model learns the state judgment, and a deterministic solver computes
the structural planning. The model then spends its capacity only on the
decisions that need the scene, and a 7B model plans better than
planners that learn both kinds. Existing planners draw the line
elsewhere: end-to-end planners [2, 10, 6] learn
both kinds, and formalize-then-plan methods
[5, 11, 12, 13, 14] have an untrained
model write the input of a classical planner, which then produces the
plan (Sec. II).

NSDL (Neuro-Symbolic Division of Labor) implements this division
(Fig. 2). The trained model writes its judgments as a
plan sketch: the goals that still need action and the intended
operations (ops) in order, each assigned to a robot. A deterministic
solver Φ\Phi expands the sketch into the executable plan: it adds
prerequisite actions and handoffs, breaks each op into primitive
actions, and schedules them. The model works in one multi-turn dialogue
(a trajectory) with two tools. detect returns the objects and spatial
relations it observes, and schedule runs the solver; when the solver
rejects a sketch, schedule returns the reason, and the model revises the
sketch. The model is trained by supervised fine-tuning and then by
reinforcement learning with the solver in the loop.

We evaluate NSDL on the public VIKI-L2 benchmark, the task-planning
level of VIKI-Bench [2], and on LOCUS-Bench, which we build
because public benchmarks fold both kinds of failure into one score.
LOCUS-Bench sets state-judgment and structural-planning difficulty on
two separate five-level scales, and its out-of-distribution splits
raise the difficulty of one kind, the other, or both. On both
benchmarks and with three backbones from 3B to 8B, NSDL outperforms
end-to-end planners and formalize-then-plan baselines; the 7B model
reaches 97.0% out-of-distribution accuracy on VIKI-L2.

Our contributions are as follows.

NSDL. A framework for embodied multi-robot task
planning in which a trained model makes the decisions that depend on
the scene and writes them as a plan sketch, and a deterministic solver
expands the sketch into the executable joint plan.

LOCUS-Bench. A benchmark that sets state-judgment and
structural-planning difficulty on separate five-level scales, so that
a failure can be traced to either kind.

Findings. Once the solver writes the structure, the
runtime almost never rejects a plan for its ordering or scheduling, and
these errors return when the model is trained without the solver. The remaining failures are misjudged
states. Most goals the model misses are ones it never lists rather
than ones it misreads, and ground-truth evidence does not reduce their
number.

1. NSDL. A framework for embodied multi-robot task
planning in which a trained model makes the decisions that depend on
the scene and writes them as a plan sketch, and a deterministic solver
expands the sketch into the executable joint plan.

2. LOCUS-Bench. A benchmark that sets state-judgment and
structural-planning difficulty on separate five-level scales, so that
a failure can be traced to either kind.

3. Findings. Once the solver writes the structure, the
runtime almost never rejects a plan for its ordering or scheduling, and
these errors return when the model is trained without the solver. The remaining failures are misjudged
states. Most goals the model misses are ones it never lists rather
than ones it misreads, and ground-truth evidence does not reduce their
number.

title: Rethinking Actions: Continuity-Aware Priors for World-Model Planning
authors: Shaobo Yang,Zichen Ai,Ziyang Ma,Qian Yang,Bin Fang
abstract:
Actions in expert demonstrations exhibit temporal structure. An
ordered-versus-shuffled analysis across five environments confirms this
dependence. We ask whether action proposals that better reflect expert
continuity can improve visual world-model planning. Rather than imposing
generic smoothness, we learn continuations from the temporal structure of
demonstrated actions. Our locality-gated
deep-kernel Gaussian-process prior, LG-DKGP, combines recent and longer-range
executed action history, predicts a neural continuation, and learns a temporal
Gaussian-process (GP) residual. A training-derived exploration scale initializes search around
the corrected mean; a frozen world model evaluates progress toward the goal.
Training first fits the neural mean, then jointly optimizes the prior with
the GP residual using expert future actions.
The resulting planner achieves 87.07% macro success across five simulated
tasks spanning native and fragment-level goal attainment, compared with
71.03% for INTACT, 61.66% for PRISM, and 58.66% for LeWM.
Component interventions and expert-relative action-structure comparisons
support demonstration-informed continuations and reveal task-dependent effects
of visual conditioning, history length, and planning horizon.
introduction:
Expert behavior is organized in time. A reaching command follows the direction
of an ongoing reach; a manipulation command depends on the phase of contact.
Neighboring expert actions usually carry information about the ongoing behavior. Treating a future action chunk
as an unconstrained collection of vectors overlooks this structure.

We test this observation by comparing expert trajectories with within-episode permutations of
the same actions. Across five held-out cohorts, preserving the original order
reduces adjacent standardized action changes. This motivates the question:
Can proposals that better reflect the continuity structure of expert
action sequences improve goal-directed world-model planning?

Visual world models provide a natural evaluation interface: roll candidate
actions forward and compare the predicted latent state with a visual goal.
Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn image and video features through
embedding-space prediction [1, 2].
LeWorldModel (LeWM) learns such action-conditioned predictors from pixels [19].
PRISM guides imagination with a learned action prior [32],
whereas INTACT learns an intent-to-action mapping for direct
execution [29].

We introduce a locality-gated deep-kernel Gaussian-process action prior,
LG-DKGP. A history encoder dynamically combines recency-biased local attention
and global attention over retained executed actions. The gate allows recent
motion and older phase information to contribute according to context. A
neural mean models nonlinear action continuations, and a temporal Gaussian-process learns
residual structure across forecast positions. Search starts around their
combined mean with an exploration scale derived from expert training
action increments. The frozen world model remains responsible for evaluating
goal attainment (Fig. ).

The target is the continuity exhibited by experts. A constant command
may have small variation yet be inappropriate for a moving expert reference.
We therefore assess both control success and discrepancy from expert
transition structure.

Our contributions are:

A held-out action-order study that motivates expert-relative continuity as a design principle for world-model planning.

A locality-gated neural/GP action prior that combines local and global action-history information with training-derived search initialization.

A five-task evaluation of control performance, component interventions, history/horizon sensitivity, and expert-relative transition structure.

1. A held-out action-order study that motivates expert-relative continuity as a design principle for world-model planning.

2. A locality-gated neural/GP action prior that combines local and global action-history information with training-derived search initialization.

3. A five-task evaluation of control performance, component interventions, history/horizon sensitivity, and expert-relative transition structure.

title: Reins: Frontier Multimodal Models Driving Real Robot Arms on Long-Horizon Tasks, Zero-Shot
authors: Pengfei Ye,Zhiyang Dou,Yuxiang Ma,Haonan Chen,Heng Yang,Edward H. Adelson
abstract:
Frontier models such as GPT-6.1 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 can now plan and call tools, yet they
still struggle to drive real robots through long-horizon, contact-rich manipulation, blind while the arm
moves and while they think. We present Reins, a harness in which an off-the-shelf model operates a
dual-arm robot with 3D perception tools and atomic actions that report contact and grip. The model chains
actions in one call, each with a condition that must hold, stopping at the first that fails; a second
instance, the narrator, watches the cameras continuously and reports what changed with every result.
From images, Reins also builds a simulation-ready twin of the scene for continual policy learning. With
natural-language prompts and no task-specific code, GPT-6.1 Sol succeeds in 88% of real episodes
on five tasks; without the harness, it fails every shell game, taking 8 times as long. Three frontier
models perform alike but differ in tracking a scene that changes while the actor thinks. Code will be
released upon publication.
introduction:
Frontier models that plan and call tools [35, 28] now run as robot policies
without robot training, mostly in simulation, where benchmarks find a gap between understanding and
executing a task [37, 34, 10, 14, 39, 31]. On real
hardware, Show-Harness [8] moves a Franka and a bimanual AgileX in 2–4 cm steps,
mostly pick-and-place. Trained policies struggle too: on RoboDojo’s real Sweep Blocks, ten
vision-language-action models trained on 100 demonstrations each never succeed [7].

Earlier language-model systems compose skills, write programs or spatial targets, or feed scene
descriptions back to the model [1, 23, 22, 29, 32, 16, 15, 24, 17, 36, 25];
others learn control from robot
data [38, 9, 4, 19, 3, 27, 12] or
sequence learned skills [13, 21, 2]. In Reins, the model drives the
arms through atomic actions, with no skill library or task code; two choices set it apart. First,
the model attaches stopping conditions to each chain of actions, checked at every step, as in
guarded moves [33, 26] and the action conditions of task and motion
planning [11], but written at run time; Show-Harness runs its action
chunks open-loop [8]. Second, another instance of the model, the narrator, watches
every camera frame while the actor thinks and keeps a running account; VoLo’s agent
monitors its own execution at 0.2 Hz [6]. We contribute
(i) Reins with its guarded chains, (ii) the narrator and its latency analysis, and (iii) a real-robot evaluation of three frontier models on five long-horizon tasks, with time and cost.

title: STVLA: Spatial-aware and Temporal-memory forVision-Language-Action Models
authors: Zhuo Han,Yeqiang Wang,Xinran Wang,Hongwei Han,Yi Xiong,Zunian Wan,Jianbo Mao,Huan Peng,Yongcheng Liu,Wei Shan,Maoqing Yao
abstract:
Robotic manipulation often requires both spatial scene understanding and task history. However, many vision-language-action (VLA) policies rely primarily on current observations, without explicitly integrating spatial structure and task history. Appearance-based memories can be sensitive to occlusion and viewpoint changes, while spatial representations of the current scene alone do not preserve how the scene has changed during task execution. We introduce STVLA, a framework that incorporates features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal memory alongside visual representations. This allows the policy to recall past scene structure as context for current action decisions.
To select informative history, STVLA uses a mathematically grounded scoring rule that balances relevance to the current observation with complementary evidence from memory.
Across evaluations on LIBERO, LIBERO-Mem, MIKASA-Robo, and SimplerEnv Bridge, STVLA achieves the highest average success rate among the compared methods on each benchmark. On real-world block stacking, object organization, and phone packaging, it improves success over π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 58.3358.33, 30.0030.00, and 35.0035.00 percentage points, respectively. These results support integrating scene geometry into temporal memory to improve manipulation requiring both spatial precision and task history.
Project website: https://stvla.github.io/.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) policies have achieved strong performance in robotic manipulation [1, 2, 3], yet many condition each action primarily on the current observation, leaving both task history and spatial scene structure only implicitly represented. Everyday manipulation tasks are often non-Markovian from the policy’s perspective: visually similar observations can correspond to different task states, causing a current-frame policy to repeat completed steps or stall. When the action further depends on the geometric structure of the scene — the height of a surface, whether a location is still free — 2D features extracted from a single frame and a single view do not express that structure. In everyday manipulation, the two demands often arise together.

Memory-augmented policies retain information from previous observations to support decisions over longer horizons [4, 5, 6, 7, 8], while spatially aware policies enrich visual representations with depth, 3D structure, or features learned by geometry models [9, 10, 11]. These capabilities, however, are commonly introduced as separate components. A memory built on appearance features inherits the weaknesses of appearance itself: once the gripper
occludes the workspace or the viewpoint changes, the current frame no longer resembles the stored frame that shares its physical configuration, and retrieval fails in exactly the situations where memory should matter most. A spatial representation computed on the current observation alone has the mirror-image problem: it describes what the scene is, but not which parts of it the policy has already changed. This motivates a simple principle: the spatial representation of the scene should be part of what the policy remembers.

We introduce STVLA, a VLA architecture that integrates spatial
representations directly into bounded temporal memory(Fig. ). A frozen pretrained visual geometry model [12] extracts scene geometry features from a multi-frame window of RGB observations, and a trainable compressor maps its intermediate features into compact spatial tokens. These spatial tokens are paired with the backbone’s visual tokens and stored in a single bounded memory bank. At each step, the current visual and spatial representations jointly retrieve relevant information from the stored history through cross-attention. Retrieved spatial information conditions the action expert through a dedicated prefix segment. This design allows spatial information and temporal context to interact during memory retrieval while preserving the backbone’s pretrained image-language representation.

Our contributions are summarized as follows:

We introduce a memory paradigm for VLA policies that incorporates
features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal
memory. This makes past scene structure available for action generation,
enabling the policy to use both appearance and geometry as historical context.

We develop a joint visual-spatial retrieval mechanism for conditioning
action generation on useful history. A relevance–non-redundancy score, computed from
current–memory feature similarity and normalized feature difference, serves as an entry-level
attention prior without introducing an auxiliary learned scorer.

We evaluate STVLA on four simulation benchmarks and three real-world
tasks. STVLA improves average success over our
π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline on each simulation benchmark and improves success by
30.030.0–58.358.3 percentage points on real-world tasks that jointly stress
geometry-sensitive manipulation and progress tracking.

1. We introduce a memory paradigm for VLA policies that incorporates
features from a pretrained visual geometry foundation model into temporal
memory. This makes past scene structure available for action generation,
enabling the policy to use both appearance and geometry as historical context.

2. We develop a joint visual-spatial retrieval mechanism for conditioning
action generation on useful history. A relevance–non-redundancy score, computed from
current–memory feature similarity and normalized feature difference, serves as an entry-level
attention prior without introducing an auxiliary learned scorer.

3. We evaluate STVLA on four simulation benchmarks and three real-world
tasks. STVLA improves average success over our
π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline on each simulation benchmark and improves success by
30.030.0–58.358.3 percentage points on real-world tasks that jointly stress
geometry-sensitive manipulation and progress tracking.

title: Input-output characterization of robotic grasping: Connecting design parameters to grasp behavior through the admittance
authors: Julien Vanderheyden,Guillaume Drion,Pierre Sacré,Fulvio Forni
abstract:
Low-impedance grippers make the dynamics of a grasp matter. Current grasp metrics, however, are static: they describe how a held object resists constant loads, not how it responds to time-varying ones. To quantify this,
we rely on small-signal analysis to characterize a grasp by its admittance, the transfer matrix relating load perturbations to object displacements around an equilibrium. This transfer matrix recovers the stiffness and stability of the grasp at zero frequency and captures its natural frequencies and peak gain under time-varying loads.
We apply this characterization to a planar two-finger gripper under proportional-derivative control. We show that two grasps of the same object in the same position and with the same contact forces can differ in stiffness by two orders of magnitude. Likewise, two grasps that share the same stiffness can exhibit very different resonances. Nonlinear simulations confirm the effectiveness of our small-signal analysis in capturing the dynamic behavior of grasping.
introduction:
Grasping with low-impedance grippers is a dynamic problem. Compliance has long been recognized as useful in manipulation [1, 2, 3], but only recently have grippers started to implement it,
thanks to advances in actuator design [4], low-inertia fingers [5], direct-drive actuation [6], and elastic elements [7, 8]. These grippers promote force transparency, high-bandwidth feedback, and fast, contact-rich motions, and thus challenge the long-standing treatment of grasping and manipulation as quasi-static problems [9]. Their low stiffness and friction also yield lightly damped resonances at low frequencies, which these motions can excite. Wimböck et al. [10] showed experimentally that the dynamics of such grippers should not be neglected.

Current grasp metrics, however, do not describe how a held object responds to time-varying loads. Standard criteria, such as the Ferrari–Canny ϵ\epsilon-metric [11] and stiffness-based quality measures [12], evaluate whether a hand can withstand arbitrary wrench disturbance magnitudes in static conditions. They treat finger links as massless and so neglect mechanical inertia, joint damping, and coupling resonances. Yet low-impedance grippers are designed for unstructured environments, where fast inertial perturbations and contact impacts are expected during standard manipulation, such as pushing or insertion. Dynamic metrics exist but address other questions, such as the accelerations a hand can impart to the object [13] or the outcome of grasp acquisition under pose uncertainty [14]. A tool is therefore needed to quantify the response of a held object to time-varying loads, and to relate it to the gripper parameters, which include both the morphology parameters and the control parameters.

To quantify this response, we characterized a grasp by its admittance, 𝐇⁡(s)=(𝐌​s2+𝐃​s+𝐊)−1\mathbf{H}(s)=(\mathbf{M}s^{2}+\mathbf{D}s+\mathbf{K})^{-1},
the transfer matrix relating load perturbations to displacements of the grasped object around an equilibrium. In contrast to classical stiffness-based measures that relate static load perturbations to static displacements, the admittance includes inertia and damping, thereby capturing the full spectrum of time-varying perturbations. At zero frequency, the admittance recovers the stiffness; at nonzero frequencies, it reveals critical dynamic behavior, such as resonances, that quasi-static metrics miss. Crucially, the gripper parameters directly shape the admittance, establishing a connection between these design parameters and the grasp dynamics.

On a minimal gripper (Fig. 1), we showed that grasps that are equivalent under static metrics can respond differently to fast load perturbations. Closed-form expressions are hard to derive in general without dropping terms that can destabilize the grasp [15]. We therefore considered a minimal model that keeps these terms and remains analytically tractable: a planar two-finger gripper under joint proportional-derivative (PD) control, holding a disk through rigid frictionless contacts. With this model, we also showed that the same gripper can hold an object in qualitatively different ways. Nonlinear simulations confirmed that the admittance, although derived from a linearization, predicts the main dynamic features of the nonlinear model.

Section II introduces the model used throughout the paper.
Section III presents the input-output characterization of a grasp by its admittance, obtained by linearization.
Section IV then derives the static equilibria and their stability.
Section V studies the dynamic response, showing how the gripper parameters shape the admittance 𝐇⁡(s)\mathbf{H}(s) and how far this admittance predicts the nonlinear response.
Finally, Section VI discusses the results and their limitations. The main symbols and the parameter values
are summarized in Table I.

title: Robots That Talk Too Much and Don't Listen Enough
authors: Graham Wilcock,Kristiina Jokinen
comment: presented at EMF Workshop, HRI 2026, Edinburgh, Scotland
abstract:
Until recently, the biggest obstacles to natural spoken
interaction with social robots were speech recognition errors
and turn-taking failures.
Advances in speech recognition have enabled much better spoken interaction,
but turn-taking failures and other misunderstandings
continue to be far too prevalent.
This short paper looks back at earlier methods for
improving speech recognition and turn-taking in interaction
with social robots, and then looks at what can be done today,
arguing that multimodal bidirectional streaming
is needed to reduce the frequency of turn-taking failures.
introduction:
Once upon a time, robots did not talk much.
They would say Moving left 10cm or something equally robotic.
Then they learned to talk a lot.
We made our own contribution to this by developing WikiTalk for Nao robots in 2012 (Csapo et al., 2012),
which is described in Section 2.

Unfortunately, many social robots now have a problem.
They talk a lot, but they don’t listen enough.
For example, many shopping malls in Japan introduced
humanoid robots about 10 years ago
to welcome customers and provide information.
However, the robots had problems understanding what the customers asked,
and they kept saying Irrashaimase! (Welcome)
repeatedly without answering customers’ questions.
It has been said that by 2019, a majority of Pepper robots used in Japan
were returned without renewing their rental
contracts.
"Only about 15% of businesses renewed their three-year contracts.
The robot’s limited conversational ability, inability to handle complex tasks,
and high ongoing costs made it difficult to justify for many
organizations." (Fankhauser, 2026).

Until recently, the biggest obstacles to natural spoken
interaction with social robots were speech recognition errors
and turn-taking failures.
Impressive advances in speech recognition have enabled much better spoken interaction,
but turn-taking failures and other misunderstandings
continue to be far too prevalent (Skantze, 2021).

This paper looks back at some earlier methods for
improving speech recognition and turn-taking in interaction
with social robots, and then looks at what can be done today.
The paper argues that bidirectional streaming
is urgently needed to reduce the frequency of turn-taking failures.
Bidirectional audio streaming allows robots to listen
while they are speaking, in case the user attempts to speak.
Video streaming of user facial expressions allows robots to
detect, while they are speaking, that the interaction is not going smoothly
or something is wrong.
Both improvements will enable more natural and fluid interactions between humans and robots.

title: RGB-D SLAM on the Edge: Benchmarking and Profiling RTAB-Map and ORB-SLAM3 on the Raspberry Pi 5
authors: Himanshu Patil,Jaideep Joshi,Rohit Saluja,Ganesh Ramakrishnan
abstract: Micro aerial vehicles that operate without GPS often run SLAM on ARM-based edge boards, yet there is little published data on how standard RGB-D SLAM systems behave on such hardware. We benchmark RTAB-Map and ORB-SLAM3 on the Raspberry Pi 5 using six TUM RGB-D sequences at three image resolutions, recording tracking coverage, trajectory error, time per frame, memory, CPU load and temperature for every run, and we profile both systems at the stage and function level. RTAB-Map was configured to process and keep every frame, so its back end runs on every frame rather than at its default rate of 1 Hz. On the sequences that every configuration tracked, its front end takes 38–74 ms per frame and its full pipeline 150–462 ms, compared with 13–45 ms and 26–62 ms for ORB-SLAM3. RTAB-Map’s main cost is optimizing a pose graph that keeps growing, because its working memory is unbounded by default; ORB-SLAM3’s local bundle adjustment costs about as much as its tracking but runs in a parallel thread. At quarter resolution, both systems lose tracking on most sequences, and runs that lose tracking finish sooner and report lower error on the poses they keep, so time and accuracy must be read alongside coverage. Timing is repeatable to within 1–5%, but trajectory error varies by up to 27% between identical runs, so the accuracy differences between the two systems are inconclusive. No thermal throttling occurred.
introduction:
Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) lets a robot build a map of an unknown environment while estimating its own pose within it. For micro-UAVs operating indoors without GPS, onboard SLAM is a necessity, and the computer that runs it is a primary design constraint: a tight payload budget for compute and sensing rules out desktop GPUs and high-power accelerators, leaving ARM-based edge boards as the practical choice.

RTAB-Map and ORB-SLAM3 are two widely used open-source RGB-D SLAM systems. ORB-SLAM3 [1] is among the most accurate open-source feature-based systems, with parallel tracking, local mapping and loop closing. RTAB-Map [2] offers configurable cost through its memory management and supports visual, RGB-D and inertial inputs through one interface, which makes it a common choice for embedded deployment. To our knowledge, the only peer-reviewed evaluation on the Raspberry Pi 5, whose Cortex-A76 cores are a large step over its predecessor, covers ORB-SLAM3 alone [3]; RTAB-Map has not been measured on the board, and the two systems have not been compared under one protocol.

This paper reports such measurements. It does not propose a new method; it provides:

A benchmark of RTAB-Map [2] on the Raspberry Pi 5 at three image decimation levels over six TUM RGB-D sequences [4], reporting tracking continuity, trajectory error, time per frame, memory, CPU load and temperature for every run, with recorded software provenance and repeatability measurements.

A stage-level and function-level profile of RTAB-Map on the Raspberry Pi 5 showing where per-frame time goes.

The same measurements and profiling for ORB-SLAM3 under the closest equivalent configuration, with a run-by-run comparison against RTAB-Map.

title: HALO: Human-Aligned Data Collection for WhoLe-body MObile Manipulation
authors: Shuai Yang,Fangyi Xu,Yishu Shen,Kecheng Zheng,Yinghao Xu
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
End-to-end robot policies and imitation learning Zhao et al. (2023); Chi et al. (2025); Kim et al. (2024); Black et al. (2024); Li et al. (2026); Wu et al. (2026) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of real-world manipulation tasks. However, most prior work focuses on tabletop settings, where robots are confined to a fixed workspace. Real-world applications instead require robots to extend their workspace through mobility while continuing to manipulate objects, motivating coordinated whole-body bimanual manipulation Fu et al. (2024). Learning such behaviors requires efficient collection of demonstrations that jointly capture locomotion and manipulation.

Existing approaches to whole-body data collection make different trade-offs in preserving natural human coordination.
Indirect teleoperation methods (e.g., VR-based interfaces Zhu et al. (2022); Rakita et al. (2018); Honerkamp et al. (2025)) provide less direct manipulation control and lack force feedback.
Leader–follower systems (e.g., Mobile ALOHA Fu et al. (2024)) provide more direct manipulation through leader arms and kinesthetic teaching, but the spatial separation between the operator’s hands, viewpoint, and robot end-effectors introduces a perception gap and constrains natural operator mobility.

Retargeting-based approaches (e.g., UMI Chi et al. (2024) and HoMMI Xu et al. (2026)) instead preserve unconstrained human motion by mapping human demonstrations to robot behavior through retargeting or whole-body control.
Taken together, existing approaches balance direct robot control, perception–action alignment, and natural operator mobility in different ways, often emphasizing one property over another.
These trade-offs across perception, manipulation, and mobility are summarized in Tab. 1.

Effective whole-body demonstration requires preserving the robot’s native action constraints and direct physical feedback while aligning the operator’s perception–action space with the robot and preserving the operator’s natural mobility, as illustrated in Fig. 1. We adopt two design principles:
First, the manipulation interface should preserve direct robot control and feedback. We therefore retain the robot arms and use kinesthetic teaching Akgun et al. (2012), keeping the operator close to the end-effectors to reduce the perception gap while preserving direct visual and force feedback.
Second, the mobility interface should preserve the operator’s natural locomotion without requiring control of the mobile base. We therefore remove the mobile base during demonstration, reducing the mobility gap and allowing natural body motion for repositioning.

While these interfaces enable more natural whole-body demonstrations, the resulting human–robot coupling introduces visual and control distribution shifts between demonstration data and autonomous deployment Xu et al. (2026). We identify these discrepancies and introduce a deployment aligned post-processing pipeline that removes demonstrator-induced artifacts from both visual observations and control signals, aligning the collected demonstrations with policy execution.

Together, these design choices improve demonstration efficiency and whole-body coordination. Compared with Mobile ALOHA and VR teleoperation, HALO enables up to 2.9×2.9\times faster demonstration collection while maintaining higher success rates. The resulting policies achieve sub-millimeter manipulation precision and a 73.3% success rate on a six-stage long-horizon mobile manipulation task involving repeated coordinated base and arm motion. These results demonstrate that human-aligned data collection supports efficient, dexterous, and coordinated whole-body policy learning. Our contributions are threefold:

Human-aligned data collection system. We introduce a whole-body bimanual teaching system that aligns the operator’s perception–action space with the robot while preserving natural mobility, enabling efficient collection of coordinated and dexterous mobile manipulation.

Human-aligned data collection system. We introduce a whole-body bimanual teaching system that aligns the operator’s perception–action space with the robot while preserving natural mobility, enabling efficient collection of coordinated and dexterous mobile manipulation.

Deployment-aligned data post-process. We identify and mitigate demonstrator-induced artifacts in visual observations and control, enabling demonstrations collected under tight human–robot coupling to be used for autonomous policy learning.

Systematic real-world evaluation. We evaluate the proposed system in terms of data-collection efficiency and demonstration success, and we further study the effects of different inference strategies as well as the achievable precision and efficiency of the learned policies.

title: VOKE: Visual Object Kinematics Estimator for Dexterous In-Hand Manipulation
authors: Shengjia Zhu,Wenqiang Xu,Lin Shao
comment: . Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA 2027). Project page:this https URL
abstract: Vision-based dexterous in-hand manipulation requires knowing not only where an object is, but also how it moves. However, most robotic manipulation systems rely on off-the-shelf visual perception models whose outputs are limited to static object masks, geometry, or 6D poses, leaving downstream controllers to infer object dynamics implicitly from noisy visual observations. We present VOKE, a kinematics-aware perception framework that augments existing object and hand-object pose estimators to recover a complete object kinematic state comprising pose, linear and angular velocity, and linear and angular acceleration. VOKE contains two core perception modules and a downstream application study. First, a Pluggable Kinematics Module (PKM) attaches to the output of a standard pose estimator and predicts the object’s linear and angular velocity and acceleration from temporal visual features. Second, a Kinematics-guided Pose Refinement Module (KPRM) converts this motion vector into a second-order, motion-prior reference pose and refines the per-frame pose estimates. We evaluate VOKE on DexYCB and OakInk, where it consistently improves object pose estimation across three different backbones and substantially reduces velocity and acceleration estimation error compared with pose differencing. As a downstream application, we use Kinematics-Augmented Reinforcement Learning (KARL) to compare a kinematics-augmented policy with a pose-history baseline. After training the policies in simulation, we transfer the kinematics-augmented policy to the physical robot without policy fine-tuning, demonstrating the complete perception-to-control pathway in the target domain. More results and visualizations are available at https://voke-project.pages.dev/.
introduction:
Estimating an object’s complete kinematic state—its 6D pose together with linear and angular velocity and acceleration—from visual data is a crucial step toward enabling more physically informed robotic manipulation. This is especially true for contact-rich tasks such as dexterous in-hand manipulation, where the object is frequently occluded and its motion changes rapidly. However, this problem is challenging for two main reasons. First, modern pose-estimation and tracking systems typically expose object pose rather than a complete kinematic state [1, 2], leaving downstream modules to infer velocity and acceleration from observation histories. Second, directly computing higher-order derivatives from noisy, image-based pose estimates is difficult because differentiation amplifies measurement noise, particularly for acceleration [3]. We address these challenges with a kinematics-aware perception framework that makes the complete object kinematic state an explicit, first-class output of the visual pipeline.

To improve robustness against occlusion and temporal instability, previous studies have leveraged temporal relationships in videos to refine pose estimates or construct temporally consistent supervision [4, 5]. These methods use motion-related cues without explicitly outputting the object’s complete kinematic state. This valuable physical information is therefore unavailable to downstream control tasks. Our work fills this gap by designing a lightweight, pluggable module that predicts velocity and acceleration directly from temporal visual features and uses these estimates for both pose refinement and policy learning.

Our framework, VOKE (Visual Object Kinematics Estimator), operates on a sequence of RGB(D) hand-object observations, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Its perception core contains two modules. First, a Pluggable Kinematics Module (PKM) attaches to an object or hand-object pose estimator: it shares the image encoder of the base model, aggregates the features of the last kk frames, and regresses the motion vector Vt=(vt,ωt,at,βt)V_{t}=(v_{t},\omega_{t},a_{t},\beta_{t}), containing linear and angular velocity and acceleration. Second, a Kinematics-guided Pose Refinement Module (KPRM) integrates VtV_{t} into a second-order, motion-prior reference pose and refines the per-frame pose with a small MLP-based pose refiner. The refined pose and motion vector jointly form the complete kinematic state Kt=(Pt,fin,Vt)K_{t}=(P_{t,\mathrm{fin}},V_{t}). We further use Kinematics-Augmented Reinforcement Learning (KARL) as a downstream application protocol in which a manipulation policy receives KtK_{t} as part of its observation.

We evaluate VOKE primarily as a perception method. On the DexYCB [6] and OakInk [7] benchmarks, we integrate VOKE into three representative pose estimators (gSDF [8], HFL-Net [9], and HOISDF [10]) and measure object pose and reconstruction quality; we additionally report the accuracy of the predicted velocity and acceleration as a reference baseline for future work on visual object kinematics estimation. As a downstream application, we train a dexterous in-hand cube reorientation policy for a Shadow Dexterous Hand in Isaac Sim. The kinematics-augmented policy converges faster during training. With VOKE-predicted object states, it achieves a higher success rate (78.90% vs. 68.20%) and a lower final rotation error (8.90 vs. 12.75 degrees) than the pose-history baseline. We then deploy the frozen simulation-trained policy on the physical robot, where real-time VOKE predictions replace the simulator object state to form the policy observation and close the perception-to-control loop.

Our contributions are threefold:

A pluggable kinematics module (PKM) that endows existing pose estimators with explicit velocity and acceleration prediction and supports temporally informed pose refinement.

A kinematics-guided pose refinement module (KPRM) that introduces a second-order motion prior between consecutive frames and improves frame-wise pose estimates.

A systematic empirical study on DexYCB, OakInk, and a simulated dexterous in-hand manipulation dataset, including quantitative reference baselines for image-based object velocity/acceleration estimation in hand-object interaction, a simulated study of kinematics-augmented RL (KARL), and real-world deployment in which online VOKE predictions provide object-state inputs to a simulation-trained robot policy.

2. A kinematics-guided pose refinement module (KPRM) that introduces a second-order motion prior between consecutive frames and improves frame-wise pose estimates.

title: BlinkMimic: Training a Humanoid Motion Tracker in Minutes on a Single GPU
authors: Fuyi Chen

introduction:
A humanoid that can follow arbitrary reference motions is a building block for teleoperation, imitation and whole-body skills (Peng et al., 2018; He et al., 2024; Liao et al., 2025). Training such a tracker has been expensive: with on-policy reinforcement learning, a policy for a library of motions takes hours to days on several GPUs (Luo et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2025). SuperMimic (Liao et al., 2026) took a different route. It learns a differentiable world model of the robot from parallel simulation and improves the policy by backpropagation through time (BPTT) in that model, replacing the high-variance policy-gradient estimate with a pathwise one. This cut the cost of training a tracker substantially and made training time a quantity worth optimizing in its own right. InstantTrack (Dao, 2026) then showed in an open implementation that a few changes, an averaged deployed policy, Muon updates (Jordan et al., 2024) and a policy that outputs a correction to the reference, bring training on the 40 LAFAN1 clips (Harvey et al., 2020) down to minutes. Training in minutes changes how such controllers are developed: a change to the reward, the retargeting or the robot model can be tested within the same hour on one workstation.

This paper builds on both and asks how far, and why, this training can be made faster. Our recipe, BlinkMimic, trains one policy for all 40 clips to a strict target, three consecutive checkpoints with a mean return of at least 0.82 and no failed clip, in 3.4 minutes on one RTX 4090 (Figure 1). Recipes like this tend to accumulate changes without a clear account of which ones matter. We organize ours around a simple identity: the time to the target is the cost of an iteration times the number of iterations, and the iterations split into a fit phase, until the mean return reaches 0.82, and a tail phase, until the last failing clips stop failing. The three terms are limited by different things. We assign each ingredient, inherited from SuperMimic and InstantTrack or new, to one of them, and add new ingredients where a term was not yet addressed.

The imagined gradient is accurate over the horizon on which the policy acts, and regression onto a perfect teacher needs no fewer updates than learning from the imagined gradient. What remains is how much each update achieves. Muon updates, here applied to both the policy and the world model, and the residual policy shorten this phase, and we add a step size that starts high and falls once training has progressed.

The last failures occur at a few states that the deployed policy reaches only after minutes of tracking. These states are learnable: the hardest clip trained alone stops failing early, but in the mix the states before its hard spot receive about 1% of the practice, and failure statistics taken during training point at the wrong places. A periodic probe with the deployed policy under deployment conditions finds these states directly.

At these model sizes the GPU often waits for the CPU. We capture the whole iteration, including the MuJoCo-Warp (Google DeepMind and NVIDIA, 2025) physics step and episode resets, as CUDA graphs, and halve the imagination batch, which costs fewer extra iterations than it saves per iteration.

A leave-one-out ablation of the final recipe, with three seeds per ingredient, checks that each ingredient acts on the term it was chosen for. Our contributions are:

BlinkMimic, a single-GPU recipe that trains one policy for 40 LAFAN1 clips in 3.4 minutes, with code and per-seed results (Table 1).

A design organized by where training time goes, with a short analysis for each ingredient: how model error enters the gradient, why the reward favors a residual policy, why the step size should fall, why normalized updates produce a batch knee, and why failure statistics from training misdirect practice (Section 4).

A leave-one-out ablation on a common baseline (Table 2) and measurements that explain it: gradient comparisons between the model and the simulator, a perfect-teacher reference, batch forks with a prediction registered before the run, and attribution tests for the tail (Section 5).

title: I See What You Want: Decoding Hierarchical Operator Intent from Visual Teleoperation History
authors: Xiangyi Jia,Kaixian Qu,Shengzhi Wang,Chenyu Yang,Robert Katzschmann,Marco Hutter
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
