abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) have become a powerful foundation for robotic scene understanding, task planning, and language-conditioned control. A natural question follows: can these models also decode what a human operator intends while teleoperating a robot, without any explicit instruction? We formulate this as hierarchical intent prediction, jointly inferring the ongoing atomic action and the broader mission it serves from a short visual teleoperation history. To study this, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot sources with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission annotations. Large proprietary models struggle with this problem: on held-out episodes, GPT-4o reaches Sentence-BERT similarities of only 0.563 and 0.470 for action and mission, and GPT-5.6 Luna achieves only 0.581 and 0.554. Fine-tuning a VLM on VI AMO yields our Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which raises these scores to 0.825 and 0.821 and still reaches 0.726 and 0.717 on the 35.4% of test actions with both labels absent from training. Finally, as a downstream application, VIM’s predicted mission enables a vision-language-action (VLA) policy to take over from the operator mid-task in a real-world environment unseen during VIM fine-tuning, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna, while cutting intent-prediction latency by roughly 70% on average.
introduction:
Vision-language models (VLMs) have emerged as a key backbone for robotic perception and reasoning. SayCan [1] grounds language plans in learned
affordances, Code as Policies [2] generates executable robot
programs from language, and Inner Monologue [3] closes the
loop with textual feedback. PragmaBot [4] uses visual
feedback and lessons from real-world experience to refine robot task plans.
On the execution side, vision-language-action
(VLA) policies map a language instruction and visual observations directly to
motor
commands [5, 6, 7, 8]. All of these translate human language into robot behavior. We ask the inverse
question: given only the partial visual history of a teleoperated robot, can a VLM
decode what the human operator intends, without an instruction ever being
provided?

Recent work has begun to explore this direction.
VOSA [9] identifies candidate
target objects through detection and segmentation, and
CASPER [10] uses VLM reasoning over teleoperation history to
select a skill–object pair from a predefined library and then executes that
skill. Both represent intent at the level of the current step, as a target object or
position, or as a skill drawn from a predefined library. However, these methods do not explicitly infer the broader mission behind the current action, yet it is what a robot needs in order to
continue: grasping an apple does not by itself reveal whether the apple should
go on a plate, to a person, or into a basket. Progress is further limited by data: existing
demonstration
corpora [11, 12, 13]
mainly provide episode-level instructions, while existing intermediate supervision is either synthetically generated from task instructions [14], or annotated at the primitive-skill level [15], rather than providing temporally aligned action–mission supervision for instruction-free intent inference.

We therefore model operator intent as a hierarchy. The ongoing
action (OA) is the atomic manipulation step currently being performed, such
as “pick up the apple,” and the ongoing mission (OM) is the
immediate goal it serves, such as “put the apple on the plate.” Both are expressed as open-vocabulary natural language, so the predicted
mission can serve as the instruction of a language-conditioned policy without
a fixed skill library. The difficulty is that a useful prediction must
arrive early: at handoff time only part of the action has been observed, so
the model must commit from a few frames and a short record of what has
already been completed.

To study this problem, we introduce VI AMO (Vision Intention Action and
Mission Ongoing), a dataset of 6,600 episodes from eleven robot source
families with 13,653 temporally aligned action annotations and 9,702 mission
annotations. Without task-specific training, even
strong proprietary models fall short in predicting the ongoing mission: GPT-4o and GPT-5.6 Luna reach mission Sentence-BERT (SBERT) similarities of only 0.470 and 0.554. Fine-tuning an open-source VLM on VI AMO yields the
Vision-Intention Model (VIM), which outperforms the two proprietary VLMs, two robotics-specialized foundation models, and its untuned backbone across different evaluation metrics, achieving a mission SBERT similarity of 0.821 compared with at most 0.564 for the baselines.
On the 35.4% of test actions whose action and mission labels are both unseen during training, VIM achieves 27.2% higher action SBERT and 27.1% higher mission SBERT than the strongest baseline for both action and mission prediction.

Finally, we test the utility of the inferred mission in shared autonomy, where
a robot continues a task that the operator
began [16, 17]. VIM’s predicted mission conditions a VLA policy that takes over mid-task and completes the remaining manipulation in real-world scenarios unseen during VIM fine-tuning. With five trials per task for each
VLM condition, VIM reduces human teleoperation time by 34.6%
relative to GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna. Each intent prediction takes approximately 0.7 s on a consumer GPU, compared with 1.9–3.5 s for the API-based baselines.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We formulate hierarchical intent prediction from visual
teleoperation history, jointly predicting the ongoing action and the
mission it serves as open-vocabulary language, and introduce VI AMO, a
dataset of 6,600 episodes with aligned action–mission annotations to
train and evaluate it.

We present VIM, a VLM fine-tuned on VI AMO that outperforms GPT-4o,
GPT-5.6 Luna, two embodied foundation models, and its untuned backbone on
different metrics, reaching 0.825 and 0.821 Sentence-BERT similarity for action and
mission on the VI AMO test set versus at most 0.581 and 0.564 for the best
baseline.

We evaluate VIM as the intent module of a shared-autonomy system
across five real-world tasks in scenarios unseen during VIM fine-tuning.
Its predicted missions serve as language instructions for a VLA
policy, reducing human teleoperation time by 34.6% relative to
GPT-4o and 39.8% relative to GPT-5.6 Luna.

1. We formulate hierarchical intent prediction from visual
teleoperation history, jointly predicting the ongoing action and the
mission it serves as open-vocabulary language, and introduce VI AMO, a
dataset of 6,600 episodes with aligned action–mission annotations to
train and evaluate it.

2. We present VIM, a VLM fine-tuned on VI AMO that outperforms GPT-4o,
GPT-5.6 Luna, two embodied foundation models, and its untuned backbone on
different metrics, reaching 0.825 and 0.821 Sentence-BERT similarity for action and

title: Remember What Changes the Odds: Critic-Gated Event Memory for Long-Horizon Manipulation
authors: Xuanzhuo Liu,Chuankang Li,Maoqing Yao,Guanghui Ren
abstract:
In long-horizon manipulation, a robot may need to take different actions under identical observations, depending on task progress and the outcomes of earlier attempts.
We refer to this ambiguity as decision aliasing.
Resolving it requires the policy to maintain memory of its execution history.
To reduce the cost of processing full observation histories, recent methods build compact event memories using perceptual, semantic, or kinematic cues.
However, these criteria may miss events that matter for task success.
We instead propose an outcome-grounded principle: remember events that substantially change the predicted probability of eventual success.
Following this principle, we introduce CGEM, a critic-gated event memory that uses a critic to select events with large estimated changes in success probability.
Positive and negative changes are encoded as progress and failure records, respectively.
Failure records are discarded once the corresponding subtask is completed.
In a ten-subtask diagnostic environment with exactly computed success probabilities, CGEM achieves 88.0%88.0\% success, compared with 0.0%0.0\% for both a 36-step observation window and a kinematic event memory.
Removing failure records reduces success to 1.7%1.7\%.
introduction:
Consider a robot at its home pose beside a button (Fig. 1a). The current observation may look the same before a press, after a recoverable failure, and after a successful press. Yet these situations call for different action strategies: attempt the press, retry, or advance to the next subtask. We call this ambiguity decision aliasing. Reactive policies based on robot foundation models [4, 3] generate actions from current observations and language instructions. When these inputs are identical, the policy cannot distinguish whether an interaction remains untried, has failed, or has succeeded.

Resolving decision aliasing therefore requires the policy to maintain a memory of its execution history. To reduce the cost of processing full observation histories, recent methods build compact memories around key events selected using perceptual, semantic, or kinematic cues [14, 10, 12, 13]. However, these cues may miss events that matter for task success. A large arm motion may be easy to detect without changing what the robot should do next. A failed contact may leave no lasting visual trace but require a different retry strategy. Selecting events for memory therefore requires more than detecting changes in appearance or motion.

To decide what to remember, we seek a signal that reflects what each event reveals about the likelihood of completing the task. Learned value estimates provide information about task progress or expected return [5, 6, 2]. We use a critic’s prediction of eventual success to obtain such a signal for memory selection. A substantial change in this prediction indicates that an event has provided new information about the estimated chance of task success. This leads to our outcome-grounded principle: remember events that substantially change the predicted probability of eventual success.

Following this principle, we introduce CGEM (Critic-Gated Event Memory), which uses a critic to select events with large estimated changes in success probability (Fig. 1b). Positive and negative changes are stored as progress and failure records, respectively. These records track which subtasks have been completed and which strategies have failed. Retaining failure records allows the policy to distinguish an untried subtask from a failed attempt and adjust its retry strategy. After subtask completion, obsolete failure records are discarded.
Theoretically, under a fixed reference policy and threshold, we establish a horizon-independent bound on the expected number of large changes in conditional success probability, motivating sparse event selection. We also characterize when event records preserve the information needed for subsequent decisions.

We evaluate this mechanism in an exact-value diagnostic that isolates the effects of event selection, failure records, and consolidation. We also analyze whether learned critics on real robot data provide reliable event-detection signals and outline a proposed integration with π0.5\pi_{0.5} (Fig. 1b).

Contributions.
(i) Theoretically, we show that the expected number of large changes in success probability has a bound independent of task length, motivating sparse event memory.
(ii) We introduce CGEM, a critic-gated memory of progress and failure events, and propose an architecture that integrates it with π0.5\pi_{0.5}.
(iii) We evaluate CGEM and its ablations in an exact-value diagnostic and assess learned critics for event detection on real robot data.

title: ManiLadder: Benchmarking Robot Manipulation Through a Categorized and Multi-Difficulty Level Task Ladder
authors: Chongkai Gao,Jieao Shi,Zhaoyu Mu,Yudi Lin,Xuanwei Liu,Wei Ken Ng,Baiye Cheng,Anqi Chen,Kerun Liu,Zhuoran Li,Xuchuan Huang,Haoyang Li,Shengjia Zhu,Nga Teng Chan,Yuxuan Zhang,Xingyu Chen,Lin Shao
abstract: Recent advances in robotic manipulation have enabled increasingly complex and dexterous behaviors, yet existing benchmarks still focus on simple pick-and-place tasks and lack a systematic framework for measuring progress in robot learning along the axis of task difficulty. We present ManiLadder, a large-scale and organized simulation benchmark for robotic manipulation. ManiLadder contains 112 carefully designed tasks stratified into 4 difficulty levels, with 8 categories in each level, spanning rigid-body and deformable-object manipulation, single-arm and dual-arm settings, and gripper and dexterous-hand end-effectors. To calibrate difficulty, we fix the data amount the same for every task and use a unified flow-matching imitation learning policy under the same training and evaluation protocols, then use its evaluation success rate as an operational empirical difficulty signal. All tasks are iteratively refined until they fall into target difficulty ranges, which are then verified across different random seeds, policies, and agentic learning systems. We further analyze the task properties, compare different policy performances and training settings, analyze task transfer and data scaling behaviors, and conduct real-world experiments showing that the designed tasks preserve their difficulty ordering beyond simulation. ManiLadder provides a calibrated ladder for measuring, comparing, and advancing robotic manipulation capabilities. More results are on https://maniladder-benchmark.github.io/.
introduction:
Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in robotic manipulation, driven by increasingly accessible hardware [12, 13], large-scale datasets [14, 15], powerful foundation models [16], effective learning algorithms [17], and agentic learning systems [18]. Robots can now perform highly complex real-world tasks such as scrambling eggs [19], tying plastic bags [20], and cardboard box folding [21]. However, current benchmarks in robotic manipulation lag considerably behind this huge progress: most existing robotic simulation benchmarks [9, 7, 8] primarily expand task diversity horizontally, by recombining relatively simple manipulation skills across different scenes and objects, such as pick-and-place, pushing, and door opening. While they are useful for evaluating generalization or semantic reasoning, they offer limited resolution for measuring the vertical growth of manipulation capability, i.e., they cannot reveal whether a model has truly expanded the frontier of solvable manipulation tasks. We therefore ask a capability-oriented question: what level of manipulation difficulty can a model reliably solve? Answering this requires a benchmark organized by calibrated difficulty levels, so that the capability boundaries of current methods can be measured directly.

Building such a benchmark raises two challenges: (1) how to determine task difficulty, and (2) how to construct diverse tasks with well-calibrated difficulty. Prior works characterize difficulty through theoretical measures [22], subskill composition [23], manually defined predicates [24], or contact patterns [25], but these abstractions are difficult to scale to diverse modern manipulation tasks. Instead, we adopt an empirical definition: under a standardized training protocol, what success rate can a robot learning algorithm achieve on the task? This becomes increasingly practical as modern imitation learning methods [26, 12] perform effectively across a broad range of tasks. Meanwhile, although modern simulators and procedural generation tools [11, 4] simplify task creation, they do not guarantee task difficulty. Initialization ranges, perception complexity, and object geometry can make tasks unintentionally too easy or too hard. Constructing a meaningful difficulty ladder therefore requires iterative, metric-driven task calibration.

In this work, we present ManiLadder, a large-scale simulation benchmark that evaluates robotic manipulation along two complementary axes: calibrated task difficulty and manipulation diversity, as shown in Figure . ManiLadder contains 112 carefully designed tasks across 4 difficulty levels, organized by object properties, robot embodiments, and manipulation skills. The tasks cover both rigid-body and deformable-object manipulation, spanning four embodiment types: single-arm grippers, single-arm dexterous hands, dual-arm grippers, and dual-arm dexterous hands. Within each task suite, we further cover disparate manipulation skills or object types, resulting in 3 to 4 concrete tasks per suite. For example, in each deformable-object manipulation suite, we design tasks targeting 1D (e.g., rope), 2D (e.g., cloth), and 3D (e.g., clay) deformable object types, respectively. To stratify task difficulty, we provide a fixed number of demonstrations for every task and train a unified flow-matching [26] imitation learning policy under a standardized protocol, using its evaluation success rate as an empirical difficulty signal. We then iteratively calibrate each task to the desired difficulty range by adjusting interpretable factors such as object geometry, initial randomization, perceptual difficulty, temporal coordination, and error tolerance. The calibrated task difficulties are then verified across demonstration recollection, retraining, different policies, and agentic learning systems. Building on these calibrated difficulty levels, we establish standardized benchmarking protocols and an Attained Level metric to quantify the highest task difficulty level a given algorithm can reliably solve. This makes ManiLadder not only broad in task coverage but also explicitly calibrated as a ladder of manipulation difficulty.

To highlight the flexibility and potential of ManiLadder for studying manipulation capability across different dimensions, we conduct a set of studies, including: 1) analyzing the task properties across different levels; 2) comparing small and large VLA models [16] on ManiLadder; 3) studying the multi-task training results compared to single-task training results; 4) studying task transfer ability and data scaling behaviors across different task families; 5) examining whether the difficulty ordering calibrated in simulation is preserved between simulation and real-world settings. Together, ManiLadder provides a platform for studying many future questions in robot learning, and also provides a calibrated and organized difficulty ladder that measures how far robotic manipulation has climbed toward general-purpose manipulation intelligence, and how far it still has to go.

title: MotionSkill: From Bipedal Motion Video to Control across Embodiments
authors: Philip Niu,Xiaofeng Han,Sylvie Pan,Yang Wang
comment: . Fortune AI technical report
abstract: Reusing a demonstrated gait can reduce the work of specifying the same motion for each biped. A video captures the timing of a step, but each robot must execute it with its own limbs and actuators. MotionSkill recovers a timed reference once from monocular video and adapts it to each target in simulation. It aligns root motion and body landmarks in a common frame and records which landmarks are available at each instant. At each source timestamp, the mapper preserves limb directions, uses the target segment lengths, and solves inverse kinematics under joint limits and closure constraints. In MuJoCo, we train a separate residual policy for each of ten bipeds on its mapped reference from one four-second walking clip. Each policy uses the measured robot state to correct joint commands during contact. From initial states held out during training, MotionSkill completed 98% of trials on the original video and 26% with the upper body occluded for one second.
introduction:
A video shows a person shifting weight and advancing one foot. A compact biped and a robot with longer legs or a closed knee linkage need different joint trajectories for that step. Both can use the directions of the limbs and the order and timing of foot motion.

In MotionSkill, a skill is the timed motion reference recovered once from a demonstration. To deploy it on another body, we reuse the same samples and timestamps, map them to that robot, and train its feedback policy. Limb directions specify what to match. Segment lengths and joint constraints determine the target pose at each instant. Physical contact and feedback determine when the robot actually reaches it.

We use one filmed walk across ten robots. Nine complete all five trials on the original input, and the tenth completes four. With the upper body masked for part of the clip, we measure how many robots receive a feasible joint trajectory and how many trials reach the end of that trajectory. A longer recorded walk tests repeated stepping, and a change in source cadence tests how closely the feet follow the demonstrated rhythm.

The work makes three contributions.

A timed representation of root motion, landmark geometry, and point availability that can be recovered once per video and reused across target bodies.

A mapping and control procedure that preserves native segment lengths and closure constraints and uses reference conditioned joint residuals to track the motion in simulation.

Paired video trials that measure mapping feasibility and execution on ten bipeds, and a cadence experiment that measures foot timing on four robots using their pretrained locomotion controllers.

1. A timed representation of root motion, landmark geometry, and point availability that can be recovered once per video and reused across target bodies.

2. A mapping and control procedure that preserves native segment lengths and closure constraints and uses reference conditioned joint residuals to track the motion in simulation.

3. Paired video trials that measure mapping feasibility and execution on ten bipeds, and a cadence experiment that measures foot timing on four robots using their pretrained locomotion controllers.

title: Memory-Efficient Parallel Policy Learning for Collapse-Reactive Retreat via Hybrid Terrain Modeling
authors: Yuki Kadokawa,Ritsuki Matsunaga,Yuqi Yang,Edgar Anarossi,Takamitsu Matsubara
comment: under review
abstract: Robots deployed at disaster sites and on unstable slopes may cross ground that gives way only after it is touched, so that cameras or prior inspection cannot reveal the hazard. This paper presents a way to train, in simulation, a single control policy for a wheeled quadruped that drives normally and, when a wheel loses support, keeps its balance and backs out to firm ground using only its onboard joint and inertial measurements. Training such a policy requires thousands of simulated robots that each experience their own ground collapse. Giving every robot its own copy of a collapsible terrain model quickly exhausts GPU memory, whereas letting the robots share one model allows a collapse caused by one robot to affect the others. Our framework instead represents the collapsible ground by computed contact forces that depend on a small collapse state kept for each robot, while the rest of the terrain is simulated as usual. On a single GPU, this supported over 100 times as many simulated robots as fine rigid-block terrain and reached a converged policy more than 50 times faster, and the trained policy worked without additional training on a real robot in four constructed collapse scenarios. New types of collapse can be added by defining their state and update rules, without building new terrain geometry. Because the policy relies only on proprioception, it may mistake a traversable downward step for a collapse; where such steps are common, combining it with terrain sensing is advisable.
introduction:
Disaster sites and unstable slopes may contain terrain that subsides or collapses under robot contact, altering support conditions for subsequent contacts [1, 2]. For legged robots, including wheeled-legged systems, localized loss of support can disturb posture and cause falls [3, 4, 5, 6]. Collapse risks may not be apparent from visual cues before traversal and may emerge only after contact [7, 8]. This paper therefore aims to learn a policy for a wheeled quadruped without prior terrain inspection or exteroceptive detection of hazardous regions. Using only proprioceptive observations, the policy performs normal locomotion, responds to collapse-induced posture disturbances and support loss, and retreats to non-collapsible terrain (Fig. 1, top).

Reinforcement learning (RL) is a promising approach to acquiring such a policy by optimizing it with samples from diverse robot–terrain interactions [16, 11, 17, 18]. To collect samples efficiently, massively parallel RL is widely used for locomotion-policy learning, simulating many robots simultaneously [19, 20, 21]. For fixed terrain, multiple robots can share a single terrain model within the same simulation space while maintaining independent experiences by disabling direct robot–robot interactions [19]. Because contact does not alter fixed terrain, one robot cannot change the terrain conditions experienced by others. This sharing avoids per-robot terrain duplication, reducing memory consumption and the computational load on the physics engine.

However, this terrain-sharing approach cannot be directly applied when robot contact changes the terrain state (i.e., its shape and support conditions). Although rigid bodies can simulate ground collapse [12], sharing changing terrain causes a region collapsed by one robot to affect the contact conditions and motion of others, even when direct robot–robot interactions are disabled. We refer to this terrain-mediated effect as indirect interference (Fig. 1, bottom). Assigning independent changing terrain to each robot prevents this interference but requires duplicating terrain objects, i.e., the simulated bodies and colliders that represent the terrain, across parallel environments [12, 22, 23]. Finer terrain discretization further increases the number of terrain objects and memory requirements, limiting the number of environments that can run simultaneously [23]. Thus, the challenge is to achieve computationally efficient parallel policy learning while ensuring that the state–action experiences needed to learn collapse-reactive retreat are generated without indirect interference.

Our key insight is that, although ground collapse can be simulated using rigid bodies, explicitly modeling the collapsing terrain as rigid bodies is not necessarily required for policy learning. The goal is not to reproduce collapse processes in detail, but to efficiently generate the state–action experiences needed to learn collapse-reactive retreat. We therefore represent collapse through changes in contact responses, particularly support loss and contact forces.

Based on this insight, we propose a memory-efficient parallel policy-learning framework for collapse-reactive retreat via hybrid terrain modeling. The framework adopts hybrid terrain modeling, which combines rigid-body simulation of the robot and non-collapsible terrain with virtual contact forces for collapsible regions, eliminating the need for terrain objects in these regions. To enable independent robot–terrain interactions within this hybrid approach, we introduce a State-Multiplexed Contact Model (SMCM) that 1) shares reference terrain geometry and a contact-response law across parallel environments, 2) maintains independent collapse states, and 3) computes virtual contact forces according to these states. This allows each robot to experience support loss, subsidence, and lateral slip without indirect interference. Using this environment, we train a proprioceptive policy for both normal locomotion and collapse-reactive retreat through massively parallel RL. Simulation experiments show that the framework supports over 100 times as many parallel environments as fine-resolution rigid-block terrain within the same GPU memory limit. This scalability speeds up sample collection and, together with improved sample efficiency, enables over 50 times faster policy convergence with comparable retreat performance. Sim-to-sim and real-robot experiments further demonstrate successful retreat under multiple tested collapse conditions.

title: Alloy: A Multi-Material Physics Engine for Robot Learning
authors: Pranay Gupta,Deepanshu Rohilla
comment: . Code:this https URL
abstract:
Robots handle much more than rigid objects: towels, cables, water, sand. The simulators used to train robots at
scale are strongest on rigid bodies, and adding another material usually means a second engine and hand-written
glue between the two. We present Alloy, an open-source physics engine for robot learning in which rigid robots,
cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft bodies share one scene. Each object is described once; Alloy
assigns it to a solver suited to its material, couples the solvers inside every control step, and runs the scene
in many parallel worlds on one GPU, or on a CPU. Every world carries
a health grade, to help tell a failure of the physics from a failure of the policy. Alloy is built on Newton, MuJoCo Warp and Warp, and it is
written to be driven by coding agents: its documentation ships inside the package, every error names its fix, and
the engine is exposed as tools over the Model Context Protocol. In a cold test, agents that had never seen Alloy installed a pre-release from the package index and trained policies for walking, cable handling and pouring on a single GPU.
We also report how throughput grows with the number of worlds, depth-camera throughput, agreement with closed-form
references, and a reliability test over a thousand worlds.
introduction:
Much of what a useful robot must do involves things that are not rigid. A kitchen robot pours and wipes. A factory
robot routes cables and seats connectors. A laundry robot folds. Learning these skills in simulation needs two
things at once. The first is physics for each material: cloth that drapes, liquid that flows, cables that bend. The
second is scale: reinforcement learning tries a task millions of times, so the simulation has to run in thousands
of copies at once and stay correct in every one.

Today these two needs pull apart. Engines built for robot learning at scale are at their best with rigid bodies.
Solvers for cloth, liquids or granular material often come as separate programs with their own scene
descriptions. A team that wants a robot arm to pour water often writes its own bridge between a rigid-body
engine and a liquid solver, chooses time steps by hand, and builds its own checks for worlds that have quietly
gone wrong.

There is also a new kind of user. More and more simulation code is written by coding agents, which read
documentation, write a scene, run it and read the errors. An engine that agents can use well needs short
documentation that travels with the package, errors that say what to change, and a way to tell a broken simulation
from a bad policy.

Alloy is our answer to these three problems. Its contributions are:

One scene for many materials. Rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft
bodies are added through one Python interface. A router assigns each object to a solver suited to it and
records why (Section 3.2).

Coupling inside every control step. Solvers exchange poses and contact forces through proxy bodies,
with step sizes chosen from the stiffness of the interface and refined per world when needed
(Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

A health grade for every world. Each parallel world is graded OK, DEGRADED or
INVALID; an invalid world is frozen while the others continue (Section 3.5).

An interface made for coding agents. Documentation inside the package, errors that carry their fix,
a command-line tool that speaks JSON, and a tool server for the Model Context Protocol
(Section 3.7).

Evidence from cold users. Agents that had never seen Alloy installed it and trained policies on a
single GPU; we report those results with their protocol, together with scaling, camera, accuracy and reliability
measurements (Section 4).

1. One scene for many materials. Rigid robots, cloth, cables, liquids, granular material and soft
bodies are added through one Python interface. A router assigns each object to a solver suited to it and
records why (Section 3.2).

2. Coupling inside every control step. Solvers exchange poses and contact forces through proxy bodies,
with step sizes chosen from the stiffness of the interface and refined per world when needed
(Sections 3.3 and 3.4).

3. A health grade for every world. Each parallel world is graded OK, DEGRADED or
INVALID; an invalid world is frozen while the others continue (Section 3.5).

4. An interface made for coding agents. Documentation inside the package, errors that carry their fix,
a command-line tool that speaks JSON, and a tool server for the Model Context Protocol
(Section 3.7).

5. Evidence from cold users. Agents that had never seen Alloy installed it and trained policies on a
single GPU; we report those results with their protocol, together with scaling, camera, accuracy and reliability
measurements (Section 4).

title: Hibikino-Musashi@Home 2026 Team Description Paper
authors: Soma Fumoto,Ryohei Kobayashi,Taiki Watanabe,Yuga Yano,Akinobu Mizutani,Naoki Yamaguchi,Ryo Terashima,Ryusei Sakakibara,Kazuma Futami,Keita Okumura,Kosei Isomoto,Koshun Arimura,Yuta Ohno,Tomoaki Fujino,Sojiro Shimada,Yuichiro Tanaka,Takeshi Nishida,Hakaru Tamukoh
abstract:
This paper presents an overview of the integrated technologies developed for the Open Platform League at RoboCup@Home 2026 in Incheon.
A vision system integrated with learning-based, training-free models enables robust object recognition for both known and unknown objects.
We introduce a RoomPlan-based method that semi-automatically registers furniture geometry and labels to generate semantic maps.
Additionally, a large language model-based planner interprets the instructions recognized by Whisper and generates primitive skill sequences for execution.
A reservoir-computing framework serves as a lightweight temporal-processing model for action recognition. Its field-programmable gate array-based implementation enables low-power, real-time operation.
This is key to removing operational time constraints for service robots.
Open-source releases, including task environments, dataset tools, and navigation frameworks, enhance reproducibility, reuse, and continuous progress within the RoboCup@Home community.
introduction:
Hibikino-Musashi@Home (HMA) is a robot development team composed of students from the Kyushu Institute of Technology and University of Kitakyushu in Japan.
The team was founded in 2010 and has consistently participated in the RoboCup@Home and RoboCup JapanOpen @Home Leagues.
In addition to RoboCup, the team participated in the World Robot Challenge 2018 and 2020 in the service robotics category of the Partner Robot Challenge (real space), as well as the World Robot Summit 2025 Future Convenience Store Challenge.

HMA addresses various challenges in realising service robots capable of working in real-world environments.
First, in environments containing diverse objects, robots must adapt to a wide variety of items and appearances.
We use two methods for object recognition, You Only Look Once 11 (YOLO11) trained by our custom dataset, and training-free models such as Grounding-DINO, NanoSAM, and Cutie.
Second, in household environments, service robots must understand the surrounding 3D space to perform tasks appropriately.
We developed an automated system using a smartphone for constructing semantic maps.
Third, the tasks a robot must perform in household environments change with the situation and the user’s instructions.
We developed a dynamic task planning system based on a large language model (LLM).
Finally, high power consumption is a bottleneck for long-term operation required for practical service robots.
We introduced a system with reservoir computing (RC) implemented on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA) to achieve low power consumption.

By integrating these components, our goal is to build a service robot system that can robustly handle various environments and tasks.

title: Robot Navigation and Obstacle Avoidance from Randomly Positioned External Cameras
authors: Raul Steinmetz,Jair Augusto Bottega,Ayanori Yorozu,Akihisa Ohya
comment: accepted as a regular paper for the 2027 IEEE/SICE International Symposium on System Integration
abstract: We study robot navigation in indoor environments from fixed exocentric cameras (infrastructure-mounted, external to the robot). We show that standard Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), which succeeds with onboard cameras, fails to learn this navigation end-to-end in our setup. This failure results from the perspective mismatch between exocentric observations and egocentric action and goal formulations, which is too complex to resolve from the reward signal alone. To address this, we propose Viewpoint-Invariant Navigation from Exocentric Cameras (VINE). VINE uses an obstacle map estimation network, trained with supervised learning, that takes exocentric images, camera pose, robot pose, and room dimensions as input and produces a viewpoint-invariant obstacle map. This map can be used either by a PPO policy or by a planner such as A*. VINE’s map estimation performs better than perspective mapping approaches, handles cameras placed across a wide range of positions and orientations without view-specific tuning, requires only approximate camera pose estimates (noise with a standard deviation of 30 cm per axis in xx, yy, and zz and about 20∘ of rotation error on average), is robust to intrinsic variation, and extends to two-camera setups with partial coverage. Despite operating from cameras randomized in position during evaluation, VINE surpasses the navigation success rate of PPO with an onboard camera in simulated environments.
introduction:
Navigation is a fundamental capability for autonomous mobile robots. Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) has emerged as a prominent approach for learning navigation policies directly from raw sensor data, yet nearly all prior work focuses on policies that act on onboard sensors, such as cameras and LiDAR mounted on the robot [1]. Learning to navigate from exocentric cameras, mounted in the environment rather than on the robot, remains largely unexplored, despite such sensors being ubiquitous in indoor environments. These cameras offer concrete advantages over onboard sensors for robot navigation, since their wider, sometimes global point of view can give instant information about the layout of a room, which onboard sensors would need multiple observations from different robot positions to recover, and they can be connected directly to power, avoiding drain on the robot’s battery.

Human intuition suggests that navigating a robot from an exocentric viewpoint should be straightforward, as we can easily reason about spatial layouts from a third-person perspective and teleoperate robots from overhead views, but this intuition does not transfer to reinforcement learning within our setup. We find that PPO [2], which achieves near-perfect PointGoal navigation from onboard sensors [3], fails to learn navigation from exocentric images. The failure results from the perspective mismatch between the images, which are mostly agnostic to the robot’s position and heading, and the egocentric actions and goal of DRL-based navigation, a mapping that proves intractable to resolve from the reward signal alone within our training budget and leaves the policy unable to reliably avoid obstacles.

Based on the findings about PPO, we present VINE, an agent composed of a supervised-learned neural network that estimates obstacle maps from exocentric camera images and a controller, either a navigation policy trained with PPO or a planner such as A*, that drives the robot towards a point goal using the estimated map. Our agent can navigate using cameras placed within wide ranges of positions without view-specific tuning, does not require intrinsics, and needs only an approximate camera pose, along with the robot pose and room dimensions. The obstacle map estimation network extends to setups where two cameras with partial views are used, and in all our comparisons it outperforms perspective mapping approaches. Despite operating from cameras randomized in position during evaluation, VINE surpasses the navigation success rate of PPO with an onboard camera.

title: Direct-Ink-Writing of Soft Thin Film Force-Sensitive Resistors with Velostat and Printed-Carbon Sensing Elements
authors: Mostafa Mo. Massoud,Paulo H.T.F Alves,Timothy Kennedy,Jacqueline Libby
comment: to be published in: IEEE Sensors
abstract: Flexible resistive force sensors are useful for wearable, rehabilitation, and human–machine interfaces, but their performance depends on sensing-material architecture and fabrication. This work presents a parameterized Voltera NOVA-based direct-ink-writing workflow using printed silver electrodes with multilayer Velostat sensing elements on PET and TPU substrates, together with an exploratory fully printed carbon architecture. Velostat sensors containing 1, 2, 4, and 6 sensing layers exhibited strongly nonlinear force–voltage responses, with the greatest sensitivity at low forces. Best-fit straight-line R2R^{2} values ranged from 0.475 to 0.641, area-based hysteresis from 3.90% to 7.47%, and 5-min voltage drift from 1.9% to 7.3%, with no consistent monotonic relationship between layer count and these metrics. Selected PET6 and TPU6 devices showed less than 0.05 V change in peak output between the first and final 100 cycles of a 10,000-cycle test. Printed-carbon devices demonstrated the feasibility of a more fully printed architecture, but configurations with six or fewer layers saturated below approximately 0.5 N or were nonfunctional, while the eight-layer device responded primarily below approximately 2 N. These results establish the feasibility of the printed-electrode Velostat workflow while identifying printed sensing materials as a key area for further development.
introduction:
Flexible force sensors are important in wearable systems, rehabilitation devices, soft robotics, and human–machine interfaces because they enable contact loads to be measured at curved, compliant, or moving interfaces [1, 2]. Recent developments in flexible bioelectronics and wearable
sensing further emphasize the importance of mechanically compliant materials and flexible electronic platforms for stable,
human-compatible sensing interfaces [3, 4]. In this paper, force denotes the total normal load transmitted through the sensing region, whereas pressure denotes force normalized by a defined contact area. Because the devices developed here are calibrated directly against an applied force rather than an area-normalized or spatially distributed pressure, they are referred to throughout as force sensors.

Flexible force sensors can employ piezoresistive, piezoelectric, capacitive, optical, triboelectric, or magnetic transduction [1, 2]. This study focuses on piezoresistive sensing because changes in electrical resistance can be measured under both static and cyclic loading using a comparatively simple voltage-divider circuit. In a piezoresistive sensor, mechanical deformation, changes in conductive pathways, or changes in interfacial contact alter the resistance of the sensing element, which is converted to an output voltage by the readout circuit. Piezoresistive architectures can be inexpensive and mechanically compliant, but their performance may be affected by nonlinear response, hysteresis, time-dependent drift, and variability associated with the sensing material, electrode contact, and assembly conditions [5, 6].

Force-sensor performance must be evaluated under defined mechanical, electrical, environmental, and temporal conditions. The principal quantities considered in this study are sensitivity, calibration nonlinearity, hysteresis, drift, response time, and cyclic stability. Sensitivity is the change in a specified sensor indication relative to the corresponding change in force, whereas hysteresis is the difference between loading and unloading outputs at the same applied force. Drift describes a time-dependent change in output under a constant load. Cyclic stability describes changes in performance following prolonged repeated loading made under the same conditions. The settling criterion used to calculate response time must also be stated explicitly [7, 8, 6].

Flexible force sensors can be fabricated using microfabrication, screen printing, inkjet printing, coating and lamination, vision-based systems, molding, and digitally controlled direct-write processes [9, 10, 11, 12, 13]. Microfabrication can provide high feature resolution and mature batch processing but generally requires substantial equipment and process infrastructure. Screen printing is well suited to repeated, high-throughput deposition but normally requires a dedicated screen for each pattern. Inkjet printing is maskless and material-efficient but imposes strict requirements on ink viscosity, particle size, surface tension, wetting, and nozzle operation.
Direct ink writing is an established extrusion-based process in which a digitally defined toolpath is used to deposit functional inks without a patterned mask [14, 15]. DIW can accommodate comparatively viscous inks and facilitate design changes and multilayer deposition, although its performance depends on ink rheology, nozzle dimensions, wetting, layer registration, curing, and interlayer adhesion [12, 16, 17, 15].
Vision-based systems provide spatial maps of contact shape and indentation depth, but their camera, lighting, and calibrated image processing imply a bulkier system that is harder to integrate into thin, conformable devices [13].
In the present work, DIW is used to print conductive electrodes and, for the printed-carbon architecture, the sensing layers.

Direct printing and DIW have previously been applied to tactile and force- or pressure-sensitive devices. Vatani et al. [18] fabricated compliant multilayer piezoresistive tactile sensors through a hybrid DIW/stereolithography process. Van Dommelen et al. [19] reported fully 3D-printed mechanical pressure sensors based on multiple sensing mechanisms, and Baghini et al. [20] directly wrote graphite-based soft piezoresistive pressure sensors. These studies preclude a claim that the present device is the first force sensor fabricated using any DIW process. The contribution of the present study should instead be framed around its Voltera NOVA-based fabrication workflow (rather than a more expensive bioprinting process), parameterized geometry, selected commercial materials, and comparative characterization of the resulting force sensors.

Velostat is a carbon-loaded polyethylene sheet whose electrical resistance changes under compression and has been widely used in low-cost resistive force sensors [21, 22, 23, 24]. Its device-level behavior is influenced by electrode contact, preload, geometry, material relaxation, and loading history, which can result in nonlinear response, hysteresis, and drift. Bartunek et al. [25] evaluated sensors containing 1, 3, 4, 5, 10, 20, and 30 Velostat layers and found that multilayer designs reduced force-estimation error relative to a one-layer design and a commercial force-sensing resistor under static, cyclic, and finger-loading evaluations. However, that study focused primarily on measurement error and did not comprehensively examine hysteresis, time-dependent output, response behavior, high-cycle stability, or PET-versus-TPU substrate effects within a common printed-electrode architecture. These remaining questions motivate the multilayer Velostat investigation in the present study.

Printed carbon composites can exhibit piezoresistive behavior, but their performance depends on conductive-filler concentration, matrix properties, microstructure, rheology, curing, and printed geometry. Recent DIW work using MWCNT/PDMS nanocomposite inks illustrates that printability and electromechanical response must be optimized together when developing a pressure- or force-sensitive material [26]. In contrast, ACI SC1502, the carbon material used in this study, is marketed as a stretchable carbon conductor for printed circuitry rather than as a purpose-designed force-sensing ink [27]. The printed-carbon device is therefore evaluated here as an exploratory test of whether stacked conductor prints can produce a reproducible force-dependent resistance response within the proposed architecture.

Based on the preceding literature, the unresolved question is not whether
DIW can be used to fabricate force-sensitive devices, but how the proposed
Voltera NOVA-based workflow performs with the selected sensing materials,
layer arrangements, and substrates. This study addresses three research
questions: (1) How does increasing the number of Velostat layers from one
to six affect the force-dependent response and selected performance measures
of sensors with printed electrodes? (2) How does replacing a PET substrate
with TPU affect the response of otherwise comparable multilayer Velostat
sensors? (3) Can a more fully printed force-sensor architecture, in which
both the conductive electrodes and sensing element are fabricated using the
Voltera NOVA, produce a measurable force-dependent response using a
commercial printed-carbon conductor?

To address these questions, this paper: (1) describes a parameterized
CAD-to-DIW and assembly workflow for flexible resistive force sensors;
(2) characterizes Velostat sensors containing 1, 2, 4, and 6 sensing layers
on PET and TPU substrates; (3) evaluates an exploratory printed-carbon
architecture as a demonstration of a more fully printed sensor fabricated
using the Voltera NOVA; and (4) quantitatively evaluates force-dependent
sensitivity, calibration nonlinearity, hysteresis, drift, and cyclic
stability using a voltage-divider readout. The limitations of the present experimental system for resolving sensor response time are also discussed. Section II describes the materials, design, fabrication, assembly, and electrical readout; Section III presents the characterization procedures and results; Section IV discusses the experimental findings, comparisons, and limitations; and Section V summarizes the conclusions and future work.

title: What Can a VLA Learn from the Agent That Calls It? Task-Level Experience Distillation for Embodied Navigation
authors: Jinze Tao,Yuxiao Han,Kangkang Dong,Yancong Wei,Xiaojun Zhu,Bokui Chen,Houde Liu
abstract:
Navigation agents use a large language model (LLM) planner to call a vision-language-action (VLA) model.
Each episode needs the LLM, adding cost and delay. We distill successful agent experience into the VLA
instead of distilling the planner. The VLA then navigates alone at test time. Agent sessions are not
VLA demonstrations. They include motions driven by planner tools and sub-instructions,
along with detours. We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method that converts these sessions
into VLA training data. Every motion becomes a VLA action under the original task instruction, with the
resulting poses as targets. H2E masks the loss on steps that move away from the goal. It labels
every visited state within 1 m of the goal as a stop. We then update the VLA with low-rank adaptation. The
VLA learns to stop at the goal and find goals the base model never reaches. On all 31893189 REVERIE-CE val-unseen
episodes, H2E raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from 35.0% to 44.9%.
introduction:
Goal-directed navigation asks a robot to find a remote object that an instruction describes, such as
go to the second-floor hallway and pick up the picture above the table [27]. The
robot sees only its own camera views [15, 36]. Strong recent systems split
this task in two [51, 18]. A frontier LLM planner looks at the scene and keeps a map of visited
places. It hands short goals to a vision-language-action (VLA) model and corrects the VLA when it goes
wrong. The planner calls the LLM throughout every episode. On our test episodes this costs a median of 70k
tokens per episode, and an episode takes more than twice as long as with the VLA alone.

The sessions of such an agent show the VLA succeeding with help. We ask whether the VLA can learn from
these sessions and then work alone. Current agents keep the VLA frozen [51], and distillation
from such agents has so far shrunk the planner [9, 41, 21]. We instead train the
VLA itself and remove the LLM at test time.

A session is hard to use as training data for the VLA. The planner often moves the robot with its own
tools, and it often gives the VLA new sub-instructions. Together these produce 45% of the motion in our
sessions. The sessions also contain detours that the planner later fixes, so nearly a quarter of the steps
move away from the goal.

We present H2E, a task-level experience distillation method. Figure 2 gives an overview.
H2E uses three simple rules. First, it labels every motion in a session as a VLA action under the
original task instruction, whoever made the motion. Second, it masks the loss on steps that move away from
the goal. Third, it labels every visited state near the goal as a stop. A LoRA update then trains the VLA,
which runs without the LLM at test time.

H2E works well on the full REVERIE-CE val-unseen split. It raises the success rate of an 8B VLA from
35.0% to 44.9%, while geodesic adaptation gives no gain. The distilled VLA learns two
skills from the agent. It stops in the right place far more often, and it finds goals that the base VLA
never reaches. Against the full agent, the distilled VLA reaches a higher success rate with no LLM tokens
and about a quarter of the time per episode.

Our contributions are as follows.

We distill a frontier LLM navigation agent into the VLA that it calls, so that the VLA navigates
without the LLM at test time.

We present H2E. It turns whole agent sessions into VLA training data with task-level labels,
progress masking and one stop rule. We also show why an L1L_{1} loss with this stop rule teaches the VLA to
stop.

We show that H2E clearly beats the base VLA and geodesic adaptation on unseen scenes. We also
show that the distilled VLA outperforms the agent at a small fraction of its cost.

1. We distill a frontier LLM navigation agent into the VLA that it calls, so that the VLA navigates
without the LLM at test time.

2. We present H2E. It turns whole agent sessions into VLA training data with task-level labels,
progress masking and one stop rule. We also show why an L1L_{1} loss with this stop rule teaches the VLA to
stop.

3. We show that H2E clearly beats the base VLA and geodesic adaptation on unseen scenes. We also
show that the distilled VLA outperforms the agent at a small fraction of its cost.

title: BWM-Forge: Agentic World Programming for Embodied Intelligence
authors: BWM Team
comment: Technical Report
abstract: Generating diverse robot videos requires control over scene geometry, robot motion, and viewpoints. End-to-end video generation offers limited direct access to these variables, making targeted edits and reuse across tasks difficult. We present BWM-Forge, a code-driven framework for controllable video generation in robotics. Given robot assets and a task description, the framework accepts an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video. A coding agent constructs editable Blender scene programs that specify objects, robot motion, and cameras. The resulting proxy videos provide structural and motion references for a video generation model, which adds visual detail. A multi-agent harness coordinates input processing, scene construction, review, and rendering. Automated evaluation and user feedback support iterative refinement, while an experience repository stores and retrieves reusable modeling and rendering rules. This design supports multiple robot embodiments, synchronized viewpoints, and appearance variation from a shared scene program. We evaluate the framework on 15 tasks covering five robot types. Compared with LingBot-World Base Cam on these tasks, BWM-Forge achieves higher aesthetic quality, imaging quality, subject and background consistency, motion smoothness, and RoboJudge-9B physical adherence and instruction alignment scores. The baseline scores higher in dynamic degree. Qualitative cases illustrate viewpoint control, scene variation, feedback-driven edits, and experience reuse across scenes. These results demonstrate a practical approach to generating controllable robot videos through editable, executable scene representations.
introduction:
Video provides a natural representation of physical-world dynamics, motivating video world models that predict future visual observations. When world state is represented implicitly in generated frames, however, users have limited direct access to scene objects, robot configurations, and camera trajectories for editing and reuse. For embodied data generation, these limitations concern changing a task object while preserving the surrounding scene, observing the same interaction from another camera, and adapting an existing scene to a different robot. Recent code world models offer a complementary approach. WorldCoder and subsequent work represent world dynamics as executable programs for prediction and decision making [1, 2]. Code World Model and Code2Worlds extend this direction toward code-mediated visual generation and the construction of 3D scenes and motion [3, 4]. These approaches motivate an explicit, executable representation through which scene structure and motion can be inspected, modified, and rendered.

Inspired by this direction, we introduce BWM-Forge, a framework for agentic world programming that generates controllable videos for embodied intelligence (Figure 1). In BWM-Forge, world programming means expressing scene objects, spatial relationships, robot motion, and camera states as executable scene programs; agents construct, execute, inspect, and revise these programs using tools and feedback. The goal is to generate diverse visual data across tasks, robot embodiments, and viewpoints, motivated by the need for broad robot interaction coverage reflected in datasets such as DROID and BridgeData V2 [5, 6]. A unified pipeline accepts robot assets and task descriptions together with an initial image, an image with motion data, or a human demonstration video, and produces high-fidelity videos of interactions between robots and their environments. The same workflow covers robotic arms, humanoid robots, quadrupeds, and dexterous hands by loading their corresponding assets and using the available motion evidence. These videos provide potential training material for embodied video generation and world modeling.

Prior work uses language models to generate robotic simulation tasks and scenes [7, 8], while robot-conditioned video generation uses explicit robot structure or rendered conditions to guide visual synthesis [9, 10]. BWM-Forge combines executable scene construction with appearance generation through proxy videos as an intermediate representation. A coding agent controls Blender to construct task scenes, import robot description packages for different embodiments, and coordinate robot motion and camera trajectories. Scene geometry, motion, and viewpoints remain directly editable in the program. Loading a different robot description package adapts the model to the target embodiment’s structure, while the scene program retains editable objects and camera parameters. A 3D engine executes the program and renders proxy videos, which provide structural and motion guidance for a video generation model to add visual detail.

This representation supports interactive refinement and flexible viewpoint control. The coding agent can modify scene code and parameters in response to user feedback, including object placement, robot motion, and camera settings. Multiple fixed cameras produce synchronized views of the same task, while camera trajectories enable continuously varying viewpoints. Because proxy videos share a scene program and motion timeline, their geometric relationships and motion remain temporally aligned. These shared references guide subsequent high-fidelity generation. This provides complementary observations of the same interaction for learning robot motion and its relationship to the environment. Reusing the scene program with different robot assets or camera configurations provides a practical basis for expanding visual observations across embodiments and viewpoints.

The agentic workflow is implemented by a Harness that coordinates four specialized agents. The Preprocessing Agent parses requests, validates robot assets and motion data, and extracts visual evidence. The Building Agent constructs and animates scenes through code. The Review Agent inspects visual and numerical evidence, identifies defects, and applies local corrections. The Rendering Agent uses the resulting proxy videos, reference images, and prompts to generate and evaluate high-fidelity outputs. Automated checks and optional user feedback guide revisions to both proxy and rendered videos. Stage summaries and execution traces supply candidate experience entries, which the Harness consolidates and retrieves for later tasks. This cycle of programming, execution, review, and experience reuse connects the framework’s editable world representation to its embodied data generation goal.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Agentic world programming for embodied data generation. We introduce BWM-Forge, a framework that converts multimodal task inputs into executable scene programs and uses their rendered outputs to guide high-fidelity robot video generation.

Agentic world programming for embodied data generation. We introduce BWM-Forge, a framework that converts multimodal task inputs into executable scene programs and uses their rendered outputs to guide high-fidelity robot video generation.

Explicit control over scenes, embodiments, and viewpoints. Editable scene programs expose object geometry, robot motion, and camera states for targeted revision, synchronized multi-view rendering, and adaptation to different robot assets.

A collaborative generation and refinement workflow. A four-agent Harness combines input validation, scene construction, evidence-based review, rendering, user feedback, and reusable experience to support iterative video generation across tasks.

1. Agentic world programming for embodied data generation. We introduce BWM-Forge, a framework that converts multimodal task inputs into executable scene programs and uses their rendered outputs to guide high-fidelity robot video generation.

2. Explicit control over scenes, embodiments, and viewpoints. Editable scene programs expose object geometry, robot motion, and camera states for targeted revision, synchronized multi-view rendering, and adaptation to different robot assets.

3. A collaborative generation and refinement workflow. A four-agent Harness combines input validation, scene construction, evidence-based review, rendering, user feedback, and reusable experience to support iterative video generation across tasks.

title: A Coupled Control Barrier Function Approach to Deadlock-Free Multi-Robot Conflict Resolution
authors: Gary Rostomyan,Ketan Savla,Petros A. Ioannou
abstract:
Many robotic applications involve scenarios where multiple robots interact and the decisions of one robot influence the behavior of others. This paper presents a quadratic programming (QP)-based feedback controller for multi-robot conflict resolution with input constraints. Safety is enforced using coupled Control Barrier Function (CBF), while a yielding matrix encodes how robots influence each other. Unlike existing methods with fixed or hard priorities, the proposed framework enables yielding preferences while guaranteeing deadlock-free operation by design. Sufficient conditions are established for the controller to be locally Lipschitz.
The optimal CBF sign-indefinite slack is shown to admit a finite uniform bound, which is compensated through an enlarged CBF safety margin to obtain a forward invariant set contained within the desired safe set. The analysis also identifies an irreducible slack component due to finite maximum deceleration that cannot be eliminated by increasing the slack penalty. Finally, sufficient conditions on the yielding matrix and nominal controller are derived to exclude deadlock states.
Simulations demonstrate adaptive coordination across yielding preferences and robustness to robot failures.
introduction:
As logistics and warehouse operations continue to expand, mobile robots have become essential for automating material transport, order picking, and replenishment, thereby improving productivity, accuracy, and operational efficiency [1, 2]. Modern warehouses deploy mobile robot fleets for prioritized transport tasks. When robots enter shared conflict zones along planned corridor routes, collisions and deadlocks may occur (Fig. 1). Thus, safety and deadlock-free
operation are key design objectives.
The conflict resolution problem shown in Fig. 1 involves interactions among multiple autonomous robots. Planning in such interactive environments is inherently complex since each robot’s state and control affect the others.

Multi-robot interactions can be modeled as differential games [3, 4].
However, computing equilibria requires solving coupled optimal control problems, making these approaches computationally intractable for real-time applications [5].
Prior works have also modeled multi-robot interactions as dynamic potential games, enabling the computation of a generalized Nash equilibrium by solving a single optimal control problem rather than multiple coupled problems [6]-[7]. However, these approaches require restrictive cost structures (e.g., action-independent inter-agent costs) to preserve the potential game property, thus precluding general non-potential costs. Moreover, they compute open-loop Nash equilibria, even when implemented in a receding-horizon fashion, and provide no guarantees of recursive feasibility.

In contrast, the proposed approach supports non-potential cost functions and yields a well-defined, optimization-based feedback controller. Since state parametrized optimization-based controllers are not necessarily locally Lipschitz [8], establishing this property is essential for guaranteeing existence and uniqueness of the closed-loop smooth solution.
In [9], local Lipschitz continuity is established for a QP-based controller with two constraints by explicitly characterizing all possible active sets and deriving closed-form Lagrange multipliers. This approach, however, does not readily scale to QPs with many constraints, for which the number of possible active sets grows exponentially.
In contrast, we provide verifiable sufficient conditions for the local Lipschitz continuity of a QP-based controller under multiple input constraints. We further present the unexplored interplay among safety, deadlock-free operation, and well-posed closed-loop motion under multiple input constraints.

Earlier work in [10] proposed an optimization-based centralized controller for multi-robot collision avoidance; however, it neither accounts for coupling costs that encode yielding relationships between robots nor establishes feasibility over a set of initial conditions.
The proposed feedback controller enables the specification of pairwise yielding preferences among robots without imposing a fixed a priori crossing order through the conflict zone. These yielding preferences are encoded in the optimization cost rather than enforced through hard ordering constraints, thereby influencing the robots’ motions toward the desired yielding behavior.
Unlike the ad hoc braking strategy in [11], which may induce deadlocks when safety constraints become infeasible, and reactive deadlock-resolution methods, our framework balances local Lipschitz continuity of the QP-based controller and forward invariance of a subset of the safe set with deadlock prevention through a conservative design margin.
Recent work [12] analyzes two-robot deadlock resolution using a closed-form QP solution without input constraints. It uses fixed pairwise separation for safety constraints, whereas our formulation uses speed-dependent stopping-distance margins.
Moreover, [12] identifies a deadlock as an unstable saddle equilibrium, whereas our analysis provides constructive conditions on the controller parameters that eliminate deadlock for NN robots.

The main contributions are threefold. First, sufficient conditions are established
for a locally Lipschitz feedback controller with input constraints that guarantees safety and deadlock-free operation by design, with yielding preferences encoded in a yielding matrix.
Second, to maintain the desired safety in the presence of sign-indefinite CBF slack, a compensation mechanism is introduced by enlarging the safety margin to guarantee forward invariance of a set contained within the desired safe set. Finally, simulations demonstrate that multi-robot coordination adapts to assigned yielding preferences, resulting in yielding behavior, while also maintaining coordination robustness against robot failures.

title: Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning with Task-Centric Perception
authors: Sahit Chintalapudi,Xiaoyan Wang,Aryan Zoroufi,Aditya Agarwal,Nancy Kanwisher,Tomás Lozano-Pérez,Leslie Pack Kaelbling
abstract: Long-horizon manipulation under uncertainty remains a challenging problem in robotics. We present VA-TAMP, an algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning. VA-TAMP extends existing deterministic task and motion planning solvers to partially observable object rearrangement tasks, while still being able to take advantage of the efficiency and compositional generalization over long horizons of the base solver. This extension interleaves sensing actions into a plan skeleton that assumed full observability, and uses a novel persistent object-based memory to fuse observations into object mesh hypotheses and an observed occupancy map. We evaluate VA-TAMP on real-world tabletop rearrangement tasks which feature heavy occlusion and partial visibility and demonstrate that it outperforms baselines that do not perform active perception or have persistent memory.
introduction:
A longstanding challenge in robotic manipulation is completing long-horizon tasks in heavily occluded environments with unfamiliar objects. When object models and poses are known a priori, Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) solvers [1, 2] can efficiently compose manipulation skills to achieve a goal. Otherwise, object models can be estimated from an observation and passed to a TAMP solver [3, 4]. These approaches assume that the initial observation models the scene accurately enough to find a goal-achieving plan.

Consider a tabletop rearrangement task, such as the one illustrated in Figure 1, where the robot has to place the cleaning supplies on the red tray. In the initial observation, the full extent of the tray (which already has other cleaning supplies on it) is not visible to the robot, and the cleaning supplies that the robot has to manipulate are partially occluded by the cardboard boxes. This setting is partially observable; the robot does not know the full shape of any of the objects in the scene, and thus it must make a plan from raw observations which are noisy and incomplete.

The naive approach to this problem, re-estimating and replanning with every new observation, suffers from two main shortcomings. First, any single observation is not sufficient to accurately model the scene. Second, TAMP solvers output strictly goal-oriented plans, meaning that they cannot direct the perception toward the task-relevant parts of the scene or remove occluding objects. In Figure 1, no single view shows the far edge of the tray, and a plan that only reaches for the eraser never looks behind the boxes that occlude it. On the other end of the spectrum, belief space planners explicitly model uncertainty in the environment state and search for plans by reasoning over full observation distributions obtained by each action [5, 6, 7, 8]. However, modeling geometric uncertainty requires reasoning over extremely high-dimensional distributions which quickly becomes intractable.

Our approach exploits the compositional generalization and efficiency of TAMP solvers while tracking object model accuracy and unobserved regions of space. VA-TAMP augments off-the-shelf TAMP solvers with action constraints requiring the robot to verify its object models before interacting with the objects. These constraints induce information gathering actions that provide observations for refining the models.

In order to build and refine our scene representation as we observe more of the scene and objects move, we define an Object-Based Memory module (OBM). The OBM collects a history of observations and maintains two complementary representations of the scene. The first representation is an occupancy grid, which accumulates depth data and tracks the regions of space that have not yet been observed. The second representation is a set of objects that are believed to exist in the scene after being detected in individual observations. The OBM associates these detections on a per-object basis and leverages a generative image-to-3D reconstruction model [9, 10] to hypothesize a complete 3D mesh geometry from partial RGBD observations. The OBM is resource-rational and task-centric: it focuses its computation time on objects that the planner has decided are relevant to the task. In the example, the eraser and tray are refined into complete meshes (Figure 1(d)) while the cardboard boxes are left as the coarse hulls from the first frame (Figure 1(b)).

Given a set of object meshes, we can leverage existing classical TAMP solvers to generate a plan skeleton: an optimistic plan that assumes the current object meshes are accurate and is entirely goal-oriented. To guard against this optimism, we require that every plan be justified. This means that any time the plan requires the robot to move through space, it must have observed that the space is collision free. Any time the plan requires the robot to grasp an object at a given pose, it must have observed that the object surface exists in between the fingers at that pose. To justify a plan, the planner has to find motions that move the camera to viewpoints where the desired regions are visible. The initial hull of the green eraser (Figure 1(b)) does not justify a grasp; the planner inserts the wrist view in Figure 1(c), which reveals the eraser’s full extent and lets the grasp proceed.

VA-TAMP extends fully observed TAMP to partially observed domains by coupling object-based memory with scene-model verification. The memory supplies object meshes and an occupancy grid, and the planner constructs a goal-reaching plan that also validates the meshes. As observations arrive, the remaining plan guides refinement of task-relevant objects. Figure 2 illustrates this coupling. Our contributions are as follows.

VA-TAMP: An algorithm for Visibility-Aware Task and Motion Planning.  VA-TAMP augments classical TAMP solvers with a persistent memory system and task-driven information gathering behavior. We show that this method outperforms systems which don’t perform active perception or do not associate object detections across observations.

A task-centric, resource-rational OBM.  Accurately modeling a scene is a computationally expensive task, with state-of-the-art completion models taking 4-5 seconds per object in a single frame. Rather than completing every object in every frame, the OBM prioritizes reconstruction on objects that are task-relevant and do not yet have a good model.

Efficient information gathering in partially observable problems by leveraging a fully observed TAMP solver.  We use the result of an existing TAMP solver to define which regions of space the robot interacts with, either as motion in assumed free space or contact with assumed object surfaces. We make the observation of these regions of space a precondition to acting, forcing the robot to collect more observations and update its models as needed.
