title: QVS-LIVO RiskMap: Health- and Information-Aware View Selection for Multi-Camera LIVO and Off-Road Risk Mapping
authors: Zihan Pan,Jinghan Wang,Hang Li,Feng Cheng,Tianchen Liu,Gaoliang Peng
comment: 17pages, 9 figures
abstract:
Multi-camera observations in off-road environments vary significantly in reliability, posing challenges when complementing degraded geometric constraints. Motivated by this, we propose Quality-aware View Selection Lidar-Vision Odometry Risk Mapping (QVS-LIVO RiskMap), which decouples visual processing for state estimation from that for semantic mapping. The front end evaluates camera observations through read-only pretracking on a shared lidar–inertial posterior, combining observation health with geometric complementarity. Channel health memory and switching hysteresis govern selection of at most one eligible view for direct photometric correction. The posterior is retained when no view is eligible or the correction fails acceptance. The mapping back end integrates semantic observations from all available views in a shared world grid. Vehicle-scale geometry constrains semantic risk corrections, while spatial and temporal evidence supports risk confirmation. The system also produces a local bird’s-eye-view (BEV) risk map and a global 2.5D semantic-terrain risk map with obstacle instance voxels. On two field sequences, QVS-LIVO achieved horizontal root mean square errors of 0.910 m and 1.664 m. It reduced error by 43.3% relative to FAST-LIO2 on the degraded long-route sequence. Across 12 controlled camera-fault configurations involving dropout, black frames and 60 ms timestamp shifts, it maintained complete trajectories with errors of 1.54–2.23 m. When deployed onboard an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, the system generates local and global maps at 9.94 Hz and 2.00 Hz, respectively, with a median local mapping latency of 32.4 ms. These runtime results demonstrate the real-time feasibility of selective visual state updates alongside multi-view semantic mapping under challenging off-road conditions. The code and related resources are available at:
https://github.com/zihanPan-HIT/QVS-LIVO.
introduction:
Off-road mobile robots performing autonomous inspection, search and rescue, and environmental reconstruction in forests, grasslands and unstructured terrains must continuously estimate their poses and motion with limited prior map information while assessing, in real time, the traversability risks posed by the surrounding terrain. Unlike structured roads, off-road environments lack clear lane markings and flat roadbeds. Pronounced terrain variations, intermittent canopy occlusion and abrupt illumination changes can degrade geometric or visual observations during motion. These conditions disrupt the continuity of features used for motion estimation and increase ambiguity in surface-material recognition and traversability-risk assessment. These challenges motivate robust state estimation under sensor degradation. They also motivate traversability representations that integrate terrain geometry and appearance while accounting for vehicle traversal capabilities 1, 2.

Heterogeneous sensor fusion provides a physical foundation to address these challenges: lidar supplies accurate metric geometry and structural scale, cameras capture rich surface textures and semantic appearance, and the inertial measurement unit (IMU) provides high-frequency motion priors and inertial constraints. However, combining these modalities does not ensure sufficient measurement constraints throughout operation. Insufficient geometric structure can weaken lidar pose constraints along specific degrees of freedom 3. Motion blur, occlusions, and lighting changes can make visual tracking unreliable 4. Surround-camera configurations substantially expand the field of view, but image quality and contributions to pose constraints vary considerably across viewing directions, compounded by asynchronous multi-camera arrivals. On resource-constrained edge platforms, identifying and selecting visual observations that provide reliable and complementary constraints along weakly constrained lidar pose directions from asynchronous multi-view streams is a key challenge in containing error propagation and leveraging camera redundancy.

State estimation and semantic mapping also impose different requirements on multi-camera observations. For state estimation, incorporating degraded views or observations with incorrect temporal associations increases computational cost and risks corrupting the pose estimate. For environmental mapping, an image excluded from the current pose update may still capture surfaces or obstacles outside the primary field of view, conversely, a single view that supports stable visual tracking may not cover all terrain requiring assessment. This distinction motivates two complementary design objectives. The front end should evaluate observation health and geometric complementarity on a shared lidar–inertial posterior to govern visual updates. It should retain that posterior when no view is eligible or an update is rejected. Independently, the mapping pipeline should integrate semantic observations from all available views while enforcing vehicle-scale geometric constraints and spatiotemporal risk confirmation.

Prior research relevant to these challenges spans three areas: multimodal localization under geometric degeneracy, multi-camera temporal coordination, and geometric–semantic terrain mapping.

(1) Multimodal localization and constraints under degeneracy. Tightly coupled LIVO combines geometric, photometric and inertial constraints for state estimation. LVI-SAM couples visual–inertial and lidar–inertial subsystems through factor-graph optimization 5. R3LIVE and FAST-LIVO combine lidar–inertial estimation with direct photometric alignment 6, 7. FAST-LIVO2 sequentially applies lidar and visual updates within an error-state iterated Kalman filter (ESIKF), using point-to-plane registration and image-patch alignment 8. Omni-LIVO extends this approach to synchronized surround cameras through cross-view photometric transfer, joint multi-view updates and adaptive covariance inflation 4. Asynchronous camera arrivals and limited computing resources motivate selective visual updates. Candidate selection and update acceptance must account for observation reliability before modifying the current lidar–inertial posterior.

(2) Multi-camera observation utilization and asynchronous coordination. Multi-camera systems provide redundancy against visual degradation confined to individual viewing directions. MIMC-VINS fuses asynchronous camera and IMU measurements through on-manifold state interpolation and maintains estimation under sensor failures 9. MAVIS extends visual tracking and visual–inertial optimization to multiple cameras 10. VINS-Multi uses dynamic feature quotas and frame-priority coordination for asynchronous camera streams 11, while ARTI-VIO combines feature recall with time-interpolated optimization 12.

Information-aware visual cue selection and active feature matching balance estimation accuracy and computational cost 13, 14. For multi-camera VIO, Zhang et al. maintain a fixed total feature budget across cameras while jointly estimating motion 15.

Observation health and geometric complementarity describe distinct properties of a visual observation. Eigenstructure-based degeneracy analysis identifies uneven constraints across pose directions 16, 3. Photometric residuals, tracked point counts and image freshness characterize observation health, but do not directly measure visual support along weakly constrained lidar directions. A healthy view may reinforce directions already well constrained by lidar, while a complementary view may be unreliable. We therefore evaluate both properties on a shared LIO posterior and retain that posterior when no view is eligible or a correction is rejected.

(3) Off-road risk mapping through semantic and geometric fusion. Terrain geometry provides measures of slope, step height, roughness and obstacle structure for traversability assessment. Probabilistic elevation mapping accounts for localization and range-measurement uncertainty 17, while GPU-based elevation mapping supports efficient terrain processing 18. Forkel et al. estimate terrain surfaces separately from obstacles 19. Xue et al. combine multiple lidar frames with spatiotemporal inference for terrain modeling and traversability analysis 20.

Visual terrain-property prediction provides complementary appearance information 21. Multilayer Bayesian mapping jointly represents semantic occupancy and traversability 22. Beycimen et al. fuse appearance classifications and geometric statistics in a 2.5D traversability grid 1. RoadRunner learns elevation and traversability from camera and lidar features in a unified BEV representation 2.

Combining geometric and semantic observations in unstructured field navigation introduces two practical challenges. The first is asymmetry in decision authority. Appearance semantics is susceptible to misclassification caused by domain shift, shadows, or debris (e.g., misclassifying a low obstacle as vegetation associated with a low appearance-risk prior). The second challenge is spatiotemporal risk confirmation. Transient classification flicker and point-cloud edge outliers can produce false alarms. Risk confirmation should distinguish direct obstacle evidence from slope- or step-induced candidates that require additional spatial and temporal support. Furthermore, restricting semantic mapping to the cameras selected for pose estimation would limit environmental coverage; the mapping pipeline should therefore ingest semantic streams across all available views independently.

These considerations motivate coordinating two distinct uses of multi-camera observations in our framework. Through multi-view pretracking, the localization front end evaluates observation health and directional geometric complementarity to select at most one eligible view for visual correction, falling back to the current LIO posterior when updates are unavailable or rejected. Concurrently, the mapping back end aggregates semantic streams across all available views under explicit geometric constraints and spatiotemporal confirmation. Anchored to a shared state reference, this separation limits the visual correction workload while retaining semantic coverage from all available views.

To address the robust perception and mapping for off-road environments, we present Quality-aware View Selection Lidar-Vision Odometry Risk Mapping (QVS-LIVO RiskMap), a multi-camera localization and dual-scale risk-mapping framework. It separates visual state-update selection from semantic observation utilization while sharing pose estimates and registered point clouds. The main contributions are as follows:

Selective visual state updates via health- and complementarity-aware view selection.
The front end performs view-specific, read-only pretracking across four non-overlapping cameras on a shared LIO posterior. Candidates are evaluated jointly by observation health and geometric complementarity to weakly constrained lidar pose directions. Four-state channel health management and switching hysteresis govern the selection of at most one eligible view for direct photometric correction. The correction is committed only after post-solve acceptance checks; the current LIO posterior is retained when no view is eligible or the correction is rejected.

Selective visual state updates via health- and complementarity-aware view selection.
The front end performs view-specific, read-only pretracking across four non-overlapping cameras on a shared LIO posterior. Candidates are evaluated jointly by observation health and geometric complementarity to weakly constrained lidar pose directions. Four-state channel health management and switching hysteresis govern the selection of at most one eligible view for direct photometric correction. The correction is committed only after post-solve acceptance checks; the current LIO posterior is retained when no view is eligible or the correction is rejected.

Dual-scale semantic risk mapping via available-view aggregation and geometry-constrained confirmation.
Independently of localization-view selection, the mapping pipeline integrates semantic observations from all available views into a world-anchored 2.5D grid. Source-timestamp pairing, spatial projection and temporally decayed accumulation support this integration. Bounded semantic risk corrections preserve direct hard-obstacle constraints. Hard obstacles meeting the occupancy-confidence threshold are confirmed immediately, whereas slope- or step-induced candidates require additional spatial and temporal support. By preserving continuous risk, confirmation, and unknown states, the mapping pipeline produces a Local Risk BEV and a global 2.5D Semantic–Terrain Risk Map with Obstacle Instance Voxels.

Systematic experimental validation via real-world field benchmarks, controlled camera faults, and onboard deployment.
Sequences collected with the Multi-sensor AMR platform support internal mode comparisons and benchmarking against external SLAM baselines. Twelve controlled single-camera fault configurations, covering dropout, black frames and timestamp shifts, assess trajectory continuity and localization error. Onboard deployment on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin benchmarks the generation latencies of both local and global maps, verifying the real-time performance of the complete system.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the platform and sensor configuration. Section 3 presents the localization and risk-mapping methods. Section 4 reports the experiments and discusses their implications and limitations. Section 5 concludes the paper.

title: PERA: Plug-in Experts for Robotic Actions in Continual Whole-Body Control
authors: Shangchao Hu,Yadan Sun,Xibo Yu,Wei Huang
abstract: Motion imitation enables humanoid robots to acquire whole-body skills such as walking and dancing. However, fine-tuning an entire policy for a new skill can affect existing behaviors, while training a separate policy for each skill increases training and maintenance costs. We present PERA, a method for learning new skills by reusing existing motion capabilities. PERA freezes a pretrained mixture-of-experts policy and trains an additional task expert and its routing score using task rewards or teacher-action supervision. In Unitree G1 simulation, each added task module contains approximately 1.03% of the parameters of the base actor. Built on our pretrained policy, PERA successfully completes all ten new tasks. Disabling the expert restores the original computation path of the base policy, which still fully executes all 126 original motions. Enabling the expert also improves the execution of some dance motions not used to train that expert, indicating that its benefits extend beyond its training motions. Experiments with HoloMotion further demonstrate the applicability of PERA to different base policies.
introduction:
Reference-based motion imitation provides an effective approach to humanoid whole-body control. With advances in motion data and policy learning, a single controller can perform walking, dancing, and a range of highly dynamic motions [1, 2, 3]. However, new tasks may involve contact patterns, posture constraints, or motion objectives not covered during training. Existing motion-tracking capabilities alone do not guarantee success on these tasks. It therefore remains necessary to learn new skills while preserving access to existing motion capabilities.

Directly fine-tuning an entire policy applies new-task gradients to shared parameters and can change existing control behaviors. Maintaining a separate controller for each new task can isolate parameter updates, but requires repeated model storage and makes it difficult to share computation during execution. Skill expansion therefore calls for both reuse of existing motion knowledge and independent access to the original policy. We address this objective by combining a frozen base policy with additional task modules (Figure 1).

Mixture-of-experts (MoE) networks provide a structural basis for incremental expansion. Experts reuse shared features and an action-output interface, while routing determines their participation and mixing weights from the input. Task-related feature transformations can thus be learned within an additional module. A new candidate can also change the selection and mixing of existing experts, so control outputs may change even when shared parameters remain fixed. Expert expansion must therefore specify both how additional modules are learned and how the original policy path is recovered when they are disabled.

PERA learns task experts independently on a frozen MoE base policy, updating only the additional expert and its routing score. Training and execution use the same competitive routing, allowing a task module to learn while participating in control. We use proximal policy optimization (PPO) when task rewards are available, and behavior cloning with online DAgger when reliable teachers are available. During execution, an explicit switch enables the chosen expert on demand; disabling it bypasses the additional module and restores the original computation path.

Our main contributions are: (1) an expert-expansion architecture and training method for continual robot skill learning, in which new experts reuse existing motion representations while the pretrained policy remains frozen; (2) an evaluation of the improvements provided by expert learning, showing higher task completion and improved tracking accuracy on some unseen motions; and (3) a modular skill library that supports independent training, storage, and on-demand invocation of task experts, allowing the skill set to grow through incremental module additions.

title: JustRUA: A Controlled Study of GPT-6 Robot-Use Agents
authors: Zefan Wang,Yufan Dang,Xuanwei Shi,Mingqi Gao,Cheng Yin,SikYuen Tam,Hanyu Liu,Yasheng Wang,Yaxi Lu,Songyang Zhang,Xin Cong,Yuan Yao

abstract:
GPT-6 Astra can drive a robot arm directly through a fixed harness, and scores of such robot-use agents on RoboDojo have risen quickly since.
Reported systems differ in harness and test subset and often change several designs at once, so it is hard to tell which choices produce the gains.
We take these designs apart and test them in one framework, along the harness around the model, the action interface, the reuse of experience and the scene geometry given to the model.
A lean harness that keeps the full episode history and stops each motion early goes a long way.
Reusing experience changes how the model acts but is not a free lunch, and scene geometry helps most, even when depth is predicted from RGB alone.
JustRUA starts from the official L3 harness and keeps only what matters most.
Even with no learned policy, self-improvement loop or task-specific tuning, this simple harness raises the score on the RoboDojo simulation benchmark substantially, from 29.7 to 50.3.
introduction:
Frontier multimodal models can now control robots without any robot-specific training.
GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI, 2026b) drives a bimanual arm through a harness, the software that turns each of its decisions into end-effector targets for a motion planner (Zhang et al., 2026; Galbot Team et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026a).
No vision-language-action (VLA) model sits in between.
The model looks at camera images, decides where each gripper should go next and reads the outcome, much as a computer-use agent looks at a screen and decides where to click (Xie et al., 2024).
By analogy such a system is called a robot-use agent (RUA) (Isola, 2026; Yang et al., 2026b).
On the RoboDojo simulation benchmark (Chen et al., 2026a), RUAs built on GPT-6 Astra have improved quickly, and each new system adds components of its own, such as depth and point clouds (Qu et al., 2026; Zhou et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026), affordance models (Kim et al., 2026; Yang et al., 2026b), in-context demonstrations (Guo et al., 2026; SenseNova and Joint Research Team et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) and self-improvement loops that write and refine their own skills (Li et al., 2026a; OpenSenseNova, 2026).

Our starting point was a discrepancy.
The first evaluation of GPT-6 Astra on RoboDojo found it weak on tasks that require precision under the official L3 harness (Zhang et al., 2026), and a broader study saw a similar gap between its task decisions and reliable physical control (Galbot Team et al., 2026).
Yet a few reasonable fixes to the harness and the action loop, with no elaborate design on top, brought its Precision score to the level of the strongest VLA models of the time (Section 3).
We came to suspect that much of the reported weakness lay in the harness rather than in the model.

If the harness matters this much, the gains reported by recent systems are hard to read.
These systems start from different harnesses, run on different subsets of the benchmark with different budgets, and often change several parts of the design at once.
A reader who sees a higher score cannot tell whether it comes from the new component, from the loop it was added to or from the episodes it was measured on.
Reproducing each system in full would carry these differences over.
We instead take the designs apart and test them on one testbed and one evaluation set, changing as little as we can between runs.

We start from the official L3 harness and group the designs that recent systems add along four axes (Figure 2): the harness around the model, the action interface, the reuse of experience from other episodes and the scene geometry in each observation.
Three tools keep the comparison affordable and readable.
Since the official evaluation of 2,100 episodes is costly to repeat for every design, we build a 111-episode evaluation set that covers all 42 tasks and spends more episodes on the tasks with high evaluation uncertainty.
Since a score says how much of a task was completed and not how the attempt went, we review every first-round episode from its video and count behaviours the score does not show, such as empty grasps and dropped objects.
And since an episode resends its whole history at every decision, we report what each configuration costs per episode.
A design is kept only if it helps on the evaluation set at a reasonable cost and does not draw on the tasks being scored.

The result is JustRUA.
It keeps three kinds of change to the official harness.
The loop keeps the full episode history and stops each motion after 20 control steps, the observation carries the robot’s own grip readings and depth predicted from RGB, and the model may run code to solve 3D coordinates from pixels.
With no learned policy, no self-improvement loop and no task-specific tuning, it raises the evaluation-set score of the official harness from 29.7 to 50.3 (Figure 1).
Our findings are as follows.

A lean harness goes a long way (Section 3).
Keeping the full episode history and stopping each motion after 20 control steps lift the score from 29.7 to 38.0.
Relative targets, named skills and model-chosen step counts do not beat plain absolute targets.

Reusing experience is not a free lunch (Section 4).
Demonstrations and a self-written skill library change how the model acts, but neither clearly beats the default, and both make an episode more expensive.
They also draw on the tasks being scored, so their scores are not comparable with a standard evaluation.

Scene geometry helps most (Section 5).
Depth images cut empty grasps from 41 to 16 in the first round, even when Depth Pro predicts the depth from RGB alone and is off by tens of centimetres.
With code that solves 3D coordinates from pixels and no decision cap, the score reaches 50.3.

Remaining failures are mostly long-tail (Section 6).
Most failures left in our best configuration are specific to one task, such as plans that do not suit the arm, unplanned knocks and slipping grasps.
Fixing them would take trial and error on each task, which comes close to tuning on the test tasks.

title: DexRemo: A Force-Sensing Hand Platform and Task Suite for Contact-Rich Removal Manipulation
authors: Liman Wang,Hanyang Zhong,Sun Zhaole,Wenting Cao,Babar Jamil,Andy Tyrrell,Shan Luo,Jihong Zhu
comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Robotics (T-RO), 2026. Project website:this https URL
abstract:
Many manipulation tasks require separating adhered, embedded, contaminated, or mechanically constrained targets. We study this setting as removal manipulation, where progress depends on evolving contact states that are only partially observable from vision and kinematics. We introduce DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario real-robot task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. To make multi-finger force observations easier to fuse, we express fingertip forces in a shared wrist-centered frame, giving force components consistent geometric meaning across fingers and time. Using an Action Chunking Transformer backbone, policies fuse multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and force observations to predict closed-loop action chunks from demonstrations. Evaluation uses six core benchmark tasks for controlled fingertip-input and force-frame ablations, plus three extension scenarios for additional held-out coverage. Across these evaluations, the learned policies achieve consistent removal performance, and ablations show that wrist-frame forces, especially with fingertip pose, improve stability and generalization over local-frame force inputs and no-force baselines. https://dexremo.github.io.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation in unstructured environments often involves targets that cannot be directly manipulated because they are adhered, embedded, contaminated, or constrained by surrounding materials. Such tasks require prior separation before conventional manipulation can proceed. We term this class of problems removal manipulation: tasks in which a robot progressively separates, exposes, or cleans a target through contact-rich behaviors such as detachment, peeling, scraping, prying, wiping, or uncovering, as illustrated by representative human examples in Fig. 1(b). Success in these tasks depends not only on object geometry, but also on evolving physical constraints such as adhesion, frictional wedging, deformation, occlusion, and surface contamination.
Removal manipulation is challenging because progress depends on the evolving contact state between the target and its surroundings. This state is only partially observable from vision and kinematics: visually similar scenes may correspond to different adhesion, friction, deformation, or occlusion conditions, while small contact changes can determine whether the robot initiates separation, maintains contact, or damages nearby material. Successful behavior therefore requires force-capable interaction, geometrically consistent multi-finger contact feedback, and temporally adaptive policies that revise actions as contacts form, slide, stick, and break.

Prior work on contact-rich separation has mainly addressed specific tasks, including robotic peeling [1], compliant surface cleaning [2], and tactile-driven excavation or retrieval in deformable or particulate media [3, 4]. Tactile sensing has also supported slip detection, contact geometry inference, and compliant surface following [5, 6]. Although these studies demonstrate the value of contact feedback, removal behaviors have not been systematically evaluated in a common real-robot setting that combines force-capable multi-finger hardware, task-level physical success criteria, and tasks involving adhesion, contamination, burial, and occlusion.

To address this gap, we introduce DexRemo, a three-finger robotic hand with three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a real-robot task suite spanning adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. The suite captures recurring contact-rich separation challenges under different physical constraints, with explicit preparation procedures, physical success criteria, and held-out variations in object geometry, pose, color, and attachment conditions. Table I reports pullout strength and power density as task-relevant capability indicators. Across tasks, peak fingertip loads frequently reach tens of newtons (Sec. V-D), reflecting the sustained contact required by the evaluation criteria.

A central design issue is how to represent multi-finger force measurements for learning. Each fingertip sensor measures forces in its local frame, which rotates with finger articulation. As a result, the meaning of each local force component varies with fingertip pose and across fingers, complicating cross-finger fusion. We therefore transform all fingertip forces, using forward kinematics, into a shared wrist-centered frame with consistent geometric meaning across fingers and time (Fig. 1). This deterministic transformation follows classical task-frame representations; our goal is to evaluate its practical value for multimodal imitation learning with 20 demonstrations per task and articulated fingertip force sensors.

For policy learning, we use an Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) [7] as the multimodal sequence-prediction backbone. The policy fuses multi-view vision, proprioception, fingertip pose, and fingertip force observations, and predicts short-horizon joint action chunks in a receding-horizon loop. ACT provides a consistent temporal imitation-learning backbone for studying how force sensing and force representation affect contact-rich removal performance.

Under the two-tier evaluation protocol, task-specific policies achieve consistent held-out performance across the suite. Controlled ablations on the six core benchmark tasks show that combining fingertip pose with wrist-frame force sensing improves stability and generalization over local-frame force inputs, no-force baselines, and other evaluated fingertip-input configurations. These results identify shared-frame force alignment as a practical representation choice for multimodal learning in the evaluated setting of 20 demonstrations per task.

The contributions of this work are:

A force-sensing hand platform and real-robot removal task suite. We introduce DexRemo, a reproducible three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and integrated three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario suite covering adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. The hand reaches a measured pullout strength of 62.562.5 N and a power density of 3.0643.064, the highest among the hands compared in Table I, at a hand cost of about $200 plus $170 per optional fingertip sensing unit (Table II). The suite defines preparation procedures, physical success criteria, held-out tests, and a two-tier evaluation protocol.

A controlled empirical study of shared-frame force alignment for multi-finger imitation learning. We represent fingertip forces in a wrist-centered frame grounded in classical task-frame formulations, and compare wrist-frame, local-frame, and no-force inputs while holding the hand, demonstrations, policy backbone, training schedule, and rollout protocol fixed. Real-robot ablations show that explicit force alignment, especially when combined with fingertip pose, yields the strongest and most consistent performance among the evaluated configurations.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work. Section III defines the local removal setting and presents the DexRemo platform, sensing system, and wrist-frame force representation. Section IV presents the multimodal imitation-learning framework. Section V describes the task suite, experimental protocol, and evaluation results. Section VI discusses limitations, future work, and conclusions.

The hardware design files, simulation models, software, and supplementary videos are being released in stages on the project website.

1. A force-sensing hand platform and real-robot removal task suite. We introduce DexRemo, a reproducible three-finger robotic hand with high-force actuation, modular fingertips, and integrated three-axis fingertip force sensing, together with a nine-scenario suite covering adhesive detachment, surface cleaning and self-cleaning, and occluded retrieval. The hand reaches a measured pullout strength of 62.562.5 N and a power density of 3.0643.064, the highest among the hands compared in Table I, at a hand cost of about $200 plus $170 per optional fingertip sensing unit (Table II). The suite defines preparation procedures, physical success criteria, held-out tests, and a two-tier evaluation protocol.

2. A controlled empirical study of shared-frame force alignment for multi-finger imitation learning. We represent fingertip forces in a wrist-centered frame grounded in classical task-frame formulations, and compare wrist-frame, local-frame, and no-force inputs while holding the hand, demonstrations, policy backbone, training schedule, and rollout protocol fixed. Real-robot ablations show that explicit force alignment, especially when combined with fingertip pose, yields the strongest and most consistent performance among the evaluated configurations.

title: Video-Action Models for Data-Efficient Industrial Manipulation
authors: Eugenio Chisari,Stefanos Charalambous,Oliver Sanchez,Thomas Umbach,Michael Gentner,Fabio Quattrini,Norica Bacuieti,Sabin Grube Doiz,Valentin Bertle,Sigmund Hennum Hoeg,Alain Ryser,German Rodriguez,Mario Arduini,Dang Nguyen,Florian Aumann,Felix Hegg,Manuel Meier,Philipp Wand,Julian Lotzer,Alessio Desogus,Benedek Forrai,Michael Bloesch,Stephan-Daniel Gravert,Stefan Weirich,Patrick Lanners,Elvis Nava

abstract:
Industrial manipulation requires precise alignment and controlled handling of rigid, deformable, and flexible components.
Yet, the benefits of pretrained visuomotor policies remain underexplored in settings where limited access to specialized hardware, components, and fixtures constrains demonstration collection and evaluation.
Understanding task-specific data requirements is important for assessing their scalability across diverse processes on the factory floor.
We investigate whether video pretraining can support reliable industrial manipulation with limited action data.
We propose FLUX-mimic, a video-action model, motivated by the potential of video pretraining to capture motion and interaction patterns that enable sample-efficient training.
FLUX-mimic is built on a backbone pretrained on large-scale web and industrial task data, and an action expert to generate robot trajectories.
We train our policy by joint video-action training.
Across four automotive manufacturing benchmark tasks and two bimanual robot platforms, FLUX-mimic outperforms all considered baselines on the dexterous robot platform and matches π0.5\pi_{0.5}’s average success rate on the gripper-based robot platform.
On a deformable part kitting task, FLUX-mimic reaches 77.5% success with as little as two hours of task-specific action-labeled demonstrations.
introduction:
Physical foundation models have been shown to bridge web-scale pretraining and real-world deployment, allowing robots to acquire manipulation behaviors that are difficult to specify through hand-engineered rules and controllers.
However, their adoption in industrial automation remains limited, as high task specificity with characteristic visual and physical properties and scarce demonstration data present significant hurdles.
For example, in the automotive industry, typical tasks include inserting components into rigid fixtures with tight clearances, routing flexible cables through constrained geometry, and picking parts from unstructured bins into ordered slots (see Fig. ), yielding scenes with metal panels, foam and rubber components, wire harnesses, and densely populated trays.
These tasks require precise control under visual and geometric variation, and are substantially different from standard web-scale priors.

Popular large-scale robot datasets, such as Open X-Embodiment [1] and DROID [2], provide diverse robot demonstrations with everyday objects in household environments.
Such generic datasets are often used during pretraining, but components and interactions encountered in industrial settings are not well covered.
To address this, we collect demonstrations of industrial tasks with materials and objects used in real production environments.

While vision-language-action models (VLAs), such as RT-2 [3], OpenVLA [4], and π0.5\pi_{0.5} [5], provide strong language-visual semantics, industrial tasks place particular demands on physical reasoning about geometry, contact, and object dynamics.
Video-action models (VAMs), such as mimic-video [6] and DreamZero [7] address this by predicting robot actions based on representations from a generative video model.
These representations inherently capture how a scene changes over time and provide a strong foundation for physical reasoning.

In this work, we present FLUX-mimic [8], a VAM trained on both video and action data of industrial tasks, that builds on top of a large-scale pretrained video backbone.
We study whether this approach improves performance and how it compares with alternative policies when action-labeled demonstrations are scarce.

We evaluate our policies on two bimanual platforms: Franka Robotics 7-DoF arms with dexterous hands, and Trossen Widow X robotic arms with two-finger grippers.
The benchmark covers four tasks from automotive manufacturing operations on Franka and two of these tasks on the Trossen set-up.
FLUX-mimic achieves higher or on par success rates when compared to π0.5\pi_{0.5} and single-task flow matching policies.
We also study sample efficiency and show that FLUX-mimic exceeds both baselines’ full-data performance using only one quarter of the action data for policy training.

The main contributions of this work are:

FLUX-mimic, a video-action model for industrial manipulation that combines a large-scale pretrained video backbone with joint video-action policy training.

A real-robot evaluation on two bimanual robot platforms with different end effectors, covering four automotive tasks on Franka and two on Trossen.

A study of sample efficiency on a deformable part kitting task, using six training data budgets, and an ablation of the joint video-action prediction objective used in our model.

1. FLUX-mimic, a video-action model for industrial manipulation that combines a large-scale pretrained video backbone with joint video-action policy training.

2. A real-robot evaluation on two bimanual robot platforms with different end effectors, covering four automotive tasks on Franka and two on Trossen.

3. A study of sample efficiency on a deformable part kitting task, using six training data budgets, and an ablation of the joint video-action prediction objective used in our model.

title: COMBS: Concealed Object Multi-modal Bayesian Search
authors: Taylor Bergeron,Kevin Leahy
abstract: This work addresses the problem of finding a concealed object in an environment by unifying formalisms for partially observable environments with multi-modal priors drawn from a mix of ontologies, semantic networks, LLMs, and VLMs. We propose a concealment-adaptive mixed-observability MDP (CA-MOMDP), a Bayes-adaptive setting where uncertainty is over both object locations and which nodes can conceal them, held as a hypothesis with a bounded ontology prior and resolved only by interaction. We define a hierarchical transition system (HTS) to abstract the environment into room and object nodes that can be planned over via our CA-MOMDP. We further propose a COMBS-score: a multi-modal fusion of a human informed semantic network, LLM, and VLM, to initialize the belief over object locations, which grounds our abstractions and reduces reliance on a single model. Belief is maintained via Bayes’ rule, which never lets a look rule out a closed container. We prove a present target is found in a bounded number of searches under exact perception and that its location is never ruled out given missed detection under noisy perception. We ablate each component to demonstrate their significance. Across five simulator configurations, from a gridworld to Matterport3D with a real detector, COMBS finds 92–100% of in-distribution and 92–100% of out-of-distribution targets, matches or beats the baselines in processing speed, significantly outperforms a per-step LLM policy at lower cost on the larger scenes, recovers more out-of-distribution placements than a TidyBot ranking, and matches an LLM-only prior at a fraction of its per-decision latency. COMBS is the only standalone method that can declare a target absent at a stated error level, and the per-step LLM policy offered a termination action abandons 12–22% of targets that were present, against 1.6–3.2% for COMBS on the same episodes.
introduction:
Modern perception models give a robot many partial, uncertain views of a scene, but a planner needs a belief it can act on, and building that belief in a principled way remains an open problem. Building an abstraction of the environment to reason over requires grounding the perception observations, which can draw on learned models, ontologies, and knowledge of how the environment layout limits what the robot can see. Consider searching for a target object that may be fully occluded in a partially known environment. Solving this task requires principled fusion of these data streams together with a hierarchical search that accounts for perception and observation uncertainty.

Semantic scene structure has largely asked what structure best represents a scene for a downstream task regardless of exploration techniques, but the structures typically do not account for what perception has not seen, meaning it becomes difficult to reason about where an object may be–a requirement for this problem [1, 2].
Works on semantic search consider a single data source or pretrained model and only consider a fully observable environment, which are not robust to LLM-related drawbacks or out-of-distribution data  [3, 4, 5, 6, 7].
Some works focus on searching for partially to fully occluded objects using existing models
but require spatial descriptions of where an object can be found  [8, 9, 10]. Other occluded-object search works train a network to guide container search, but
explore each container in turn rather than trading off opening against searching elsewhere and
fail on out-of-distribution placements [11].
Belief-based search models uncertainty about the locations of things already known to exist, rather than uncertainty over what exists at all, which is required for searching for a concealed target [12, 13].
Manipulation-based approaches search for an occluded object by moving clutter [14],
sometimes reasoning about target-object geometry relative to the scene [15], but they do not consider higher-level exploration. Conversely, household domain approaches [16, 17] focus on placement, so the answer is a destination to execute rather than a hypothesis to test, and a wrong guess is never contradicted by observation.

We develop a framework, Concealed Object Multi-modal Bayesian Search (COMBS) to both leverage environment hierarchy though abstraction and semantic knowledge through multi-modal data fusion to find an object without any additional input or location descriptions.

Our contributions are: 1) a hierarchical transition system (HTS) whose edges are the robot’s actions and whose nodes grow only when an action reveals objects, the structure concealed-object search requires, since a hidden object is reached only by opening what holds it; 2) the CA-MOMDP, a factored Bayes-adaptive mixed-observability formulation, planned over the HTS, in which the robot’s uncertainty covers not only where the target is but which nodes could be hiding it; and 3) a multi-modal prior, fused in log-odds with bounded influence from any single source, which initializes the CA-MOMDP’s belief.

title: MOSAIC: Modular Obstacle and Spatial-Aware Framework for Manipulation In Cluttered Scenes
authors: Richard Shi,Mohammad Mahdavian,Mehrdad Momeni Zadeh,Mohammed Elmahgiubi,Amir Rasouli
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong performance in robotic manipulation, yet most rely primarily on 2D visual observations and language instructions, leaving scene geometry and obstacle relationships to be inferred implicitly. This limitation is particularly problematic in cluttered environments, where small spatial errors can lead to unintended contacts or collisions. We propose MOSAIC, a modular spatial- and obstacle-aware framework that can be integrated with pretrained VLA policies to improve object-level scene understanding and action generation. Our method augments the VLA backbone with an auxiliary semantic grounding task that predicts role-specific masks for the target object, destination region, and surrounding obstacles. We further combine the target and destination masks with depth estimated from 3D scene reconstruction to construct role-specific geometric tokens that are injected directly into the action expert. In addition, we propose obstacle-aware attention supervision that emphasizes obstacles near the robot body during task execution. The resulting attention features are subsequently injected into later action-expert layers to further guide action generation. Together, these components provide explicit semantic, geometric, and obstacle-aware cues while preserving the underlying pretrained VLA architecture. We evaluate our framework on pretrained VLA model using the RoboPRO benchmark, including visual perturbation tests, and further validate it on real-world manipulation tasks. MOSAIC improves the success rate by 5.1% in cluttered scenes, and by 9.7% under visual perturbations, with gains of up to 25.0% in the most challenging environment. We will release our code and dataset upon acceptance at the following Github page: https://mmahdavian.github.io/MOSAIC/
introduction:
VLAs have emerged as powerful robotic foundation models for understanding task context, spatial reasoning, and executing physical-world tasks. VLAs typically build on Vision-Language Models (VLMs) [1, 2] by extending their interfaces with proprioceptive inputs and action outputs. Actions are commonly generated either through discrete token prediction [3, 4] or specialized action experts based on diffusion [5, 6] or flow matching [7, 8, 9]. Despite their strong performance, generalization to unseen scenarios remains challenging, particularly for manipulation in cluttered scenes [10].

Several approaches improve VLA generalization through large-scale pretraining [11], cross-embodiment learning [12], and world or future-state modeling [13], however at the cost of substantial data and computation. Recent methods incorporate explicit spatial grounding through 3D geometry [14] or task-relevant objects understanding [15, 16], providing richer scene representations for more generalizable manipulation. However, these approaches generally do not explicitly model surrounding obstacles as a separate component.

To improve object understanding of VLA models, existing approaches condition the policy on object-level 2D information, such as target-object masks [17] or target and destination regions [15], or inject depth and 3D point-cloud information directly into the action expert [18, 19, 16]. While such grounding improves the spatial representations available for action generation, these methods at best focus on the target object and its destination. In cluttered environments, the lack of explicit obstacle awareness can lead to unintended contacts, collisions, and ambiguous actions.

A further challenge caused by object clutter and visual noise is that they can divert the policy’s attention away from task-relevant regions. Prior work shows that VLA action experts naturally attend to the target object and destination [20]. Several methods further guide this attention by aligning model attention maps with human gaze estimates or target-object masks to improve performance and interpretability [21, 22]. But these approaches rarely guide attention toward surrounding obstacles, which are critical for safe and reliable manipulation in cluttered scenes.

To improve spatial and object-level reasoning in VLA models, we propose MOSAIC (Fig. 1), a modular framework that combines semantic masks from the VLA backbone with VGGT-Ω\Omega [23] to extract role-specific object geometry. These 3D features are encoded as tokens and injected into the action expert for clutter-aware manipulation. We further introduce contact-point-aware attention supervision over the obstacles, and re-inject the resulting attention features into later action-expert layers to guide action generation.

In summary, our main contributions are as follows:

We propose MOSAIC, a novel modular framework that enhances object-centric understanding and spatial reasoning in VLA models, enabling more effective manipulation in cluttered environments.

We propose MOSAIC, a novel modular framework that enhances object-centric understanding and spatial reasoning in VLA models, enabling more effective manipulation in cluttered environments.

Our modules augment a pretrained VLA with components that explicitly model surrounding obstacles using its own backbone, while injecting semantic object-level depth information into the action-generation process.

We guide VLA attention beyond the target object and destination region toward surrounding obstacles, improving action generation in cluttered scenes.

We demonstrate improvements in manipulation performance when applying our proposed modules to pretrained VLA models, evaluated on the RoboPRO benchmark and experimented with real-world robots.

1. We propose MOSAIC, a novel modular framework that enhances object-centric understanding and spatial reasoning in VLA models, enabling more effective manipulation in cluttered environments.

2. Our modules augment a pretrained VLA with components that explicitly model surrounding obstacles using its own backbone, while injecting semantic object-level depth information into the action-generation process.

3. We guide VLA attention beyond the target object and destination region toward surrounding obstacles, improving action generation in cluttered scenes.

4. We demonstrate improvements in manipulation performance when applying our proposed modules to pretrained VLA models, evaluated on the RoboPRO benchmark and experimented with real-world robots.

title: Runtime Safety and Emergency Stops on a Full-Size Humanoid: Deployment Lessons and a Case for Graduated Force Authority
authors: Max Conway,Yutong Zhang,Allen Devaraj,William Xie,Alessandro Roncone,Nikolaus Correll
abstract: Full-size humanoid robots are being considered for hazardous industrial work such as disassembling electric-vehicle batteries. We describe the safety mechanisms of an open-source autonomy stack for the Unitree H1-2 humanoid and what deploying them taught us. All joint commands pass through a safety layer that runs separately from the control software. It enforces joint position, velocity, and torque limits, and it stops the robot when a state estimate becomes stale or when the hard-wired emergency stop (e-stop) is pressed or disconnected. We pushed the standing robot until it lost balance. With a model-predictive lower-body controller it never recovered, and the operator had to press the e-stop in every trial. Pressing it removes balance control, and the robot falls. The safety layer’s own limits trigger the same stop, and limits chosen for manipulation were exceeded during normal walking. Near an operator or a battery pack, the fall can be more dangerous than the cause of the stop. Joint limits bound how much force a robot can apply, but not when applying it is appropriate. Drawing on research on responsibility and on child and adolescent development, we therefore make a case for granting robots force authority in stages, with a person or organization explicitly responsible for its use.

title: RUMI: A Robotiq-Matched Universal Manipulation Interface for Robot Learning with Augmented Reality and Haptic Feedback
authors: Kevin Avdiu,Seongjin Bien,Yannik Blei,Philine Meister,Johannes Hechtl,Philipp Schmitt,Kai Wurm,Georg von Wichert,Wolfram Burgard
abstract:
Many manipulation tasks require carefully controlled contact forces for successful execution, yet large-scale, force-aware datasets remain scarce.
Handheld interfaces can help by transmitting interaction forces directly through the operator’s arm, but most existing designs are tailored to simple linear grippers and do not match the nonlinear mechanics of widely used robotic grippers. We present RUMI, a handheld universal manipulation interface matched to the Robotiq 2F-85 with exchangeable fingertip sensors that preserves the target gripper geometry while enabling natural input before contact and force measurement after contact. By integrating the tracking system into a virtual reality headset, our method provides real-time augmented reality feedback about the kinematic feasibility of motion on the target robot platform.
We further introduce a haptic feedback mechanism that supports force-aware teleoperation for simulated and real robots. A user study shows fewer episodes containing joint-limit violations with live robot visualization and pose initialization (3/50) than without augmented reality (16/50). We additionally train imitation policies from demonstrations, collected using two different fingertip modalities enabled by the gripper-matched hardware, and assess the haptic interface’s capability for collecting force-aware teleoperation datasets in simulation. The code and assets for RUMI are available at: https://utn-air.github.io/RUMI/.

title: Prediction-Error-Tightened MPC for Socially Compliant Crowd Navigation
authors: Alessandro Febbraro,Federico Rollo,Marcello Farina,Luca Bascetta,Navvab Kashiri
comment: . Submitted to the European Control Conference (ECC 2027)
abstract: Autonomous navigation of mobile robots in crowded environments, while preserving pedestrians’ psychological comfort, requires distinguishing pedestrians from other obstacles, predicting their future motion, and accounting for uncertainty in the predicted trajectories of both pedestrians and the robot. This work extends a previous MPC framework by integrating obstacle and pedestrian detection, Koopman-based motion prediction, and online prediction-error estimation directly within the collision-avoidance mechanism. To reduce collision-avoidance complexity in crowded scenarios, nearby obstacles are aggregated, thereby reducing the number of collision-avoidance constraints. Simulation studies evaluate the prediction-error margins and the computational benefits of semantics-aware aggregation. In a paired 300-seed closed-loop comparison with a moving generic obstacle, Markov residual tightening reduces the fraction of runs with physical contact from 10.0%10.0\% to 1.33%1.33\%, at a mean travel-time cost of 0.680.68 s. In a separate crowd-navigation semantic ablation, the offline robot-footprint/personal-space overlap occupies 2.11%2.11\% of observed time with pedestrian-aware handling versus 22.84%22.84\% with generic-obstacle handling.
introduction:
Mobile robots operating in crowded human environments must not only avoid collisions, but also move predictably and comfortably around pedestrians. This requires preserving suitable interpersonal distances, anticipating human motion, and avoiding abrupt maneuvers [1, 2], particularly for assistive platforms such as autonomous wheelchairs [3].

Socially aware navigation has been addressed through model-based, learning-based, and hybrid approaches [1, 4]. Learning-based methods can capture complex interactions but require substantial data, may generalize poorly to unseen scenarios, and typically lack explicit safety guarantees [1, 5, 2]. MPC offers an attractive model-based alternative because tracking, actuation limits, obstacle avoidance, motion smoothness, and proxemic requirements can be handled within a unified optimization framework [6, 7, 8]. Its effectiveness, however, depends on reliable motion prediction and on maintaining real-time solvability as collision-avoidance constraints increase [7].

Prediction uncertainty has therefore received increasing attention in MPC-based navigation. Uncertainty-aware objectives and constraints can introduce conservatism depending on their formulation [9], while conformal-prediction methods construct uncertainty regions from offline calibration data [10] or adapt them online from observed errors [11]. In this work, collision cones are used to identify relative velocities that may lead to a collision with an obstacle [12, 13, 14] and prediction errors are taken into account in both collision-cone detection and the collision-avoidance constraints of the MPC.

Short-horizon motion prediction remains challenging,
particularly when pedestrians change direction.
Koopman-based models approximate nonlinear motion
through linear evolution in a lifted space and have
been investigated for pedestrian and moving-obstacle
prediction [15, 16].
Here, a finite-dimensional Koopman operator is
updated online for each tracked dynamic obstacle.

A further challenge is computational scalability in crowds, where each obstacle may generate constraints over multiple prediction steps [7]. Unlike group-level representations aimed primarily at modeling pedestrian-group motion [17], we use grouping as a constraint-reduction mechanism. Nearby detections are aggregated while retaining pedestrian personal spaces and the detected geometry of generic obstacles; the resulting group representation is used both for collision-cone screening and for constructing a reduced set of separating constraints.

Using the linear-MPC/input–output-linearization architecture in
[8] as the nominal control backbone, the main contributions
of this work are:

a prediction-error-tightened collision-avoidance formulation in which
errors affecting collision-cone screening and separating constraints are
characterized online through second moments and incorporated through
Markov-based margins; and

a semantics-aware obstacle-aggregation strategy that preserves
pedestrian personal spaces and generic-obstacle geometry while reducing
the number of separating collision-avoidance constraints.

title: Robot-Induced Bias in Movement Smoothness Metrics for Rehabilitation: Quantification and Correction in Simulation
authors: David Regev,Alex Scherbakov,Eran Beeri Bamani
comment: . Submitted to the 2027 IEEE International Conference on Rehabilitation Robotics (ICORR)
abstract: Robot mechanics can bias kinematic measures of recovery and limit comparisons across rehabilitation devices. We developed a closed-loop human–robot simulation calibrated to published healthy and stroke group kinematics. Paired runs held motor-control parameters and movement plans fixed to quantify bias in seven metrics relative to a low-impedance reference, normalized using external repeatability benchmarks. Within a subset informed by published device specifications, median log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) bias was 0.930.93 and 1.791.79 benchmark units for stroke and healthy profiles, respectively. Sobol analysis identified Coulomb friction and apparent mass as leading contributors; LDLJ bias persisted across 11 robustness variants. LDLJ bias increased as simulated movements became less fragmented. If recovery similarly reduces fragmentation, this effect could partly mask improvement in measured smoothness. Correction combining identified robot dynamics and observed metrics with gradient-boosted trees reduced median normalized absolute error from 0.770.77 to 0.100.10 for LDLJ and from 0.240.24 to 0.080.08 for spectral arc length (SPARC) in the device-informed subset of a random 20% hold-out. Median smoothness residuals remained at or below 0.150.15 benchmark units across four separately held-out parameter regions. Under an alternative controller, LDLJ error decreased from 1.601.60 to 0.170.17 without retraining, although transfer varied across metrics. These simulation results support mechanical characterization and movement-dependent correction toward more comparable robotic assessments, motivating validation in patients.
introduction:
Robotic devices are increasingly used not only to deliver therapy but also to measure recovery. End-effector robots such as MIT-MANUS record hand kinematics, yielding measures of smoothness, speed, straightness, and endpoint accuracy that track recovery after stroke and correlate with clinical scales [1, 2]. Test–retest studies provide minimal detectable change (MDC) estimates for interpreting changes within specific robotic assessment protocols [3]. Video-based gait and balance assessment also relies on reliable clinical measures [4, 5, 6]; repeatability alone does not establish cross-device comparability. Interpreting unadjusted differences across devices as differences in patient function assumes that robot mechanics do not materially influence these measures. That assumption is questionable, because the robot is part of the dynamical system that produces the movement. Its apparent mass, viscous and Coulomb friction, and residual controller impedance load the arm during every reach. Such effects can introduce systematic shifts that repeated measurements on the same device may reproduce rather than reveal, making repeatability alone insufficient to establish comparability. Robot dynamics can alter wrist smoothness in ways that depend on movement configuration and metric selection [7]. In stroke survivors, higher peak acceleration and mean jerk were observed on the low-impedance DORIS robot than on the HapticMaster [8]. A recent systematic review further highlights the need for consistent methods to evaluate robot transparency and support comparisons across studies and devices [9].

What remains open is (i) how large these effects are across standard assessment metrics, expressed against repeatability benchmarks; (ii) which robot properties drive them and how their effects interact with motor control; (iii) how compensation for robot dynamics changes the bias; and (iv) how accurately this bias can be corrected. Simulation enables matched comparisons of the same motor-control model across parameterized robots, isolating mechanical effects while systematically varying patient and recording factors. This is particularly useful when motor-control variability and adaptation would otherwise make it difficult to attribute a metric difference to a specific mechanical property. Quantifying these effects provides a basis for interpreting device-dependent scores and identifying assessment metrics that are less sensitive to robot mechanics.

We address these questions through a closed-loop simulation of reaching with parameterized end-effector robots. Figure 1 illustrates the three stages of the approach. The first stage pairs each simulated reaching condition with a run on the low-impedance reference robot, preserving the motor-control parameters and movement plan. The second stage quantifies the resulting metric shifts; the middle panel shows simulated hand-speed profiles alongside the computed smoothness biases. Finally, the identified robot dynamics and measured movement features are used to predict and subtract the bias, yielding an estimate of the corresponding reference-device metric. Our main contributions are:

A simulation of human-robot reaching calibrated to published healthy and stroke group kinematics, incorporating delayed feedback, motor noise, and different levels of compensation for robot dynamics.

A quantitative analysis of robot-induced bias in seven assessment metrics, normalized using published MDC values and repeatability-derived benchmarks, with global Sobol sensitivity analysis to identify the contributions of robot, motor-control, and recording parameters.

A correction method that combines robot dynamics identification with measured movement features to estimate metrics on a specified low-impedance reference robot. On a random 20% hold-out of simulated cases, it reduces median absolute bias in log dimensionless jerk (LDLJ) from 0.770.77 to 0.100.10 benchmark units. Further evaluations compare the method with a regression baseline and test its transfer to held-out conditions and an alternative motor-control model.

title: What World Model Does Active Object Search Need? A Study under Imperfect Detection
authors: Kyeongryeol Go
comment: Accepted in CoRL 2026 Workshop on Do Robots Need World Models
abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions. Through comprehensive ablations in Isaac Sim and HSSD houses, we examine the roles of these representations and their update mechanisms across different detector configurations. Notably, target belief and its update mechanisms are critical to search performance, with their contribution generally increasing as detection errors become more prevalent. These findings highlight the importance of maintaining and updating target beliefs to support reliable active search under uncertain detector observations, providing insights into the design of world models for embodied agents. Code is available in our GitHub repository.
introduction:
In active object search, a robot chooses where to point its camera until it can state where a target object
is [2, 32]. Consider a mobile manipulator instructed to “bring me the mug” while the mug is
behind a box on a shelf. Before grasping, it must decide where to look next and when it has gathered enough evidence. When a
view yields no detection, the target may be occluded, outside the frame, or visible but missed by the detector (a
false negative). Open-vocabulary detectors miss targets often enough that a non-detection alone cannot distinguish
these cases. They also report objects that are absent (false positives), so a single detection does not settle
the target’s location either.

Interpreting such observations calls for a world model. Most robot world models reconstruct the scene or predict future
observations [4, 23, 26]. Active object search, however, depends on a narrower
quantity: the probability that a view detects the target, given the detector’s error rates. Previous methods already
maintain beliefs over the target and model visibility [32, 11], but few predict
detection from probabilistic occlusion and fitted detector error rates together [31, 34, 33].
To our knowledge, no controlled study has isolated which of these components the decisions
use [29, 22, 35]. We therefore ask which world-model representations active
object search requires when the detector is imperfect.

We make two contributions. First, we present Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS), a belief-based world model
that predicts detection rather than the scene (Section 2). It maintains a target belief over the target’s
location and size and an occupancy belief used only to predict visibility, and it trains no network. Second,
the separable components enable a controlled study with an oracle and two open-vocabulary detectors in
Isaac Sim [27] and in Habitat Synthetic Scenes Dataset (HSSD) houses [21] in
Habitat-Sim [28]. The study replaces the occupancy belief with the true geometry, ablates each
component, crosses view and stop rules, and injects detector errors.

Probabilistic object search updates a belief after non-detections, with a hand-set
detection probability and binary occlusion [32, 31], or with a point
target [11, 34]. BAMOS instead fits the detector’s error rates and treats the target’s
size as uncertain. Open-vocabulary object navigation uses real detectors [29, 6] and
lowers map values where nothing was detected, with heuristic weights [35, 22]. BAMOS
replaces these weights with a likelihood. World models reconstruct the
scene [17, 25, 24, 20] or predict
observations [14, 15, 1], although a model need only be accurate in the
quantities a decision depends on [13, 30]. BAMOS is a case study of this principle
(Appendix E).

title: GraSLA: A Lightweight Spatial-Language-Action Model with Grasp Hypotheses as Geometric Priors
authors: Jibao Yuan,Zixiang Zhao,Wensong Xu,Siqi Lu,Shaofei Chen
abstract:
This paper focuses on improving the behavioral diversity and effectiveness of language-conditioned manipulation policies trained through imitation learning.
Recently, continuous-action policies have become mainstream in robotic manipulation, but the lack of diverse demonstrations tends to restrict their behavioral diversity.
For grasping, a fundamental subtask of manipulation, 6-DoF grasp detection provides diverse grasp hypotheses, but open-loop execution constrains responsiveness in dynamic environments.
This motivates us to combine the diversity of grasp hypotheses with the adaptability of continuous-action policies.
To this end, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight and effective spatial-language-action model with grasp hypotheses as geometric priors.
In particular, we employ spatial and language foundation models to encode scene geometry and task semantics, and integrate them with grasp hypotheses through bidirectional cross-attention for continuous action prediction.
On LIBERO, GraSLA achieves an average success rate of 99.30%.
introduction:
In language-conditioned manipulation, robots use observations to perform tasks specified by language instructions [31]. Despite progress in language-conditioned methods [2, 19], translating instructions into precise actions remains challenging. In doing so, robots must account for task-relevant spatial relationships in the environment. Accordingly, using these relationships for action generation has attracted increasing research interest [17, 29].

In this work, we focus on manipulation with parallel-jaw grippers. Based on their execution pipelines, existing methods can be broadly divided into two categories [45]: (1) pose-based methods, which predict target end-effector poses and use motion planning for execution [13, 31]; (2) continuous-control methods, which directly predict actions for robot control [2, 6]. Each has its strengths and limitations. The former can provide diverse target poses [34], but open-loop execution of planned motions limits responsiveness in dynamic environments [40]. The latter support closed-loop execution, but demonstration coverage may limit behavioral diversity [6].

A natural idea is to combine the strengths of both approaches [7, 15, 30, 40]. Specifically, diverse target poses can reveal different interaction possibilities, guiding continuous-control policies toward a variety of action sequences. These possibilities depend on the spatial relationship between the gripper and the environment, for which 6-DoF grasp detection provides a large set of grasp hypotheses as geometric priors [34, 36]. Meanwhile, language foundation models (LFMs) capture instruction semantics [8], while spatial foundation models (SFMs) encode 3D scene structure [49], together providing complementary information for interpreting grasp hypotheses. In this context, can these hypotheses be integrated with language and spatial representations to guide continuous action prediction?

Building on this idea, we propose GraSLA, a lightweight spatial-language-action (SLA) model that uses grasp hypotheses to guide continuous action prediction. Specifically, we first obtain spatial tokens from multi-view point clouds with Utonia [49], language tokens from instructions with BERT [8], and grasp tokens by projecting grasp hypotheses from GSNet [36]. These tokens interact through bidirectional cross-attention, integrating grasp hypotheses with scene geometry and instruction semantics. Finally, an action decoder [50] predicts a chunk of continuous actions from the fused tokens and robot state.

In our experiments, we evaluate GraSLA on LIBERO [25], conduct ablation studies, and report inference latency. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

We propose GraSLA, a lightweight spatial-language-action model that incorporates grasp hypotheses as geometric priors for language-conditioned continuous control.

We propose GraSLA, a lightweight spatial-language-action model that incorporates grasp hypotheses as geometric priors for language-conditioned continuous control.

We design a spatial-language-grasp interaction module that fuses grasp, spatial, and language representations through bidirectional cross-attention.

LIBERO results show strong task performance, and ablations confirm the value of grasp hypotheses and cross-modal fusion.

1. We propose GraSLA, a lightweight spatial-language-action model that incorporates grasp hypotheses as geometric priors for language-conditioned continuous control.

2. We design a spatial-language-grasp interaction module that fuses grasp, spatial, and language representations through bidirectional cross-attention.

3. LIBERO results show strong task performance, and ablations confirm the value of grasp hypotheses and cross-modal fusion.

title: Embedded Sim-to-Real Visual Servoing: Learned Reaching and Force-Guided Placement
authors: Dezhi Sun,Duy Khang Banh,Kenan Niu
comment: . Accepted at IEEE ROBIO 2026
abstract:
Embedded perception-to-control systems must combine visual targeting
with reliable contact handling under tight computational constraints.
We present a shared architecture on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin
controlling a Franka Research 3 through Cartesian impedance control.
RealSense D435i observations, YOLO11-seg segmentation, depth
back-projection, and hand–eye calibration provide metric robot-frame
targets. We compare two strategies: compact proximal policy
optimization (PPO) policies transferred from simulation for object-
and hole-region reaching, and force-guided Cartesian placement
using approximately 2 N normal contact and spiral search.
The PPO policies achieved 87.2% and 83.1% success over 1000
simulation episodes each. Across 50 real-robot trials per strategy,
the learned hybrid and force-guided analytical pipelines achieved
70.0% and 74.0% completion, respectively.
Mean perception latency with TensorRT was 34.55 ms.
These results support an embedded architecture combining learned
free-space reaching with explicit contact correction.
introduction:
Embedded visual manipulation integrates perception, motion generation, and physical interaction under computational constraints. RGB-D sensing supports free-space targeting, but constrained placement remains sensitive to localization and orientation errors. Robotic imaging combines visual perception with contact-force regulation [1, 2] and coordinated motion control [3]. Contact and geometric jamming further require compliant local correction [4, 5].

Visual feedback supports robotic control [6, 7, 8], while learning-based manipulation acquires target-conditioned behavior from interaction [9, 10]. RLBench provides simulation-based training [11], and domain or dynamics randomization facilitates sim-to-real transfer [12, 13]. Impedance control, spiral search, and residual learning address contact-rich placement errors [14, 15, 16, 17], with related compliant-control applications in robotic catheterization [18] and ultrasound scanning [19].

Large-scale visuomotor policies offer broad manipulation capabilities but typically require substantial models and robot data [20, 21, 22]. We instead evaluate compact state-based PPO reaching and force-guided analytical placement on a shared embedded platform. YOLO11-seg processes eye-in-hand RGB-D observations on a Jetson AGX Orin to reconstruct targets in the Franka Research 3 (FR3) base frame. Both strategies share sensing, calibration, hardware, and Cartesian impedance execution; the analytical branch additionally uses force and end-effector height during placement.

The main contributions are: (1) Embedded architecture—a Jetson-based pipeline integrating RGB-D segmentation, metric target reconstruction, and compliant FR3 execution; (2) Matched comparison—compact sim-to-real PPO reaching and force-guided analytical placement under common sensing and execution conditions; and (3) Experimental validation—1000 simulation episodes per policy and 50 real-robot trials per strategy. Physical manipulation evaluates an approximately aligned square object, while perception covers all four classes.
