title: Recover, Don't Just Continue: Learning from Feedback for Physical Failure Understanding and Correction
authors: Miao Pan,Kaixiang Yao,Xiaohe Zhou,Xu Wang,Qinfeng Li,Wenqi Zhang,Xuhong Zhang
abstract: Multimodal large language models are increasingly regarded as the cognitive foundation of embodied intelligence, yet planning from instructions alone does not make them reliable embodied brains. During physical execution, actions deviate from intended effects, and what can be realized is jointly constrained by the embodiment, controller, and environment. An embodied brain must therefore understand why execution deviates, identify what the current execution system can reliably realize, and revise decisions using interaction experience. These three requirements correspond to causal failure localization, capability-constrained adaptation, and experience-driven revision, which are complementary and non-substitutable. Although current embodied foundation models have advanced spatio-temporal reasoning, physical-world modeling, and high-level planning, they still largely lack these capabilities. To address this gap, we introduce Embodied-Corrector. We construct controlled failure–recovery data by injecting a single controlled perturbation at subtask boundaries of successful trajectories (navigation, reachability, grasp pose, control timing, articulation state, task prerequisite, or target grounding), replaying the affected subtask, and retaining only failures that are observable from public execution evidence and recoverable from the current state; we then align actions, observable consequences, failure causes, and executable recoveries into Judge–Cause–Sub–Fine supervision. Training uses evaluation-first SFT: the model first learns Judge and Cause, and then learns Sub and Fine conditioned on accurate Judge/Cause prefixes. Because SFT uses accurate prefixes while deployment can only use self-generated prefixes, evaluation errors propagate into recovery planning, and response-level rewards are too coarse to locate the affected planning tokens. We therefore use OPD to internalize the planning distribution under accurate Judge/Cause prefixes into the planning distribution under self-generated prefixes: during training, the model generates plans from self-generated Judge/Cause prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate Judge/Cause prefixes compares token probabilities and reinforces or suppresses planning tokens; at deployment, this contrastive branch is removed and no labels are exposed. Experiments on embodied failure reasoning and planning benchmarks show stronger failure-cause analysis and corrective planning: with a frozen VLA, composite task success improves by 6.1 percentage points, and with fixed GPT-5.5 execution, embodied manipulation and navigation tasks improve by 13.9 percentage points.
introduction:
Multimodal large language models are becoming an important foundation for embodied intelligence (Driess et al., 2023; Brohan et al., 2023a; Ahn et al., 2022a; Reed et al., 2022). By combining visual understanding with language reasoning, they can interpret task goals, reason about scene relations, and decompose complex instructions into executable steps (Liang et al., 2023a; Huang et al., 2022a; Singh et al., 2023; Song et al., 2023; Pan et al., 2026a). Recent embodied foundation models such as RynnBrain (Dang et al., 2026b), RoboBrain 2.0 (BAAI RoboBrain Team, 2026), and Embodied-Reasoner (Zhang et al., 2026a) have advanced spatio-temporal memory, physical-world reasoning, and embodied planning; VeBrain-1.5 (VeBrain Team, 2026) further unifies multimodal perception, spatial reasoning, and robot control in a shared decision interface. However, a reliable embodied brain requires more than planning. During physical execution, actions deviate from intended effects, and what can be realized is jointly constrained by the embodiment, controller, and environment (Anonymous, 2026b). An embodied brain must therefore understand why execution deviated, recognize what the current executor can reliably realize, and adjust decisions using interaction experience. This raises the central question: how can a multimodal model evolve from planning what to do into an embodied brain that understands physical interaction, adapts to execution capability, and corrects its behavior after failure?

We argue that this requires three related but non-substitutable capabilities. First, physical causal understanding and failure localization (Ying and others, 2026; Liu et al., 2026a; Anonymous, 2026d) requires determining not only that an execution failed, but also which action, physical relation, or unmet prerequisite caused it. Existing failure-memory and detection methods can flag unsuccessful outcomes (Ying and others, 2026), yet a model may observe an object not placed into a container while failing to distinguish incorrect grasp timing, inappropriate contact pose, or an earlier uncompleted step. Effective correction requires tracing execution back to the condition that first invalidated progress. Second, execution-capability identification and adaptation (Physical Intelligence Team, 2026; Ghosh et al., 2024) requires translating intent into a form the current executor can reliably realize. Even a correct diagnosis is ineffective if the recovery exceeds the controller’s capability. The brain should adapt instruction content and granularity, e.g., decomposing a long request into state-conditioned subtasks for a frozen VLA Physical Intelligence Team (2026); Brohan et al. (2023b); O’Neill et al. (2024). Third, in-context learning from interaction experience (Chen et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026c; Sridhar et al., 2025) requires information from one execution to change the next decision. Prior work indicates that a robot’s own physical interaction experience can support in-context learning even when the policy model is frozen (Chen et al., 2026). Failure observations, previous actions, and successful corrections should become evidence for planning rather than accumulating in context while the model repeats the same behavior (Anonymous, 2026a; Anonymous, 2026c).

We first examine whether current embodied brains possess these capabilities. On failed EB-ALFRED (Yang et al., 2025b) executions, we supply frozen multimodal models with the same task goal, visual observations, executed actions, and execution feedback, and inspect predicted failure cause and proposed next-step correction. As shown in Figure 1(a), models such as RynnBrain (Dang et al., 2026b), MiMo-Embodied (Xiaomi MiMo Team, 2026), and InternVL3 (OpenGVLab, 2025) frequently produce plausible descriptions while failing to identify the condition that actually blocks progress, and their plans often fail to repair it. This exposes weak physical causal understanding and failure localization. The missing capability is not merely recognizing failure, but transforming execution evidence into an explanation of why it failed and what must change next.

We next ask what form this missing information should take. Keeping the evaluated brain, visual input, action interface, and decoding fixed on EB-ALFRED, we vary only the feedback after failure. As shown in Figure 1(b), repeating the failed outcome provides little benefit (Shinn et al., 2023a), whereas supplying the concrete failure cause consistently improves performance. For RoboBrain2.5-4B, MiMo-Embodied-7B, and InternVL3-8B, cause-level feedback changes task success from 0.220.22 to 0.280.28, from 0.200.20 to 0.270.27, and from 0.200.20 to 0.240.24. Useful feedback does not simply state failure; it identifies which expected condition was violated and why that prevents progress, revising the brain’s interpretation of the task state. Together, these diagnostics indicate that current models lack not only failure analysis, but also execution-capability adaptation and in-context learning from interaction: outcome repetition alone does not change subsequent decisions, and only explicit causal feedback enables correction.

Motivated by this, we introduce Embodied-Corrector, which couples the three capabilities through data, training, and inference. For physical causal understanding and failure localization, we build controlled failure–recovery data by branching successful trajectories at subtask boundaries and intervening on navigation, reachability, grasp pose, control timing, articulation state, task prerequisites, and target grounding. Each branch shares the preceding successful context while changing one controlled factor, and we retain only failures observable from public execution evidence and recoverable from the realized state. The resulting paired failure–recovery experience connects what changed, what consequence it caused, and what must be restored.

To obtain such data at scale, we build an automated pipeline that coordinates simulation environments, robot execution interfaces, multimodal models, and tools for trajectory generation, failure construction, cause annotation, and correction verification, with a Harness providing runtime support for interaction and data collection. Each sample contains four fields: Judge determines whether the current subtask is completed; Cause identifies the failure cause supported by observable evidence; Sub decides whether to advance to the next subtask or redo the current subtask; and Fine specifies how to execute Sub, including actions, target arguments, execution order, and verification steps. Learning from such data is challenging: Judge/Cause errors contaminate Sub/Fine; SFT trains Sub/Fine with accurate Judge/Cause prefixes, whereas deployment can only use self-generated Judge/Cause, creating a prefix distribution mismatch; response-level rewards are too coarse to locate the planning tokens affected by evaluation errors; and Fine must satisfy the realizability constraints of a frozen executor. We therefore adopt “evaluation-first SFT + OPD internalization.” In the first stage, we train Judge/Cause, and then supervise Sub/Fine generation with accurate Judge/Cause prefixes. In the second stage, we use OPD: during training, the model generates Sub/Fine from self-generated Judge/Cause prefixes, while a contrastive forward pass with accurate Judge/Cause prefixes compares token probabilities and reinforces planning words supported by accurate diagnoses or suppresses contradictory ones. Accurate diagnoses are used only for scoring and do not replace self-generated prefixes; at deployment, the contrastive branch is removed, and the model still autonomously generates Judge/Cause and Sub/Fine. Thus, a single inference outputs the complete Judge–Cause–Sub–Fine and produces state-conditioned recovery plans realizable by a frozen executor.

Experiments evaluate corrective reasoning and execution with fixed backends. First, on brain-level corrective reasoning, Embodied-Corrector substantially improves failure-cause analysis and produces recovery plans consistent with the identified physical cause, demonstrating stronger physical causal reasoning rather than outcome classification alone. Second, with the VLA frozen, execution-aware decomposition improves π0.5\pi_{0.5} by 5.4 percentage points on Composite-Seen tasks and by 6.1 percentage points on Composite-Unseen tasks, showing that the brain can adapt task granularity to reduce the burden on a fixed executor. Third, with the GPT-5.5 code generator, robot functions, perception module, and execution budget all fixed, feeding Embodied-Corrector’s diagnosis and recovery back into the next planning context improves all ten execution conditions over the untrained corrective brain, with a macro-average gain of 13.9 percentage points. This shows that execution feedback is not merely stored in history: it changes the next workflow produced by the same planner. Our contributions are threefold:

We identify physical causal understanding, execution-capability adaptation, and in-context learning from interaction feedback as three complementary capabilities for corrective embodied reasoning, and diagnose their absence in current multimodal embodied brains.

We introduce Embodied-Corrector and a controlled failure–recovery data construction pipeline connecting actions, observable physical consequences, failure causes, and executable recoveries, together with evaluation-first SFT.

We evaluate correction from brain-level failure reasoning to fixed-backend execution, showing the learned brain can explain failures, adapt instructions to a frozen VLA, and provide corrective context that changes the subsequent thinking of a code generator.

1. We identify physical causal understanding, execution-capability adaptation, and in-context learning from interaction feedback as three complementary capabilities for corrective embodied reasoning, and diagnose their absence in current multimodal embodied brains.

2. We introduce Embodied-Corrector and a controlled failure–recovery data construction pipeline connecting actions, observable physical consequences, failure causes, and executable recoveries, together with evaluation-first SFT.

3. We evaluate correction from brain-level failure reasoning to fixed-backend execution, showing the learned brain can explain failures, adapt instructions to a frozen VLA, and provide corrective context that changes the subsequent thinking of a code generator.

title: Single-View RGB-D Force--Deformation Estimation for Robotic Manipulation of Elasto-Plastic Materials
authors: Dezhi Sun,Marijn van Hilten,Kenan Niu
comment: . Accepted at IEEE ROBIO 2026
abstract:
Persistent deformation complicates elasto-plastic manipulation by
coupling physical interaction with spatially distributed shape changes.
We investigate the force–deformation relationship using a standard
robot, a single eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, and intrinsic force estimates.
A 7-DoF Franka Emika FR3 performs normal indentations while an Intel
RealSense L515 captures pre- and post-contact surfaces. Point-cloud
processing localizes deformation and estimates displaced volume.
Force–volume characterization includes 27 measurements over nine
force levels. A compact multilayer perceptron (MLP), trained on
52 force–volume pairs at four levels, achieves a held-out RMSE of
1.857 N and R2=0.440R^{2}=0.440. A separate comparison shows lower error
for a quadratic model at 16 N and for the MLP at 19 and 23.5 N.
An eight-step experiment at 4 N per interaction demonstrates
cumulative deformation localization from the second indentation onward.
These results establish a practical measurement basis for
deformation-aware manipulation using intrinsic force estimates
and single-view geometry.
introduction:
Robotic manipulation of deformable objects is challenging because each interaction changes both object geometry and subsequent dynamics. For elasto-plastic materials, the deformation persists and is spatially distributed, while the observable response depends on surface state, interaction history, and material condition. A robot must therefore connect a commanded physical interaction to the resulting surface change without assuming rigid-body behavior [1, 2, 3].

Recent systems have advanced geometric shaping of clay, dough, and related materials. RoboCraft learns particle dynamics for model-predictive shaping, and RoboCook extends learned interaction models to long-horizon tool use [4, 5]. SculptBot learns clay dynamics from point clouds, whereas SculptDiff learns goal-conditioned policies from demonstrations [6, 7]. PinchBot addresses long-horizon pinch actions with guided diffusion, and hierarchical text-to-3D shaping combines learned actions with high-level reasoning [8, 9]. Related approaches use compliant hardware, reinforcement learning, differentiable system identification, or learned predictive control [10, 11, 12]. Dough shaping and robotic pizza stretching further illustrate task-specific sensing and action design [13, 14]. These systems chiefly target goal geometry, learned dynamics, demonstrations, or policy learning.

Related studies have integrated robotic interaction with image-based
perception for ultrasound reconstruction [15],
force-controlled tissue segmentation [16], and
fluoroscopic guidance [17].Sensing choices range from multimodal measurements to vision-only feedback [18, 19]. RGB-D probing has been used to track deformation and classify non-rigid response [20]; visual shaping of plastic material has also been demonstrated with specialized actions and model-free image feedback [21, 22]. RoPotter instead exploits pottery-specific priors to reduce the state dimension and recover occluded geometry [23]. Fewer studies isolate a directly measured link between intrinsic interaction force and persistent geometric deformation from a single commodity view. We address this measurement problem with standard robotic hardware. The scope is controlled indentation of one Play-Doh-type material; closed-loop target-shape reproduction is outside the present evaluation.

We pair pre- and post-interaction observations, compute the estimated displaced volume from registered point clouds, and map it to force using a quadratic model and a compact multilayer perceptron (MLP). A separate sequence tests cumulative localization. The contributions are:

a minimal-sensing real-robot interaction framework combining a 7-DoF robot, a single eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, and intrinsic force estimation for controlled interaction with an elasto-plastic material;

a point-cloud deformation pipeline that localizes the affected surface region and computes an estimated deformation volume relative to a local reference surface; and

a real-robot evaluation covering force–volume characterization, analytical and MLP-based force estimation, system repeatability, and cumulative deformation localization across sequential interactions.

title: Helping Hand: A Continuum Robotic Grasper for Traction in Single-Channel Endoscopic Submucosal Dissection
authors: Bendavid Maimon,Thompson Wong,Aedan Mangan,Sukjun Kim,Michael C. Yip,Tania K. Morimoto
abstract:
Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is a minimally invasive approach for removing large polyps from the colon and offers many benefits compared to other surgical approaches. However, ESD is technically very challenging to perform, leading to limited adoption by physicians. We propose the Helping Hand, a two-segment continuum robotic grasper that, together with an electrosurgical knife, enables tissue traction and cutting within a single 3.7 mm working channel.
We achieve this functionality by creating a slot at the base of the Helping Hand that lets the electrosurgical knife extend out, enabling countertraction and cutting through one instrument lumen. We evaluate the Helping Hand’s workspace and its ability to provide traction forces from different starting configurations. Finally, we demonstrate the full workflow by isolating and removing tissue in an ex vivo chicken thigh, illustrating the potential for the Helping Hand to help improve ESD procedures.
introduction:
Approximately 3.9% of people in the United States will develop colorectal cancer during their lifetime [1].
For patients with precancerous colorectal lesions or selected superficial cancers, endoscopic resection offers a means of removing the lesion while preserving the bowel [2].
Endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) can capture and remove small lesions with a snare, but large lesions often must be removed in several pieces, which makes it difficult to confirm complete excision and increases the risk of recurrence [2].
In contrast, in endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD), the physician uses an electrosurgical knife to incise the mucosa around the lesion and dissect the submucosal tissue beneath it, permitting en bloc removal that preserves the resection margins for pathological assessment [2]. ESD thus allows large lesions to be removed without colectomy, which for nonmalignant polyps carries a 14% rate of major adverse events and 0.7% 30-day mortality [3, 4].

Despite the many benefits of ESD, the procedure is technically very challenging to perform. In particular,
maintaining a clear view of the tissue immediately ahead of the knife is challenging as the lesion separates from the bowel wall and the partially freed mucosal flap often obscures the plane between the lesion and the underlying muscle. Applying traction to the flap exposes this plane and places the submucosal fibers under tension, facilitating dissection [5, 6]. The direction of traction is also critical, where a pull that initially exposes the submucosa may become less effective as the cut advances [6]. The procedural challenge is therefore to maintain traction in a direction that keeps the dissection plane both visible to the physician and accessible to the knife.

Several devices have been proposed to maintain traction on the mucosal flap during ESD.
One approach has been to mount the grasper externally, leaving the working channel available for the knife. The Olympus FlexLifter, for example, advances and retracts forceps from a fixed position on a distal cap.
This approach results in a dependence between the angle at which the forceps approach the flap and the orientation of the endoscope [7].
Lou et al. have developed an externally mounted soft pop-up robot that articulates a grasper at the tip of the endoscope [8]. However, even when folded, the robot measures approximately 33×32×633\times 32\times 6 mm, adding bulk at the tip that may make it harder to navigate narrow or tortuous anatomy.
Other robotic end caps mount to the endoscope tip and articulate instruments passed through the working channel, adding distal dexterity without a second channel [9].

A second approach has been to use separate working channels for traction and cutting. The Fujifilm TRACMOTION uses an articulating, rotatable grasper to adjust the direction of traction while an electrosurgical knife passes through the second working channel [10].
Connor et al. passed two concentric push-pull steerable sheaths through the 3.7 mm and 2.8 mm channels of a standard dual-channel colonoscope, one steering forceps for countertraction and the other an electrosurgical tool, and showed that users with no prior ESD experience could complete ex vivo resections [11].
Gao et al. developed a bimanual telerobotic system that passes a 3.5 mm manipulator for tissue traction and a 2.5 mm manipulator for dissection through the two working channels of a commercial endoscope [12].
However, the externally mounted approaches add bulk at the tip of the endoscope, and the multichannel approaches require a dual-channel endoscope, whose acquisition cost limits its availability in many endoscopy units [13]. These constraints motivate a device that provides articulated traction and knife access through a single working channel.

The contributions of this work are as follows: (1) We present the Helping Hand, a two-degree-of-freedom continuum robotic grasper that houses all the tools needed for endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) within a single 3.7 mm colonoscope working channel (see Fig. 1). A slot at its base, rather than the usual tip exit, lets the electrosurgical knife extend through the grasper, enabling countertraction and cutting through one instrument lumen without any externally mounted tools or a second working channel.
(2) We evaluate the Helping Hand’s workspace and ability to provide retraction forces. We also demonstrate the full workflow by isolating and removing tissue in an ex vivo chicken thigh benchtop model.
To the best of our knowledge, this is the first demonstration of robotic ESD with countertraction and cutting performed through a single working channel.

title: EMS-Nav: Embodied Multi-Scale Navigation
authors: Zenghui Yang,Xinan Wang,Danyang Li,Zhe Xu,Zheng Yang,Jingao Xu,Qiang Ma
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: including appendices
abstract: Applications such as industrial inspection require robots to autonomously reach different work areas and specific pieces of equipment. These destinations span spatial scales from regions to objects, so robots must relate each target to its surroundings to interpret the task and determine where to go. Existing methods support multi-scale navigation through rich environment representations, but at substantial computational and storage cost. These costs limit deployment where wireless coverage is incomplete and robots must rely on onboard computation to keep navigating. We introduce EMS-Nav, a biologically inspired multi-scale navigation framework for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is to organize perception, spatial understanding, and navigation around regions, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. EMS-Nav groups objects and their relationships into functionally meaningful spaces and builds a hierarchy from local areas to the broader environment. This organization supports efficient map construction alongside the interpretation and execution of language goals at different scales. In multi-scale navigation experiments, EMS-Nav achieves the highest success rates across all four target categories: objects, rooms, regions, and specific instances. It outperforms representative state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods, improving overall first-attempt success by 9.39 percentage points over the strongest baseline while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Local deployment in real indoor environments further demonstrates its applicability to on-device embodied navigation. By establishing regions as the organizing basis for perception, spatial understanding, and language-guided action, EMS-Nav provides a system that combines multi-scale understanding with computational efficiency to support diverse language goals on resource-constrained robots.
introduction:
Navigation is a fundamental capability of embodied robots, connecting perception of the physical world to action within it. Mobile robots support warehouse logistics (Brown, 2022), hospital deliveries (Toyota Motor Corporation, 2026), industrial inspections (ANYbotics, 2025), and so on. These tasks require robots to identify destinations and navigate to them. When tasks are specified in natural language, destinations may be described at different spatial scales.

A user may ask a robot to reach a room, a functional region, or an object, or combine these scales in one instruction. For example, “Find the laptop on the mint-green computer desk in the office” identifies the target through its room, desk attributes, and spatial relationship to the desk. Recognizing the laptop alone is insufficient: multi-scale semantic navigation requires connecting object details with their surrounding spaces (Werby et al., 2024; Miao et al., 2026).

Existing studies support such multi-scale semantic navigation through hierarchical representations and spatial context. HOV-SG (Werby et al., 2024) organizes floors, rooms, and objects to localize language goals, while SG-Nav (Yin et al., 2024) uses relationships among objects, object groups, and rooms for object-goal search. LangMap (Miao et al., 2026) evaluates goals at the scene, room, region, and instance levels.

However, constructing rich environment representations can incur substantial computation and storage costs (Gu et al., 2023; Werby et al., 2024). Where wireless coverage is incomplete, as in industrial inspection (ANYbotics, 2023), robots must continue navigating with limited onboard compute and memory, constraining the deployment of these methods.

To reduce these costs, other work explores more efficient map construction and use. Clio (Maggio et al., 2024) builds compact online scene graphs by retaining task-relevant objects and regions. OneMap (Busch et al., 2025) reuses semantic maps for successive object searches on embedded hardware, while FindAnything (Laina et al., 2026) improves object semantic map construction and storage efficiency.

Despite these advances in semantic representation and efficiency, the object-level scene graph methods above largely follow an object-first paradigm: they first reconstruct individual objects, then use those representations to infer spatial relationships and higher-level structure. Separating object reconstruction from spatial organization creates two limitations for on-device multi-scale navigation: the cost of processing a growing body of object information, and the difficulty of recovering functional spaces from object representations.

∙\bullet Building and interpreting an environment around objects places increasing computational demands on the system as the scene grows (Gu et al., 2023; Werby et al., 2024). As exploration extends, the map accumulates more objects and relationships. If a local change triggers reprocessing across a wider area, map maintenance and spatial interpretation repeatedly revisit unrelated object details. This mismatch consumes scarce on-device resources and limits efficient online mapping and spatial understanding as coverage expands.

∙\bullet Object reconstruction may leave navigation-relevant spatial structure implicit. A laboratory’s preparation, storage, and measurement areas can occupy the same room and contain similar object categories. Their differences depend on local layouts, boundaries, and arrangements of objects. Room boundaries alone cannot distinguish these areas, and object labels alone cannot determine their extent (Hughes et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2024). The same function can also occur in different layouts, limiting the usefulness of fixed spatial partitions. Thus, even when a target object is already mapped, a robot may be unable to determine whether it lies in the functional space named by the instruction. Resolving this ambiguity requires a map that connects objects to the functional spaces they collectively form and represents hierarchical relationships among those spaces.

Addressing these limitations poses three connected challenges for on-device multi-scale navigation. The first is to make sense of local space from partial observations: objects may be recognizable, but which objects form a coherent space, and how they should be organized, are not given. The second is to derive spatial hierarchies that align with everyday understanding and language. Functional relationships need not follow walls or fixed architectural levels, limiting predefined partitions. The third is to retrieve goal-relevant spatial knowledge under limited resources without processing every scale in each decision.

When people seek a destination, they connect visible objects to their surroundings and draw on spatial knowledge at the scales relevant to the description. This motivates us to look to biological spatial cognition for design inspiration. Studies of local layout perception (Epstein and Kanwisher, 1998), hippocampal cognitive maps (Iaria et al., 2007), and prefrontal goal and contextual control (Koechlin et al., 2003) suggest a functional division among local perception, spatial integration, and goal-directed decisions. We draw from this division a design principle: use local spaces to connect object perception with understanding of the broader environment, and access different levels of spatial knowledge according to the navigation goal. This leads us to place regions at the center of perception, understanding, and navigation.

We introduce EMS-Nav, a multi-scale language-guided navigation framework designed for online, on-device operation. Its core innovation is a region-centered organization that extends spatial structure beyond an interpretation added after object reconstruction, making it foundational to perception, understanding, and navigation (Figure ).

EMS-Nav addresses the three challenges within a shared spatial organization. Perceptual structuring inspired by the scene-selective cortex (SSC) forms spatial units from local layouts and object relationships, establishing how the local environment is represented. Hippocampus-inspired spatial parsing constructs a multi-scale hierarchy from functional relationships, supporting spatial understanding beyond fixed room partitions. Goal-directed navigation inspired by the prefrontal cortex (PFC) selects knowledge at the scales relevant to an instruction and uses it to determine the destination. All three modules organize computation around regions: local changes are updated primarily within the relevant spaces, while broader understanding builds on region summaries. Resource constraints thus inform perception, parsing, and navigation throughout the framework.

Our contributions are threefold:

We introduce EMS-Nav, a multi-scale language-guided navigation framework for online, on-device operation. It connects environmental mapping, spatial understanding, and language-guided goal decisions, enabling robots to use a shared map for navigation instructions at different scales under limited computational resources.

We propose a spatial organization that uses regions to connect perception with semantic parsing, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. By extending object understanding to functional regions and their hierarchical relationships, this organization allows multi-scale spatial understanding and efficient mapping to support one another.

Large-scale evaluation and real-world deployment demonstrate improvements in both multi-scale navigation and computational efficiency. Across 18,628 instructions covering object, room, region, and specific-instance targets, EMS-Nav achieves the highest navigation success rates in all four categories, outperforming representative state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Real-world deployment on an RTX 4060 Ti reaches a peak on-device processing throughput of 5.19 frames per second (FPS), further demonstrating the framework’s practical applicability. We will release the source code for EMS-Nav.

1. We introduce EMS-Nav, a multi-scale language-guided navigation framework for online, on-device operation. It connects environmental mapping, spatial understanding, and language-guided goal decisions, enabling robots to use a shared map for navigation instructions at different scales under limited computational resources.

2. We propose a spatial organization that uses regions to connect perception with semantic parsing, making local spaces the basic units of both environmental understanding and computation. By extending object understanding to functional regions and their hierarchical relationships, this organization allows multi-scale spatial understanding and efficient mapping to support one another.

3. Large-scale evaluation and real-world deployment demonstrate improvements in both multi-scale navigation and computational efficiency. Across 18,628 instructions covering object, room, region, and specific-instance targets, EMS-Nav achieves the highest navigation success rates in all four categories, outperforming representative state-of-the-art open-vocabulary mapping and navigation methods while reducing mapping overhead and language-model input size. Real-world deployment on an RTX 4060 Ti reaches a peak on-device processing throughput of 5.19 frames per second (FPS), further demonstrating the framework’s practical applicability. We will release the source code for EMS-Nav.

title: Generalized Inverse Kinematics via Conditional Flow
authors: Kaitlyn Zhang,Tomás Lozano-Pérez,Leslie Pack Kaelbling
abstract:
Inverse kinematics (IK) is a foundational primitive in robotics, mapping the task-space objectives expressed by higher-level planners to robot configurations that realize them. Traditional IK methods generally treat each query as an isolated pose-to-configuration problem, but planners often need a distribution over valid realizations that accounts for future reachability and preferences such as collision avoidance and stability. We introduce GenGenIK, a generative modeling approach that supports mobile bases, multiple end-effectors and targets, scene awareness, and preferences over robot behavior within a common interface. Experiments show that GenGenIK outperforms existing methods in both solve rate and runtime across tasks such as bimanual lift and flip-up, while allowing flexible control over the sampled distribution and remaining effective under partial scene observations.
Website: https://icra-2027-gengenik.github.io/.
introduction:
Many robot operations are most conveniently described in Cartesian end-effector
coordinates: for example, opening a door, grasping or pushing an object on a
table, pouring liquid, etc. However, safety verification, motion
planning, and many control processes require a full configuration space (C-space)
realization of the robot. The problem of generating valid joint configurations that satisfy constraints on the end-effector is known as the inverse kinematics (IK) problem. For redundant robots, in which the dimension of the C-space exceeds the dimension of the end-effector space, the IK problem is computationally difficult, and most often addressed by non-linear optimization or other numerical methods.

When planning for long-horizon manipulation tasks, it is generally necessary to
consider many alternative IK solutions to individual steps, for example,
considering different base positions for opening a door or reaching into a
cupboard [1]. Numerical methods for IK generate single solutions; they can
typically be guided into generating multiple solutions but that process can be slow and may not reliably cover the feasible solution space.

For highly redundant robots, such as humanoids, it is not
sufficient to generate samples of configurations consistent with an
end-effector constraint. We will typically have a large number of additional
constraints and preferences on the resulting configuration: the robot should be
stable, the hand should be in the field of view of the camera, multiple
end-effector positions should be reachable from the same base position, the robot should
not be in self-collision or in world-collision, etc. Generating large
numbers of solutions and rejecting them on the basis of the constraints is not
practical. Numerical IK solvers can accept a rich set
of constraints and preferences, but as indicated earlier, are slow when multiple
solutions are required.

In this paper we address the generalized IK problem. We assume the robot
has a base and a set of end-effectors, such as hands or posable cameras.
We specify a sequence of targets for the end-effectors, scene collision geometry,
and a set of preferences, such as high manipulability. The desired result
is a set of whole-body configurations for each of the targets that achieve the
specified end-effector pose and which approximately optimize the preferences.

We model generalized IK as conditional generation over whole-body configurations
or trajectories. We learn a Transformer model [2], GenGenIK, based on a masked representation
that lets a single learned model handle different numbers of targets and end-effectors, mobile bases, and partial configuration or trajectory completion
without changing the architecture. Our contributions are:

Generalized IK as conditional C-space completion: a
unified formulation encompassing IK over multiple targets,
multiple end-effectors, mobile bases, warm starts, and partial configuration or
trajectory infill.

Scene-conditioned generation: a generative solver that
directly conditions the distribution on scene geometry, concentrating
samples on collision-free regions of solution space rather than
relying on scene-agnostic proposals followed by online search or
optimization.

Realization under constraints and preferences: a method for incorporating constraints and preferences via auxiliary training losses, such as keeping the end-effector in the robot’s view; guided sampling for differentiable constraints, such as manipulability and static stability; and preference conditioning, which biases the sampled distribution according to non-differentiable requests such as torso use and arm posture.

title: Reading the Table: Sim-to-Real Game State Detection for the Chef's Hat Card Game
authors: Connor Gäde,Matthias Kerzel,Hauke Bünning,Jan-Gerrit Habekost,Mariana Barros,Stefan Wermter
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: Presented at the Dungeons, Neurons, and Dialogues workshop (DnD-SIDC 2026) at ICANN 2026, this https URL
abstract: Tabletop games offer a compelling scenario to study the interaction between artificial and human agents, combining social interaction with game state tracking and physical manipulation. To assess the game state, a robot needs to precisely detect closely related game objects, such as different card designs, requiring dedicated training data that is costly to annotate in the real world. Instead, we develop a fully automated synthetic data collection pipeline, using re-projection of known 3D coordinates to generate labels automatically and domain randomization to bridge the reality gap. This approach is used to collect a dataset of 25413 samples to finetune an object detection and a segmentation model, which are combined to assign detected cards to game-relevant zones and infer the game state. When evaluated on a real NICO humanoid robot, our pipeline achieves an F1-score of 0.906 for card-to-zone assignment, thus providing the perceptual foundation for a robot that can autonomously play Chef’s Hat against human players.
introduction:
Enabling robots to participate in multiplayer tabletop games with human players combines multiple challenges in robotics and AI. The robot needs to naturally interact with the other players, accurately infer and track the game state, and perform fine-grained object manipulation to execute game actions. Recent advances in embodied robot agents utilize an LLM [1] or VLM [6] for high-level interaction, scene understanding, and task-planning, combined with detection and action modules for object localization and manipulation. While these agents generally use open-vocabulary detectors to interact with everyday items [1, 6], task domains with visually similar objects or specific class labels require specialized detection models and thus training data [7].
A card game like Chef’s Hat represents one such domain, where visually similar cards must be distinguished by value and their placement in specific playing field zones identified.

Collecting training data for such tasks on a real robot requires meticulously annotating bounding boxes for each card and segmentation masks of the playing field by hand, which is time-intensive, prone to errors, and can introduce biases towards specific camera poses, lighting conditions, or object placements, making a trained model generalize poorly. Simulators provide a more scalable alternative, allowing the free arrangement of objects in the scene and automatically generating labels through re-projection using the known object poses and camera parameters. However, due to the reality gap caused by lower visual fidelity and simplified assumptions of a simulator compared to reality, models trained on synthetic data generalize poorly to real-world input. Domain randomization [19] mitigates this gap by altering visual and environmental parameters of the simulation to increase the resilience of a trained model to domain shifts and thus its ability to interpret the unseen real-world domain.

In this work, we develop a fully automated synthetic data collection pipeline in CoppeliaSim11
1
https://www.coppeliarobotics.com and create a game state detection approach for the Chef’s Hat card game to play it on a real humanoid robot. For this, we create a dataset of 25413 samples consisting of paired domain-randomized and non-randomized canonical images showing the Chef’s Hat playing cards on the playing field and custom 3D-printed cardholders. Each image is labeled with card identities, zone assignments, and the projected 2D image coordinates for individual cards and playing field zones, from which bounding boxes and segmentation masks can be derived. Each sample further includes the 6D simulation poses of all objects, camera parameters, and a random seed, allowing the reconstruction of any scene in simulation and enabling future extensions such as card pose estimation or motion planning for physical manipulation.
With this synthetic dataset, we finetune an object detection model to detect playing cards and a segmentation model to determine different zones of the playing field, combining them to determine which cards are placed in which zone. When evaluated on real-world data without additional finetuning, our model assigns the correct cards to the correct zones with an F1-score of 90.6%, enabling valid game actions in most situations.

title: What Makes a VLA Reactive? A Study of Execution Strategies for Dynamic Manipulation
authors: Zhuoyue Li,Zhendong Han,Pankhuri Vanjani,Wenting Li,Rudolf Lioutikov
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
comment: Efficient Foundation Models for Real-Time Embodied AI, CoRL 2026 Workshop
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models predict chunks of future actions, and when objects move, those chunks go stale before they are executed. We study what makes a pretrained VLA reactive, using π0.5\pi_{0.5} on two dynamic simulation benchmarks and three real-robot tasks. We vary the prediction and execution horizons, compare synchronous and asynchronous inference, test methods that deliver actions sooner or keep successive chunks continuous, and adapt the policy with motion cues and latent-space reinforcement learning. The best prediction horizon is about one second, and the best execution horizon depends on the checkpoint. Short horizons help more with asynchronous execution, and methods that keep the trajectory continuous outperform those that only reduce latency. Adapting the policy repairs targeted failures, but on the conveyor task changing the execution horizon gained as much. Reactivity depends on the execution pipeline as much as on the policy, so both should be evaluated together.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models predict action chunks to support coherent motion with fewer inference calls.
When objects move during inference and execution, these predictions can become stale. Shorter execution horizons allow more frequent replanning, but increase inference demand and can introduce discontinuities between chunks. Dynamic manipulation therefore requires balancing observation freshness, computational cost, and execution stability.
Recent approaches address these challenges through faster action generation, asynchronous execution, trajectory continuity, and temporal information [1, 11, 14, 5]. We used π0.5\pi_{0.5}  [9] on DOM [14], DOMINO [5], and three real-robot dynamic tasks. In this work, we investigate: (1) How do prediction and execution horizons affect performance? (2) How do scheduling and trajectory continuity affect the benefits of frequent replanning? (3) Can temporal information and reward-guided adaptation, including DSRL [13], improve dynamic manipulation? Our results show that frequent replanning alone does not ensure better performance: its benefits depend on the execution pipeline and the learned policy.

title: ActionCodec2: A Streaming Action Tokenizer
authors: Zibin Dong,Yicheng Liu,Shiduo Zhang,Tianyuan Yuan,Baijun Ye,Jinqiu Wang,Hang Zhao
abstract: 未获取到摘要
introduction:
In an autoregressive (AR) VLA, the action tokenizer encodes continuous actions into discrete tokens for training and decodes predicted tokens into executable actions [Zitkovich et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024; Pertsch et al., 2025; Dong et al., 2026]. Most existing action tokenizers encode one to two seconds of motion as a chunk (Figure 1, left), following a formulation widely used in diffusion policies [Chi et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2023; Bharadhwaj et al., 2024]. For example, FAST [Pertsch et al., 2025] exploits temporal correlations by compressing DCT coefficients with BPE, while VQ-VAE-based tokenizers [Mete et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026a; Kang et al., 2026; Dong et al., 2026] learn compact latent representations of action chunks. With chunkwise tokenization, the robot can react to new observations only at chunk boundaries, and an erroneous token may affect multiple actions within a chunk. Real-time chunking [Black et al., 2025b] allows earlier reactions by replanning before a chunk ends, but reacting at every control step would require repeatedly predicting overlapping chunks. A streaming tokenizer instead releases actions as their symbols become available, allowing the policy to incorporate new observations at each control step without regenerating entire chunks.

The simplest streaming tokenizer is per-dimension binning, as in OpenVLA [Kim et al., 2024], which assigns one token to each action dimension. For 7-dimensional actions at 15​Hz15\,\mathrm{Hz}, this requires 105 tokens per second, substantially increasing autoregressive decoding latency. An alternative is to shorten the chunks of learned VQ-based tokenizers to one or two steps [Mete et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026d; Liu et al., 2026a]. However, their fixed codebooks concentrate reconstruction accuracy on the training distribution, with no guarantee for unfamiliar motions (Figure 1, right). More importantly, accurate reconstruction of individual actions does not guarantee accurate trajectories, as small errors in incremental actions accumulate over time. In a replay test on LIBERO (Figure 2), FAST reconstructs individual actions to within 1​mm1\,\mathrm{mm} but accumulates about 40​mm40\,\mathrm{mm} of drift per episode, achieving only 90%90\% replay success. The other chunkwise baselines reach at most 80%80\%, whereas ActionCodec2 keeps the drift below 5​mm5\,\mathrm{mm} and achieves 97%97\% replay success.

ActionCodec2 addresses trajectory drift by accounting for the quantization error left by previous steps. The encoder maintains the same reconstructed state as the decoder and uses it to select the next motion primitive, keeping the reconstructed trajectory within a prescribed tolerance of the original. Rather than allowing small errors to accumulate, each step corrects the error remaining from earlier steps. This reduces the range that needs to be quantized to the possible one-step motions and the residual tracking error, rather than the robot’s entire workspace. We derive the minimum number of discrete motion symbols required to guarantee this error bound.

The motion primitives guarantee bounded tracking error, but representing every possible combination of primitives with a separate VLA token would require an enormous vocabulary. Representing each coordinate separately avoids this problem but produces long token sequences. We therefore compress these symbols without changing the reconstructed actions. Standard BPE [Sennrich et al., 2016; Pertsch et al., 2025] merges only adjacent symbols under a fixed coordinate ordering, limiting its ability to capture correlations across dimensions. We introduce Set-BPE, which losslessly merges co-occurring symbols across coordinates and neighboring steps, regardless of coordinate order. At 15​Hz15\,\mathrm{Hz}, ActionCodec2 requires only 8.88.8 tokens per second for end-effector control and 10.810.8 for joint control.

ActionCodec2 is fitted without gradient-based optimization: its primitive sets are determined by the motion bounds and prescribed tolerances, while Set-BPE learns its merges by counting symbol co-occurrences. In addition to benchmark-specific tokenizers fitted on each dataset’s training corpus, we fit universal variants on about 2020k hours of data from 2424 embodiments for plug-and-play use across robots and tasks. Our contributions are:

We formulate bounded-error streaming action tokenization as a covering problem and prove the optimality of fixed motion primitives among one-symbol-per-step decoders, with an exact solution for translation and constant-factor-tight bounds for rotation.

We introduce Set-BPE, which losslessly merges co-occurring primitive symbols across coordinates and neighboring steps, without relying on a fixed coordinate ordering. This allows merged tokens to capture coordinated motion patterns that standard BPE may miss, while reducing token count by 6.66.6–10.7%10.7\% on held-out data.

Using the same G0.5 VLA [Liu et al., 2026c], ActionCodec2 achieves 98.2%98.2\% on LIBERO, 93.8%93.8\% on SimplerEnv, and 79.5%79.5\% on LIBERO-Plus, outperforming FAST, OAT, X-Tokenizer, and ActionCodec. It also achieves 73.9%73.9\% task progress across four zero-shot Franka tasks.

We show that ActionCodec2 tokens can serve as a direct control interface for VLM agents, which store successful token sequences as reusable macros that carry over across attempts and to new tasks.

1. We formulate bounded-error streaming action tokenization as a covering problem and prove the optimality of fixed motion primitives among one-symbol-per-step decoders, with an exact solution for translation and constant-factor-tight bounds for rotation.

2. We introduce Set-BPE, which losslessly merges co-occurring primitive symbols across coordinates and neighboring steps, without relying on a fixed coordinate ordering. This allows merged tokens to capture coordinated motion patterns that standard BPE may miss, while reducing token count by 6.66.6–10.7%10.7\% on held-out data.

3. Using the same G0.5 VLA [Liu et al., 2026c], ActionCodec2 achieves 98.2%98.2\% on LIBERO, 93.8%93.8\% on SimplerEnv, and 79.5%79.5\% on LIBERO-Plus, outperforming FAST, OAT, X-Tokenizer, and ActionCodec. It also achieves 73.9%73.9\% task progress across four zero-shot Franka tasks.

title: FloCOS: Predicting Compact Forward Occupancy Sets of Surrounding Vehicles via Conditional Flow Matching
authors: Chuansheng Dong,Yinxiao Zhan,Zongdian Li,Peng Hou,Jin Wang,Jiayu Fan
abstract: Existing methods for predicting surrounding vehicles’ forward occupancy may under-approximate the ground-truth occupancy, exposing the ego vehicle to collision risk, or produce overly conservative regions that unnecessarily restrict feasible space and cause planning failures. To address these issues, we propose FloCOS, a conditional flow-matching framework that predicts compact forward occupancy sets with high occupancy coverage. FloCOS represents the forward occupancy set as a time-varying union of half-space convex polygons parameterized by temporal basis coefficients. Conditional flow matching captures the conditional distribution of these coefficients to govern the temporal evolution of the convex components, trained under coverage and union-area losses that penalize missed occupancy and excess area. For downstream trajectory optimization, the predicted nonconvex union is directly incorporated into hyperplane-based collision-avoidance constraints. Evaluations on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset show that FloCOS generates compact forward occupancy sets with high coverage and achieves a higher interaction completion rate than evaluated baselines. Real-world vehicle experiments further confirm its ability to support collision-free planning in interactive scenarios.
introduction:
Motion prediction is a key component of autonomous driving because the ego vehicle must anticipate the future behavior of surrounding traffic participants before planning safe and efficient maneuvers [1, 2, 3]. For optimization-based motion planning, these predictions ultimately determine the spatial regions excluded by collision-avoidance constraints [4, 5]. Uncertainty in collaborative perception [6] and real-to-sim domain shifts [7] pose challenges to reliable autonomous driving. Because future behavior depends on uncertain driving intent and traffic interaction, the predicted regions must account for multiple plausible behaviors. If a predicted region fails to cover the ground-truth occupancy, the planner may treat space that the vehicle can actually occupy as collision-free. Conversely, overly enlarged regions unnecessarily shrink the feasible space and may render planning infeasible in confined environments [8, 9], as illustrated in Fig. 1. A practical prediction representation for motion planning must simultaneously achieve high coverage of plausible future occupancy and geometric compactness.

Modern motion predictors can represent complex future behavior, but their native outputs are commonly trajectories or probability distributions instead of bounded geometric sets that can be enforced directly in collision-avoidance constraints. Converting these predictions into forward occupancy sets introduces an additional design problem: vehicle geometry and prediction uncertainty must be represented without excluding unnecessary free space. This problem becomes particularly acute when plausible future occupancies are spatially separated, because a single convex enclosure also occupies the space between them. Representing forward occupancy as a union of compact convex components can naturally capture separated regions without filling the intervening free space.
To this end, we propose FloCOS, which predicts compact forward occupancy sets of surrounding vehicles as unions of occupancy components. Conditional flow matching [10] generates temporally coherent component sequences from scene context, and the ground-truth occupancy at each prediction step supervises the geometry passed to the planner. The training objectives jointly penalize missed occupancy coverage and unnecessary occupied area over the occupancy union.

Our main contributions are as follows:

We propose FloCOS to predict compact forward occupancy sets of surrounding vehicles by a conditional flow-matching method. This method achieves sufficient and tight coverage of possible forward occupancy regions of surrounding vehicles.

We integrate the predicted occupancy unions into trajectory optimization through hyperplane-based collision avoidance constraints. This allows the planner to use the nonconvex occupancy representation without replacing it with an approximate convex enclosure.

We validate FloCOS on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset and in real-world vehicle experiments. The results demonstrate that FloCOS produces more compact occupancy predictions than existing methods and enables collision-free planning for ego vehicles.

title: SPARC: RoboCup Standard Platform for Autonomous Rescue Competition with Initial Datasets, Software, and Simulation Environments
authors: Yuezhong Wang,Bichi Zhang,Zhongli Yin,Pingcong Li,Raimund Edlinger,Sören Schwertfeger
comment: IEEE SSRR 2026
abstract: The RoboCup Standard Platform for Autonomous Rescue Competition (SPARC) is a new competition under development of the RoboCup Rescue Robot League that uses the Unitree A2-W as a common robot platform. SPARC aims to make research on artificial intelligence for autonomous rescue robots accessible to a broader research community, including groups without expertise in developing and maintaining custom robot hardware. By providing a capable standard platform and established benchmark environments, researchers can focus on autonomous navigation, perception, manipulation, and embodied AI for challenging disaster-response scenarios. This paper introduces the SPARC competition, its benchmark environment, and the Unitree A2-W standard platform. Furthermore, we present the first open SPARC datasets collected during the IEEE ICRA 2026 Legged Robot Challenges and RoboCup Rescue 2026, release an open-source software stack for autonomous navigation, and provide initial simulation assets representing RoboCup Rescue test environments. Together, these resources aim to lower the barrier to entry for autonomous rescue robotics and facilitate reproducible research and collaborative development on a common hardware platform.
introduction:
Natural and man-made disasters continue to pose significant challenges for emergency responders. Search and rescue robots are increasingly being deployed in these scenarios [19]. Consequently, rescue robotics has become an important research area [14]. Owing to the wide range of capabilities required, including robust mobility, autonomous navigation, perception, mapping, manipulation, and human-robot interaction, disaster response has been recognized as one of the most realistic and comprehensive benchmarks for autonomous robotic systems [10].

For more than two decades, the RoboCup Rescue Robot League has served as a benchmark competition for autonomous rescue robotics [17, 16, 18]. By providing realistic disaster scenarios together with objective evaluation methodologies, the league has driven research in autonomous navigation, mapping, perception, manipulation, and human-robot interaction. However, participating teams have traditionally developed and maintained their own robotic platforms, resulting in duplicated engineering effort and making reproducible comparisons between algorithms challenging. So, while RoboCup Rescue has successfully standardized benchmark environments and evaluation procedures, the participating robots have remained highly heterogeneous.

A successful solution to this problem has already been demonstrated within RoboCup. In the RoboCup Soccer Standard Platform League, all teams compete using identical robot hardware, allowing research efforts to focus on perception, localization, decision making, multi-robot cooperation, and artificial intelligence rather than hardware development [3, 8]. This approach has lowered the barrier to entry, improved reproducibility, and accelerated software development through shared tools, datasets, and open-source software.

Recent advances in commercially available quadruped and wheel-legged robots have made a standard platform feasible for rescue robotics. Platforms such as the Unitree A2-W combine high mobility, integrated sensing, and onboard computation at a price point accessible to many research groups. Their capabilities have already been demonstrated in recent competitions, with an A2-W winning RoboCup Rescue 2026 (see Fig. 1) and the closely related A2 platform winning the Best in Class Autonomy award at the IEEE ICRA Legged Robot Challenge (LRC) 2026 (see Fig. 3). These developments motivated the RoboCup Rescue League to establish the Standard Platform for Autonomous Rescue Competition (SPARC), using the Unitree A2-W as its standard robot and enabling researchers to focus on autonomous navigation, perception, manipulation, and embodied AI rather than hardware development. SPARC is under active development, and contributions from the research community are encouraged. The latest competition rules, technical specifications, and updates can be found at https://rrl.robocup.org/sparc/.

This paper introduces the SPARC competition together with the first SPARC open research resources for the community, provided by the winner of both the RoboCup Rescue 2026 competition and the IEEE ICRA 2026 Legged Robot Challenges (LRC), and by the winner of the Best in Class Autonomy award of the ICRA 2026 LRC. The main contributions of this paper are:

We introduce the RoboCup Standard Platform for Autonomous Rescue Competition (SPARC), including its motivation, competition format, benchmark tasks, evaluation methodology, and the Unitree A2-W standard platform.

We introduce the RoboCup Standard Platform for Autonomous Rescue Competition (SPARC), including its motivation, competition format, benchmark tasks, evaluation methodology, and the Unitree A2-W standard platform.

We release the first public SPARC datasets, including data collected with the Unitree A2 Pro during the IEEE ICRA 2026 Legged Robot Challenges (LRC) and with the Unitree A2-W during RoboCup Rescue 2026 in Incheon, Korea.

We open-source a complete software stack for autonomous navigation on the SPARC platform, enabling researchers to build upon state-of-the-art competition-winning solutions.

We publish initial simulation assets representing RoboCup Rescue test environments to support simulation-based development and evaluation.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section II reviews the related work. Section III introduces the SPARC arena, the standard hardware platform, and the competition concept. The datasets released alongside this paper are presented in Section IV, while the open-source software stack is described in Section V. Section VI introduces the simulation environment, and Section VII concludes the paper.

title: Actuation and Control of Passive Tendon-Driven Soft Extensions Through Rigid Manipulator Motion
authors: Ignacio Cuiral-Zueco,Gonzalo López-Nicolás,Youcef Mezouar
comment: . Soon to be submitted to the IEEE Transactions on Robotics. Code:this https URL. Interactive pages and video:this https URL
abstract:
Industrial manipulators offer reach and precision but can damage nearby
structures in confined spaces. Soft robots provide compliant contact but
typically have limited reach. Rigid–soft systems combine their advantages,
although they often require dedicated actuation and control hardware. We propose
actuating a passive tendon-driven soft extension through manipulator joint
motion. As the robot moves, the exterior spans of tendons anchored to upstream
links change, altering tendon tension and deforming the extension.
Inspection through narrow apertures, for example, constrains the motion of
the end effector (EE). We develop a controller that regulates the soft tip
while preserving such EE constraints.
A differential model separates rigid transport from soft deformation,
combining analytic arm and tendon kinematics with a locally identified
span-to-deformation map. We also derive a local upper bound on the number
of independent deformation directions transmitted by the tendons under
the EE constraint, and conditions for the exponential convergence of the
tip error. A quadratic program with control barrier functions imposes
obstacle clearance, fulcrum limits, and model-validity conditions.
Simulations and real experiments show tip and shape regulation under free,
position-constrained, and fulcrum-constrained EE motion.
introduction:
Industrial manipulators are widely available, offer large
workspaces and precise positioning, and come with mature control
infrastructure. Their rigidity, however,
can pose safety risks and cause damage when operating in confined spaces. On the
other hand, soft and continuum robots can deform around obstacles and provide
compliant contact with their surroundings
[1, 2, 3], but typically have limited reach.
Mounting a soft robot at the end effector (EE) of a rigid manipulator combines
the rigid arm’s reach with the soft robot’s compliant access to confined
spaces. Existing rigid–soft combinations, however, typically require dedicated
actuation and control hardware for the soft robot, increasing integration
effort and adding mass near the EE [4, 5] (see
Fig. 1).

We instead propose using the joint motion of the rigid manipulator (hereafter,
the robot) to actuate a passive tendon-driven soft extension (hereafter, the
extension). The extension is mounted at the robot’s EE, and each tendon runs
from an anchor on an upstream arm link to an entry point at the extension’s base
(Fig. 2). We call the portion of each tendon between its
anchor and entry point its exterior span. As the robot moves, changes in
these spans alter tendon tension and deform the extension. The robot can thus
position and deform the extension using its existing joints, and the extension
needs no dedicated actuators, sensors, or electronics.

This approach is particularly relevant to the inspection of hard-to-reach
spaces, where EE motion is often constrained to ensure proper insertion and
safety. For example, an inspection aperture may require a fixed EE position
while allowing reorientation, whereas a laparoscopic port permits pivoting and
axial insertion but prevents lateral motion at the entry point. Both cases
impose EE constraints, which can be expressed at the velocity level as

Our main contributions are:

Manipulator-driven actuation of a passive soft extension.
We propose using rigid manipulators’ joint motions to actuate passive soft
extensions through tendons anchored to upstream manipulator links, without
requiring dedicated actuation or control hardware for the extensions. This
approach enables low-cost and efficient integration of soft robotic capabilities into
existing industrial robots and control infrastructure.

Manipulator-driven actuation of a passive soft extension.
We propose using rigid manipulators’ joint motions to actuate passive soft
extensions through tendons anchored to upstream manipulator links, without
requiring dedicated actuation or control hardware for the extensions. This
approach enables low-cost and efficient integration of soft robotic capabilities into
existing industrial robots and control infrastructure.

A differential model separating rigid transport from soft
deformation. We define a differential model relating joint velocity to
soft-tip velocity. The model separates the transport of the extension
from its coupled tendon-driven deformation, where transport denotes its
translation and rotation with the EE at fixed shape. We compute transport
and tendon transmission analytically and propose a data-driven approach to
identify the local span-to-deformation map. The decomposition also provides
a local upper bound on the rank of the constrained deformation Jacobian
(Section V), which limits the number of independent
deformation directions transmitted by the tendons. This bound accounts for
the number of taut tendons, anchor placement, soft-body mechanics, and the
null-space motion allowed by the EE constraint.

Constrained tip control with safety and model-validity
conditions. We treat the EE constraint as the primary task and use a damped
least-squares control law to regulate the soft tip in its null space. For
the nominal control law on the constraint manifold, we prove that a weighted
tip-error Lyapunov function is nonincreasing. The tip error converges
exponentially when the constrained tip Jacobian satisfies the rank and
spectral conditions of Corollary 3. We also formulate a
quadratic program using control barrier functions (CBFs) to maintain
clearance between obstacles and the extension, respect the
geometric limits of the fulcrum, and keep the spans within the identified
span domain.

Simulation and experimental validation. We evaluate the
approach in simulation and on a physical UR10 robot arm. The simulation uses a
Cosserat-rod model of the extension, and its code and interactive
browser-based implementation are publicly available.11

title: Low-Cost Mobile Bimanual Manipulation for Long-Horizon Toilet Cleaning
authors: Sven Schreiber,Bernard Burdiek,Lasse Huber-Saffer,Yung-Hui Li,Donglin Chen,Shang-Ching Liu,Jianwei Zhang
abstract:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising capabilities
for robot manipulation, but their performance on accessible mobile
bimanual platforms remains underexplored. We present a low-cost and
reproducible mobile bimanual platform integrating two LeRobot SO-101
manipulators with a TurtleBot 4 and a LeRobot–ROS 2 software stack.
Using long-horizon toilet cleaning as a case study, we collect 250
real-world demonstrations and evaluate π0\pi_{0}, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, SmolVLA,
and GR00T under the same embodiment and task conditions. We further
evaluate variants using SARM-derived task-progress signals and
short-term MEM observation history. Among the evaluated models,
π0\pi_{0} performs best, achieving 60% strict and 70% relaxed
autonomous success, increasing to 90% with limited human intervention.
In contrast, the evaluated progress- and memory-augmented variants do
not improve their corresponding baselines. Our results demonstrate the
feasibility of long-horizon mobile bimanual manipulation on accessible
hardware while highlighting remaining challenges in reliable VLA
deployment. Project website: https://so101-turtlebot4.github.io/mobile-bimanual-cleaning/.
introduction:
Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have rapidly advanced from
task-specific manipulation toward generalist robot policies capable of
dexterous, bimanual, and increasingly long-horizon behaviors [1, 2, 3, 4].
However, translating these advances into reproducible real-world
systems remains challenging [5]. Existing models are typically evaluated
on different robot embodiments, datasets, and task settings, making it
difficult to understand how they compare when deployed under the same
physical conditions [5, 6]. This challenge is particularly pronounced for
mobile bimanual manipulation, where locomotion, dual-arm coordination,
perception, and contact-rich manipulation must operate reliably over
extended task sequences [7].
In this work, we present a low-cost mobile bimanual platform for
studying VLA policies in such settings, as shown in Fig. 1. The platform combines two
LeRobot SO-101 manipulators with a TurtleBot 4 mobile base, custom
3D-printable mechanical structures, and a multi-camera perception
system. A modular LeRobot–ROS 2 software stack supports whole-robot
teleoperation, data collection, human-in-the-loop correction, policy
training, and deployment. The system is designed to provide an
accessible and reproducible testbed for physical evaluation of modern
VLA policies.

We evaluate the platform through a long-horizon toilet-cleaning case
study that requires mobile navigation, bimanual coordination, tool
manipulation, contact-rich cleaning, and sequential task execution.
Using 250 real-world demonstrations collected on the same platform, we
fine-tune and physically evaluate representative open VLA models,
including π0\pi_{0} [3], π0.5\pi_{0.5} [4], SmolVLA [8], and GR00T N1.7 [9, 10]. We additionally
evaluate two temporal variants based on SARM-derived task-progress
signals [11] and short-horizon MEM observation history [12].

Our experiments reveal substantial differences between VLA
configurations under identical physical conditions. Among the evaluated
models, π0\pi_{0} achieves the strongest autonomous performance, whereas
the evaluated SARM- and memory-augmented variants do not improve task
success in our setting. The experiments further expose recurring
failure modes in embodiment adaptation, stage transitions, and
long-horizon execution, while showing that limited human intervention
can recover a substantial fraction of otherwise unsuccessful
π0\pi_{0} rollouts. These results highlight the remaining gap between
the capabilities demonstrated by modern VLA models and reliable
deployment on accessible mobile bimanual hardware.

The main contributions of this work are:

We present a low-cost and reproducible mobile bimanual
platform based on dual LeRobot SO-101 manipulators and TurtleBot 4,
with custom 3D-printable structures, multi-camera perception, and
an integrated LeRobot–ROS 2 software stack.

We establish a real-world long-horizon toilet-cleaning case
study with 250 demonstrations and five sequential task stages,
requiring mobility, bimanual coordination, and contact-rich tool
manipulation.

We provide a controlled physical evaluation of representative
open VLA models and temporal variants on the same embodiment and
dataset, and analyze their task performance and characteristic
failure modes.

1. We present a low-cost and reproducible mobile bimanual
platform based on dual LeRobot SO-101 manipulators and TurtleBot 4,
with custom 3D-printable structures, multi-camera perception, and
an integrated LeRobot–ROS 2 software stack.

2. We establish a real-world long-horizon toilet-cleaning case
study with 250 demonstrations and five sequential task stages,
requiring mobility, bimanual coordination, and contact-rich tool
manipulation.

3. We provide a controlled physical evaluation of representative
open VLA models and temporal variants on the same embodiment and
dataset, and analyze their task performance and characteristic
failure modes.
