title: Bind-WAM: Binding-Uncertainty-Guided Selective Future Imagination in World Action Models
authors: Chenhao Qiu,Shuyi Chen,Songen Gu,Shufeng Nan,Tianyu Wang,Siyu Lin,Yifan Li,Bingwen Zhu,Yanwei Fu
abstract:
World Action Models (WAMs) can improve robot learning by jointly predicting future
visual states and actions, but generating a visual future at every replanning
step is expensive and sometimes unnecessary. This raises a critical question: when should a robot
policy imagine the future? In this paper, we propose Bind-WAM, a binding-uncertainty-guided
WAM for selective future imagination. Bind-WAM introduces language-object binding
uncertainty, selectively invoking joint future-action generation when the
current observation does not support stable task-relevant action generation. An offline
labeling pipeline uses complete demonstrations and action context to identify task-relevant objects and detect reference
mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift. The resulting pseudo-labels
supervise a lightweight router that predicts binding uncertainty from the
current observation and language instruction. At inference, a
shared WAM policy invokes selective future imagination according
to the predicted uncertainty and its change
between consecutive replanning steps.
Simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate that Bind-WAM can
establish binding uncertainty as a strong, interpretable signal for
selective future imagination.
introduction:
World Action Models (WAMs) improve robot policies with the ability to imagine
how a scene may evolve. By jointly predicting future visual states and actions,
they can exploit temporal and physical structure that is absent from a purely
reactive observation-to-action interface [1]. Yet traditional WAMs
always make an implicit assumption: future imagination should be triggered at every
replanning step. This uniform strategy ignores a basic property of
policy execution: the value of dreaming ahead is state dependent. In many states the
current observation already specifies the relevant objects and action, whereas
in others the policy must resolve missing, ambiguous, or unstable visual
evidence before acting.

This leads to the central question of this paper: when should
a robot policy imagine the future? Existing work like Fast-WAM [2] shows that video co-training can benefit action prediction
even when future imagination is totally removed at deployment,
and Faster-WAM [3] finds that future representations can improve robustness under
visual distribution shift. The important distinction
is therefore not whether future prediction is globally useful, but whether its
additional information is useful for the current state. Recent methods
such as AdaWAM [4] enable adaptive inference by routing among
action-only, visual, and textual reasoning according to the execution context.
However, this identifies the need for future prediction mainly through execution
phases, but when imagination is truly necessary for the current state
remains unclear. Selective future imagination requires an interpretable signal to determine whether joint future-action prediction should be invoked.

We choose language-object binding uncertainty as such a signal. A
language instruction assigns semantic roles to objects in the scene. For
example, in
“place the bowl on the plate,” the bowl is the affected object and the
plate is the relational reference. The policy’s decision is fragile when a
required object is invisible, when similar instances compete for the same role,
or when an object’s tracked identity changes during execution. These cases
are jointly defined by language and vision, arise before low-level action
generation, and directly threaten task completion, therefore
requiring future imagination to provide additional guidance. Stable language-object
bindings, in contrast, provide a clear setting for policies to skip future
generation and predict correct actions.

In this paper, we propose Bind-WAM, a binding-uncertainty-guided WAM for selective future
imagination. Bind-WAM introduces an offline labeling pipeline that leverages
Qwen3-VL [5], SAM 3.1 [6] and
DINOv3 [7] to generate uncertainty
labels representing role mismatch, invisibility, and identity drift, which are
used for training a 6.65M-parameter lightweight predictor. At deployment, the
predicted uncertainty value switches
one shared WAM between direct action prediction and joint future-action
denoising.

Our contributions are threefold. First, we formulate selective future
imagination in World Action Models as a state-dependent
problem, and introduce language-object binding uncertainty as an
interpretable signal for deciding when joint future-action prediction should
be invoked. Second, we develop Bind-WAM, which constructs binding uncertainty
supervision from an offline labeling pipeline, and predicts uncertainty with
a lightweight predictor to route a shared WAM between direct and joint
inference. Third, simulation and real-world experiments demonstrate
that binding uncertainty can identify the states where future
imagination is useful.

title: Interactive Perception of Granular Materials via Robotic Scooping and Force-Torque Sensing
authors: Samuli Hynninen,Mohammad Amman,Meri Mäkelä,Anirvan Dutta,Ville Kyrki
abstract: Granular materials exhibit complex and highly variable interaction dynamics, making their reliable manipulation challenging without knowledge of their physical properties. We present an interactive perception framework that infers granular material properties directly from force–torque measurements acquired during scooping. The proposed Latent Filter++ combines a bio-inspired frequency–temporal filter-bank representation with a causal latent dynamical model, allowing the representation to evolve as interaction observations become available while avoiding hand-crafted signal preprocessing. The learned latent representation captures physically meaningful variation in granular materials and supports estimation of properties including grain size and bulk density. Evaluated on 2626 diverse granular materials, the approach generalizes to materials excluded from training and enables few-shot adaptation of property-specific mappings using a small number of additional interaction samples. Finally, we demonstrate the relevance of the inferred properties to downstream manipulation by examining their correlation with the maximum acceleration the materials can withstand without spilling from the spoon during transport.
introduction:
Granular materials are ubiquitous in robotic manipulation, from food handling and agriculture to construction and manufacturing, yet their complex physical behavior makes them particularly challenging to manipulate reliably. Unlike rigid objects, their macroscopic response emerges from interactions among many particles and depends on properties such as particle size, shape, packing, and compaction [1]. Reliable perception of these properties is therefore important for manipulation and transportation, where the same action can produce substantially different outcomes across materials.

Existing approaches to granular-material manipulation have primarily relied on either real-world sensory feedback or physics-based simulation. Real-world methods have used visual, tactile, and vibrational signals to estimate quantities such as scooped mass and material flow [2, 3]. While these approaches demonstrate that interaction signals contain rich information about granular materials, they often target task-specific quantities or predefined material categories rather than generalizable physical properties. Simulation-based approaches provide an alternative for modeling granular-material interactions without extensive real-world data [4, 5]; however, accurately capturing granular behavior remains challenging because of the high-dimensional particle state and complex inter-particle interactions. Moreover, transferring simulation-based models to real materials requires correspondence between simulated and physical material behavior, often involving material-specific calibration. These limitations motivate learning physical representations directly from real interaction data.

A key challenge is to extract such properties from the temporal evolution of the interaction rather than from isolated observations, i.e., through interactive perception. In this work, we consider scooping with a spoon as the interaction. When interaction forces during scooping are measured with a force-torque (F/T) sensor, the resulting F/T signal combines slowly varying loads arising from bulk interaction with higher-frequency fluctuations caused by grain-scale contacts. Humans similarly infer material properties during interaction, while different populations of mechanoreceptors exhibit distinct sensitivities to the temporal and frequency characteristics of skin deformation [6, 7]. Inspired by this organization, we introduce a learnable frequency–temporal filter-bank encoder that explicitly determines which frequencies to emphasize and over what time intervals to integrate. This provides a structured inductive bias for learning from limited interaction data while avoiding handcrafted signal decomposition or dataset-specific preprocessing.

Building on this encoding technique, we extend the latent-filter framework of Dutta et al. [8] into a causal sequential model for granular-material perception. The proposed Latent Filter++ operates directly on raw F/T measurements and maintains a temporally evolving representation of the interaction and material properties. This is particularly important for granular materials, for which some physical properties can be measured independently, while others are difficult to characterize directly and may only become apparent through interaction. Rather than requiring explicit supervision for every relevant property, the model learns a latent representation from the observed interaction dynamics. We introduce an innovation pathway and observation masking to encourage the latent representation to capture temporal interaction dynamics, and explicitly evaluate its ability to generalize to materials unseen during training. Separating the learned representation from the property-specific readout further allows adaptation to a new material using only a small number of interaction samples, without retraining the interaction model.

This study makes the following contributions:

We introduce a bio-inspired frequency–temporal filter-bank encoder that provides a structured inductive bias for F/T measurements without hand-crafted preprocessing, with more consistent performance across observation-window lengths than CNN encoders.

We extend the sequential latent-filter framework as Latent Filter++ with an innovation pathway and observation masking to enable causal online inference from raw F/T measurements, improve latent representation learning, and infer physical properties from interaction dynamics.

We demonstrate that the learned representation captures physically meaningful variation, enabling estimation of grain size and bulk density for unseen materials and adaptation of property-specific mappings from a small number of interaction samples.

We evaluate the approach on a real robotic setup with 2626 diverse granular materials and demonstrate its downstream utility by showing how the inferred properties are related to maximum accelerations that the materials can withstand without spilling from the spoon during transportation.

title: BiPOP: Partial-Order Planning for Long-Horizon Bimanual Robotic Manipulation
authors: Kun Chu,Xufeng Zhao,Jan-Gerrit Habekost,Cornelius Weber,Stefan Wermter
abstract: Bimanual robotic manipulation offers substantial versatility, yet its central challenge lies not only in executing dexterous motion with each hand, but also in coordinating the two arms for long-horizon manipulation under coupled spatial and temporal constraints. Prior work has largely focused on endowing robots with human-level manipulation skills, paying comparatively less attention to the structure of bimanual behaviour itself: many practical tasks are best understood as a coordinated composition of reusable unimanual skills together with a small set of synchronous bimanual skills. This makes high-level spatio-temporal coordination, rather than skill acquisition alone, a key bottleneck for efficient bimanual execution. Therefore, we propose BiPOP, a framework that couples Large Language Models (LLMs) with Temporal Partial-Order Planning for long-horizon bimanual manipulation. At its core is an explicit spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and captures inter-arm dependencies, arm assignment, synchronization requirements, and opportunities for safe concurrent execution. Building on this model, an LLM translates natural-language instructions into a formal PDDL specification, while a temporal planner enforces the constraints and schedules actions, yielding plans that are logically consistent at the symbolic level and efficient through parallel execution. On simulated long-horizon tasks of varying complexity, BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with strong reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency, and the full pipeline runs end-to-end on a real bimanual robot NICOL. A failure analysis further shows that LLM-only planners mainly violate spatial and temporal coordination constraints, which motivates delegating these constraints to a symbolic planner. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Kchu/BiPOP.
introduction:
Humans effortlessly perform bimanual tasks, from tying shoelaces to flipping book pages while holding a coffee cup, orchestrating complex spatial and temporal synchronization without conscious thought. Robots, in contrast, struggle even with apparently simple bimanual tasks, which demand planning, synchronization, and coordination. Bridging this gap remains an inherent challenge in robotics [1, 2].

Deep learning techniques ease the acquisition of dexterous bimanual manipulation, such as folding shirts [3], cutting vegetables [4], and scooping food [5]. However, most approaches focus on learning human-level skills as a whole and overlook high-level task planning, which demands task decomposition, subtask assignment between the arms, execution sequencing and parallelization over long horizons.

Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong reasoning and planning abilities across domains [6], and recent work applies them to robotic task planning [7, 8, 9, 10]. Yet generating embodiment-aware, executable plans is difficult for complex manipulation, where LLMs remain prone to long-horizon reasoning errors and hallucinations [11, 12], especially in spatially constrained scenarios. To mitigate these limitations, LLMs have been combined with classical symbolic planners [13]: by translating natural-language instructions into declarative representations such as PDDL [14], LLMs enable plans with logical-correctness guarantees. However, these approaches generally do not address the spatio-temporal coordination intrinsic to bimanual manipulation, in particular inter-arm dependencies, task allocation, synchronization, and parallelization. Our research question is therefore: how can LLMs be integrated with symbolic planning to achieve efficient spatial and temporal coordination for long-horizon bimanual robotic tasks?

To address this, we propose BiPOP (Bimanual Partial-Order Planning), a framework (Fig. 1) for long-horizon bimanual task planning that integrates semantic reasoning with explicit spatio-temporal coordination. Our contributions are threefold. First, we introduce a spatio-temporal model that partitions the workspace by arm reachability and encodes inter-arm dependencies, synchronization, and safe concurrency as durative PDDL actions with mutual-exclusion predicates. Second, we couple LLM-based problem generation with temporal planning: an LLM translates the task description and scene information into a PDDL problem, and a temporal planner computes a validated partial-order plan with a short symbolic makespan. Third, we evaluate BiPOP against open-loop and closed-loop LLM planners on three simulated bimanual task domains and deploy it on a real bimanual robot NICOL [15]. The results show that BiPOP outperforms open-loop planning with recent OpenAI and DeepSeek reasoning models and closed-loop ReAct-style planning in success rate, planning time, and plan efficiency.

title: APG-Planner: Learning Vision-Based High-Speed Trajectory Planning via Analytic Policy Gradient
authors: Jinwoo Lee,Geunsik Bae,Changseung Kim,Jiwoo Kim,Woojae Shin,Hyondong Oh
abstract: Vision-based high-speed navigation requires a trajectory planner that can reactively generate smooth, collision-free trajectories from onboard visual observations. Deep reinforcement learning offers a promising approach to vision-based trajectory planning, as it enables the optimization of sequential decision-making policies in complex environments. However, model-free policy gradient methods rely on sample-based policy gradient estimation, which yields noisy gradient estimates and inefficient training. To this end, we propose a framework for learning trajectory planning policies using the analytic policy gradient (APG) method and use it to train APG-Planner, a vision-based high-speed trajectory planner. The proposed framework leverages differential flatness to analytically reconstruct vehicle states from planned trajectories, thereby enabling differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without requiring an explicit low-level dynamics model. By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct a differentiable episode rollout and analytically compute policy gradients from episode-level losses, improving both training efficiency and policy performance. After approximately 30 minutes of training on a single GPU, APG-Planner demonstrates comparable or superior performance to existing baseline methods in simulation and achieves speeds of up to 11 m/s in real-world flight experiments. We further validate the proposed framework on a skid-steer ground robot, demonstrating its applicability to differentially flat robotic systems beyond quadrotors.
introduction:
Vision-based high-speed flight has been widely studied to fully exploit the agility of quadrotors. The central challenge is to plan collision-free trajectories online from visual observations under limited onboard computation. Conventional systems reconstruct a geometric representation of the environment and then perform a trajectory search or optimization [1, 2, 3]. Although effective, these approaches introduce computational latency that may limit rapid replanning for obstacle avoidance. To address this limitation, recent studies have proposed learning-based planners that directly generate trajectories from depth observations [4, 5, 6, 7].

Recent works on learning-based trajectory planning have adopted training paradigms such as imitation learning [4, 5] and guidance learning [7]. Imitation learning can offer advantages in sample efficiency but is limited by the availability and quality of expert trajectories. Guidance-based learning removes the need for expert demonstrations by exploiting gradients from a predefined planning-cost landscape, but such guidance remains local to each planning decision.

In high-speed flight, each planned trajectory affects future states and decisions, influencing overall flight performance. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a promising approach to this problem, as it optimizes sequential decisions with respect to task-level objectives. However, training model-free RL policies for high-speed flight remains challenging, as model-free policy gradient methods rely on sampled rollouts to estimate policy gradients. These estimates can exhibit high variance, making training sample-intensive and slowing convergence [8]. An alternative should enable task-level optimization while providing more accurate policy gradients.

Analytic policy gradient (APG) methods provide such an alternative by constructing a differentiable episode rollout and backpropagating task-loss through it [9, 10]. Previous studies have employed APG to learn control policies, typically by propagating system states through differentiable dynamics. Recent work has successfully applied this approach to learn an end-to-end control policy for vision-based high-speed drone flight [8]. However, this approach required a differentiable dynamics simulator calibrated using real-world flight data, necessitating recalibration of parameters such as aerodynamic drag across vehicles, while its end-to-end formulation limits interpretability. Therefore, learning high-speed trajectory planners remains a distinct and important research direction, providing explicit trajectories that facilitate interpretation and fallback design while integrating with existing low-level controllers to reduce reliance on low-level dynamics modeling.

In this work, we propose a learning framework that uses APG to train APG-Planner, a vision-based high-speed trajectory planner. The proposed policy outputs trajectory segments in the flat-output space, while an existing low-level controller tracks the planned trajectories. Training a trajectory planning policy with APG requires differentiable state transitions between successive planning steps. We construct these transitions directly from planned trajectories using differential flatness, instead of explicitly simulating low-level vehicle dynamics.

Differential flatness enables quadrotor states to be represented in terms of position, heading, and a finite number of their derivatives [11], and has been widely exploited for trajectory optimization [2, 3]. We take this idea a step further by using differential flatness not only to parameterize trajectories, but also to define the state transition between successive planning decisions. Following a receding-horizon scheme, we analytically evaluate the planned trajectory at each replanning instant and reconstruct the corresponding vehicle state through the flatness map for the subsequent planning decision. This enables differentiable trajectory-level state transitions without explicitly modeling or unrolling low-level vehicle dynamics.

By iteratively performing trajectory planning and differentiable state transitions, we construct differentiable episode rollouts and directly compute policy gradients from episode-level losses. This allows the planner to account for the downstream effects of sequential planning decisions during policy optimization while avoiding sampling-based policy-gradient estimation.
Furthermore, by leveraging the flatness map of the target system, our framework enables the training of trajectory planners without requiring platform-specific low-level dynamics models. Moreover, the proposed framework is not limited to quadrotors and can be extended to other differentially flat robotic systems.

The main contributions of this work are as follows:

We formulate differentiable trajectory-level state transitions using differential flatness, without explicitly modeling low-level system dynamics.

Based on this formulation, we propose an APG-based framework for training trajectory planning policies. Using this framework, we train APG-Planner in just 30 minutes on a single GPU.

We demonstrate the performance of APG-Planner through extensive experiments, achieving competitive results in simulation and peak flight speeds of 11 m/s in real-world quadrotor flights. Further experiments on a skid-steer ground robot validate its applicability beyond quadrotors.

1. We formulate differentiable trajectory-level state transitions using differential flatness, without explicitly modeling low-level system dynamics.

2. Based on this formulation, we propose an APG-based framework for training trajectory planning policies. Using this framework, we train APG-Planner in just 30 minutes on a single GPU.

3. We demonstrate the performance of APG-Planner through extensive experiments, achieving competitive results in simulation and peak flight speeds of 11 m/s in real-world quadrotor flights. Further experiments on a skid-steer ground robot validate its applicability beyond quadrotors.

title: Autonomous Trail Racing with a Bicycle Robot
authors: Fabian Jenelten,Deepana Ishtaweera,Pablo Garcia,Liana Margolese,Igor Bogoslavskyi,Luca Buonocore,Jan Migliazza,Aleksandrs Ecins,Annika Wollschlaeger,Dario Bellicoso,Gabriel Nelson,Abel Gawel,Marco Hutter
comment: (incl. appendix with supplementary figures and tables). Submitted to The International Journal of Robotics Research. Project page:this https URL. Code:this https URL
abstract:
Navigating off-road trails on a mountain bike requires diverse locomotion skills, including aerial maneuvers, cornering, and slip recovery, paired with sophisticated perception for scene understanding. Translating these capabilities to autonomous, two-wheeled robots remains a formidable challenge.
We show that autonomous, high-speed trail navigation can be achieved through a single idea: encoding the trail as a semantic layer of the terrain. In simulation, this layer embeds the navigation task into the training environment; during deployment, it is reconstructed onboard from camera and LiDAR data.
First, we introduce a unified learning framework that treats local navigation and locomotion as a joint optimization problem, bypassing the twist or pose command interface of classical control hierarchies. With fixed reward weights, the same framework produces both trail racing and agile parkour, shaped only through terrain semantics and episode length.
Second, our perception pipeline combines a frozen vision foundation model with a lightweight dual-head decoder that predicts per-pixel terrain semantics and confidence scores, which are fused with LiDAR range measurements into an egocentric semantic elevation map at 30 Hz30\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} onboard an NVIDIA AGX Orin.
We validate our framework on the  UMV (UMV), a bicycle robot that autonomously raced across all sections of a kilometer-long, unstructured mountain bike trail at speeds exceeding 5 m/s5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} and averaging 3.26 m/s3.26\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s}. In simulation, our policy fails up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines while driving faster.
We release our simulation and perception tools as open source.
introduction:
Off-road mountain biking demands a robust fusion of high-level world understanding, spatial planning, and split-second physical coordination. Deploying statically unstable systems, like a bicycle robot, on a mountain bike trail is inherently difficult because uneven, unpredictable terrain in outdoor forests makes it hard to plan and execute maneuvers. Friction fluctuates with changing ground conditions, seasonal shifts alter vegetation, and changing sun positions and cloud coverage introduce unpredictable shadows and harsh lighting variations. Therefore, autonomous trail racing emerges as a profoundly challenging, tightly coupled perception-and-control problem. It combines research challenges from navigation (Ravichandran et al., 2022; Rana et al., 2023; Lee et al., 2024; Werby et al., 2024; Rajvanshi et al., 2024), autonomous hiking (Miki, 2025; Mattamala et al., 2025; Reed et al., 2025; Giusti et al., 2016), legged parkour (Hoeller et al., 2024; Cheng et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2025), high-speed autonomous ground vehicle racing (Kabzan et al., 2020; Cataffo et al., 2022; Betz et al., 2023), and drone racing (Loquercio et al., 2021; Kaufmann et al., 2023; Bahnam et al., 2026), while adding the complexity related to the unstable bike dynamics. Autonomous trail racing sits at the intersection of these domains, here summarized as “time-optimal traversal of mountain bike trails relying strictly on onboard compute and sensing using wheeled, statically unstable platforms”. Each of the aforementioned fields addresses one or more relevant aspects, but no method provides a complete solution to trail racing. We tackle this challenge by (i) unifying local navigation and control and (ii) casting pathfinding as an explicit perception problem, without the need for a global map or destination-based planning.

The prior work by Bokser et al. (2026) presented the UMV, a two-wheeled bicycle robot capable of high-speed driving up to 8 m/s8\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} on flat ground. Two actuated DOF in the upper body allow the robot to trigger vertical jumps reaching 1 m1\text{\,}\mathrm{m} in height. While it demonstrated the physical feasibility of driving down a trail within a human-operated experiment, we consider the UMV the ideal platform to push toward full autonomy and high-speed racing. Expanding upon this hardware foundation, we integrate onboard perception, develop real-time visual world understanding, and learn vision-locomotive skills to present a comprehensive framework for autonomous trail racing (Fig. 3 and multimedia extensions E1 and E2).

We break this challenge down into two core scientific contributions. First, we introduce a platform-agnostic  MDP (MDP), herein referred to as  TENa (TENa) (subsection 3.2). By encoding the traversable path as a semantic layer directly into the terrain mesh and treating it as a soft boundary during training, locomotion and local navigation collapse into a unified optimization problem. To support our specific application, we also present the  TL (TL), an approach for the procedural generation of diverse, unidirectional synthetic trails that enables zero-shot deployment of racing policies (subsection 3.1). Second, to render the semantic path observable to the control policy during real-world deployment, we introduce  SemMap (SemMap) (subsection 3.3). This module constructs a two-layered, robot-centric elevation map containing both geometric and semantic path information. Leveraging a frozen  VFM (VFM) paired with a lightweight decoder, incoming RGB images are processed at up to 90 Hz90\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz} in isolation and fused with LiDAR range measurements at 30 Hz30\text{\,}\mathrm{Hz}, producing a 2.5D elevation map that holds the path as a segmented trail.

We demonstrate autonomous deployment on a kilometer-scale, real-world mountain bike trail, sustaining average speeds of 3.26 m/s3.26\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} and peaking above 5 m/s5\text{\,}\mathrm{m}\text{/}\mathrm{s} (Fig. 2A). Compared to prior work Bokser et al. (2026), our work (i) introduces a single training environment applicable to both trail racing (subsections 4.4, 4.5) and parkour (subsection 4.2) with fixed reward weights; (ii) removes the human operator by following a trail observed by SemMap (subsections 4.3, 4.4); (iii) outperforms the teleoperated policy by a factor of 2.3 in speed on a real-world mountain-bike trail where baseline data is available (subsection 4.5); (iv) in simulation, fails up to an order of magnitude less often than hierarchical baselines built on the policy of Bokser et al. (2026), including one with a learned navigation policy, while driving faster (subsection 4.6); and (v) integrates the necessary state-estimation tools and onboard perception hardware (subsection 3.4). title: DroneDiffusion: Uncertainty-Guided Diffusion Path Planner for UAV Navigation
authors: Ivan Valuev,Iana Zhura,Valerii Serpiva,Miguel Altamirano Cabrera,Dzmitry Tsetserukou
abstract: We present DroneDiffusion, a perception-aware diffusion planner for local 3-D UAV trajectory generation that explicitly models and avoids failure zones caused by lens flare, overexposure, and reflective surfaces. A vision-language perceptual safety estimator produces a pixel-aligned reliability map that highlights regions of degraded sensing. A denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) is conditioned on this map together with the onboard RGB image, goal point, and initial velocity to generate egocentric 3-D trajectories. To enforce obstacle avoidance at inference time without retraining, we apply training-free CHOMP guidance over a 3-D Euclidean signed distance field. The model is trained entirely in simulation and deployed zero-shot on a real drone. Reliability conditioning raises the mean perceptual reliability along generated trajectories to 0.710.71, compared with 0.630.63 for a geometric baseline, while guidance halves the collision rate of the learned prior from 14.7%14.7\% to 7.8%7.8\%. Perceptual safety conditioning and geometric guidance are therefore complementary: treating sensor reliability as a first-class signal reduces incursions into unreliable regions while maintaining competitive navigation performance.
introduction:
Autonomous UAV navigation in cluttered indoor environments exposes onboard sensors to perceptual hazards that geometric planners routinely ignore: overexposed corridors, lens flare, transparent walls, and specular surfaces. A planner unaware of such failures may route a drone confidently through a region where the sensor stream cannot be trusted.

Diffusion models have recently emerged as expressive trajectory generators for navigation and manipulation, offering flexible multimodal conditioning and strong generalization from data [1, 2, 3]. Yet existing diffusion planners condition only on geometric and semantic cues such as RGB images, goal specifications, or occupancy maps. They provide no mechanism to reason about input reliability when the image is saturated or the depth measurements are invalid. Vision-language tools such as CLIPSeg [4] and AnyTraverse [5] can detect such failure zones, but have not been integrated into trajectory-level planning.

We present a diffusion planner for 3-D UAV trajectory generation that treats a perceptual safety map as a first-class conditioning signal alongside the RGB image, goal point, and initial velocity. A CLIPSeg-based estimator produces a pixel-aligned reliability map that penalizes overexposure, lens flare, and transparent surfaces. A DDPM denoiser generates egocentric 4-DoF paths (x,y,z,ψx,y,z,\psi) of 24 waypoints at 10 Hz conditioned on this map, naturally steering away from unreliable regions. Training-free CHOMP guidance on a 3-D ESDF enforces geometric obstacle avoidance at inference time. The model trains in simulation and transfers to real drone flights without fine-tuning.

The main contributions are:

A perceptual safety map formulation that encodes sensor failure zones as a spatial reliability prior for diffusion trajectory planning.

A conditional DDPM planner for 3-D UAV navigation
jointly conditioned on visual context and perceptual reliability, with sim-to-real transfer validation.

A training-free guidance module
enforcing obstacle avoidance and goal reaching without retraining.

2. A conditional DDPM planner for 3-D UAV navigation
jointly conditioned on visual context and perceptual reliability, with sim-to-real transfer validation.

title: Are We Ready for Snow-tonomous Driving? Challenges Toward Robust Automated Driving in Extreme Weather
authors: Eren Erdal Aksoy,Abu Mohammed Raisuddin,Thien-Thu Ngo,Eren Aydemir,Osman Tahir Ekşi,Paula Litkey,Petri Manninen,Heikki Hyyti,Jyri Maanpää,Tarmo Kivioja,Tuomas Herranen,Väisänen Sofie,Niemi Kalle,Isabelle Morvan,Pierre Duthon,Ian Marsh,Martin Sanfridson,Henrik Toss,Thanh Bui,Yuri Poledna,Maikol Funk Drechsler,Mikko Tarkiainen,Matti Kutila,Topi Miekkala,Stefan Parzefall,Valentina Donzella,Pak Hung Chan,Sogol Kharrazi,Mario Ceccarelli
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract:
Automated driving has gained remarkable momentum over the past decade, with both industry and academia investing substantial resources in developing perception and control solutions to advance vehicle autonomy.
However, these efforts have largely focused on clear-weather scenarios, leaving harsh conditions, such as snow, rain, and fog, comparatively understudied.
As a result, inclement weather remains one of the most significant hurdles for autonomous vehicles,
often leading to substantial performance degradation in downstream perception and control tasks.
introduction:
Over the past decade, automated driving research has undergone a quantum leap, largely driven by rapid and exciting advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI). Both academic research institutions and companies have invested substantial resources in developing and demonstrating AI-based perception and control systems across increasingly impressive real-world scenarios. Notable examples include Waymo’s autonomous robotaxi fleet11
1
https://waymo.com/ operating continuously in the US and the large-scale deployment of Baidu’s robotaxis22
2
https://ir.baidu.com/ across multiple cities in China [1].
Despite these remarkable achievements, a fundamental question remains: why do we not yet see robotaxis navigating autonomously in harsh weather (e.g., under heavy rain or snowfall)?

This breakdown in autonomy under extreme environmental conditions highlights a lack of systemic resilience. The challenge is particularly pressing considering the fact that, for instance, in March 2025 alone, nearly 3 million km2 of Europe was covered by snow [2].
Thus, until Autonomous Vehicles (AVs) can robustly perceive and safely act in such adverse, unpredictable conditions, the vision of truly reliable autonomy remains unfulfilled.

Severe weather is a natural phenomenon that poses significant challenges for current AVs.
Sensors can become partially (or fully) occluded or contaminated by water droplets, mud, snow, and ice (see Fig. -1), leading to degraded sensor measurements and impaired perception performance.
For example, 3D LiDAR scans can be severely affected by precipitation, which in turn degrades downstream tasks such as object detection and semantic segmentation.
Likewise, road surface conditions can deteriorate rapidly, for instance, due to ice formation or aquaplaning. This compromises tire–road friction and reduces controller reliability and safety. Testing and validation under such conditions remain particularly challenging, as severe weather is both sporadic and difficult to reproduce in a controlled and scalable manner.

To address these weather-related challenges, the EU-funded Horizon Europe project ROADVIEW33
3
https://roadview-project.eu/ (RObust Automated DriVIng in Extreme Weather) aims to develop robust, weather-aware perception and control modules that enhance the performance of connected and automated vehicles under severe conditions, including snow, rain, and fog (See Fig. -1).
With 15 partners from seven countries, ROADVIEW targets a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) 7 automated driving stack deployed across five distinct vehicle platforms, including passenger cars and trucks (See Figs. -1, 0, and 3).
Building on four years of intensive development and real-world deployment in ROADVIEW, we pose a fundamental question to the research community: are we truly ready for snow-autonomous driving?

Drawing on lessons learned from multiple ROADVIEW demonstrations, we, as members of the ROADVIEW consortium, identify ten core challenges as key obstacles to achieving autonomy resilient to weather-induced disturbances. These challenges are summarized as follows:

Lack of annotated harsh weather datasets:
Although several autonomous driving datasets [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9] include all-weather scenarios (see Table I), most contain only a limited amount of annotated data representing severe weather conditions. For example, snowy scenes account for merely 2%2\% of the ZOD [6] dataset and approximately 12%12\% of Ithaca365 [7]. Some datasets are specifically designed for winter environments [8, 5]; however, they typically focus on a single perception task, such as 3D object detection in the CADC dataset [8] or 3D semantic segmentation in SemanticSTF [5]. Furthermore, existing publicly available datasets lack comprehensive ground-truth annotations for jointly evaluating multiple multimodal 3D perception tasks under harsh winter conditions. Thus, the research community is in urgent need of multimodal datasets that span multiple seasonal conditions, ensure balanced data distributions, and provide supervision signals for multiple perception tasks.

Lack of annotated harsh weather datasets:
Although several autonomous driving datasets [3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9] include all-weather scenarios (see Table I), most contain only a limited amount of annotated data representing severe weather conditions. For example, snowy scenes account for merely 2%2\% of the ZOD [6] dataset and approximately 12%12\% of Ithaca365 [7]. Some datasets are specifically designed for winter environments [8, 5]; however, they typically focus on a single perception task, such as 3D object detection in the CADC dataset [8] or 3D semantic segmentation in SemanticSTF [5]. Furthermore, existing publicly available datasets lack comprehensive ground-truth annotations for jointly evaluating multiple multimodal 3D perception tasks under harsh winter conditions. Thus, the research community is in urgent need of multimodal datasets that span multiple seasonal conditions, ensure balanced data distributions, and provide supervision signals for multiple perception tasks.

Multimodal sensing and data quality:
Sensing is a fundamental component for bootstrapping autonomy.
Severe weather, however, introduces dynamic and modality-specific degradations, such as reduced visibility in RGB images, snow-induced noise in LiDAR point clouds, and signal ambiguities in RADAR data.
The challenge arises when noise in raw 2D images and 3D point clouds propagates to downstream perception tasks, leading to degraded performance.
Contemporary research tackles these heterogeneous disturbances that vary over time and space by applying conventional statistical noise filtering techniques [10, 11, 9, 12, 13] or advanced AI-based supervised denoising methods [14, 15, 16], which are unimodal and require substantial amounts of annotated data.
Still, the development of sensor-agnostic and generic filtering methods remains largely underexplored.
Furthermore, there is no established consensus on a metric to quantify data quality levels, akin to Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) [17].
Therefore, multimodal data quality degradation and sensor impairments need to be assessed from sensor installation at the hardware level to object detection at the machine learning level [18, 19].

Real-time weather-aware multimodal perception:
While multimodal sensing provides complementary information and enhances robustness through increased redundancy, achieving real-time perception while continuously adapting to changing weather conditions remains a significant challenge.
A key limitation of current approaches is that they remain context-agnostic and follow static fusion strategies, in which the relative contributions of each modality are fixed and fail to adapt to variations in scene context, such as weather-induced degradation.
Although recent methods explore attention-based cross-modal fusion [20] and availability-aware weighting schemes [21], their applicability in real-time settings is often limited by computational complexity.
Consequently, balancing robustness, adaptability, and computational efficiency remains an open challenge for ensuring safe and reliable autonomy.
To further enhance resilience against harsh weather conditions, more advanced perception solutions are required, for instance, to distinguish various weather types, estimate road-surface slipperiness, and predict the visibility of the drivable area, among others.

Weather-aware map-based positioning:
Accurate vehicle positioning relative to the surrounding roadway is fundamental for AVs. In addition to satellite-based positioning, High-Definition (HD) map-based positioning is widely used to estimate the vehicle’s pose with respect to a prior map of the environment, enabling centimeter-level accuracy and lane-level semantic understanding [22].
HD maps commonly use a set of points and line segments in a global reference frame to represent detectable features in the environment.
These features include lane markings, road boundaries, lane dividers, curbs, sidewalks, pedestrian crossings, and both vertical and horizontal traffic signs.
Owing to their rich and precise representation of the road environment, HD maps are considered among the most suitable priors for localization [23].
However, many of these features become partially or fully obscured under harsh winter conditions, when snow obscures most road markings.
Positioning the automated vehicle within the required accuracy of 10 cm [24] under these conditions is therefore challenging and requires novel, robust methods.

Collective perception via V2X communication:
Collective perception enables vehicles and roadside units to extend their understanding of the environment by sharing high-level perception results. Current V2X [25] deployments remain limited to connected-vehicle self-announcements, which provide insufficient situational awareness, especially at low market penetration or in the presence of non-connected road users, such as pedestrians or animals. The next generation of V2X services introduces the Collective Perception Message (CPM) to share the outputs of a single sensor or a multimodal perception system, including sensor metadata, perception regions, and perceived objects. Within ROADVIEW, we investigated how adverse weather affects the quality of perception systems and which quality-related information should be shared in CPMs [26]. To support this work, an infrastructure-based perception system was installed in Northern Finland to evaluate the impact of harsh weather conditions on the sensing performance. We also explored methods [27] to mitigate systematic errors in roadside sensing by performing offline deviation analysis with a high-precision probe vehicle.
The integration of V2X-based collective perception into automated driving requires reliable temporal and spatial alignment between local perception and CPMs received from roadside units or other vehicles. This alignment depends on the availability of uncertainty descriptors, detection confidence, and kinematic precision to support robust fusion.
Early deployment phases will involve only a limited number of CPM-capable vehicles or roadside units, but the system must remain scalable as penetration increases. To avoid radio channel congestion, value-of-information-based mechanisms [28] are needed to dynamically adapt CPM transmission frequency and message size.
Cross-vendor interoperability also remains a significant challenge: standardization activities for CPMs are still evolving, and additional profiling work is required to ensure consistent implementation across manufacturers, including recommended parameter settings and harmonized interpretation of quality fields.
These lessons highlight that large-scale deployment of collective perception depends on both high-quality perception outputs and continued progress in standardization and profiling activities.

Weather-aware decision making:
Adverse weather affects automated driving not only by degrading perception but also by altering the vehicle’s safe operating envelope. Reduced visibility, sensor degradation, heavy snowfall or rain, fog, and low tyre–road friction can increase braking distance, reduce maneuverability, and make safe speed selection dependent on uncertain environmental estimates. Prior work has studied friction-aware vehicle control [29] and LiDAR-based visibility estimation in fog [30], [31], but a key unresolved challenge remains: how to translate these uncertain, spatially variable estimates of road and weather conditions into reliable driving decisions. This includes determining when the vehicle should reduce speed, increase safety margins, restrict maneuvers, or trigger a minimum-risk maneuver. The difficulty is that weather-related estimates cannot be directly converted into control commands; they must be interpreted alongside vehicle dynamics, route geometry, ODD limits, and uncertainty to ensure safe automated driving under changing conditions.

Sim-to-real gap in noise modeling:
In AI-based driving systems that rely heavily on sensor data, it is essential to simulate and emulate large volumes of data for training, validation, and verification. However, since driving functions are safety-critical, collecting sufficient real-world data to cover extreme conditions and complex scenarios is practically infeasible. Within ROADVIEW, significant effort has been devoted to sensor data generation and augmentation to enable thorough system testing under conditions where data cannot be collected or controlled, with a particular focus on adverse weather, including snow, rain, and fog.

Nevertheless, the use of such synthetic or augmented data must be accompanied by a rigorous analysis of its validity for the specific testing scope and environment (see the following subsection), complemented by validation against real-world data. This validation is necessary to assess the Sim2Real (Simulation-to-Real) gap. In this context, ROADVIEW has evaluated the impact of weather-induced noise models (i.e., rain, fog, and snow) on camera, LiDAR, and 4D RADAR data, considering both data-driven and physics-based approaches [32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39]. The key lessons learned are summarized as follows:

i. Importance and controllability of real data for validation.
Noise models need to be evaluated against real data collected in a controlled manner (e.g., with gradually increasing snowfall intensity) and, ideally, include ‘paired frames’, meaning identical scenes captured both with and without noise under the same conditions. In practice, achieving this is extremely challenging, as even minimal variations in environmental factors (e.g., wind or illumination) can significantly affect the captured data, even in controlled outdoor setups. To address this challenge, ROADVIEW developed and curated the REHEARSE dataset [40] with noise annotations [41].

ii. Lack of standardized metrics. There is currently no widely accepted evaluation framework in this domain. Within ROADVIEW, we propose a structured methodology based on point cloud metrics [42] and image quality metrics [43] to assess the Sim2Real gap. However, this approach provides only a partial evaluation, and further work is needed to develop holistic methods for assessing the Sim2Real gap in generated data and digital twins.

iii. Purpose-driven fidelity.
Even when highly accurate models are available, we recommend that future Sim2Real gap evaluations be linked to downstream perception performance of the overall automated driving pipeline [44]. Generating extremely realistic data is not inherently beneficial if system performance is not sensitive to such fidelity. Instead, it is crucial to understand how AI-extracted features relate to data artifacts and representations, and to focus evaluation efforts on those aspects that meaningfully affect system behavior.

XiL testing and validation:
XiL (X-in-the-Loop) testing systems enable early verification and validation of automotive software through virtual environments [45].
At advanced levels of integration, where the software is deployed on the target hardware (Hardware-in-the-Loop), real-time simulation constraints become essential to guarantee reproducible and accurate evaluations [46].
The integration of complex models, such as weather models, introduces a trade-off between fidelity and computational cost, often limiting their applicability to a restricted set of weather conditions.
Meaningful and generalizable applications require deep integration into simulation engines, which, in turn, makes models tightly coupled to specific simulation environments and hinders interoperability across simulators.
Moreover, the lack of standardized methods for accessing simulation physics and for applying sensor manipulation remains a critical barrier to the broader adoption of XiL systems.

Despite recent initiatives to create databases of LiDAR reflectivity44
4
                  
                  
                  
                https://www.persival.de/material-database, material properties are still not comprehensively cataloged.
Furthermore, current standards do not support the dynamic adaptation of these properties under varying weather conditions.
For example, in the modeling of road slipperiness, existing standards do not allow the definition of spatially varying or dynamic slippery zones, thereby limiting testing under realistic, changing conditions55
5
                  
                  
                  
                https://www.asam.net/standards/detail/opencrg/.
Similarly, standard models available in open-source simulators are often simplified [47] and limited in their representation of real-world complexity [48].
The lack of high-fidelity, low-latency sensor models continues to constrain the application of XiL systems, hindering the development and validation of automated systems not only in the automotive domain but across the broader robotics ecosystem.

Recent EU regulations explicitly encourage the use of simulation for AV validation, emphasizing the need to validate simulation results against proving-ground and real-world testing [49, 50, 51].
However, methodologies for validating simulation credibility are not yet fully defined, and the extrapolation of validation results to real-world scenarios remains insufficiently addressed.
Furthermore, reliance on proprietary interfaces for data exchange between sensors and control units limits the ability to perform standardized assessments and homologation of production vehicles using sensor data injection.
The industry, therefore, requires standardized interfaces and clear validation methodologies to ensure the credibility of simulations, as their absence impedes the large-scale adoption of XiL approaches for AVs and delays their deployment.

Transparency in perception and control:
A key challenge in AI-based perception and control is the lack of transparency in how AI models transform sensor inputs into predictions. These systems often operate as opaque black boxes [52], making it difficult for human experts to assess whether their predictions rely on relevant, sufficient, and meaningful input features. Such opacity poses a fundamental challenge for the verification and validation of AI-based systems against safety requirements, where reliable performance shall be guaranteed across diverse ODD conditions, including harsh weather. Without sufficient transparency and traceability, it is challenging to ensure system safety during operation.

Another challenge lies in establishing trustworthiness when perception outputs are directly consumed by downstream control modules for safety-critical decisions [53].
For example, a weather-aware control module may rely on perception-based estimates of weather conditions and visibility. In such cases, quantifying uncertainty and detecting out-of-distribution scenarios are essential to prevent overconfident predictions from propagating into unsafe actions in severe weather [19].

Standardizations and regulation:
Despite their potential, the large-scale commercialization and deployment of weather-resilient AV perception and control solutions remain constrained by regulatory and policy barriers. To fully unlock their benefits, policymakers (e.g., the EU and its Member States) must align fragmented connected and automated vehicle regulatory frameworks, clarify liability regimes, and establish harmonized and standardized testing and validation methodologies for adverse weather conditions.
In addition, clear and enforceable guidelines on AI transparency, data governance, privacy, and V2X communication standards are essential to enable scalable deployment while preserving public trust and ensuring regulatory compliance.
Policymakers should actively foster cross-border collaboration, invest in resilient transnational data-sharing infrastructures, and streamline regulatory processes to support consistent and safe deployment.

title: PolyMorphWBC: Whole-Body Control from End-Effector Trajectories for Quadrupedal Mobile Manipulation across Arm Morphologies with Extended Reach
authors: Heng Li,Yang Li,Yifan Duan,Ren Fang,Matao Duan,Wenhao Yu,Lu Zhang,Jianmin Ji,Yanyong Zhang
abstract:
Quadrupedal mobile manipulators can extend their manipulation workspace by coordinating the mounted arm with the mobile base.
At the task level, short-horizon end-effector (EE) trajectories provide an interface for specifying the desired manipulation motion without prescribing how it should be realized by the arm and base.
However, executing such trajectories remains challenging because the controller must determine when and how the base should move, and this decision depends on the mounted-arm morphology.
We therefore present PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical controller that takes an EE trajectory as the sole task-level motion command and generates coordinated arm–base motions across four families of 6-DoF mounted arms, with extended-reach trajectories beyond the initial fixed-base reach.
Within PolyMorphWBC, a trajectory-conditioned coordinator determines the base motion from previewed EE targets, while arm-specific Inverse Kinematics (IK) tracks the current target, and a frozen locomotion backend executes the resulting motion.
Cross-arm reuse is enabled by a Unified Robot Description Format (URDF)-derived morphology conditioning, together with online residual-wrench feedback.
We train PolyMorphWBC on procedurally generated arms and structured trajectories within and beyond fixed-base reach.
In IsaacLab, it achieves 93.95% completion with 2.30 cm position error and 4.81∘ orientation error on held-out trajectories and arm morphologies.
In MuJoCo evaluation against UMI-on-Legs, PolyMorphWBC reduces EE position error by 69–72% and orientation error by 91–97% across four within- and extended-reach trajectories.
On a physical Go2–ARX5 system, we demonstrate language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place using EE trajectories from π0\pi_{0} without vision-language-action (VLA)-generated base commands.
introduction:
Quadrupedal mobile manipulators combine legged mobility with the reach and dexterity of robotic arms, enabling manipulation beyond the arm’s fixed-base workspace [1, 2].
Exploiting this capability requires whole-body control (WBC) to coordinate the mounted arm with the mobile base while maintaining physical stability.
Existing approaches typically achieve such coordination through model-based optimization or learned control [3, 4, 5, 6, 7].
Despite substantial progress, task interfaces may still require explicit base-motion commands, while controllers are often tailored to a particular arm–base configuration.
These dependencies complicate integration with task-level policies and controller reuse across arm morphologies.

Meanwhile, recent visuomotor and VLA policies increasingly predict short action sequences [8, 9, 10].
For mobile manipulation, a short-horizon EE trajectory provides a natural task-level interface: it specifies the intended manipulation motion without prescribing how motion should be distributed between the arm and the mobile base.
UMI-on-Legs [11] demonstrates EE-trajectory-driven posture adjustment and stepping beyond fixed-base reach, although spatial coverage remains a challenge for learned tracking controllers [12]. MLM [13] extends the EE-trajectory interface to multiple tasks.
However, these controllers are developed for fixed mounted-arm morphologies.
Cross-arm reuse of the control hierarchy under the same EE-trajectory interface remains largely unexplored, especially for trajectories beyond initial fixed-base reach.
Fig. 1 summarizes this trajectory-to-motion interface together with cross-arm workspace variation and reach extension through base motion.

Addressing this problem involves two coupled challenges.
First, extending manipulation reach requires the controller to anticipate when base motion is needed: keeping the base fixed may leave upcoming EE targets unreachable, whereas premature or excessive motion can degrade EE tracking.
Second, this coordination is morphology dependent. For the same EE trajectory, kinematic differences change the feasible arm motion and required base response, while mass distribution and realized arm motion change the disturbances transmitted to the base.
We study these challenges on a compact Unitree Go211
1
            
            
          Unitree Go2: https://www.unitree.com/go2 base, where arm reachability, base motion, and stability are tightly coupled.
A reusable hierarchy must therefore combine future task motion, arm morphology, and interaction feedback.

In this work, we design and develop PolyMorphWBC, a hierarchical controller that converts short-horizon EE trajectories into coordinated arm and base motion across mounted-arm morphologies.
The EE trajectory serves as the sole task-level motion command, while the controller resolves morphology-dependent base motion and retains arm-specific kinematic execution.
A shared whole-body coordinator determines the required base motion, while an arm-specific IK module tracks the active EE target and a locomotion backend executes the resulting base command.

Our key design insight is to use future task motion to anticipate base coordination, while combining static arm morphology with online interaction feedback to adapt that coordination across arms.
To extend reach, the coordinator uses trajectory preview to anticipate the need for base posture adjustment or locomotion.
To support reuse across arms, we encode the known URDF arm model into a compact representation pretrained with kinematic and dynamic supervision, while retaining arm-specific IK for exact kinematic constraints.
Online residual-wrench feedback further captures realized arm–base interaction beyond this static model.

We evaluate PolyMorphWBC in simulation and on a physical Go2--ARX522
2
            
            
          ARX: https://arx-x.com/ system.
In simulation, we test held-out trajectories and mounted arms from four kinematic families using the same coordinator and frozen locomotion backend without policy fine-tuning.
On hardware, we demonstrate EE-commanded teleoperation and language-conditioned extended-reach pick-and-place with π0\pi_{0} [10].
Our study uses a common Go2 base platform and considers known arm models and smooth, low-speed EE trajectories.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

We present PolyMorphWBC, a shared whole-body control hierarchy that uses EE-trajectory preview to generate morphology-dependent arm–base motion within and beyond initial fixed-base reach, without task-level base commands.

We combine URDF-derived morphology conditioning with online residual-wrench feedback to reuse the same learned coordinator and locomotion backend across mounted-arm morphologies, while retaining arm-specific IK.

We evaluate cross-arm and extended-reach tracking on held-out trajectories and arms from four kinematic families in simulation, and demonstrate language-conditioned manipulation with π0\pi_{0} on a physical Go2–ARX5 system.

1. We present PolyMorphWBC, a shared whole-body control hierarchy that uses EE-trajectory preview to generate morphology-dependent arm–base motion within and beyond initial fixed-base reach, without task-level base commands.

2. We combine URDF-derived morphology conditioning with online residual-wrench feedback to reuse the same learned coordinator and locomotion backend across mounted-arm morphologies, while retaining arm-specific IK.

3. We evaluate cross-arm and extended-reach tracking on held-out trajectories and arms from four kinematic families in simulation, and demonstrate language-conditioned manipulation with π0\pi_{0} on a physical Go2–ARX5 system.

title: Elastra: A Simulation Framework for Elastic Bodies
authors: Youran Sun,Chugang Yi,Xingyu Ren,Haizhao Yang
abstract:
When robots interact with elastic surfaces such as mattresses and trampolines, changes in loading cause the surfaces to deform and rebound, altering subsequent contact locations and forces.
We present Elastra, a simulation framework for modeling this interaction and supporting the training and evaluation of robot control policies.
Elastra represents each surface using elements that move only vertically, with elastic connections and damping to model deformation and recovery.
Contact forces drive surface motion, and the updated surface geometry is used to compute subsequent contact forces.
We systematically validate our simulations against an independent implementation and a real mattress load curve.
We further use Elastra to train the Unitree G1 humanoid to stand up on mattresses and trampolines.
Using the pretrained HoST policy and ProtoMotions motion tracker as original controllers, we train residual policies through reinforcement learning to add corrections to their joint targets.
Adding these residual policies increases the success rate with HoST from 44.1% to 72.5%, and from 55% to 89% on the trampoline.
With ProtoMotions, the success rate increases from 19.0% to 45.0% for initial poses not encountered during training.
The code and video are available on GitHub.
introduction:
To use the motion skills of a robot in different environments, one has to consider how changed contact conditions affect the execution of a motion.
Mattresses, sofa cushions and trampolines sink where they are pressed and recover when the load moves on, so every push changes where the next contact lands and what force it meets.
Robot learning environments usually treat the ground as rigid.
This paper builds Elastra, a simulation framework in which mattresses and trampolines deform under the robot and the deformed surface enters the contact computation.
As the demonstration task we use standing up after a fall (Fig. 1), which loads and unloads the surface with several body parts in turn.
HoST [1] and HumanUP [2] have demonstrated humanoid standing up from many fallen postures and on varied terrain, and Singh et al. [3] achieved humanoid walking on a mattress and soft foam.
This paper instead simulates the support itself as a body that moves under the robot.

The contributions are (1) Elastra, a mattress and trampoline simulation framework for robot learning that incorporates local deformation, neighboring-region motion, and post-unloading recovery into the contact computation, (2) a systematic validation of Elastra against (i) an independent implementation and (ii) a real mattress load curve, and (3) a demonstration in which residual reinforcement learning on top of a pretrained standing policy enables the Unitree G1 to stand up on both mattresses and trampolines, evaluated across different stiffness levels and on fallen postures unseen during training.

title: Decide Before You Move: Diffusion-Generated Search Reference for Zero-Shot Open-Vocabulary Object Navigation in Semi-Static Environments
authors: Yuxuan Feng,Fujing Xie,Sören Schwertfeger,Hermann Blum
abstract:
Open-world navigation requires a robot to locate a user-specified target in an indoor scene under open-vocabulary queries.
Realistic indoor environments are semi-static: walls and furniture largely persist while smaller objects move, relocate, or vanish between visits.
Prior-map systems answer queries from object poses recorded at reconstruction time, which expire as soon as objects move, whereas online methods re-derive where to look from current observations every few steps, often through expensive calls to a vision–language model.
Assuming that walls and large furniture do not move, we keep their map to plan paths, but use a target–furniture co-occurrence prior to decide where to search.
We present PreNav, an ObjectNav framework on semi-static environments.
Rather than invoking a vision-language model at each step, PreNav generates a single global search reference before the robot moves: an LLM converts target–furniture co-occurrence into a spatial prior, a conditional diffusion model turns that prior and the persistent structure into an ordered centerline with a band around it, and the robot approaches the target once it is detected online.
Experiments on a Gibson ObjectNav benchmark show that PreNav outperforms a strong online baseline under matched structural priors, using a generator trained only on room-level ScanNet++ scenes and applied to floor-level Gibson without fine-tuning. Real-world experiments under object relocation and open-vocabulary queries further validate the approach.
introduction:
Object navigation requires a robot to move through an indoor environment and find a target specified only by a user query [1, 2]. Existing methods keep either too much of the building or too little. Prior-map systems answer queries from dense object-level maps [3, 4], whose object poses expire as soon as objects move. Map-free methods use no prior knowledge of the building and decide where to look online, re-deriving candidate regions from current observations every few steps, often through expensive calls to a vision–language model [5, 6]. Real buildings are semi-static: walls and large furniture such as wardrobes and tables barely move, whereas objects such as keys and cups change position between visits.

Between these extremes, two lines of work handle the semi-static building differently. One follows what changes: systems for changing scenes keep a semantic map of objects and update it online as they move, adding and removing voxels [7] or tracking whether each object instance is still in place [8], yet their search still runs over the whole maintained map, movable objects included. The other builds on what persists: osmAG [9], a lightweight, text-based hierarchical map of areas such as rooms and corridors, supports localization [10] and LLM-based map understanding and navigation [11, 12] even when incomplete, and osmAG-LLM [13] uses it to reliably identify the room that holds a moved or never-mapped target. Within that room, however, the robot can only check candidate locations recorded during mapping, namely viewpoints along the mapping trajectory and past object positions, which need not cover where the target now lies. With the search already narrowed to a room, and tracking every object as it moves requiring continual map maintenance, we ask whether the part of the room that barely changes, its walls and large furniture, suffices to plan where to look, and in what order, before the robot moves.

We argue that it does. Real buildings are semi-static: walls and large furniture persist across missions, while movable objects, including the target, may change location. Therefore, instead of continually updating object locations, or treating the environment as a completely unknown scene, we treat only the objects as unknown and rely on the layout of walls and furniture to infer where the target may be. Thus, even if the target has moved, we do not rely on previously recorded target locations. Instead, we use semantic scores between the target and furniture to guide the search: a cup may be near a dining table, whereas a television is unlikely to be near a toilet.

We propose PreNav, which uses this prior knowledge of a scene to pre-plan an informed object search for a given query whenever a query arrives. An LLM scores target–furniture co-occurrence once, offline, and the scores are projected onto the mapped furniture as a spatial prior. A conditional diffusion model then turns this prior, the wall raster, and the start pose into what we call the search reference: a globally planned reference path that optimizes the order of where to search in a floor or room. The reference is thus both an order to follow and a region to sweep. Trained on references from a solver for the traveling salesman problem (TSP), the generator produces one in about a second rather than tens of seconds. The robot then follows the reference, detects the target online, and approaches it, without repeated foundation-model calls or query-conditioned global replanning.

We evaluate PreNav on an expanded Gibson [14] ObjectNav benchmark, asking three questions: whether it outperforms online baselines under matched structural priors; how generation efficiency trades against navigation quality when compared with its TSP teacher; and whether it transfers to real-world robots under open-vocabulary queries.

As a summary, our main contributions are:

We propose PreNav, an ObjectNav framework for semi-static environments: it guides online search through a search reference that is globally optimized with respect to the known room layout and semantic areas.

We introduce an open-vocabulary interface that projects any user query onto the persistent furniture through LLM-generated co-occurrence scores between the query and each furniture category. As the generator’s only query-dependent input, these scores let a conditional diffusion model plan a search reference for any query without retraining.

We demonstrate zero-shot transfer from room-level ScanNet++ training to floor-level Gibson scenes, without fine-tuning the generator on Gibson. On the six-category benchmark, our method outperforms SGM under matched structural priors and achieves navigation performance comparable to its TSP teacher with an order of magnitude less generation time. We further demonstrate deployment on a real mobile robot with open-vocabulary queries.

1. We propose PreNav, an ObjectNav framework for semi-static environments: it guides online search through a search reference that is globally optimized with respect to the known room layout and semantic areas.

2. We introduce an open-vocabulary interface that projects any user query onto the persistent furniture through LLM-generated co-occurrence scores between the query and each furniture category. As the generator’s only query-dependent input, these scores let a conditional diffusion model plan a search reference for any query without retraining.

3. We demonstrate zero-shot transfer from room-level ScanNet++ training to floor-level Gibson scenes, without fine-tuning the generator on Gibson. On the six-category benchmark, our method outperforms SGM under matched structural priors and achieves navigation performance comparable to its TSP teacher with an order of magnitude less generation time. We further demonstrate deployment on a real mobile robot with open-vocabulary queries.
