title: CrowdMAPS: Crowdsourcing Multiple Actions per State for Real-World Imitation Learning
authors: Yilong Song,Harshvardhan Chandirasekar,Karthik Desingh,Chen Zhu-Tian
comment: Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
abstract: Real-world robot imitation learning is often limited by the cost of collecting physical demonstrations, which typically yield only one action label per visited state. We present CrowdMAPS, a web-based crowdsourcing paradigm for augmenting real-robot datasets with Multiple Actions per State (MAPS). After or during standard robot data collection, CrowdMAPS distributes visited robot states to remote annotators through a web-based 3D interface, where they specify alternative valid actions without requiring access to physical robot hardware. This expands robot datasets along a complementary “width” dimension—by increasing the number of actions per visited state—rather than only by collecting more trajectories. We evaluate CrowdMAPS using keyframe-centric goal-pose annotations supplied by non-expert annotators and train imitation policies on the resulting MAPS data. Across five real-world manipulation tasks, increasing MAPS width from one to ten actions per state improves sample efficiency and increases average success rates by 35.6 percentage points for keypose policies and 33.0 percentage points for trajectory policies. These results show that software-mediated human annotations can augment physical robot data to afford denser supervision, establishing CrowdMAPS as a scalable digital layer for real-robot data collection.
introduction:
Robot learning needs large, diverse, high-quality datasets, yet real-robot data remains expensive because each demonstration often requires physical execution, specialized hardware, and real-time human control [20, 5]. In language and vision, large-scale datasets leverage internet-scale human activity and web-based annotation [6, 23, 25, 9, 14]. Inspired by this success, recent systems crowdsource robot data by allowing remote users to teleoperate real robots through web interfaces [15, 17, 16, 1].

However, robot crowdsourcing is inherently constrained by embodiment. One robot can execute only one action from one physical state at a time. Existing web-based systems therefore follow a synchronous “one user controls one robot” model, where every contribution requires physical hardware and throughput remains bounded by the number of robots and trajectory execution time. When contributors outnumber robots, users wait; moreover, noisy demonstrations can be less sample-efficient than expert data. Web-based teleoperation thus broadens who can contribute without removing the physical execution bottleneck.

We approach this bottleneck from a different angle: instead of using the crowd only to collect more trajectories, can we use the crowd to extract more supervision from each trajectory already collected?
Our key observation is that a single visited robot state often admits multiple valid next actions, especially in manipulation tasks with geometric redundancy, multimodal task orderings, or alternative feasible grasps. Standard imitation-learning datasets record only the action that happened to be executed, leaving these other valid actions unobserved. This suggests a different decomposition of robot data collection:
real robots are needed to acquire physically grounded states, but additional valid actions for those states can be annotated asynchronously in software.

We present CrowdMAPS, a web-based crowdsourcing paradigm for augmenting real-robot datasets with Multiple Actions per State (MAPS).
During or after standard robot data collection, CrowdMAPS distributes visited robot states to remote non-expert annotators through a web-based 3D interface, where they specify alternative valid goal-pose actions without requiring access to physical robot hardware.
This process performs action densification: it expands robot datasets along a complementary “width” dimension by increasing the number of valid actions associated with each visited state, rather than only increasing the number of collected trajectories.

Across five real-world table-top manipulation tasks, increasing MAPS width from one to ten actions per keyframe improves sample efficiency with respect to robot time and increases average keypose-policy success rates by 35.6 percentage points, with larger gains on longer-horizon and more multimodal tasks. For trajectory policies, co-training with width-ten MAPS data improves average success by 33.0 percentage points and consistently outperforms adding an equal or greater number of expert teleoperated trajectories. These results show that action densification can improve imitation learning without proportionally increasing hardware-bound data collection.

Our contributions are:

CrowdMAPS, an asynchronous crowdsourcing framework that decouples hardware-bound state acquisition from software-scalable action annotation, bypassing the one-user-one-robot bottleneck of synchronous web teleoperation.

Multiple Actions per State (MAPS), a data structure for imitation learning that densifies supervision by associating each visited state with multiple valid action labels.

An empirical evaluation across five real-world manipulation tasks and two policy formulations, showing that increasing MAPS width improves policy success rates and sample efficiency, especially for longer-horizon and multimodal tasks, and that MAPS data can outperform adding an equal or greater number of expert teleoperated trajectories.

title: MiniPose: Miniature-Based Real Data Collection for 6D Pose Estimation of Large Industrial Pipe Segments
authors: Hyunjun Kim,Youngjin Seo,Sungwon Seo,Jiyou Shin,Kunwoo Kim,Chanyong Park,Hyungpil Moon
comment: . Submitted to IEEE Robotics and Automation Letters (RA-L)
abstract:
6-DOF pose estimation of large and heavy industrial objects, such as large piping systems in shipyards and structural components in petrochemical plants, remains relatively underexplored in robotic perception.
Repeatedly repositioning large objects is physically and spatially demanding, making it difficult to acquire real training data with sufficient pose diversity.
Synthetic data offer a scalable alternative, but faithfully reproducing real RGB-D observations, particularly the structured measurement errors of real depth sensors, remains difficult.
We propose MiniPose, a practical pipeline for miniature-based real RGB-D data collection that addresses both the data-acquisition burden and the sim-to-real gap.
We fabricate a scaled-down replica and capture RGB-D data of it in diverse poses using a real RGB-D camera.
RGB images are used directly, while depth maps are converted to a geometrically consistent representation of the full-scale object via a simple inverse scaling transformation.
This allows training to incorporate real appearance and sensor measurement characteristics that are difficult to reproduce using synthetic data alone.
To examine whether the benefit depends on a particular network, we evaluate two RGB-D pose estimators with different formulations, PVN3D and RDPN6D.
Mixing at most 1,000 miniature images per pipe type, less than 10% of the training data, with 10,000 synthetic images
improves the mean ADD-S AUC across pipe types over synthetic-only training for both estimators.
A comparison with training on full-scale real data further suggests that miniature data can serve as a proxy where full-scale collection is difficult, reducing the data-collection burden for large industrial objects.
introduction:
Recent deep learning-based 6D pose estimation methods have achieved strong performance.
However, existing research has largely focused on small objects that can be directly handled by robotic manipulators [1, 2].
In contrast, 6D pose estimation for physically large and heavy industrial components remains comparatively underexplored [2].
Existing studies on such components use geometry-based vision measurement to guide assembly rather than learned pose estimators [3, 4].
Small objects can be freely repositioned by hand or on a turntable to collect real training data from diverse poses.
Large objects cannot be moved this way due to their size and weight, which makes it difficult to acquire training data with sufficient pose diversity.
Camera placement is also more challenging because capturing the full shape of a large object requires positioning the camera farther away.

To address this data scarcity, many studies generate synthetic data from 3D CAD models and reduce the sim-to-real gap [5, 6].
For RGB, domain randomization of lighting, backgrounds, and textures can reduce the appearance gap relatively easily [7], whereas realistically reproducing the behavior of real depth sensors remains difficult [8, 9, 10].
Depth noise has been handled either by explicitly modeling it or by correcting the measurements, but both depend on the characteristics of a specific sensor [11, 12, 13].
Consequently, a sim-to-real gap can remain between synthetic training data and real observations, degrading model generalization to real-world environments [10, 9].

Rather than further complicating the simulation model, we address both the data scarcity and the sim-to-real gap at the data-acquisition stage by proposing MiniPose, a miniature-based RGB-D data collection pipeline.
Scaled-down replicas of large objects are easy to reposition, enabling more efficient collection of real RGB-D data across diverse poses than with the full-scale objects.
They can also be captured at a shorter camera distance, reducing the space required for data acquisition.
Because a miniature is captured with a real RGB-D sensor, it provides both real RGB and real depth at once, without a noise model of the camera.
The captured data are adapted to the full-scale training domain through a simple geometric transformation and combined with synthetic data.
This provides a convenient way to incorporate real observations into training without repeatedly manipulating the full-scale object.

We validate the proposed method on six representative industrial pipe types commonly used in heavy-industry settings.
Mixing depth-scaled miniature images, which constitute less than 10% of the training set, with synthetic images increases the average ADD-S AUC over synthetic-only training for both PVN3D [14] and RDPN6D [15], and also outperforms a Time-of-Flight (ToF) noise model and test-time depth correction with the Camera Depth Model (CDM) [13].
A comparison with training on directly captured full-scale real data further shows comparable performance, indicating that miniature-based data collection can serve as a viable alternative to collecting real training data from full-scale objects.

The contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

We propose MiniPose, a pipeline that captures real RGB-D data from diverse poses using a scaled-down miniature replica, avoiding the physical difficulty of repeatedly repositioning large industrial objects.

Extensive experiments and ablations show that MiniPose improves 6D pose estimation over synthetic-only training and outperforms depth noise modeling and correction.
Both real RGB and real depth contribute to this gain, and MiniPose can serve as a practical alternative to full-scale real data.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows.
Section II reviews related work, and Section III introduces MiniPose for miniature-based data collection.
Sections IV and V describe the experimental setup and results, respectively.
Finally, Section VI concludes the paper and discusses future directions.

1. We propose MiniPose, a pipeline that captures real RGB-D data from diverse poses using a scaled-down miniature replica, avoiding the physical difficulty of repeatedly repositioning large industrial objects.

2. Extensive experiments and ablations show that MiniPose improves 6D pose estimation over synthetic-only training and outperforms depth noise modeling and correction.
Both real RGB and real depth contribute to this gain, and MiniPose can serve as a practical alternative to full-scale real data.

title: Does Your World Model Know Actions Have Consequences?
authors: Ayush Gaggar,Jared Berry,Todd D. Murphey
comment: Presented at "Do Robots Need World Models?" Workshop at Conference on Robot Learning (CoRL) 2026
abstract:
Embodied world models (WMs) are implicit learning systems that predict the next future latent state directly from observations and actions.
Unique from other end-to-end learning systems, the dynamics predictor of WMs can simulate the environment’s response to alternative actions without physical deployment or pre-specifying states of the dynamical system.
Current metrics focus on the quality of model outputs, e.g., clarity of reconstructions or task success, but fail to assess the fidelity of modeling consequences of counterfactual actions.
Inspecting the forced response to action perturbations through sensitivity analysis is one way to audit how well WMs can predict the consequences of counterfactual actions.
Deploying WMs on hardware will require new evaluation frameworks to analyze the tradeoffs between state error and accurate sensitivity prediction.
introduction:
“World models” (WMs) have become an increasingly overloaded term, and refer to any combination of forecasting models, dynamics predictor models, latent-imagination based planners, video predictors, and synthetic data generators  [20].
WMs in robot learning, referred to as embodied world models, have gained traction because of the promise of an end-to-end system that can sense the environment, reason over action-conditioned dynamics, and perform a given task.
Although vision-language-action models (VLAs), reinforcement learning (RL), imitation learning (IL), and model predictive controllers are also end-to-end techniques, the strength of a WM is, by definition [5, 13], predicting multiple possible state evolutions without pre-specifying the state of the dynamic system.

Traditional learned dynamics models require specifying joint positions, object pose, friction, deformation modes, and other underlying mechanical properties.
On the other hand, a full WM stack (Fig. 1) learns an implicit representation p(zt+1:t+H∣o≤t,at:t+H−1)p(z_{t+1:t+H}\mid o_{\leq t},a_{t:t+H-1}) directly from observations (e.g., pixels). Given the current state of the environment (sts_{t} if known, st=ots_{t}=o_{t} if from observations)

and a history of state-action-reward pairs ht={(st−H,ut−H,rt−H),h_{t}=\{(s_{t-H},u_{t-H},r_{t-H}), ...(st,ut,rt)}...(s_{t},u_{t},r_{t})\}, a world model predicts the temporal response of the implicit state representation directly from raw observations.

Counterfactual auditing [17], i.e., the “imagined” environment response under action sets (ut1,ut+11,…)(u_{t}^{1},u_{t+1}^{1},\mathrm{...}) vs. (ut2,ut+12,…)(u_{t}^{2},u_{t+1}^{2},\mathrm{...}), can be evaluated in terms of these observables.
Inspecting counterfactual actions provides roboticists a window into auditing the decision making of end-to-end learning systems which would otherwise be impossible without physical rollouts.

Therefore, accurate dynamic predictions are a prerequisite for counterfactual auditing.
Current WM metrics are ill-posed for verifying planning utility (Fig. 2).
A world model with poor reconstruction capability can still be perfectly adequate for successful planning; in model-based RL, low state reconstruction error does not necessarily translate to task performance [10].
Similarly, an overfit, highly brittle WM may have high task success within its training distribution but poor generalization.

Auditability of embodied WMs requires both interpretability [8]—model predictions are human interpretable—and actionability—the effects of alternative actions can be both imagined and executed.
Chain-of-thought semantic reasoning of modern VLAs [2, 21, 9, 16] is unreliable for robot trajectories [11, 4];
although interpretable, language is a non-auditable proxy for predicting dynamic state evolution.
WMs with latent transition models  [7, 19, 1, 14] and World Action Models [18] are best suited for counterfactual auditability because the learned dynamics models are both action-conditioned and interpretable via decoders.

title: Genie Sim Benchmark: Real-to-Sim Fidelity and Evaluation
authors: Di Yang,Da Huang,Yang Lv,Fan Yang,Yi Lu,Zheyuan Xing,Linting Guo,Jiaen Shen,Wenjun Sun,Maoqing Yao,Qian Wang
abstract: We evaluate Genie Sim Benchmark through paired real–simulation tasks and complementary system-identification studies. Across 22 robot–task pairs spanning 16 task names, task-specific π0.5\pi_{0.5} policies fine-tuned on real-robot data achieve a descriptive Score correlation of 0.9686 (MAE 0.0405; RMSE 0.0520), with simulation–real differences from −-0.110 to +0.080. G2 crsB experiments assess long-horizon closed-loop position and joint-side torque agreement, while five representative object cases examine identification and cross-engine contact transfer. A separate 32.6503 s teleoperation trajectory, excluded from mechanical identification and servo-gain search, evaluates external position targets through simulated motion-controller command shaping and a calibrated position servo. Across both arms, per-joint position RMSE spans 0.00614–0.03522 rad and current-derived torque RMSE spans 0.73545–4.00099 N⋅\cdotm. Native PhysX adaptations recover three recorded interaction tasks, with case-dependent alignment gains. These results support task-specific simulation evaluation through joint assessment of task outcomes and physical-response consistency.
introduction:
A simulation benchmark is useful only when its task outcomes remain informative about real robots.

Matching joint and gripper behavior addresses only one part of the reality gap. Object geometry, contact response, rotational resistance and initial state can determine whether a grasp, handover or placement succeeds. We organize the report around Genie Sim Benchmark: which task families are covered, which execution and interaction errors can change their outcomes, and whether frozen real–simulation evaluations preserve task scores and failure stages. Section II presents benchmark coverage, the paired-evaluation protocol, reported scores and failure boundaries. Sections III and IV then explain the Real2Sim pipeline and the robot/object identification methods supporting this evaluation.

We examine 22 final Score pairs and 14 G2/Arx before/after system-identification comparisons. Robot-identification replay and five G2 object recordings provide complementary evidence on execution and contact response. The evaluation compares real and simulated task Scores and physical responses, and examines how these discrepancies change after system identification [1, 4, 5].

title: Fast Inference-Time Policy Refinement via Action-Affine World Models
authors: Run Wang,Yilin Mo,Liang Wu
abstract: Imitation policies can perform complex manipulation, yet small execution errors can accumulate and cause failure. Refinement can correct these errors, but existing approaches often require additional on-policy learning or costly online planning. Our key insight is that a pretrained policy already supplies a useful nominal behavior: refinement can focus on predicting how small action corrections change its outcome. We therefore learn this local response in a form that is cheap to optimize. Our action-affine world model (A2WM) learns local action sensitivities offline from action-perturbed policy rollouts. Given interaction history and a policy proposal, it predicts task-relevant geometry as a nominal trajectory plus a linear response to corrections. It predicts the full planning horizon directly, avoiding the propagation of intermediate errors through recursive model evaluations. Quadratic penalties on predicted task errors and linear correction constraints then yield a cheap convex quadratic program (QP). Online refinement requires one model evaluation and one QP solve, while both policy and model weights remain frozen. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, our framework achieves the highest success rate among evaluated baselines, adding only 3.8 ms of mean refinement overhead per control step, excluding base-policy sampling.
introduction:
Behavior cloning (BC) enables robots to acquire manipulation skills from expert demonstrations. Diffusion policies represent multimodal action sequences and provide useful proposals for reaching, grasping, and assembly [1, 2]. At deployment, however, execution errors can drive the robot outside the demonstrated state distribution, where further errors can accumulate and lead to failure [3]. Refining a pretrained policy through feedback offers a way to recover from such deviations without relearning the task. For precision-demanding manipulation, this refinement must anticipate the consequences of corrections while remaining fast enough to respond to new observations. The central challenge is to structure a world model so that it supports accurate prediction and cheap optimization of policy corrections.

One route to policy refinement learns an additional correction policy through environment interaction. Residual policy learning follows this route, augmenting an existing controller with learned corrections [4, 5]. ResiP applies residual reinforcement learning (RL) to precise assembly [6], Policy Decorator refines pretrained imitation policies through online interactions [7], and KoRR conditions a residual policy on Koopman-predicted states [8]. Another route selects or optimizes actions at inference time using fixed learned models. V-GPS ranks samples with an offline-learned value function [9], while LPB guides diffusion sampling toward the expert state distribution [10]. Within this second route, a learned world model can instead predict the consequences of proposed actions and support their optimization against a task objective. Our work follows this predictive refinement route.

World models support policy learning in imagined trajectories [11] and online action optimization [12, 13], including manipulation planning with predicted images or visual features [14, 15]. Sampling and gradient-based planning can require many model evaluations. Local linearization offers another approach through quadratic programming within nonlinear model predictive control (MPC), but forming the local problem still requires model derivatives [16]. More directly related to our setting, LaDi-WM and GPC use world models to refine diffusion-policy proposals [17, 18]. GPC ranks sampled proposals or optimizes them through model gradients. Although the frozen policy supplies a useful starting point, refinement still incurs candidate-evaluation or repeated differentiation costs. This motivates learning the action-response coefficients needed for optimization directly, so that deployment requires neither candidate search nor differentiation of a nonlinear rollout.

State representation matters because task objectives often depend on nonlinear geometry. For example, assembly requires controlling the relative pose between two parts, a nonlinear function of their individual poses. Making raw-state predictions affine in action corrections therefore does not automatically make the task cost quadratic. Learned control representations offer ways to address this issue. Embed to Control (E2C) learns locally linear latent dynamics [19], while Koopman approaches augment the state with nonlinear functions, called observables, and approximate their evolution using fixed or learned dictionaries [20, 21]. These representations have been used for robot control and diffusion-based imitation [22, 23]. In lifted MPC, observables can explicitly include geometric quantities used by the objective [24], allowing them to be predicted rather than recomputed nonlinearly inside the optimizer. Such augmentation does not guarantee exact linear dynamics; finite-dimensional linear representations remain structurally restrictive [25]. Our setting calls for a local approximation of how task-relevant geometry responds to corrections around a policy proposal.

A separate design choice is how to predict over the control horizon. MPC evaluates action sequences over multiple future steps [26]. Recursive one-step prediction feeds intermediate predictions back into the model, propagating their errors through subsequent evaluations [27] and requiring repeated model calls. Direct multi-step prediction learns the finite-horizon mapping instead, as studied in receding-horizon control [28] and Koopman-based MPC [29]. Since refinement ultimately requires a trajectory over the full horizon, learning that trajectory directly removes this source of error propagation and reduces sequential online model evaluations. We therefore evaluate whether this structural advantage translates into improved prediction accuracy and lower computation time over the same control horizon.

We propose an action-affine world model (A2WM) for fast inference-time refinement of frozen imitation policies, using measured robot and object states and specified geometric task objectives (Fig. 2). A useful policy proposal supplies the nominal behavior, allowing the model to focus on bounded corrections around that behavior. Our key insight is to learn trajectory predictions that are explicitly affine in these corrections, so that the corrections can be optimized efficiently. Conditioned on interaction history and the proposal, the model predicts a nominal trajectory and a matrix mapping the full correction sequence to changes in future task quantities. During each optimization, the predicted trajectory is the fixed nominal forecast plus the fixed response matrix multiplied by the correction sequence. We retain measured states, include task-relevant geometry in the prediction space, and append learned nonlinear features to represent context-dependent behavior.

We train A2WM offline on action-perturbed rollouts of the frozen policy, supervising the full predicted trajectory. At each control step, the trained model generates a new nominal forecast and response matrix from the current context, instead of computing the response through online differentiation. All horizon steps are predicted directly in one model evaluation, without feeding intermediate predictions back into the model. This aligns supervision with the controller’s prediction horizon.

Quadratic penalties on the predicted task errors and linear correction constraints define a convex quadratic program (QP). Each control update requires one model evaluation followed by a QP solve. The controller executes the first corrected action and replans from new observations, with both policy and model weights frozen. Together, the action-affine structure and direct horizon prediction make repeated feedback correction cheap without candidate search or world-model differentiation.

Our contributions are:

Action-affine world modeling. We learn a local action-response model conditioned on interaction history and a frozen policy’s proposal. By predicting task-relevant geometry explicitly, the model makes the predicted task errors affine in action corrections.

Direct multi-step action-response prediction. We formulate direct finite-horizon action-response prediction, producing the affine response in one model evaluation without feeding intermediate predictions back into the model. We assess its accuracy and computational cost against recursive alternatives that retain QP-compatible planning.

Fast closed-loop policy refinement. We integrate the predictor with constrained QP-based correction and evaluate the complete framework on four simulated manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved task-averaged success with millisecond-scale refinement overhead and no on-policy residual-policy training.

Across four simulated manipulation tasks, our framework improves task-averaged success from 27.2% for the frozen policies to 59.5% (Fig. 1(b)). It exceeds the evaluated GPC-based refiners in task-averaged success while requiring only 3.4–4.0 ms of refinement overhead per control step (Tab. I).

1. Action-affine world modeling. We learn a local action-response model conditioned on interaction history and a frozen policy’s proposal. By predicting task-relevant geometry explicitly, the model makes the predicted task errors affine in action corrections.

2. Direct multi-step action-response prediction. We formulate direct finite-horizon action-response prediction, producing the affine response in one model evaluation without feeding intermediate predictions back into the model. We assess its accuracy and computational cost against recursive alternatives that retain QP-compatible planning.

3. Fast closed-loop policy refinement. We integrate the predictor with constrained QP-based correction and evaluate the complete framework on four simulated manipulation tasks, demonstrating improved task-averaged success with millisecond-scale refinement overhead and no on-policy residual-policy training.

title: ILA: A Transferable Interface-Level Adapter for Compliant Humanoid Motion Tracking
authors: ZhuoChang Cai,Zihao Yan,Jinxuan Zhu,Yanjie Li,Hao Xiong
abstract: Humanoid motion tracking is fundamental to reproducing human motions on humanoid robots and serves as an important tool for teleoperation and motion data collection. However, directly tracking reference motions can be unsafe in constrained environments or during physical human–robot interaction, motivating the need for compliant motion tracking. We present ILA, an Interface-Level Adapter for compliant humanoid motion tracking without dedicated interaction sensors. ILA adapts motion references from the robot’s observation history, allowing the robot to respond to physical guidance while preserving the capabilities of a pretrained motion tracker. As an interface-level module, ILA can be directly plugged into different pretrained motion trackers without retraining either the adapter or the tracking policies. ILA is trained entirely in simulation to predict reference corrections induced by physical interaction. We evaluate ILA with three humanoid motion trackers and achieve a 63.6–75.4% reduction in guidance-target error compared with their original policies. Matched simulation studies and hardware experiments further show that ILA improves responsiveness to human guidance while preserving nominal motion-tracking performance. These results demonstrate compliant guidance as a reusable, sensor-free extension to pretrained humanoid motion trackers.
introduction:
Humanoid motion tracking brings diverse human motions to robots, supporting teleoperation and motion data collection [1, 2, 3, 4]. During physical interaction, faithfully following a prescribed motion can conflict with yielding to human guidance. Compliant tracking should accommodate guidance while retaining existing motion skills (Fig. ).

Learning-based compliance typically requires retraining or redesigning the motion controller [5, 6, 7]. Analytical retrofits rely on explicit wrench estimation and prescribed force–motion relations [8]. We seek reusable compliance for pretrained trackers without changing their architecture or parameters or adding dedicated interaction sensors.

We present ILA, an Interface-Level Adapter that predicts reference corrections from the nominal reference and the robot’s observation history. The pretrained tracker follows the adapted reference and handles whole-body execution and stabilization. Its architecture and parameters remain unchanged, which we term policy-preserving compliance retrofit. ILA is trained entirely in simulation using paired nominal and modified references. The trained adapter can be reused with other trackers through deterministic mappings of observations and motion references.

The same trained adapter reduces guidance target error by 63.6–75.4% across three independently trained trackers, without finetuning either the adapter or the tracking policies. Matched simulation comparisons assess guidance gains alongside nominal-motion preservation. Hardware experiments demonstrate human-guided motion with concurrent task execution and whole-body coordination.

Our contributions are:

Policy-preserving compliance retrofit. Compared with policy-training approaches and wrench-based retrofits, ILA adds physical guidance without tracker retraining or explicit wrench estimation. It learns reference corrections from causal interaction history, retaining the pretrained policy for whole-body execution and stabilization.

Cross-tracker reuse of learned compliance. ILA transfers the same learned adapter across independently trained motion trackers through deterministic observation and reference mappings. Both adapter and tracker parameters remain fixed, avoiding per-tracker compliance training.

Systematic evaluation of compliance and motion preservation. Matched comparisons and hardware experiments evaluate guidance gains together with nominal-motion tracking, spatial selectivity, and post-release recovery, including comparisons with direct policy finetuning.

1. Policy-preserving compliance retrofit. Compared with policy-training approaches and wrench-based retrofits, ILA adds physical guidance without tracker retraining or explicit wrench estimation. It learns reference corrections from causal interaction history, retaining the pretrained policy for whole-body execution and stabilization.

2. Cross-tracker reuse of learned compliance. ILA transfers the same learned adapter across independently trained motion trackers through deterministic observation and reference mappings. Both adapter and tracker parameters remain fixed, avoiding per-tracker compliance training.

3. Systematic evaluation of compliance and motion preservation. Matched comparisons and hardware experiments evaluate guidance gains together with nominal-motion tracking, spatial selectivity, and post-release recovery, including comparisons with direct policy finetuning.

title: From a Single RGB Image to Robot Execution: Metric Scene Alignment and Contact-Guided Retargeting
authors: Zhenxuan Ding,Yu Huang,Xinmiao Wang,Chenghao Sun,Ziyang Dong,Wenhao Cui
abstract:
Extending humanoid interaction generation to new environments remains limited by the need for prebuilt 3D scene assets. Reconstructing scenes directly from single RGB images offers a way to overcome this limitation, but introduces a key challenge in maintaining geometric consistency throughout motion generation and transfer. Visually plausible human motions may be misaligned with the reconstructed scene, while retargeting can introduce additional support errors due to differences between human and robot embodiments.
We present a unified pipeline that transforms a single RGB image into a humanoid motion reference. It reconstructs scene geometry from the input image, generates a human interaction conditioned on the reconstructed scene, and retargets the motion to a humanoid robot. To maintain geometric consistency throughout this process, we incorporate two complementary refinement stages before and after embodiment transfer. Before retargeting, Joint Metric Interaction Refinement (JMIR) refines human motion alignment with the registered metric scene while preserving the generated interaction structure. Following retargeting, Contact Guided Residual Retargeting (CGRR) corrects robot specific support errors to restore the intended support relationships. Together, these stages produce motion references that are consistent with the reconstructed scene and can be followed by multiple pretrained humanoid trackers without scene specific policy fine tuning. Compared with GRAIL, our method reduces refinement time from 480 s to 87 s, yielding a speedup of 5.5×\times. The complete pipeline achieves a success rate of 89% in simulation and 70% across 50 physical trials on the Unitree G1, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating executable humanoid motion references from single RGB images.
introduction:
Recent advances in humanoid motion tracking have enabled the execution of diverse reference motions [16, 17], while motion retargeting has improved the transfer of human motion across robot embodiments [9]. Despite this progress, generating suitable references for interaction with a specific environment remains a separate challenge. In interactions that depend on environmental support, motion quality is determined not only by the body trajectory but also by its geometric relationship with the scene. A reference must therefore preserve the intended support contacts while respecting the geometry of both the environment and the robot. Motion tracking alone does not resolve inconsistencies in these scenarios. Generative human object interaction (HOI) models offer a promising basis for constructing such references. HOI-Diff [4] and CHOIS [5] generate coordinated human and object motions from language and geometric conditions, while DAViD [6] models dynamic object affordances using pretrained video diffusion models. These methods provide valuable human interaction priors, but do not directly address the geometric and kinematic requirements of a target humanoid robot. GRAIL [3] advances toward robot execution by integrating interaction generation with humanoid retargeting and policy learning. However, its generation process assumes a predefined 3D scene with known object geometry and camera parameters, limiting its application to a new environment.

Direct reconstruction from a single RGB image provides an alternative to preparing the target scene assets in advance, but it introduces challenges in maintaining geometric consistency during motion generation and transfer. The generated human interaction may be semantically appropriate yet misaligned with the reconstructed scene, resulting in penetration or loss of support contact. Even after this mismatch is corrected, retargeting can introduce additional support errors due to differences in body proportions, contact geometry, and joint limits. These two sources of error motivate complementary refinement before and after embodiment transfer: the first stage aligns the human interaction with the scene and preserves its structure, while the second uses the target robot geometry and kinematics to restore the intended support contacts.

In this paper, we present a unified pipeline that generates humanoid motion references from a single RGB image for interactions that rely on environmental support. As shown in Fig. 1, we first reconstruct scene geometry using SAM 3D Objects [7] and generate a human interaction conditioned on the reconstructed scene. To maintain geometric consistency before embodiment transfer, we introduce Joint Metric Interaction Refinement (JMIR), which aligns the generated human interaction with the registered metric scene while preserving its interaction structure. The refined motion is then transferred to the target humanoid through General Motion Retargeting (GMR) [9]. Following retargeting, Contact Guided Residual Retargeting (CGRR) restores the intended support contacts through a bounded residual correction to the lower body. By separating scene alignment from robot support correction, we address geometric errors before and after embodiment transfer while retaining existing motion generation and retargeting components.
The resulting references can be used by pretrained humanoid motion trackers without scene specific policy fine tuning. We evaluate their compatibility with MimicLite [21], GMT [16], and SONIC [17], and validate the complete workflow in simulation and on a physical Unitree G1 robot. Under matched evaluation settings, our method reduces refinement time from 480 s to 87 s compared with GRAIL. The complete pipeline achieves a success rate of 89% in simulation and 70% across 50 real robot trials.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows.

A one-RGB-image-to-humanoid pipeline. We integrate scene reconstruction, human interaction generation, and motion retargeting into a unified pipeline for interactions that rely on environmental support, without requiring prebuilt assets of the target scene.

Geometric refinement across embodiment transfer. We introduce JMIR to refine human–scene geometric alignment while preserving the generated interaction structure, and CGRR to correct robot specific support errors after retargeting. Together, these stages address distinct geometric errors before and after embodiment transfer.

Experimental validation in simulation and on real robots. Experiments in simulation and on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that our pipeline generates executable humanoid motion references with reduced refinement time. We further demonstrate compatibility with multiple pretrained motion trackers without scene specific policy fine tuning.

1. A one-RGB-image-to-humanoid pipeline. We integrate scene reconstruction, human interaction generation, and motion retargeting into a unified pipeline for interactions that rely on environmental support, without requiring prebuilt assets of the target scene.

2. Geometric refinement across embodiment transfer. We introduce JMIR to refine human–scene geometric alignment while preserving the generated interaction structure, and CGRR to correct robot specific support errors after retargeting. Together, these stages address distinct geometric errors before and after embodiment transfer.

3. Experimental validation in simulation and on real robots. Experiments in simulation and on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that our pipeline generates executable humanoid motion references with reduced refinement time. We further demonstrate compatibility with multiple pretrained motion trackers without scene specific policy fine tuning.

title: Scaling VLA Serving Under Robotic Execution Constraints
authors: Yue Zhang,Zicong Ye,Lufang Chen,Dance Yang,Mingyang Li,Zhenwei Duan,Michael Zhao,Ziye Deng,Starrick Liu,Ruizhi Chengze,YongHua Chen,SongAo Han,Yu Sun,Ran Yu,Xiaofan Li,Ruyi Gan,Hao Wang
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose robotic manipulation. In our production setting, hundreds of VLA-powered robots are already operating in real-world environments, creating an immediate need for efficient fleet serving. We present XInfer, a production-deployed VLA serving system designed to reduce the inference infrastructure cost of large-scale robotic deployments.
XInfer jointly coordinates heterogeneous VLA computation with the evolving response requirements of robotic execution. By exploiting computational parallelism while managing interference, XInfer improves GPU efficiency while protecting time-critical robotic feedback.
We evaluate XInfer across three VLA models using production-derived workloads, achieving 1.26–3.75× the effective robot capacity (ERC) of state-of-the-art systems under physical-execution constraints. Our implementation is publicly available at
https://github.com/X-Square-Robot/xinfer.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models are bringing general-purpose robotic manipulation into logistics and manufacturing, where multiple robots can share GPU infrastructure to reduce serving cost. Figure id1 shows representative parcel-handling operations from our production deployment. Recent inference engines improve the efficiency of individual VLA queries (Su, 2026; Xu et al., 2026; Tan et al., 2025). However, higher inference throughput does not necessarily translate into greater physical productivity, as delayed feedback can disrupt robotic execution. We use effective robot capacity (ERC), the maximum number of concurrent robots a GPU can serve while meeting specified latency and reliability requirements, as the serving objective.

Shared VLA serving requires exploiting concurrency without compromising time-critical feedback. VLA requests traverse heterogeneous stages with distinct computational demands, creating opportunities to overlap independent work across robots. However, concurrent GPU execution also introduces interference: admitting a new stage may delay stages already in progress. Since these stages are non-preemptive, prioritizing urgent requests alone cannot prevent deadline violations caused by previously admitted work. Effective fleet serving therefore requires two coordinated decisions: which requests should be prioritized, and which stages can be admitted without jeopardizing the deadlines of current and forthcoming requests.

The cost of this interference is not uniform across requests. Robots continue executing previously predicted actions while awaiting new responses, and the consequences of delayed feedback depend on their ongoing physical execution. As a result, requests with similar computational demands may have substantially different response-time requirements, which evolve throughout task execution. Moreover, response timing influences subsequent request arrivals, coupling scheduling decisions with future workload dynamics. Fleet serving must therefore balance concurrency against interference under changing per-request deadlines, rather than optimize inference throughput or average latency alone.

Prior systems adapt action horizons and request priorities to execution context (Dai et al., 2026; Anonymous Authors, n.d.), coordinate serving for factory productivity (Jiang et al., 2026), or overlap encoding and diffusion in lockstep rounds (Adamopoulos et al., 2026). Yet effective fleet serving must reconcile the time-varying urgency of robotic feedback with the distinct computational demands of VLA stages. This calls for fine-grained scheduling that matches stage execution to available GPU capacity while controlling interference with time-critical requests.

We present XInfer, a VLA serving system that couples asynchronous execution with fine-grained, execution-aware scheduling. Its dependency-driven engine exposes parallelism across requests and heterogeneous VLA stages, allowing computation to progress as dependencies resolve. The scheduler coordinates these execution opportunities with the time-varying urgency of robotic feedback by decoupling request prioritization from stage admission. At stage boundaries, it combines per-request response-time budgets, remaining computation, and predicted interference to admit ordinary work only when protected requests remain predicted feasible. It further accounts for anticipated earlier-deadline arrivals using request history, balancing immediate concurrency gains against future scheduling demands.

We evaluate VLA-2B, π0.5\pi_{0.5}, and Wall-OSS-0.5
using production-derived closed-loop workloads and controlled experiments. With error-free
responses, XInfer achieves ERCs of 18 VLA-2B and
24 π0.5\pi_{0.5} robots, versus 10 and 15 for vLLM-Omni;
Robion serves 19 π0.5\pi_{0.5} robots.
In a separate VLA-2B evaluation with heterogeneous response-time budgets, all policies share the same backend and execution resources. Under the same real-time feasibility criterion, XInfer achieves an ERC of 18 robots, compared with 15 for Slack-Gate, 14 for FIFO, and 12 for EDF (§6). Mechanism ablations isolate the effects of asynchronous execution and scheduling decisions.

Our contributions are:

An asynchronous VLA serving engine that exposes cross-request
and cross-stage parallelism by advancing work as its dependencies complete.

Execution-aware cross-stage scheduling that coordinates shared
GPU computation by separating request priority from stage admission, accounting
for interference on current and anticipated urgent requests.

Production deployment and empirical evaluation. XInfer is deployed
in production. We characterize closed-loop workloads, compare ERC across
three VLA backends, and evaluate heterogeneous-budget scheduling and its mechanisms.

1. An asynchronous VLA serving engine that exposes cross-request
and cross-stage parallelism by advancing work as its dependencies complete.

2. Execution-aware cross-stage scheduling that coordinates shared
GPU computation by separating request priority from stage admission, accounting
for interference on current and anticipated urgent requests.

3. Production deployment and empirical evaluation. XInfer is deployed
in production. We characterize closed-loop workloads, compare ERC across
three VLA backends, and evaluate heterogeneous-budget scheduling and its mechanisms.

title: Adapting Monocular Depth Estimation in Novel Scenes through Disparity Refinement and Robot Ego-Motion
authors: Dimitrios Chatziparaschis,Georgios Georgakis,Adnan I. Ansar,Shehryar Khattak,Konstantinos Karydis
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
comment: journal
abstract:
The geometric understanding of a scene is a crucial component for safe and efficient robotic operations in novel and unstructured environments. The recent emergence of foundation models for Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) has provided an opportunity to enrich robotic perception capabilities with dense long-range depth predictions, replacing expensive onboard hardware (e.g., LiDARs and stereo cameras). However, these offline models are primarily trained on affine-invariant depth representations, and their generalization to novel scenes remains unclear. In this work we present EM-ViT, a monocular depth estimation model that learns to adapt online relative depth inputs from a foundation model prior to the metric scale with observations collected during robotic operations. Motivated by the stereo camera parameterization, our method decomposes depth prediction via dense disparity refinement to recover the scene’s relative structure and an effective baseline scalar prediction to determine the missing metric scale.
The learning process leverages sparse LiDAR points and, optionally, the robot’s Ego-Motion (EM) to rapidly train a lightweight Vision Transformer (ViT), while an internal gradient matching loss preserves the fine-grained semantic structure of the input disparity in real-time. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method on publicly available sequences, such as KITTI, and show that our online learning pipeline can adapt to novel scenes faster and with higher accuracy than existing MDE foundation models. The code and supplementary materials will be publicly available at https://emvit-mde.github.io.
introduction:
Key tasks for autonomous robots, such as exploration in unknown environments [1] and goal-directed navigation [2], depend on an accurate and reliable understanding of
the 3D geometry of a scene for traversability assessment,
path planning, and collision avoidance.
The consequences
of incomplete terrain understanding can be substantial in
long-duration missions of ground robots.
For example, the Curiosity Mars rover experienced an unexpectedly high rate of wheel punctures and cracks while traversing sharp sandstone outcrops, motivating geomorphic terrain mapping and careful path planning to avoid hazardous terrain and mitigate further wheel damage [3].
Thus, accurate geometric characterization of terrain, particularly before hazards enter the robot’s immediate vicinity, can directly reduce mobility risk during exploration.

Most existing systems employ LiDAR sensors [4, 5] due to their high metric accuracy, long range, and day-and-night operation.
However, they produce sparse measurements and may suffer from ambient conditions, such as dust particles, high-reflectance surfaces, and the skewing effect caused by abrupt and jerky movements in the wild [6, 7, 8].
Additionally, LiDARs are often expensive and heavy, making it difficult to accommodate them in constrained Size, Weight, and Power (SWaP) conditions.
Stereo cameras have been successfully used in numerous applications involving robot localization and mapping [9, 10],
but they are typically constrained by a comparatively shorter range and can be inaccurate when the robot operates in low-texture environments.
Notably, in extraterrestrial applications [2, 11] the applied stereo methods [12, 13] suffer from low solar phase and texture conditions, which causes discontinuous depth areas and makes navigation uncertain.

Monocular Depth Estimation (MDE) is a promising avenue for utilizing monocular cameras as a dense long-range depth sensor alternative [14].
However, as a result of focal and scene-scale ambiguities, MDE models that predict metric depth [15, 16, 17, 18, 19] must be fine-tuned when operating in new scenes or with different cameras.
A popular paradigm that has been shown to improve generalization to new scenes involves the formulation of an affine-invariant inverse depth estimation task [20].
Fueled by large amounts of data collected in different environments, these models show impressive zero-shot
capabilities [21].
Yet, models trained in this manner still need to be fine-tuned for metric depth in target domains (e.g., specific scenes and/or camera intrinsics) to be applicable to downstream robotic tasks.
This is not always possible when operating in unseen environments due to the absence of domain-specific data, thus leading to poor generalization of metric depth estimation in novel scenes [18].

The absence of data relevant to robotic tasks motivated earlier works to explore unsupervised learning of monocular depth estimation [22, 23, 24, 25].
These methods typically leverage ego motion from monocular video sequences using geometric constraints as substitutes for explicit ground-truth depth or camera pose supervision during training.
However, these approaches may suffer from poor initialization because they do not incorporate learned geometric priors and are limited to coarse-depth predictions.
In response, recent methods have investigated test-time adaptation [26, 27, 28] by rescaling outputs from foundation MDE models.
Still, this strategy requires repeating the optimization process needed to estimate the rescaling at every step in the sequence, and ignores image context that is important to refine initial estimates.

Since robotic platforms naturally acquire image sequences, an alternative is to recover scene geometry directly using Structure-from-Motion (SfM) or visual SLAM. However, multi-view geometric reconstruction relies on correspondence and sufficient camera parallax as classical systems typically recover geometry only at observed features or keyframes, while pure monocular SLAM additionally leaves metric scale unobservable without an external metric cue [29, 30, 31]. Dense SLAM methods can alleviate the sparsity of classical approaches, but require persistent multi-frame correspondences and iterative joint optimization of camera motion and scene structure [32], whereas MDE can provide dense geometry over the entire visible image, including distant or newly observed regions for which sufficient parallax has not yet accumulated, from a single frame.

To address these challenges, we propose an online training pipeline for metric depth prediction that is suitable for robotic tasks.
The key idea is to use sequential observations as a self-supervisory signal for adapting a strong single-image geometric prior to metric scale, rather than relying on the sequence itself as the mechanism for reconstructing scene geometry.
To do so, we train a disparity refinement network that uses an affine-invariant inverse depth estimation input from a foundation model (e.g., Depth Anything V2 [21]) and decodes depth reconstruction via the stereo camera parameterization.
Specifically, our proposed virtual stereo system decomposes and disentangles dense disparity refinement to recover relative scene structure from an effective baseline scalar prediction to obtain the scale of the scene in real-time. By conditioning our model on camera’s focal length of the robotic task, the formed stereo parameterization becomes metrically consistent to the used camera model, with scale ambiguities (caused by different focal lenses) being disentangled by the learned quantities.
The model is supervised via photometric loss using refined odometry estimates and sparse measurements from an onboard LiDAR.
Our lightweight model comprises a small vision transformer (ViT) to allow fast domain adaptation in novel environments while the robot moves in the scene. Figure 1 illustrates our system pipeline deployed on a Boston Dynamics Spot robot in an unknown garage environment.
Our main contributions are threefold.

A lightweight virtual stereo framework producing metric and high-fidelity depth maps that greatly improve the applicability of MDE foundation models for robotic tasks.

An on-the-fly learning process that leverages ego-motion and sparse LiDAR measurements to mitigate the scale bias and camera intrinsics ambiguity during deployment in novel environments.

Extensive experiments in publicly available datasets, such as KITTI [33], CitrusFarm [34], and Perseverance Navcam[12], demonstrating faster and more accurate adaptability than existing methods that metrically tune foundation models in novel scenes.

title: The Posterior-Prior Epistemic Gap: When World Model Imagination Fails to Carry Task-Relevant Signals
authors: Jaerock Kwon,Elahe Delavari,Donghyun Kim,Haewoon Nam
abstract:
Model-based planners that roll out imagined futures assume the
transition model faithfully propagates task-relevant signals—a
property rarely measured directly. In a single-seed case study
of a Recurrent State Space Model world model with active-inference planning in the CARLA driving simulator,
we identify a posterior-prior gap—posterior
(observation-filtered) states retain obstacle information that
imagined rollout states progressively lose: a supervised obstacle
probe achieves AUC 0.85 on posterior states, but the
same probe applied to imagined prior states shows monotonic decay
(AUC 0.85→\rightarrow0.71 over 15 steps; logit separation drops
57%). Because the probe is identical, the decay isolates the
transition model---not the representation---as the information
bottleneck. Obstacle avoidance drops to 0% without privileged
runtime coordinates, and the planner’s own ensemble-based
epistemic term does not flag the loss---ensemble disagreement yields AUC 0.52 as an obstacle
classifier (chance level), making the failure an unflagged
imagination failure---an unknown unknown at planning
time.11
1
          
          
          
        Project page: https://bimilab.github.io/paper-posterior-prior-epistemic-gap/
As a secondary contribution, we show that
task-conditioned weighting of Effective Free Energy components over the
same world model yields lane keeping (81.2±1.881.2\pm 1.8% route
completion) and obstacle avoidance (28/28 avoided, using
privileged coordinates) in the CARLA simulator, with runtime weight modulation
enabling post-evasion centering.
introduction:
Model-based planning with learned world
models (Hafner et al., 2023) relies on rolling out imagined
futures and scoring candidate action sequences. Planning quality
therefore depends on whether the transition model faithfully
propagates task-relevant signals through imagination—a property
that is usually assumed but rarely measured directly.

Active inference (Friston, 2010; Parr et al., 2022) provides
one concrete instantiation: an agent selects actions that minimize
Expected Free Energy (EFE), naturally balancing goal-seeking
(instrumental value) with information-seeking (epistemic value).
We use it here as the planning framework, but the diagnostic we
propose—probing the same auxiliary head on posterior versus
imagined prior states—applies to any world-model-based planner
that distinguishes filtered and predicted latent states.

We study a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) world model (Hafner et al., 2023) with improved Cross-Entropy Method (iCEM)

title: DIVAL: Diffeomorphic Vector-Field Alignment for Nonholonomic Motion Planning
authors: Yike Qiao,Xiaodong He,An Zhuo,Zhiyong Sun,Weimin Bao,Zhongkui Li
comment: under review
abstract:
Conventional vector-field-based motion planners for nonholonomic robots consist of two steps: first designing a nominal vector field and then controlling the robot to follow it to approach the target.
However, a nonholonomic robot cannot follow the vector field instantaneously and may collide with obstacles, due to the inevitable mismatch between the robot’s initial heading and the vector field’s direction.
This paper proposes a diffeomorphic vector-field alignment (DIVAL) method, which aligns the vector field’s direction with the robot’s initial heading so the robot can follow the vector field from the start.
Specifically, the nominal vector field is locally reshaped by applying a diffeomorphic deformation to the workspace, such that the reshaped vector field has the same direction as the robot’s heading at the initial position and coincides with the nominal vector field outside the deformed region.
Since DIVAL eliminates the initial heading mismatch, the nonholonomic robot can maintain heading alignment with the reshaped vector field throughout the motion.
This heading alignment further ensures that the robot preserves the nominal vector field’s properties, including obstacle avoidance, convergence to the target, and smooth control signals.
Numerical simulations provide vector-field-tracking baselines where the nominal vector fields are reshaped with DIVAL.
Compared to the original baselines, the proposed method achieves collision-free convergence in all trials and avoids control discontinuities.
Hardware experiments on a ground vehicle further demonstrate collision-free convergence across different targets and initial conditions under real-world disturbances.
introduction:
Nonholonomic constraints of mobile robots, such as wheeled uncrewed ground vehicles (UGVs) and fixed-wing uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAVs), restrict their admissible motion to the heading direction and pose challenges for motion planning [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].
Among existing motion planning methodologies, vector-field-based motion planners are suitable for nonholonomic robots because the vector assigned to each position specifies the desired heading direction of the robot [7, 8, 9].
The prevailing paradigm of vector-field-based planning consists of two stages [10, 11, 12].
First, a vector field is designed with desirable properties, including safety, convergence, and smoothness, such that its integral curves avoid obstacles and converge smoothly to the target.
Next, an attitude tracking controller is designed to rotate the robot’s heading toward the vector field’s direction as it moves forward, so that the robot follows an integral curve once the heading mismatch is stabilized at zero.

One classic way to generate the vector field is computing the gradient of a potential function, such as artificial potential field [13, 14, 15], harmonic potential field [16, 17, 18], navigation functions [19, 20, 21], and the data-driven approaches [22, 23, 24].
Besides the gradient-based methods, some works decompose the environment into polygonal cells and directly design vector fields within each cell [25, 26].
The aforementioned vector fields are safe, convergent, and smooth along their integral curves.
Thus, when the nonholonomic robot has the same heading as the vector field, it can move along the integral curve and exhibit the prescribed properties.

Since vector fields usually disregard the robot’s initial heading, an initial heading mismatch between the robot and the vector field exists in most cases.
To handle this problem, existing works employ the attitude tracking controllers to regulate the heading mismatch[27, 28, 29, 30], which can be categorized into two types.
One type is the asymptotic tracking controllers [31, 32, 33, 34], where the robot’s heading asymptotically converges to the vector field’s direction, so that the robot can move along the vector field’s integral curve as the time goes to infinity.
The other type is the finite-time tracking controllers [35, 36], where the robot strictly moves along the integral curve once the heading mismatch converges to zero in a finite time.

However, neither controller type eliminates the initial heading mismatch instantaneously, so the heading mismatch persists during the robot’s motion.
Since the robot can only move along its heading direction, the heading mismatch inevitably causes the robot’s trajectory to deviate from the vector field’s integral curve.
This deviation may cause collision with obstacles or discontinuities in control inputs even though the vector field is inherently safe and smooth, and consequently undermine the vector field’s desirable properties under the attitude tracking controller.
Representative cases where the robot encounters collisions and fails to converge to the target are illustrated in Figure 1() and numerical simulations in Section V-B.

Instead of designing attitude tracking controllers for the robot to reduce the heading mismatch, another possible way is to reshape the nominal vector field such that its direction is aligned with the robot’s heading at the initial position.
Although such an idea is natural, reshaping the vector field remains challenging, since it involves not only altering the vector field’s direction to eliminate the heading mismatch, but also preserving desirable properties of the nominal vector field in terms of safety, convergence, smoothness, among others. Otherwise, the robot may collide with obstacles or cannot reach the destination even though it strictly follows the vector field from the start.

To address the above-mentioned challenges, we propose a diffeomorphic vector-field alignment (DIVAL) framework for motion planning of robots with 3D nonholonomic kinematics.
DIVAL defines a diffeomorphism according to the initial heading mismatch between the nominal vector field and the nonholonomic robot, and locally deforms the workspace around the robot’s initial position.
The workspace deformation induces a corresponding reshaping effect of the nominal vector field, as in Figure 1(1(b)).
At the initial position, the reshaped vector field is aligned with the robot’s heading, and hence the initial heading mismatch is eliminated.
As the deformation gradually vanishes away from the initial position, the reshaped vector field smoothly transitions back to the nominal vector field and remains identical to it outside the deformed region.

Furthermore, we design control laws to maintain the initial heading alignment established by DIVAL throughout the robot’s motion.
Under the proposed control laws, the robot moves strictly along the integral curve of the reshaped vector field in the ideal case, and within a small bounded neighborhood of that curve under disturbances.
Moreover, given that the deformation of DIVAL is a diffeomorphism, we show that the integral curves of the reshaped vector field are the images of the integral curves of the nominal vector field.
We further prove that under explicit initial conditions, the nonholonomic robot can avoid obstacles, converge to the target, and maintain continuity of control inputs as the nominal vector field.

The theoretical contributions are verified through extensive numerical simulations and hardware experiments.
In simulation, we select several vector-field-tracking baselines for comparison and reshape their nominal vector fields with DIVAL.
Compared with the baselines that rely on aggressive control inputs, DIVAL eliminates trajectory deviation and ensures collision-free convergence for all initial configurations in the given set without abrupt control changes.
The effectiveness of DIVAL in real-world applications is further examined on a UGV, which demonstrates safe convergence covering different target and initial configurations despite disturbances.

This paper is organized as follows. Section II formulates the objectives of vector-field alignment.
Section III proposes DIVAL and proves that the reshaped vector field satisfies the alignment objectives.
Section IV derives the control law and shows that the closed-loop system preserves the safety, convergence, and smoothness properties of the nominal vector field.
Section V presents the simulation results including comparisons with the baselines, and validates the effectiveness of DIVAL in real-world experiments.

title: Can I join you? Extended Social Force Based Model with Predictive Control and Barrier Functions for Humanoid Group Repositioning Amidst Obstacles
authors: Chuxuan Zhang,Niloofar Jahanshahi,Yasaman Etesam,Mo Chen,Angelica Lim
abstract: As social and service robots increasingly share interaction spaces in public, they may form groups while coordinating tasks or interacting with humans. Initial group formation alone is insufficient in dynamic settings, because it can be disrupted when a person or another agent joins, leaves, or passes through the group. Although group dynamics and repositioning have been widely studied in swarm robotics and virtual-agent settings, little attention has been given to socially appropriate repositioning behaviors in groups of humanoid robots. Existing social-force-based approaches provide a useful foundation for group behavior, but they have limited obstacle handling, and can produce unsafe behavior as environmental complexity increases. We propose a novel framework that modulates traditional Social Force, guided by Model Predictive Control (MPC) to plan ahead, bounded by Control Barrier Functions (CBF) to increase safety for robot groups repositioning behaviors. This approach aims to produce safer and socially aware group repositioning behaviors under various group formation disturbance. We evaluate the method in simulation through an ablation study and an online user study. The results show that our proposed method can produce smoother and safer repositioning behaviors in complex environments while preserving social appropriateness.
introduction:
Group repositioning is common in everyday social interactions. We may need to join or leave colleagues who are chatting in an office or navigate through crowded poster sessions at a conference. Similar situations can also arise in human–robot group interactions, for example when a person enters an elevator occupied by a group of delivery robots or approaches a group of tour-guide robots while traveling. In these situations, existing group members may need to reposition themselves to acknowledge the newcomer, provide access to the shared interaction space, or allow the person to pass through comfortably.
When existing group members fail to acknowledge and accommodate a newcomer’s joining or leaving behavior, additional time and effort may be required for the newcomer to engage with the group, while the remaining members may struggle to maintain an appropriate group formation. A lack of adaptive proxemic behavior may also be perceived as passive-aggressive toward a passerby and make navigation through the shared space uncomfortable. As humanoid robots become more widely deployed in real-world environments, improving the repositioning behavior of existing robot group members is important for enabling smooth and natural group interactions.

The Social Force Field Model (SFFM) [1] was proposed in 2008 for free-standing conversational virtual agents in obstacle-free environments. SFFM succeeds in static group formation contexts, suggesting it’s better suited to maintaining a formation once established than to producing naturalistic, adaptive dynamics [2]. Nevertheless, it still lacks the capability to maintain appropriate group formation during real-world interaction. Gao et al. [2] applied SFFM in robot group joining study, demonstrating its potential to translate from virtual agents setting to physical robot deployment. However, transferring SFFM from virtual agents to physical robot groups introduces additional safety concerns. Robots deployed in real environments rarely operate in obstacle-free spaces, and collisions involving physical robots can be expensive. In this study, we propose an Extended Social Force Field Model (ESFFM) that not only produces initial static group formation, but also adapts to disturbances in group formation.

When a social-force-inspired controller is used alone for group repositioning, force cancellation cannot be prevented, and complex environments can increase the likelihood of unsafe proxemic behavior. Therefore, we introduce receding-horizon prediction to optimize group repositioning behavior over a longer interaction horizon, together with barrier functions that provide an additional safety mechanism. While barrier functions provide an additional safety filter, they do not themselves encode social context. This motivates our framework, which combines social-force-inspired optimization with barrier-function-based safety constraints to produce safer and more natural group dynamics for social humanoids.

In this paper, we focus on modeling the adaptive behavior of existing robot group members when the group formation is disturbed by joining, leaving, or passing-by behaviors. Compared with prior work on virtual-agent group dynamics, we translate group-repositioning behavior to social robot settings and evaluate it across a variety of environments. The major contributions of this paper are summarized as follows:

An obstacle-aware Extended Social Force Field Model (ESFFM) for adaptive robot-group repositioning under interaction disturbances.

A receding-horizon controller that optimizes ESFFM behavior over a finite horizon to reduce unnecessary motion.

An ESFFM-based predictive controller with barrier-function safety filtering that enables safer robot-group repositioning across varied environments while preserving social appropriateness.

title: Learning Low-Latency Action Verification for Frozen Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Wen-Han Hsieh,Ken Jiankun Zheng,Chia-Chien Chen,David M. Chan,Trevor Darrell
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)
abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have made significant progress in general-purpose robotic manipulation. However, sampled action sequences can be ineffective, while evaluating alternatives with computationally expensive verifiers adds latency at each policy query. In this work, we propose HDH, a lightweight framework that uses hindsight from a frozen VLA’s own deployments to improve action verification. The framework has three stages. First, we deploy the policy and collect its autonomous rollouts. We then train a compact action verifier to assign each action chunk a predicted task-success score. Finally, the frozen VLA generates action candidates, and the verifier selects the candidate with the highest score for execution. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3% and on three real-world manipulation tasks, HDH improves average success over the baseline policy by 22.6%.
introduction:
Vision-language-action (VLA) models have achieved state-of-the-art performance on general-purpose manipulation, mapping visual observations and language instructions into robot actions [1, 2, 3, 4]. In deployment, however, the common practice is to sample a single action from the VLA, and execute it on the robot. Existing deployments, thus, do not exploit a fundamental property of generative policies, where the same observation and instruction can yield a full distribution of candidates with substantial variation in execution quality. To exploit this distributional generation capability, a simple test-time solution is to sample multiple candidate action chunks and select the candidate with the highest estimated quality.

The question of how to select that action is, however, an open problem. Existing work has considered several heuristic selection strategies, including random selection and candidate evaluation using large vision-language models [5, 6, 7, 8]. However, we believe that instead of relying on very large external models, the policy’s own deployment experience can provide explicit supervision for this choice. We therefore investigate whether terminal success and failure provide sufficient supervision for candidate ranking and whether a compact verifier can achieve selection performance comparable to that of substantially larger verifiers.

To address these questions, we introduce Hindsight Decision Model with History (HDH), a lightweight verifier trained on terminal outcomes from autonomous policy rollouts, without expert comparisons, synthetic preferences, or predicted futures. Each training example consists of the current observation, the executed action prefix, and the episode’s terminal outcome. To provide context about task progress, the verifier additionally receives recent observations and executed actions. At deployment, HDH assigns a predicted eventual task-success score to each candidate sampled from the frozen VLA, and the robot executes the highest-scoring prefix.

We evaluate HDH in simulation and in the real-world in four dimensions. First, does a verifier trained only from terminal outcomes improve the closed-loop success of a frozen VLA? Second, does it produce candidate rankings that improve selection performance, beyond randomly selecting from the same set? Third, does history-conditioned scoring improve candidate discrimination by revealing task progress? Finally, how does such a compact verifier compare with verifiers based on large vision-language models on task success and inference latency?

We find that hindsight supervision alone substantially improves closed-loop manipulation. Across four LIBERO-10 tasks, HDH achieves an average success rate of 82.3%, outperforming both the frozen policy and random selection from the same candidate set. On three real-world manipulation tasks, it raises average success from 44.7% to 67.3% within a real-time control budget. Furthermore, history-conditioned scoring improves candidate ranking, and the compact verifier achieves selection performance comparable to that of much larger verifiers with substantially lower inference cost.

Our contributions are thus threefold:

Problem setting. We frame VLA deployment as real-time candidate selection supervised only by the frozen policy’s own rollout outcomes.

Verifier and selection. We introduce a lightweight, history-conditioned verifier for ranking native VLA candidates without updating the policy.

Evaluation. We show in both simulation and real-world experiments that hindsight-supervised selection improves closed-loop manipulation with substantially lower inference cost than large verifiers.

2. Verifier and selection. We introduce a lightweight, history-conditioned verifier for ranking native VLA candidates without updating the policy.

3. Evaluation. We show in both simulation and real-world experiments that hindsight-supervised selection improves closed-loop manipulation with substantially lower inference cost than large verifiers.
