title: Open-Source Transtibial Prosthetic Bypass Preserving Joint Alignment: Gait Learning and Kinematic Evaluation
authors: Apolline de Vaulchier,Pablo Nocito,Yann Corbel,Nathanaël Jarrassé
abstract: Prosthetic bypasses allow able-bodied individuals to walk with a prosthesis, enabling safe early-stage testing of new prosthetic devices before clinical trials. However, existing transtibial bypasses impose constraints, such as a contralateral shoe lift or a lateral offset of the prosthesis, and their effects on gait remain poorly documented. We present an open-source transtibial prosthetic bypass that preserves part of the sagittal knee mobility without these constraints. Six able-bodied participants familiarized themselves with the bypass for approximately 10 min, then walked on a treadmill with and without it, and joint kinematics were recorded with motion capture and then extracted with OpenSim. All participants were able to walk without handrail support, although single stance remained shorter on the bypass side (27% vs. 45% of the gait cycle). Bypass-side ankle kinematics were consistent with those reported for transtibial prosthesis users, whereas peak knee flexion during swing decreased from 61∘ to 36∘ (𝒑<0.001\boldsymbol{p<0.001}) and hip range of the sound leg increased (35∘ to 51∘, 𝒑<0.01\boldsymbol{p<0.01}). Although gait with the bypass does not fully replicate that of prosthesis users, it yielded consistent gait patterns after only 10 min of learning. This bypass therefore provides a useful tool for the lower-limb prosthetics research community, facilitating preliminary experiments with able-bodied participants.
introduction:
Lower-limb amputation affects a large and growing number of people worldwide. According to a study conducted in 2022 by Bruyant et al. [1], 116,866 amputations were recorded in France between 2011 and 2020, and in the United States, the number of people living with limb loss could more than double by 2050, mainly due to diabetes and vascular disease [2]. Following amputation, several options are available to restore mobility. One of them is wearing a prosthesis: prosthetic devices help restore mobility, and thereby independence and social participation [3].

The research and development of prostheses, and in particular of active prostheses whose control laws must be tuned and validated, relies on extensive experimental testing. Performing these tests directly with people with amputation is demanding: the number of available participants is limited, each trial places an additional burden and risk on them, and ethical and medical approval processes are lengthy. To facilitate these early stages, prosthetic bypass systems have been developed [4]. They allow able-bodied individuals to walk with a prosthesis and are mainly used for prototyping.

Transtibial bypasses fall into two categories. In the first, the prosthesis is attached under the participant’s foot by means of a rigid boot fitted with a pyramid adapter [5]. This configuration requires a shoe lift on the contralateral side to compensate for the leg-length difference, and places the prosthetic joint below the anatomical one. In the second, the prosthesis is attached to the side of the leg [6], which avoids an excessive shoe lift but offsets the prosthesis laterally from the leg axis. To our knowledge, no transtibial bypass avoids both the shoe lift and the joint offset without locking the knee. Moreover, the effect of the bypass on gait has mainly been evaluated for transfemoral simulators, whereas such evaluations are lacking for transtibial simulators [4].

In this context, we propose an open-source transtibial bypass that is simple to build and preserves part of the sagittal knee mobility without requiring a shoe lift. We evaluate the learning of gait with this bypass in able-bodied participants, and then its effect on the sagittal kinematics of the hip, knee and ankle of both limbs, in order to characterise the influence of the bypass on gait.

title: SunLightBots: Turning sunlight into self-sustained, high-power motion in soft robots
authors: Yoo Jin Lee,Melanie Torres Crespo,Zhongxiao Deng,Andrew Tejada-Vega,Rebecca Kramer-Bottiglio,Wenzhong Yan,Yimin Luo
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Soft Condensed Matter (cond-mat.soft); Applied Physics (physics.app-ph)
abstract:
Soft robots built from active materials can directly convert environmental stimuli into motion, offering a route to energy autonomy and embodied control. However, environmental energy is generally harvested at low power, whereas rapid, mechanically demanding actions require high mechanical output power. Reconciling this mismatch while sustaining self-regulated cyclic actuation is challenging, particularly at the subgram scale, where limited payload capacity constrains the integration of conventional power and control hardware.
Here, we present SunLightBots, a class of subgram, sunlight-powered, untethered soft robots that achieve autonomous locomotion under continuous illumination near 1 Sun (100 mW/cm2). Their operation is enabled by a self-resetting snapping (SRS) mechanism that integrates liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) with snap-through instability to accumulate solar energy supplied at low power, release it as rapid, high-power motion, and reset through photothermal–mechanical feedback.
Through coordinated optimization of the LCE actuation temperature, photothermal conversion, actuation stress, and structural energy barrier, the system operates near 1 Sun and achieves a peak mass-specific mechanical power of 89 W/kg. At this irradiance, the optimized LCE generates an actuation stress of 0.1 MPa at approximately 60 ∘C. SunLightBots demonstrate sustained swimming, crawling, and repeated impulsive jumping. Under 1.5 Suns, the swimmer advances more than three body lengths per cycle. This work provides a materials–mechanics route toward autonomous soft robots powered entirely by the environment.
introduction:
Reactive monomers RM257 (1,4-bis[4-(3-acryloyloxypropyloxy) benzoyloxy]-2-methylbenzene) and RM82 (1,4-bis[4-(6-acryloyloxyhexyloxy)benzoyloxy]-2-methylbenzene) were purchased from Daken Chemical (Zhengzhou, Henan, China). EDDT (2,2’-(ethylenedioxy)diethanethiol), TATATO (1,3,5-triallyl-1,3,5-triazine-2,4,6(1H,3H,5H)-trione), dodecylamine, butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT), PEGDA 250 (poly(ethylene glycol) diacrylate, Mn = 250), silver microparticles (powder, 2-3.5 μ\mum), copper microparticles (average particle size = 10 μ\mum)  and triethylamine, were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich (St. Louis, MO). 4-(4-aminophenyl)butyric acid was purchased from AmBeed (Buffalo Grove, IL). Photoinitiator Irgacure 651 (2,2-dimethoxy-2-phenylacetophenone, I-651) was purchased from MedKoo BioSciences (Durham, NC). All chemicals were used without further modification unless otherwise stated. Candle soot (CS) was obtained from the incomplete combustion of a paraffin candle. An aluminum foil was positioned above the candle flame to collect soot deposits, and the accumulated CS was subsequently removed from the foil surface by gentle scraping. Water was dispensed from a Milli-Q system with a resistivity
= 18.2 MΩ⋅\Omega\cdotcm at 25∘C.

LCEs were synthesized via either amine- or thiol-based click reactions using the formulations listed in Supplementary Table S2. For amine-based LCEs, the LC monomer, chain extender, and I-651 were combined in a 20 mL scintillation vial. For thiol-based LCEs, the LC monomer, chain extender, crosslinker, BHT, and I-651 were combined in a 20 mL scintillation vial. In both cases, the mixture was heated above T​NIT\textsubscript{NI} and vortexed until homogeneous, followed by thermal oligomerization at 150 ∘C. Amine-based formulations were oligomerized for 15 h, whereas thiol-based formulations were oligomerized for 3.5 h. After oligomerization, the resulting oligomer was cast into a glass mold (10 mm ×\times 30 mm) and partially crosslinked under 365 nm UV light (intensity = 1.21 mW cm-2 ). The partially crosslinked film was then uniaxially stretched to 100% strain using a mechanical stretching apparatus, corresponding to twice its original length. While maintained under strain, the LCE film was fully crosslinked under UV light for 3 h. To promote uniform curing, the sample was flipped every 5 min during the first 30 min of irradiation and every 30 min thereafter until crosslinking was complete.

Thermomechanical characterization was performed using a dynamic mechanical analyzer (DHR 30, TA Instruments). For isometric stress measurements, aligned LCE films were cut into rectangular strips and held at a fixed length while the temperature was increased from 25 to 100 ∘C at a rate of 3 ∘C/min.

Actuation strain as a function of temperature was measured using an optical microscope equipped with a Linkam thermal stage (The McCrone Group, Westmont, IL). LCE films were first heated to 100 ∘C and then cooled to erase thermal history. The films were subsequently subjected to heating–cooling cycles between 25 and 65 ∘C at a rate of 3 ∘C min-1, during which dimensional changes were recorded to obtain strain–temperature profiles.

The light irradiance of the solar simulator was adjusted by varying the distance between the light source and the sample. The corresponding calibration curve, measured independently using a light meter, is shown in Supplementary Fig. S4.

Metal microparticles (silver and copper) were incorporated into the LCE precursor as photothermal absorbers to enhance solar absorption and temperature rise. The rise in temperature was characterized by a thermal camera (Thermal Master P3, Yantai, Shandong, China).

The LCE was combined with a curved elastomer beam to form a composite to introduce mechanical instability. The curved beam is obtained by mirroring and then extruding the height profile Yan et al. (2025) to a certain width, ww:

where HH is the overall height, dd is the nominal thickness, and LL is the span of the arc. ss denotes the length of the flat portion added at the base of the beam to facilitate the enforcement of clamped-clamped boundary conditions when integrated into a frame. The final beam geometry is obtained by offsetting the height profile h⁡(x)h(x) along its surface normal by a distance dd to account for the uniform thickness.

A photocurable mold was printed using a 3D printer (Form 4, Formlabs). Dragon Skin 10, 20, 30 (Macungie, PA) and Ecoflex 00-50 (Legal, Alberta, Canada) were cast into the molds, degassed under vacuum, and cured overnight, followed by additional curing in the oven at 65 ∘C. Afterward, the excess materials were trimmed with a razor blade and then released from the mold. The LCE and silicone were bonded together using a heat-resistant adhesive (500°F RTV High Heat Silicone Sealant, Rutland).

Autonomous cyclic motion requires a shutter design that can accommodate the full range of motion of the LCE–elastomer composite. We optimized the shutter geometry using 2D simulations to ensure that it closes completely when the composite is actuated downward to its fully deformed state (Supplementary Movie S2). This complete closure shields the LCE from sunlight, thereby allowing the LCE to cool, recover, and reverse its motion, enabling autonomous cyclic actuation.

The energy released during snap-through was quantified by impacting the composites with a hollow steel ball weighing 16.5 mg. The process was captured using two high-speed cameras (AX100, Photron, Tokyo, Japan) that simultaneously recorded side and top views of the experiment. The contact time and rebound height were extracted from the high-speed recordings (40,000 frames per second) and used to calculate the energy transferred from the composite to the ball during the snap-through event (Supplementary Movie S1).

A balsa wood frame (1.5 mm thick, Qj-solar) was fabricated by laser cutting (VLS3.50, Universal Laser Systems) following the design (Fig. S6). Two carbon fiber substrates were bonded to the bottom of the balsa wood frame using Loctite super glue (Rocky Hill, CT). The LCE-elastomer composite was then attached to the carbon-fiber-supported balsa wood frame using Loctite SI 5699 Gray adhesive (Henkel AG & Co. KGaA). The wood frame constrains the composite and enables snap-through behavior, which serves as the primary actuation mechanism for the robots.

For the crawler, starting from the primary device design, two legs and light-blocking shutters were integrated to enable directional crawling. The legs were fabricated from polyester film (0.002” thick, Dura-Lar Film, Grafix, Ohio) and cut into rectangular strips with dimensions of 12 mm × 4.7 mm. Each strip was manually folded at approximately one-third of its length to form an angle of 45°. The fabricated legs were then attached to the balsa wood substrate using cyanoacrylate adhesive. The legs were fabricated from the same polyester film (0.002 in / 0.05 mm thick, Dura-Lar Film, Grafix, Ohio). Shutters were incorporated into the device to facilitate reversible photothermal actuation of the silicone using superglue.

For the swimmer, the wooden frame was coated with a water-repellent spray to reduce water absorption and was elevated above the water surface by attaching a small piece of bubble wrap underneath the frame. A paddle was bonded directly beneath the hinge using super glue, with the hinge positioned on top of the silicone layer. A compliant hinge was formed by scoring the polyester film with a razor blade and repeatedly folding it. Swimming was recorded in a custom-built water tank under different solar illumination conditions.

For the jumper, two polyethylene terephthalate shutters (DuraLar, Grafix Plastics, Maple Heights, OH) were affixed using super glue to shade the LCE, allowing it to cool down after photothermal heating and snap-through. Two pieces of carbon fiber, which served as balancers, were attached to the bottom of the wooden frame using super glue. This enables repeatable actuation cycles after landing, even under continuous simulated sunlight, thereby allowing recovery after landing.

title: Terrain-Aware Thompson Sampling for Multi-Drone Search and Rescue
authors: Riana Gagnon Souleiman,Giovanni Beltrame
comment: Accepted to the 18th International Symposium on Distributed Autonomous Robotic Systems (DARS 2026)
abstract: In this work, we propose a decentralized terrain-aware multi-drone Thompson Sampling algorithm tailored for search and rescue (SAR) applications. A probability distribution of locating a lost person is informed by terrain data, using established SAR models (displacement ring, elevation, watershed, dispersion angle, and track offset) derived from historical SAR case data of lost person behavior. Exploration is conducted by a team of drones using Thompson Sampling, where candidate actions are selected by drawing samples from this probability distribution (a per-cell Gaussian posterior), whose mean and variance are updated through Bayesian inference. This approach enables a balance between exploration of uncertain regions and exploitation of high-probability areas with the goal of locating a lost person. Observation uncertainty is incorporated through fractional forest coverage, measuring the percent of an observation occluded by tree coverage and accounting for reduced detection performance in densely vegetated areas. Simulations are performed using real SAR case data (YOSAR) to evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to a coverage planner and probabilistic active search method in a 1.5 k​m2km^{2} and 3.8 k​m2km^{2} search region with 5,10,15, and 20 agents flying at 50 km/hr. We demonstrate that our method is able to successfully locate a lost person at a success rate of ∼87%{\sim}87\% within 6060–247247 s for an area of 1.5 k​m2km^{2}, and at a success rate of ∼75−91%{\sim}75-91\% within 161161–466466 s for an area of 3.8 k​m2km^{2}, across configurations.
introduction:
Wilderness search and rescue (WiSAR) operations are inherently arduous, time-consuming, and resource-intensive, requiring careful planning and efficient execution to maximize the probability of survival of a lost person. In land-based SAR missions, survivability decreases rapidly over time, making timely and informed decision-making critical. To support this process, a variety of models have been developed [18, 7, 23] to generate probability maps that estimate the likely locations of a missing individual. These approaches are grounded in mathematical search theory [19], which addresses the fundamental challenge of locating an unknown target within a large search space. While such probabilistic approaches significantly improve search efficiency, SAR operations still demand extensive human effort, coordination, and time to achieve successful outcomes.

Multi-robot systems, in particular teams of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), offer a promising solution by enabling rapid, parallel exploration of large areas [3, 9, 22]. However, the effectiveness of such systems depends critically on their ability to operate autonomously and in a distributed manner. Centralized coordination approaches reduce robustness in SAR scenarios due to limited communication infrastructure, bandwidth constraints, and the risk of single points of failure. To address these challenges, decentralized task allocation methods have been proposed, enabling each agent to independently and cooperatively make decisions while contributing to a shared objective [15, 24, 28].

Thompson Sampling (TS), a Bayesian decision-making framework increasingly used in search and rescue [5, 4, 20], provides a natural basis for decentralized decision-making under uncertainty. TS maintains a probabilistic belief over unknown quantities via a prior probability distribution that is updated as observations are collected (posterior). Agents sample from this posterior to select actions with the highest sampled reward, naturally balancing exploration and exploitation. When each agent maintains its own posterior and shares observations with agents within communication range, this enables a scalable, parallel decision-making process without a central coordinator.

We propose a decentralized, terrain-aware Thompson sampling framework for multi-drone SAR applications that incorporates key terrain characteristics such as linear features, elevation, and watershed structures to inform prior probability distributions based on established models of lost person behavior. Each UAV maintains a local belief over the search space and selects actions by sampling from this distribution over candidate actions. The proposed framework is evaluated in simulation using real-world SAR case data (YOSAR11

In summary, our major contributions are:

A decentralized terrain-aware Thompson sampling algorithm that leverages existing search and rescue models to assign informed priors for search of lost persons in large, remote environments.

Object detection uncertainty based on fractional forest coverage.

Experimental simulations analyzing the performance of the proposed method using real search and rescue cases.

title: An Integrated Architecture for Data-Efficient Real-Time Neural Imitation of Nonlinear Time-Optimal Model Predictive Control
authors: Maarten De Baecke,Flavia Sofia Acerbo,Andrea Giusti,Wilm Decré
subjects: Systems and Control (eess.SY); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Robotics (cs.RO)
comment: Submitted to European Control Conference 2027 (Brussels)
abstract: Nonlinear time-optimal model predictive control (TOMPC) enables highly performant control of constrained systems, but its computational cost prohibits real-time use on fast dynamical systems. Neural network imitation of the TOMPC control law can reduce online computational costs, yet existing work mostly targets quadratic cost formulations in simulation and addresses the challenges of neural controllers in isolation. This work imitates a long-horizon nonconvex TOMPC with hard terminal constraints, whose high computational cost limits training-data generation. We present (i) self-informed sampling (SIFS), a data-efficient expert-sampling strategy that uses a learned time-to-go to query the expert only where the policy deviates from time-optimal behavior, (ii) a complete training and control architecture that jointly addresses dataset correlation, suboptimal expert labels, covariate shift, constraint satisfaction and model mismatch, and (iii) real-world validation on a Furuta pendulum. SIFS matches standard dataset aggregation performance in roughly one-third of the training time and with less than half the training data. The resulting controller matches the region of attraction of the expert TOMPC while raising the control frequency from 1.4 Hz to 1 kHz. On hardware, the controller swings up and stabilizes the pendulum along trajectories closely matching the expert TOMPC solution.
introduction:
Model predictive control (MPC) has emerged as a powerful and widely applicable control strategy. In particular, nonlinear time-optimal MPC (TOMPC) seeks to steer nonlinear systems to a desired state in minimum time, thereby achieving highly performant control while accounting for system dynamics and constraints [1, 2]. Nevertheless, for nonlinear systems with fast dynamics, the high computational cost of online nonconvex optimization results in computation times often orders of magnitude higher than the available sampling interval [3]. A promising approach to overcome this limitation is to imitate the MPC control law with a neural network (NN), often through Behavioral Cloning (BC) [4], trained offline on MPC solutions [5]. Given a sufficiently small NN that accurately reproduces the MPC control law, MPC-like control can be achieved at the high control frequencies required by fast dynamical systems. Such a controller is hereafter referred to as a neural network model predictive controller (NNMPC).

Existing literature already demonstrates real-time approximation of nonlinear MPC, but almost exclusively for quadratic-tracking objectives, and predominantly in simulation [6, 7]. Hardware demonstrations remain scarce, with existing works limited to either simpler objectives, soft or no terminal constraints or comparatively simple platforms [8, 9, 10]. This work therefore tackles imitation of more computationally challenging MPC formulations, specifically a long-horizon, time-optimal formulation with hard terminal constraints. A key characteristic of such problems is that the computational cost of the MPC formulation not only restricts online deployment, but also strongly limits the generation of training data. Moreover, time-optimal control laws tend toward bang-bang behavior. Accurately approximating such laws with a smooth NN requires dense data near the switching points, increasing the demand for expert data. This makes conventional expert-data collection approaches such as Dataset Aggregation (DAgger) [11] particularly costly, motivating more efficient expert-sampling strategies. Finally, existing works address individual challenges of NNMPC, such as dataset correlation [12], suboptimal expert labels [13], controller adaptability [10], constraint satisfaction [6] and covariate shift [11], but a complete architecture integrating these solutions is currently lacking, leaving the design of a reliable NNMPC system fragmented across the literature.
Therefore, this work aims at (i) presenting an expert-sampling algorithm, referred to as self-informed sampling (SIFS), as a data-efficient alternative to DAgger specifically designed for time-optimal MPC, (ii) providing a complete training and control architecture that jointly addresses dataset correlation, suboptimal expert labels, controller adaptability, constraint satisfaction, covariate shift and efficient expert sampling, and (iii) providing real-world validation by deploying the resulting controller on a physical Furuta pendulum.

title: A Class of Bayesian Conjugate Distributions on $SE_n(3)$ for Motion Estimation
authors: Shijie Wang,Haichao Gui,Rui Zhong
abstract: This paper proposes a novel class of Bayesian Conjugate Distributions (BCDs) on extended special Euclidean groups S​En​(3)SE_{n}(3) for global motion uncertainty representation and estimation. BCDs are constructed by restricting matrix Gaussian distributions on ambient Euclidean space to S​En​(3)SE_{n}(3), avoiding singularity of local coordinates. The unique feature of BCDs is their conjugacy to a broad class of sampling distributions arising in motion estimation, enabling exact closed-form Bayesian inference. Optimal estimation with respect to BCDs is further investigated for implementing motion estimation. Two means are extracted as random state estimates, which maximize probability and minimize mean squared error, respectively. Moreover, within the BCD class, moment matching is shown to minimize the Kullback–Leibler divergence, and maximum likelihood estimation is also derived, which provide analytical methods to approximate underlying distributions with the optimality guarantee. As an application, a Bayesian estimator for pose and velocity estimation of an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) is developed within an assumed density filtering architecture. The propagation and estimate extraction leverage the optimal estimation related to BCDs, and the landmark measurements are exactly fused with the BCD prior in closed form due to the conjugacy. Numerical simulations of a UAV flight indicate the advantages of BCD-based estimators over two classic Kalman filters on Lie groups with various initial uncertainties and measurement noise.
introduction:
Motion estimation based on sensor fusion plays a crucial role in many engineering fields, including robotics[1], aerospace[2], etc. Since motion states involving attitude evolve on nonlinear manifolds with inherent constraints, conventional nonlinear filtering or optimization methods may fail to achieve accurate estimation if the underlying geometric structure is not properly considered. Meanwhile, sensors are inevitably affected by random noise, whose effects cannot be neglected and need to be carefully modeled.

When incorporating the kinematics and dynamics of systems, the main branches of motion state estimators are deterministic nonlinear observers and Kalman filters on Lie groups. Deterministic observers are directly designed on state manifolds, avoiding the singularity of local coordinates and achieving global or almost global stability for attitude estimation, pose estimation, and more complex situations [3, 4, 5]. While these estimators are distinguished by their high reliability and a sound theoretical framework, this paper focuses on estimation techniques accounting for the stochastic properties of states. Among stochastic motion estimators, an important development was the multiplicative extended Kalman filter (MEKF)[6, 7], which represents attitude by unit quaternions and approximates uncertainty in Euclidean space by Gaussian distributions. The invariant extended Kalman filters (IEKFs) further introduce the Lie group structure of the motion state space, as developed in [8, 9, 10]. IEKFs use intrinsic properties of Lie groups to linearize nonlinear systems and characterize the uncertainty of the state via a Gaussian distribution in exponential coordinates. IEKFs can provide estimates with lower errors and faster convergence rates than those of the MEKF, benefiting from their better consistency with geometric and dynamic structures. Similar methodologies are also applied to the Unscented Kalman filter (UKF) [11] and Particle Filter (PF) [12].

Concentrated Gaussian Distributions (CGDs), as presented in [13, 14], are defined on the Lie group via formulating Gaussian distributions on the Lie algebra with the exponential map. CGDs are used to construct Kalman filters on Lie groups [15] and also to characterize the uncertainty of states in the IEKF [9]. Although CGDs are described as distributions on Lie groups, the fusion and propagation involved with CGDs generally require approximation based on the Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff (BCH) formula and local coordinate representations [16, 15]. Moreover, while pose graph optimization in Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) and robotics is designed towards global optimality, its front-end preintegration and back-end optimizer often rely on local representations of uncertainty [17, 18].

Recently, there are several attempts to develop global probabilistic representations on the state manifold, and to apply them to Bayesian estimation. Matrix Fisher distributions (MFDs) [19] and Bingham distributions [20] are two primary choices for pure attitude estimation. Additionally, their joint distributions with Gaussian distributions, in the form of conditional–marginal distributions, are used to simultaneously estimate the attitude and the states in the n-dimensional Euclidean space ℝn\mathbbm{R}^{n}, such as sensor bias [21, 22]. Despite the fact that the three-dimensional special Euclidean group S​E​(3)SE(3) and its extension S​En​(3)SE_{n}(3) play important roles in motion state representation, distributions defined directly on these groups remain limited, such as [23] and [24]. These distributions on S​E​(3)SE(3) miss coupling terms between the attitude and the translation component, and have not yet been used for Bayesian pose estimation. In designing estimators with these distributions, propagation along the dynamic or kinematic equations of the system, fusion with measurement distributions, and the extraction of the optimal state estimates constitute three fundamental steps. The propagation of distributions is related to obtain the optimal approximation of underlying distributions in a certain distribution class, while the fusion involves the conjugacy [25], allowing the posterior distribution to remain within the same class of the prior and thus enabling tractable recursive estimation. For Bayesian estimators with MFDs [19], the MFD approximation of propagated distributions computed by moment matching was proven optimal in terms of maximum likelihood estimation, and they are also shown to be conjugate to von Mises Fisher and Gaussian distributions in [19, 26], which are used to characterize vector measurements. While matrix Fisher-Gaussian distributions (MFGDs) proposed in [21] carefully design the correlation terms between the attitude and states in the Euclidean space with an intuitive geometric interpretation, MFGD-based estimators cannot provide globally optimal approximation of propagated distributions and no distribution, to the best of our knowledge, have been found to be conjuagated to MFGDs, including themselves. The Bingham-Gaussian distributions (BGDs) in [27] and [22] suffer from similar issues.

Due to the absence of conjugacy to common probabilistic models of motion measurements, the approximation of the underlying posterior distributions needs to be explicitly considered in the Bayesian estimator with these joint distributions. For certain specific scenarios, such as attitude-bias estimation with unit vector measurements in [21] or pose estimation with mutually independent position and attitude measurements [28], tailored approximation strategies can be derived to obtain tractable posterior updates. These strategies are inherently problem-dependent and inevitably result in a loss of theoretical accuracy. When more general measurement models are involved, especially those containing position-attitude coupling terms such as landmark observations, constructing accurate approximations of the underlying posterior distributions with joint distributions defined on state manifolds, such as MFGDs and BGDs, is still an open problem. Moreover, obtaining an analytical solution for optimal parameter estimation, including maximum likelihood estimation or minimum Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence estimation of these distributions remains insufficiently addressed in existing literature, despite being essential for Bayesian estimators under the assumed density framework. Existing approaches either rely on marginal–conditional approximations for MFGDs [21] or require numerical optimization on manifolds for BGDs [22].

To address the absence of conjugacy and analytical solutions for optimal parameter estimation, this paper develops a conjugate probabilistic distribution class for Bayesian motion estimation on S​En​(3)SE_{n}(3), which is conjugate for common probabilistic models of motion measurements and enables analytical and optimal parameter estimation from moments or samples. Based on this distribution class, we further design a Bayesian pose estimator that incorporates landmark measurements, to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed distributions to measurements involving position–attitude coupling. The three main contributions are summarized as follows.

First, this paper proposes a novel class of Bayesian Conjugate Distributions (BCDs) in Section 3, which globally represent the uncertainty of motion states on S​En​(3)SE_{n}(3). The proposed distribution class is defined by confining Gaussian distributions on the ambient space of S​En​(3)SE_{n}(3), and is designed to be conjugate to itself and a broad range of distributions characterizing measurements used in regular pose estimation tasks. The introduction of conjugacy enables rigorous and precise closed-form Bayesian inference in the form of the BCD class when fusing both pure position-/attitude-related measurements and position-attitude-coupled measurements, including GPS, magnetometer, and known and unknown landmark measurements.

In Section 4, the optimal estimation of state and parameters is developed under the BCD representation. Two estimates are given for states characterized by BCDs, which are derived from the maximum probability and minimum squared error optimizations, respectively. Then, we consider obtaining the globally optimal BCD approximation of the underlying distributions using moments and samples. All parameters of a BCD are shown to be obtained from finite-order moment matching, and the distribution with these parameters is proven to be the minimum KL divergence estimation of the underlying distribution. The joint Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) with samples on S​En​(3)SE_{n}(3) is then presented, avoiding the introduction of local sampling from Gaussian distributions on ℝn\mathbbm{R}^{n} in [12] or conditional-marginal MLE as an approximation in [21]. The solutions of both moment matching and MLE are derived analytically. Most parameters are computed in closed form, while the rest are solved from equations in ℝ3\mathbbm{R}^{3}, thereby avoiding the numerical optimization on manifolds, as in [22].

A BCD-based Bayesian estimator for estimating the pose and linear velocity of a UAV with known landmarks is presented, demonstrating the applicability of the proposed distributions to motion estimation problems with position-attitude coupling measurements. The BCD-based estimator follows the structure of assumed density filtering and includes propagation, fusion, and estimate extraction steps, illustrating how the properties in Section 3 and 4 are utilized in estimation algorithm construction. In the proposed estimator, the propagation step provides the minimum KL-divergence BCD prior approximation based on propagated moments, and the fusion with sampling distributions from measurement models is analytical and structure-preserving due to the conjugacy. The maximum probability and minimum squared error estimates are used as extracted estimates, respectively. In the simulation of a UAV flight presented in Section 6, we observe that the BCD-based estimator provides lower RMSEs and better transient response than those of two classical Kalman filters on S​En​(3)SE_{n}(3). Moreover, the estimator with minimum squared error estimates demonstrates slightly better performance compared to the estimator with BCDs using maximum probability estimates in the mean RMSE over 50 Monte Carlo simulations, indicating its long-term accuracy.

title: ScrewSense: Mapping the Invisible - Anomaly Detection and Error Classification in Screwdriving Processes
authors: Tobias Lettner,Tatyana Ivanovska,Anwar Al Assadi,Christian Bergler
comment: Accepted manuscript, 59th CIRP Conference on Manufacturing Systems (CMS 2026).
abstract: The growing volume of process data generated by screwdriving systems, combined with advancements in computing power, data storage, and algorithms, is facilitating the application of artificial intelligence in this field. Accurately detecting and classifying screwdriving errors is crucial for ensuring product quality, avoiding costly rework in manufacturing, and supporting sustainability by facilitating the maintenance, reuse, and recycling of screw-connected products. In this context, machine learning approaches offer a promising alternative to traditional monitoring techniques, such as window-based methods or envelope curves. This study examines the use of deep learning techniques for anomaly detection and error classification in screwdriving processes. The data corpus consists of multivariate time series capturing process parameters, such as torque and rotation angle. For anomaly detection, the embedding space of a vector quantized variational autoencoder was analyzed. In terms of error classification, four different model architectures were evaluated. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of anomaly detection and confirm that deep learning models can distinguish between multiple error categories beyond traditional binary classification. This extends the capabilities of conventional monitoring approaches, achieving accuracies of up to 100 %. Additionally, real-world data material was examined in order to further demonstrate model robustness. Overall the results indicate strong generalization capability and highlight the practical potential of the developed models for use in industrial screwdriving processes, eliminating the need for expert knowledge in error identification and significantly reducing manual effort and analysis time.
introduction:
Screwdriving systems have evolved into complex technologies that continuously collect process data, such as torque and rotation angle [15]. This data is primarily used to evaluate the quality of screw joints by determining whether they meet the required specifications (OK versus NOK) [6]. Traditionally, this evaluation has relied on monitoring windows that define fixed upper and lower limits for key parameters [6, 25].

However, threshold-based methods only assess limited areas of the tightening process. Envelope curves [17] can be used to analyze the entire process, but they require extensive parameterization and only indicate whether a process is acceptable or not, without identifying the underlying cause of the deviation.

The trend toward lightweight construction, advanced materials, and higher automation in industrial production is making screwdriving processes increasingly complex. This necessitates adaptive and intelligent monitoring approaches to maintain consistent assembly quality and process reliability [11].

The ongoing rise of artificial intelligence, particularly deep learning, provides innovative solutions to these challenges. They enable flexible and comprehensive analysis of the entire screwdriving process by learning complex patterns and dependencies within the data. Machine learning reduces the need for manual parameter tuning next to expert- and domain-specific rules, supporting higher levels of automation, better quality control, and more reliable processes.

The paper is structured as follows: 2 Related Work summarizes prior work, 3 Data Situation describes the data and preprocessing, 4 Methodology details the proposed approach, 5 Experiments, Results, and Discussion presents the results, and 6 Conclusion and Future Work summarizes the main findings and outlines future work.

title: Autonomous Mobile Robots on a Computing Field
authors: Yonghwan Kim,Gil-Tak Kong,Un-Sook Choi
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract:
We introduce CABot, a computational model for autonomous mobile robots in
which the discrete plane the robots operate on is not a passive stage but an
active computing medium. In the classical 𝙻𝚘𝚘𝚔\mathtt{Look}-𝙲𝚘𝚖𝚙𝚞𝚝𝚎\mathtt{Compute}-𝙼𝚘𝚟𝚎\mathtt{Move} (LCM) model
every increase in computational capability is obtained by strengthening the
robots themselves, with lights, memory or wider visibility, at a cost paid
once per robot. CABot strengthens the environment instead: each cell of the
grid holds a state from a finite set 𝒬\mathcal{Q}, the states evolve synchronously
under a uniform local rule that also senses whether a robot stands on the
cell, that is, the floor is a cellular automaton, and the 𝙻𝚘𝚘𝚔\mathtt{Look} operation
returns the states of the visible cells in addition to the positions of the
visible robots. The robots are as weak as we can make them: oblivious, silent,
lightless, myopic with visibility range 11, without multiplicity detection
and unable to write to the floor. The number of field states |𝒬||\mathcal{Q}|, rather
than any robot capability, becomes the measure of the resources required.
On an inert floor (|𝒬|=1|\mathcal{Q}|=1) such robots can neither form a line, nor gather
from scattered positions, nor explore a grid. We show that a handful of states
changes this. Line Formation from connected configurations is solvable with
four states, and field-silently, so that the floor also reaches a fixed
point, with five. Gathering from arbitrary, possibly disconnected,
configurations is solvable with three states and Line Formation from arbitrary
configurations with six; we prove that neither can be solved field-silently
with any number of states. A single robot explores every finite grid forever
with four states and every torus with two, which is optimal. Further rule
sets, validated by simulation only, equalize the spacing of robots on a row,
fill a pattern painted on the floor and guide robots through a maze, and
indicate the range of the model.
introduction:
A swarm of autonomous mobile robots is commonly studied
through the 𝙻𝚘𝚘𝚔\mathtt{Look}-𝙲𝚘𝚖𝚙𝚞𝚝𝚎\mathtt{Compute}-𝙼𝚘𝚟𝚎\mathtt{Move} (LCM) model [1, 2].
Robots are points in the plane, anonymous and indistinguishable,
all executing the same algorithm (i.e., homogeneous);
each repeatedly takes a snapshot of its surroundings (𝙻𝚘𝚘𝚔\mathtt{Look}),
computes a destination (𝙲𝚘𝚖𝚙𝚞𝚝𝚎\mathtt{Compute}), and moves there (𝙼𝚘𝚟𝚎\mathtt{Move}).
The enduring appeal of the model lies in how little it assumes.
Robots have no identifiers, no memory that persists across cycles,
and no explicit means of communication.
Every positive result is therefore a statement about
how much coordination can be extracted from almost nothing.

The price of this minimalism is a long list of impossibility results [1, 3].
Symmetric configurations cannot be broken by identical deterministic robots;
oblivious robots cannot accumulate the history a task requires;
and myopic robots, which see only a bounded neighborhood,
cannot obtain the global view that many formations implicitly need.

The standard response has been to give the robots more.
Luminous robots (ℒ​𝒰​ℳ​ℐ\mathcal{LUMI}) carry an externally visible light of constant size [4];
the sub-models ℱ​𝒮​𝒯​𝒜\mathcal{FSTA} and ℱ​𝒞​𝒪​ℳ\mathcal{FCOM} separate its use as internal memory from
its use as communication [5];
other work enlarges the visibility radius or restricts the scheduler.
Together these form a well-understood hierarchy of models.
What they all share is that capability is added per robot:
a swarm of nn robots requires nn copies of the additional hardware,
and the robots themselves must become more complex, more expensive, and less disposable.

We take an orthogonal route.
Rather than asking what must be added to the robots,
we ask what must be added to the environment so that nothing has to be added to the robots.

Real robots never move in a vacuum.
Automated warehouse floors already carry fiducial markers and RFID grids
that vehicles read as they travel;
social insects coordinate not by direct communication but by depositing
and sensing traces in their surroundings,
a mechanism known as stigmergy [13].
In both cases the environment is part of the algorithm.
The LCM model, however, treats the plane as an inert set of coordinates.

We therefore promote the environment to a first-class computational entity
and call the resulting model CABot (robots on a cellular automaton
field). The grid on which the robots operate is itself a cellular automaton:
every cell carries a state from a finite set 𝒬\mathcal{Q},
and all cells update synchronously under a single uniform transition rule
whose input is the state of the cell, the states of its four neighbors, and
the presence or absence of a robot on the cell itself.
A robot’s 𝙻𝚘𝚘𝚔\mathtt{Look} operation returns, in addition to the robot positions within its visibility range,
the states of the cells within that range. Informally: the floor is computing.

Three properties distinguish this from strengthening the robots.
Memory is attached to places, not to robots: a light travels with its
carrier and vanishes when the robot leaves, whereas a field state stays where
it was produced, survives that departure, and can be read by a different robot
arriving later. Information propagates without being carried: in the
plain LCM model information travels only as fast as the robots move or as far
as they see, while in CABot it spreads one cell per step on its own,
which is what lets robots of visibility range 11 act on circumstances they
cannot see. The field is minimal infrastructure: it is anonymous and
uniform, its rule is purely local, and it needs no identifiers, no broadcast
and no connectivity beyond nearest neighbors, so the question we ask is not
what an arbitrarily powerful environment can do but how little environmental
support suffices. Accordingly the robots are fixed at the weakest setting
throughout the paper, and the single resource we measure is the number
|𝒬||\mathcal{Q}| of field states.

Once the environment computes, the usual notion of termination is too weak:
an algorithm may halt the robots in the desired configuration while the cells
beneath them keep changing forever, so the field still consumes energy and an
observer of the field cannot tell that the computation is over. We therefore
call an algorithm terminating if every execution reaches a
configuration in which no robot moves again, and field-silent if it
reaches one in which no cell changes state again either, by analogy with
silent self-stabilization [25]. The distinction is not vacuous: our
four-state Line Formation algorithm is terminating but not field-silent, since
two cells at the ends of the formed line oscillate forever, and removing that
obstruction costs one additional state. For robots that start far apart the
distinction is even sharper: we show that no algorithm whatsoever can make
them meet field-silently.

We formalize CABot and study three fundamental problems in it,
Line Formation, Gathering and Exploration,
with robots that are as weak as the setting permits:
oblivious, silent, lightless, myopic with visibility range 11, without
multiplicity detection, agreeing on directions and operating fully
synchronously (𝙵𝚂𝚈𝙽𝙲\mathtt{FSYNC}). Table 1 summarizes the results.

The model. We define CABot as an extension of LCM in which
|𝒬||\mathcal{Q}| measures the resources supplied by the environment, and we introduce
field-silence as a refinement of termination that is specific to models with
an active environment (Section 3). With |𝒬|=1|\mathcal{Q}|=1 the model is
the plain one, in which Line Formation from connected configurations,
Gathering and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations, and Exploration
are all unsolvable (Proposition 1).

the plain one, in which Line Formation from connected configurations,

Line Formation from connected configurations. Four states
suffice on the infinite grid; the algorithm terminates but is not
field-silent (Section 4). Five states suffice for a field-silent
solution, and we identify the mechanism, a landing mark produced by decay
rather than by a persistent predicate, that makes the four-state algorithm
non-silent (Section 5).

Gathering from arbitrary configurations. Robots that start on
arbitrary distinct cells, with no connectivity whatsoever, gather with three
states (Section 6). We also prove that no algorithm, with
any number of states, solves Gathering or Line Formation from arbitrary
configurations field-silently (Proposition 4).

Line Formation from arbitrary configurations. Six states
suffice (Section 7). The algorithm combines the region
painting of the gathering algorithm with a landing zone, a cell that
knows a robot is directly above it, which makes the approach collision-free
although the converging robots cannot see each other.

Exploration. A single robot visits every cell of every finite
torus and of every bounded grid infinitely often with four states, the floor
acting as a rotor-router; on tori two states suffice, which is optimal
(Section 8).

Further examples. Three more rule sets, validated by simulation
only, illustrate other uses of the floor: as a ruler that spaces robots
equally on a row, and as an excitable medium that calls robots to target cells
painted on the floor and routes them through a maze
(Section 9).

The state counts are small enough to be striking:
four states amount to a cell being blank, occupied, or carrying a trace at one of two levels of freshness.
The computational capability that would otherwise demand a light or a memory on every robot
is recovered from a handful of states underfoot.

Section 2 surveys related work.
Section 3 defines CABot, the problems, and what an inert floor cannot do.
Sections 4 and 5 present Line Formation from connected configurations with four and with five states.
Sections 6 and 7 treat Gathering and Line Formation from arbitrary configurations.
Section 8 treats Exploration, Section 9 the further examples,
and Section 10 concludes with open problems.

title: AstroMemBench: A Benchmark for Memory Systems in Embodied Spacecraft Agents
authors: You Wu,Guhong Zhang,Hongwei Li,Xinyue Hong,Yuan Jia
comment: . Includes Appendices A-E
abstract: Long-term spacecraft autonomy requires embodied agents to use operational history under communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational constraints, and safety and reliability requirements. We introduce AstroMemBench and a Scenario–Challenge–Capability design method that maps these requirements to executable memory tests. The benchmark covers 16 memory subchallenges through 140 templates and 2240 instances across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration. A deterministic environment scores actions for task completion, state changes, safety, and resource use. Ablations under nine conditions show that the benchmark is sensitive to how accurately agents recover and use historical information and to differences in memory-system design. Main experiments compare six configurations. Mem0, Chain-of-Memory, LightMem, and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improve same-session mean scores over native Pi Agent, with no clear advantage of the three memory systems over RAG. After a session restart, Mem0 outperforms RAG by 12.25 points. Benefits favor instruction retention and result reuse over ongoing state tracking and energy reservation. AstroMemBench supports the design, development, and selection of memory systems for embodied spacecraft agents. AstroMemBench 1.0 and its evaluation code are publicly available: https://github.com/flyingView/AstroMemBench-v1.
introduction:
Advances in planetary surface operations [1], on-orbit servicing [2], and deep-space exploration [3] increase demand for unattended, long-term autonomous spacecraft operation [4, 5]. Agents based on large language models and their multimodal extensions support such autonomy through perception, reasoning, and tool use; related studies in simulated and experimental orbital operations and on-orbit servicing have explored closed-loop execution and experience reuse [6, 7, 8]. Within these agents, memory systems preserve, organize, and update interaction records so that facts and experience remain available for decisions beyond a finite context window [9, 10]. For embodied spacecraft agents on long missions, this ability supports continued adherence to task requirements, resumption from the correct execution state, and effective reuse of prior experience.

However, the suitability of current memory systems for spacecraft tasks requires dedicated evaluation. Mem0, CoM, and LightMem continue to advance [9, 10, 11], but their ability to meet specialized operational requirements remains to be established. In building information modeling, for example, general-purpose systems retrieved relevant content yet omitted required domain information [12]. This need for domain-specific validation is not fully addressed by existing memory benchmarks. MemoryAgentBench notes that static long-context evaluations inadequately capture agents’ incremental information accumulation and updating; recent research also identifies gaps between benchmark scale, metrics, and practical needs [13, 14]. The main experiments on SimpleMem [15] and LightMem [11], two recent memory systems, still use the earlier conversational benchmarks LoCoMo [16] and LongMemEval [17]. These benchmarks provide a common basis for testing long-term conversational memory, whereas evaluations of spacecraft agents must also test whether historical information helps them act correctly under the operational constraints of space missions. A dedicated benchmark is therefore needed to guide memory system design and selection.

Remote operation and limited intervention place particular demands on the use of history in space missions. The European Space Agency’s Technology 2040 identifies six challenges for autonomous space systems: communication delays, time-critical operations, environmental uncertainty, complex physical interactions, power and computational resource constraints, and safety and reliability [5]. Communication delays hinder timely ground confirmation, requiring agents to follow existing requirements and distinguish valid instructions from superseded ones; time-critical operations require agents to use valid information within action windows and remember pending tasks. Unknown environments and complex interactions require agents to revise judgments using prior observations, actual operation results, and environmental changes, while distinguishing plans from completed actions. Limited energy and computation also make experience and result reuse directly relevant to task cost. Safety imposes further demands: for example, deep-space flybys cannot pause when anomalies occur, and delayed responses may cause mission failure [4], making valid safety checks and correct task resumption after faults particularly important. To assess these requirements, memory evaluation must link history to action consequences, including task completion, safety constraints, and resource use.

We therefore develop AstroMemBench, a benchmark for memory systems in embodied spacecraft agents (Fig. 1), translating these operational requirements into executable, history-dependent tasks to examine the role of memory. Our main contributions are:

We introduce the three-dimensional SCC design method for domain coverage. Scenario–Challenge–Capability (SCC) organizes benchmark construction through a scenario–challenge applicability matrix, capability associations, and execution checks, translating domain requirements into inspectable, revisable test coverage.

We introduce the three-dimensional SCC design method for domain coverage. Scenario–Challenge–Capability (SCC) organizes benchmark construction through a scenario–challenge applicability matrix, capability associations, and execution checks, translating domain requirements into inspectable, revisable test coverage.

We construct a dedicated memory test set for embodied spacecraft agents. We refine six operational challenge categories into 16 memory subchallenges across nine tasks in planetary surface operations, on-orbit servicing, and deep-space exploration, yielding 140 templates and 2240 instances. Each instance establishes task context through 30 historical interaction turns; subsequent execution is scored deterministically by state changes, safety conditions, and resource consequences.

We demonstrate the benchmark’s sensitivity to history availability and differences among memory systems. Nine ablation conditions test the effects of historical background, session boundaries, and context windows. Comparisons of scores, baseline-relative gains, and operational costs under same-session and new-session conditions, with each instance isolated, reveal how memory benefits vary across systems and task requirements.

title: Demo: Matter-Based IoMT Telemetry and Security Analysis
authors: Muhammad Hassan,Masooda Bashir,Carl Gunter
abstract: Connected health devices increasingly support health monitoring outside clinical settings, making secure and accessible physiological data important for patients and caregivers. However, device-specific applications and interfaces complicate the integration of readings from different devices. The Matter standard provides standardized device commissioning and protected communication, but its cluster library does not represent the health attribute measurement. We present a preliminary demo study of a Matter-based IoMT testbed with a specific HealthVitals cluster. Implemented in the connectedhomeip SDK on a Raspberry Pi 5, the cluster exposes simulated heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, and body temperature. We examine commissioning, attribute retrieval, communication under simulated packet loss, and operational traffic through a reference controller. The study demonstrates that this custom telemetry model can operate within the tested Matter configuration without modifying commissioning or secure-session mechanisms. The resulting testbed gives researchers and device developers a concrete platform for investigating health-oriented extensions. It also supports exploration of local telemetry integration that could help patients and caregivers access readings across connected devices.
introduction:
Connected health devices, also referred to as Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) are increasingly becoming popular and used outside clinical settings. These devices, such as include wearables, pulse oximeters, and connected thermometers, collect health and physiological measurements [3, 8]. These devices often use different protocols and standards making interoperability difficult. As a result, a person using different IoMT devices may need separate smartphone applications or controllers to manage and view their health data. This makes it challenging for the user to view and analyze health and wellness data in a unified system [8]. Therefore, a smart and connected device protocol that can port the data in a common format so the devices can communicate and be interoperable is needed. Additionally, the protocol should protect the sensitive health data during device setup and routine network exchange [9]. This can provide a single application and controller for easier interpretation and usability for IoMT devices.

Matter is an IP-based standard developed for communication among Internet of Things (IoT). It defines a device data model, commissioning procedures, and protected operational sessions [1, 2]. These mechanisms make it useful to implement for local health telemetry. However, the Matter cluster library does not define a standard representation for the health and physiological data.

Existing Matter testbeds have examined commissioning and traffic capture across Wi-Fi, Thread, and BLE [7]. Other work has studied deployment on development platforms and provided methods for implementing custom clusters [10, 6]. Building on these efforts, we examine a custom cluster in a health-telemetry setting. We focus on how a controller retrieves its attributes after commissioning and how the resulting operational traffic appears in a network capture.

We implement a manufacturer-specific HealthVitals cluster using the connectedhomeip SDK on a Raspberry Pi 5. It exposes simulated heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), and body temperature to a chip-tool controller. We report attribute-read behavior, read completion under simulated packet loss, and observations from traffic capture and network-fabric life-cycle tests. Our objective is to assess how this custom telemetry model operates within Matter’s existing commissioning and operational workflow.

title: Robo-SWE: An Executable Issue-Resolution Dataset Mined from Robot Software Repositories
authors: Vahid Haratian,Vahid Ansari,Mohammadhossein Malmir,Alois Knoll
comment: . Submitted to the MSR 2027 Data and Tool Showcase Track. Dataset:this https URL
abstract:
Coding agents are evaluated mostly on general-purpose software, but domain-specific systems require
domain-aware evaluation. Robot software is a particularly challenging case: Robot Operating System 2
(ROS 2) packages have their own build tools, simulators and learning frameworks are built on physics
engines, and behavior that depends on timing and hardware is hard to test. We present robo-swe, a
dataset of 236 executable issue-resolution tasks mined from merged pull requests in 28
public robotics repositories in four domains: ROS 2 systems, simulation and physics engines, robotics
algorithm libraries, and robot-learning frameworks. Each task contains the original issue text, a container recipe
for the repository at the commit before the fix, the developers’ fix, and the developers’ tests,
which fail before the fix and pass after it in repeated offline runs. The dataset also keeps a provenance
ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests, with the stage each reached and the reason
for every rejection, and, as a first use, 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups
with recorded patches and 3,529 available trajectories. Across three runs per primary setup,
resolve rates range from 45.8% for Claude Sonnet 5.5 to 56.5% for Claude Opus 5.5; GPT-6.1 Sol
reaches 54.1% at maximum effort and 52.5% at medium effort, and GPT-6 Astra 51.4%.
GLM-5.3 resolves 46.2%, and Kimi K3.1 Pro 43.9%. The tasks are validated by execution; verification of their fairness by human reviewers
is future work. The dataset and public leaderboard are available online.
introduction:
Robot software consists of large, interdependent stacks of reusable components [1].
A mobile manipulator built on the Robot Operating System (ROS), in its current generation
ROS 2 [2], combines navigation, control, perception, hardware
drivers, and middleware across C++ and Python packages built with colcon and CMake. Development
depends on simulators and physics engines, while robot-learning frameworks add substantial codebases for
policies trained in simulation before deployment to hardware [3, 4]. Maintaining these
stacks is central to robotics engineering, yet testing them is difficult: behavior depends on timing,
concurrency, and hardware, and practitioners still rely heavily on field testing [5].

These characteristics distinguish robot-software repair from repair in self-contained applications.
Correctness spans packages and processes: a patch may compile yet violate a ROS message or lifecycle
contract, change launch-time behavior, or fail only with a particular simulator, middleware, timing, or
hardware configuration. Reproducing a task therefore requires more than checking out source and running
unit tests. Evaluation must preserve the domain toolchain and execution environment, account for
concurrency and nondeterminism, and separate infrastructure failures from incorrect repairs; otherwise,
scores may measure environment mismatch rather than an agent’s repair ability.

Despite these domain constraints, coding agents are typically evaluated by whether they resolve
GitHub issues in general-purpose repositories. SWE-bench [6]
and its human-checked subset [7] defined the task; later datasets extended it to
more languages and automated its
collection [8, 9, 10]. None of them targets robot
software or its build systems. Roboticists, meanwhile, ask whether such agents can supply the
engineered, testable modules that robot learning does not obtain from
data [11, 12]. Current robotics benchmarks do not answer this for
existing codebases: agents write new programs against a robot application programming interface (API) or a
simulator [13, 14, 15, 16], complete single
functions [17], or repair a small curated defect set in one
stack [18].

We present robo-swe, a dataset mined from the history of robotics projects to close this gap. It is meant
for software engineering researchers who study or train coding agents, and for robotics teams who want to
know which parts of their stack an agent can maintain. It provides:

236 executable issue-resolution tasks from 28 repositories in four domains
(Table I), among them Navigation2, ros2_control, rosbag2, MoveIt 2, Newton, MuJoCo Warp,
python-control, and LeRobot. Each pairs the original issue with a pre-fix workspace, the developers’ fix, and developer tests that fail before
the fix and pass after it.

The provenance of the tasks: a 2026 refresh of a census of ROS repositories on
GitHub [19], and a ledger of all 1,567 candidate pull requests
with the stage that each reached and the reason for every rejection.

A first use: 3,540 graded attempts by five coding-agent setups, with their patches,
per-test verdicts, and trajectories.

title: Imitating the Imperfect: Offline-to-Online Robust Imitation Learning from Heterogeneous Demonstrators
authors: Cheng Pan,Nan Lu,Kai Arulkumaran,Josie Hughes
abstract:
Imitation learning (IL) typically relies on large-scale offline demonstrations collected from multiple human or algorithmic demonstrators.
However, most existing approaches assume these demonstrators are homogeneous or near-optimal experts, a convenient but unrealistic assumption in real-world applications.
In practice, demonstrations are often collected from heterogeneous demonstrators with unknown and varying levels of expertise, resulting in highly mixed-quality data.
In this work, we study a challenging yet practical setting of imitation learning from such heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators.
We propose Latent Expertise and Optimality Scoring based Imitation Learning (LEOS-IL),
a principled framework that jointly learns (i) a state-action optimality scoring model and (ii) latent expertise levels for each demonstrator from unlabeled suboptimal offline demonstrations. The learned scoring model is then integrated into an online policy optimization procedure, where the agent is trained to maximize estimated optimality scores while its online rollouts are iteratively leveraged to refine the scoring model, thereby mitigating distributional shift during online adaptation.

We further provide theoretical guarantees for optimality score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. Experiments on continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that our approach consistently outperforms existing baselines across highly heterogeneous and low-quality demonstration regimes.
introduction:
Imitation learning (IL) offers a convenient framework that enables agents to acquire skills directly from expert demonstrations Zare et al. (2024). Prior research has shown that effective policies can be learned efficiently when provided with large-scale and high-quality demonstrations Belkhale et al. (2023); Saxena et al. (2025).
However, in real-world scenarios, large-scale datasets are often collected from multiple demonstrators, and human or algorithmic demonstrators typically possess strengths in specific contexts and may perform suboptimally outside their areas of expertise.
For example, in autonomous driving data collected from electric vehicles Lee et al. (2022); Zhang et al. (2024), drivers demonstrate a wide range of skill levels, resulting in heterogeneous and imperfect trajectories with unknown degrees of expertise.
Treating all such demonstrators as perfect experts can lead to unreliable or even unsafe agent behavior, posing serious risks in safety-critical applications.

In this work, we study IL from heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators whose expertise levels are unknown and variable, naturally leading to datasets containing suboptimal demonstrations, and learn a policy online based on the estimated demonstrator expertise and data optimality.
Existing methods (see details in Section 2) addressing this setting often rely on one or more of the following assumptions: (i) demonstrators are homogeneous, i.e., with the same expertise levels, and the optimal data dominates the dataset, (ii) access to explicit labels indicating the optimality of demonstrations, or (iii) the expertise level of each demonstrator is known a priori.
These requirements are demanding and often impractical when demonstrations come from uncontrolled or large-scale sources.

This brings us to a central question:
Can we design effective IL algorithms without relying on these assumptions?
This problem setting is inherently challenging because neither demonstrator expertise levels nor demonstration optimality are observed. In the worst case, all demonstrators may exhibit very low expertise, making it extremely difficult to extract reliable signals for policy learning.

To address the challenges, we propose a novel Latent Expertise and Optimality Scoring based Imitation Learning framework (LEOS-IL) for learning from heterogeneous imperfect demonstrators. Our main contributions are summarized below.

We introduce a principled formulation in which each demonstrator is modeled as a flexible mixture of optimal and suboptimal behaviors. We characterize a demonstrator’s expertise level as the probability of selecting actions aligned with an underlying latent optimal policy. These expertise levels vary across demonstrators, naturally capturing heterogeneous demonstration quality, while remaining fully latent and unobserved. This formulation provides a principled foundation for learning from realistic mixed-quality datasets without requiring explicit supervision11
1
              
              
              
            We only require 1 expert query to resolve ambiguity from the purely unsupervised setting (Sec. 3.2.2). or curated expert data.

Building on this formulation, we propose a novel two-stage IL framework (Fig. 1).
In the offline stage (Stage 1), we jointly estimate demonstrator expertise and learn a scoring model that assigns optimality scores to each state-action pair, representing the likelihood that the pair corresponds to the (latent) optimal policy.
This is achieved through an EM-style alternating self-training method that iteratively refines the scoring model and expertise estimates based on its current hard pseudo-labels.
In the online stage (Stage 2), the learned scoring model is used as a surrogate reward function for policy optimization. To address the distributional shift arising from offline training, we introduce an online iterative refinement procedure that alternates between policy learning and scoring model fine-tuning, yielding a progressively less biased and more informative reward signal.

We provide theoretical analysis establishing optimality-score identification and conditional optimal occupancy and policy recovery under explicit sufficient conditions. Empirically, we evaluate our method in two challenging heterogeneous scenarios: (i) a wide-range setting, with demonstrator expertise levels spanning [0.1,0.9][0.1,0.9], and (ii) a low-quality setting, where all demonstrators are highly suboptimal with expertise in [0.05,0.15][0.05,0.15]. Across both regimes, our method outperforms baselines and, remarkably, achieves performance comparable to methods trained on the subset of purely optimal demonstrations. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework for learning from uncurated demonstrations with unknown and highly variable quality.

title: Where to Generate Touch: Do Image Latents Preserve Material Recognition?
authors: Wanghao Ye,Aarosh Das,Sihan Chen,Yiting Wang,Bowei Tian,Guoheng Sun,Shwai He,Zheyu Shen,Ziyao Wang,Yexiao He,Zhaoyi Liu,Meng Liu,Yuning Zhang,Meng Feng,Ziyi Wang,Yilong Dai,Yifei Dong,Siyuan Peng,Zhenle Duan,Joshua Liu,Lang Xiong,Daeun Jung,Aditya Sarkar,Parastoo Pilevar,Xiaochuan Gong,Yancheng Zhu,Yingying Fan,Qiong Wang,Ang Li
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Robotics (cs.RO)
abstract: Generated touch could extend robot learning beyond recorded contacts. A tactile generator needs a latent space, and we choose one by testing whether a material classifier trained on real GelSight presses still works on encode–decode reconstructions from pretrained image models. On ObjectFolder Real, the classifier loses 6.5 to 9.7 points on reconstructions from three 16×\times discrete tokenizers and 0.3 points on those from the Stable Diffusion VAE (SD-VAE). The 16×\times tokenizers again lose far more on Touch and Go and on DIGIT object recognition (YCB-Slide). Retraining the classifier on reconstructions, with no new labels, narrows the discrete gap. SD-VAE reconstructions also keep object identity, with 76.7% object-matching accuracy against 78.9% for real touch and 67.0% for MAGVIT-v2. We therefore select SD-VAE latents and show a photo-to-touch generator trained in them. Code will be released upon acceptance.
introduction:
Tactile data are scarce because each recording requires physical contact (Wang et al. 2026). Generating touch from object photos could expand these data (Gungor, Eppinger, and Kovashka 2025; Ye et al. 2026), provided that synthetic touch works with models trained on real recordings. GelSight and DIGIT capture elastomer deformation as RGB images (Yuan, Dong, and Adelson 2017; Lambeta et al. 2020), so the continuous autoencoders (Rombach et al. 2022) and discrete tokenizers (Esser, Rombach, and Ommer 2021; Yu et al. 2024a) of image foundation models can serve as the latent space of a tactile generator. We compare these spaces through encode–decode round trips, before any generator is trained. The comparison also shows how tokenizers from vision foundation models fare on a new sensory modality.

Beyond pixel fidelity (Ye et al. 2026), we test whether a material classifier trained on real touch still works on reconstructed presses. Continuous and discrete reconstructions both look close to the original (Figure 1, A2), yet across 71 objects the classifier loses 6.5 points on MAGVIT-v2 reconstructions and 0.3 on SD-VAE ones (A3; Figure 2, B3). Retraining the classifier on reconstructions then shows how much of this loss is a mismatch between real and reconstructed inputs.

On two GelSight datasets, real-trained classifiers lose a quarter to a half of their margin over chance on reconstructions from released 16×\times discrete tokenizers and less than one point on SD-VAE reconstructions, and on DIGIT touch from YCB-Slide the discrete tokenizers lose 21 to 28 points of object-recognition accuracy against 1.2 for SD-VAE. SD-VAE reconstructions also retain high object-matching accuracy, and Section 4 shows a photo-to-touch generator trained in this compact space.

Our contributions are (1) a transfer test that ranks latent spaces for tactile generation with encode–decode passes and a lightweight classifier on frozen features; (2) a comparison of released and fine-tuned image tokenizers on three datasets from two sensor types, with grouped splits, several classifiers and bootstrap intervals; and (3) a matched comparison that separates quantization from downsampling, with classifier retraining that narrows the discrete gap without new labels.

Tactile generators condition on local geometry (Bien et al. 2026; Bhouri et al. 2026), on a sensor-aligned view of the contact region (Li et al. 2019; Yang, Zhang, and Owens 2023; Dou et al. 2024) or on text (Tu et al. 2025). Recent tactile models generate with vector-quantized codes (Lyu et al. 2026; Huang et al. 2026; Tu et al. 2026), and TacGen predicts tactile latents from RGB (Ye et al. 2026). Our study complements these generators (Appendix I). It compares candidate latent spaces on the same presses with a downstream classifier, under splits that keep product families apart (Gungor, Eppinger, and Kovashka 2025). Foundation models for other sensors face the same choice of input representation. Time-series models reprogram signals into language-model inputs (Jin et al. 2024a) or encode them as images (Wang and Oates 2015), and language models answer questions about time series and reason over medical sensor data (Kong et al. 2025a; Langer et al. 2026). Surveys and position papers cover Transformers, large models and reasoning for time series (Wen et al. 2023; Jin et al. 2026; Jin et al. 2024b; Kong et al. 2025b).
